side_a.title: Palestinian National Charter, Articles 1 and 17
side_a.text: Article 1: "Palestine is an Arab homeland bound by strong Arab national ties to the rest of the Arab countries and which together form the great Arab homeland." Article 17: "The partitioning of Palestine, which took place in 1947, and the establishment of Israel are illegal and null and void, regardless of the loss of time, because they were contrary to the will of the Palestinian people and its natural right to its homeland …"
side_a.provenance: Palestinian National Charter (1964), English translation; adopted by the first Palestine National Council, East Jerusalem.

side_b.title: Prime Minister Levi Eshkol on the Jordan waters
side_b.text: Eshkol told Israelis and foreign governments that the National Water Carrier took only Israel's fair share of Jordan water, within the amounts proposed by the American Johnston Plan of 1955. He warned that Arab plans to divert the river's headwaters were an attack on Israel's vital rights and that Israel would defend its water supply. Israeli leaders saw the new PLO and its charter as evidence that Arab states still rejected Israel's existence.
side_b.provenance: Summary of Israeli government statements to the Knesset and foreign governments, 1964.

sources.question: The Charter calls Israel's creation "null and void", while Eshkol defends Israel's water project. Why did both sides feel threatened in 1964?

sources.source_context: On 13 November 1966 Israel sent troops, tanks and aircraft against the village of Samu, south of Hebron, in reprisal for a Fatah landmine. Fighting with the Jordanian army killed 15 Jordanian soldiers and many houses were destroyed. sources.model_answer: Israel struck a Jordanian village even though most Fatah raids were backed by Syria, and 15 Jordanian soldiers were killed. West Bank Palestinians rioted, accusing Hussein of failing to protect them, while other Arab states mocked him; the humiliation pushed Hussein to take a harder line and, in May 1967, to join Nasser.

sources.title: Source E: Israeli and Syrian Accounts of the Air Battle of 7 April 1967
sources.image_alt: Black-and-white photo of an Israeli Air Force Mirage III jet landing with its braking parachute open, trees behind the runway.
sources.caption: An Israeli Air Force Mirage IIICJ of 117 Squadron landing at Ramat David air base in northern Israel, photographed in 1970. Mirages like this fought the Syrian MiG-21s on 7 April 1967.

sources.source_context: On 7 April 1967 Syrian guns fired on an Israeli tractor ploughing disputed land in the demilitarised zone near the Sea of Galilee. Israel sent Mirage jets against the Syrian positions; in the air battle that followed six Syrian MiG-21s were shot down and Israeli jets flew over Damascus. Syria turned to Egypt for support under their defence pact.
sources.context: On 7 April 1967 a clash over a tractor in the demilitarised zone grew into an air battle in which Israel shot down six Syrian MiG-21s.
sources.model_answer: Each side blamed the other for the fighting over farmland in the demilitarised zone, so neither felt it had started the clash. Losing six MiGs in public humiliated Syria, which then demanded that Egypt honour their November 1966 defence pact; that pressure, added to taunts that Nasser was hiding behind UN troops, helped push him into the May 1967 crisis.

perspective_pair.framing_note: The same air battle was described in opposite ways; comparing the two accounts shows why each government felt justified and why the crisis escalated.

side_a.title: Israeli account of 7 April 1967
side_a.text: The Israeli army said Syrian positions on the Golan opened fire on Israeli tractors working land in the demilitarised zone that Israel regarded as its own. When shelling widened to nearby kibbutzim, Israeli aircraft were sent to silence the guns, and six Syrian MiG-21s that intercepted them were shot down without Israeli loss. Israeli leaders presented the flight over Damascus as a warning that Syria would pay for shelling and for backing guerrilla raids.
side_a.provenance: Summary of Israel Defense Forces and Israeli government statements, April 1967.

side_b.title: Syrian account of 7 April 1967
side_b.text: Syria said Israel deliberately provoked the clash by sending armoured tractors to plough disputed land in the demilitarised zone, breaking the 1949 armistice. Syrian leaders described their guns as defending Arab territory against Israeli expansion and accused Israel of preparing a larger attack on Syria. Damascus appealed to Egypt under their November 1966 defence pact, increasing pressure on President Nasser to show that he would stand by his ally.
side_b.provenance: Summary of Syrian government statements and radio broadcasts, April 1967.

questions.question: 3. Explain the importance of the Cairo Conference (1964) and the growth of Fatah for escalating tension in the Middle East in the years 1964–67. [8 marks]
questions.prompt: Use the structure strip and causal connectives below to structure your response.
questions.model:
First, the January 1964 Arab League Summit in Cairo turned water disputes and Palestinian nationalism into coordinated Arab policy against Israel. Alarmed by Israel’s completion of the National Water Carrier pumping water from the Sea of Galilee to the Negev, Arab leaders launched the Headwater Diversion Plan in Syria and Jordan and established the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) committed to armed struggle. Between 1965 and 1966, Israeli tank and air strikes bombed Syrian earth-moving equipment, making armed border clashes routine.

Second, the growth of Yasser Arafat’s Fatah movement drove a relentless cycle of guerrilla sabotage and massive Israeli reprisals that destabilised Israel’s neighbours. Launching raids from January 1965 and backed from 1966 by Syria’s radical military regime alongside Golan Heights artillery shelling, Fatah landmines provoked Israel’s November 1966 assault on Samu in Jordan and contributed to the 7 April 1967 dogfight in which Israeli Mirage jets shot down six Syrian MiG-21s over Damascus — pushing Syria to demand Egyptian military action.

tier_2m.title: 2/8 Simple Statement
tier_2m.text: The 1964 Cairo Conference and Fatah were important because Arab leaders agreed to divert Israel’s water supplies and set up the PLO, while Fatah fighters launched guerrilla attacks across Israel’s borders. This caused constant border clashes with Israel between 1964 and 1967.
tier_2m.verdict: AO1 Level 1 (1 mark) • AO2 Level 1 (1 mark). Identifies water disputes and raids broadly, without specific dates, targets, or analytical development.

tier_5m.title: 5/8 Descriptive Analysis
tier_5m.text:
First, at the January 1964 Cairo Summit, Arab League leaders responded to Israel’s National Water Carrier by planning the Headwaters Diversion Plan in Syria and Jordan and creating the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO). Israeli tanks and aircraft bombed Syrian diversion works between 1965 and 1966.

Second, Yasser Arafat’s Fatah group launched armed sabotage raids into Israel from January 1965 with Syrian backing. These attacks led to Israel’s major reprisal raid on Samu in Jordan in November 1966 and the 7 April 1967 air battle in which Israeli Mirage jets shot down six Syrian MiG-21s.
tier_5m.verdict: AO1 Level 2 (2–3 marks) • AO2 Level 2 (2–3 marks). Strong factual coverage of both elements, but describes the sequence of clashes rather than explicitly analysing how each widened regional tension.

stages.title: The 1964 Cairo Conference & PLO Founded
stages.trigger: President Nasser hosts Arab heads of state in Cairo to coordinate opposition to Israel and establish the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO).
stages.because: Arab leaders wanted to show leadership on the Palestinian issue and control growing Palestinian guerrilla activity.
stages.therefore: Put the Palestinian cause back on the world stage; Yasser Arafat’s guerrilla group, Fatah, began launching independent sabotage raids into Israel.
stages.connective: Disputes over vital water supplies soon escalated border clashes between Israel and Syria...

stages.question: Why did Arab leaders meet in Cairo and establish the PLO in January 1964?

stages.title: The Dispute Over the River Jordan Waterways
stages.trigger: Syria attempts to divert the headwaters feeding the River Jordan; Israeli artillery and tanks shell Syrian engineering machinery to stop construction.
stages.because: Israel relied on the River Jordan to irrigate its farms and towns, while Arab states sought to cut Israel’s fresh water supply.
stages.therefore: Showed that Israel was prepared to use pre-emptive military force to protect essential resources, making border shootouts a regular occurrence.
stages.connective: A radical new government in Syria began actively funding guerrilla attacks against Israel...
stages.exam_link: Q1 Consequence: Escalated border tensions between Israel and Syria, making military clashes frequent on the northern frontier.
stages.question: How did rival River Jordan water plans trigger cross-border military strikes?

stages.title: Syrian Support for Fatah Border Raids
stages.trigger: The Syrian government begins openly supplying money, weapons, and bases to Fatah fighters launching landmine raids into northern Israel.
stages.because: Syrian leaders wanted to prove they were the most radical opponents of Israel and pressure other Arab states to take action.
stages.therefore: Cross-border guerrilla attacks into northern Israel multiplied, turning the Israeli-Syrian border into the most dangerous hotspot in the region.
stages.connective: Israel launched a large retaliatory raid across the Jordanian border to deter infiltrators...
stages.exam_link: Q2 Narrative Account: Syrian state backing for Fatah provoked heavy Israeli retaliation, bringing the region closer to war.
stages.question: Why did Fatah launch raids into Israel, and how did Syria’s regime back them?

stages.title: The Israeli Raid on Samu
stages.trigger: Israeli tanks and troops raid the village of Samu in the Jordanian-controlled West Bank, destroying houses and clashing with Jordanian soldiers.
stages.because: Israel retaliated after a Fatah landmine killed three Israeli border police near the frontier.
stages.therefore: Damaged relations between Arab states: Jordan’s King Hussein blamed Nasser for failing to support him, raising public pressure on Nasser to act tough.
stages.connective: Tensions reached boiling point in a major aerial clash over the Syrian border...
stages.exam_link: Q1 Consequence: Deepened divisions between Arab leaders and pressured Nasser into taking aggressive action to restore his leadership.
stages.question: Why did Israel’s reprisal raid on Samu destabilise King Hussein in Jordan?

stages.title: The Aerial Battle of 7 April 1967
stages.trigger: After Syrian guns shell Israeli tractors in the border zone, Israeli fighter jets shoot down six Syrian MiG fighter planes and fly low over Damascus.
stages.because: Israel wanted to silence Syrian gun positions and demonstrate total command of the skies.
stages.therefore: Humiliated the Syrian government, leaving Syrian leaders demanding military help from Egypt and setting the stage for war in May 1967.
stages.connective: Desperate to deter another Israeli attack on Syria, the Soviet Union issued a fateful false warning to Nasser...
stages.exam_link: Q2 Narrative Account: The destruction of Syrian jets pushed Syria and the USSR to provoke the crisis that started the Six-Day War.

video.title: Historical Archive: Who Will Fire First? The May 1967 Brinkmanship
video.teacher_guidance: Dramatic breakdown of the rapid diplomatic unraveling in May 1967: Soviet false intelligence, Nasser massing 100,000 troops in Sinai, expelling UNEF, and blockading the Straits of Tiran. Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–05:15 • Lesson Phase: Starter Hook (0–5m). Tone Alert: Dramatic archival newsreel footage capturing the sudden plunge from uneasy peace into existential regional crisis.
video.viewing_task:
1. [01:10] Recall: What international peacekeeping force did President Nasser order to immediately evacuate the Sinai border on 16 May 1967?
  2. [02:40] Explain: Why did the State of Israel consider President Nasser's closure of the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping on 22 May 1967 an explicit act of war (casus belli)?
  3. [04:20] Challenge: Evaluate the role of political brinkmanship: did President Nasser genuinely intend to launch an unprovoked invasion of Israel, or did he become a prisoner of his own public rhetoric and regional Arab rivalry?
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: The United Nations Emergency Force (UNEF), stationed in Sinai since the 1956 Suez Crisis.
  2. Explain: The Straits of Tiran were Israel's sole maritime outlet to the Red Sea and Indian Ocean, vital for imported Persian crude oil through the port of Eilat. Following 1956, international maritime guarantees had established that closing the straits was an act of war. The blockade severed Israel's economic lifeline and forced the government to mobilize 250,000 civilian reservists, paralyzing its economy.
  3. Challenge: Declassified records suggest Nasser was engaging in political theater to reassert Pan-Arab leadership after being mocked by Jordan and Saudi Arabia for hiding behind UN skirts. However, by massing 100,000 troops, expelling UNEF, blockading the Straits, and signing defense pacts with Jordan and Iraq, Nasser created a military stranglehold that forced Israel to strike pre-emptively to survive.

  2. [03:15] Explain: Explain how Syrian military positions on the high cliffs of the Golan Heights held a commanding tactical advantage over Israeli agricultural kibbutzim in the Hula Valley below.
  3. [04:50] Challenge: To what extent was the outbreak of the Six-Day War driven by competition over vital ecological resources (freshwater) rather than purely ideological or religious hostility?
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: Israel completed the National Water Carrier; the Arab League launched the Headwater Diversion Scheme to divert the River Jordan tributaries away from Israel.
  2. Explain: The Golan Heights rose steeply hundreds of meters above northern Israeli settlements. Syrian artillery batteries heavily entrenched in basalt bunkers could shell civilian farmers, tractors, and fishing boats on the Sea of Galilee with near-total impunity, triggering retaliatory Israeli airstrikes and tank duels.
  3. Challenge: Freshwater was existential: diverting the headwaters would have cut Israel's water supply by 35%, halting agricultural and demographic development. While nationalist and anti-Zionist rhetoric dominated the airwaves, the continuous physical combat over water bulldozers and fishing rights between 1964 and 1967 served as the direct operational sparks that escalated border skirmishes into all-out war.

video.teacher_guidance: Examines the impact of Moscow's fabricated reports alleging Israeli troop concentrations against Syria, Nasser's public bravado, and King Hussein of Jordan signing a mutual defence pact with Egypt. Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–03:22 (Full Clip) • Lesson Phase: Source Analysis & Evidence. video.viewing_task:
1. [00:50] Recall: Which global superpower delivered fabricated intelligence reports to Egyptian officials on 13 May 1967 falsely claiming Israel was massing twelve brigades on the Syrian border?
  2. [01:45] Explain: Why was King Hussein of Jordan compelled to fly to Cairo on 30 May 1967 to sign a mutual defense pact with his bitter ideological rival, President Nasser?
  3. [02:40] Challenge: Analyze the explosive impact of Arab radio propaganda and mass street demonstrations in May 1967. How did public passion limit the ability of Arab leaders to pursue diplomatic compromise?
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: The Soviet Union (USSR).
  2. Explain: King Hussein ruled over a population containing hundreds of thousands of Palestinian refugees who revered Nasser. Had Jordan remained neutral while Egypt appeared ready to liberate Palestine, Hussein faced imminent revolution and the overthrow of his Hashemite dynasty. Signing the pact placed Jordan's armed forces under Egyptian command to secure regime survival.
  3. Challenge: Fiery broadcasts from Cairo declaring that 'the battle will be a general one and our basic objective will be to destroy Israel' whipped millions into a frenzy of expectation. Arab leaders became prisoners of their own nationalist myth-making: de-escalating or accepting diplomatic mediation was condemned by the street as treason, making armed confrontation unavoidable.

video.title: Kings and Generals: Six-Day War (1967) – Escalation, Alliances & Three-Front Documentary
video.teacher_guidance: Cartographic military-diplomatic documentary mapping the 1964–1967 Jordan River water clashes, Syrian border shelling, Soviet intelligence warnings, and Egyptian mobilisation in Sinai. Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–06:30 • Lesson Phase: Strategic Overview / Extension.
video.viewing_task:
1. [01:15] Recall: Why did Syria and the Arab League attempt to divert the headwaters of the Jordan River between 1964 and 1966?
  2. [03:40] Explain: Explain how cross-border Fatah raids, Syrian artillery exchanges, and the November 1966 Samu incident destabilised Israel's borders before May 1967.
  3. [05:45] Challenge: Looking at troop deployments by late May 1967, why did Israeli military planners conclude that a prolonged war of attrition along three borders was impossible to sustain?
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: To block Israel's National Water Carrier project from piping Sea of Galilee water south to irrigate the Negev Desert.
  2. Explain: Escalating guerrilla raids and Israeli reprisals—culminating in the shooting down of six Syrian MiGs in April 1967—pushed Damascus and Cairo into tighter military coordination and heightened brinkmanship.
  3. Challenge: Because Israel relied on mobilising civilian reservists, keeping hundreds of thousands of workers under arms paralysed the national economy while Arab armies consolidated positions across Sinai, the West Bank, and the Golan Heights.

video.viewing_task:
1. [00:45] Recall: What false intelligence report from the Soviet Union in May 1967 triggered Egyptian troop deployments into the Sinai Peninsula?
  2. [01:50] Explain: Explain why Nasser's closure of the Straits of Tiran on 22–23 May 1967 was treated by the Israeli cabinet as a casus belli (act of war).

video.model_answer:
1. Recall: Moscow falsely warned Cairo that Israel had massed 11–13 brigades along the Syrian border for an imminent invasion.
  2. Explain: Israel had declared since 1957 that blocking the Straits of Tiran—through which 90% of Israeli oil imports passed via Eilat—would legally constitute an act of war, and UNEF's sudden removal erased the 1957 buffer.
  3. Challenge: Nasser's prestige in the Arab world pushed him to escalate once challenged by rivals, while King Hussein's 30 May military pact placed Egyptian command on Israel's narrow waist, convincing Israeli commanders that failing to strike first risked national destruction.

key_individual.anchor_title: The Pre-Emptive Dawn Airstrike & Air Dominance (5 June 1967)
key_individual.anchor_rationale: Anchored directly adjacent to Block 2 where newly appointed Defence Minister Dayan authorized the pre-emptive air blitz destroying the Egyptian air force in three hours.
key_individual.name: Moshe Dayan
key_individual.role: Israeli Minister of Defence (1967–1974)
strategic_actions: Appointed Minister of Defence on 1 June 1967 amid national crisis to unify the Israeli war cabinet.
Authorised the pre-emptive dawn air strike that destroyed the Egyptian Air Force on the tarmac.
Directed three-front combat operations that captured the Sinai Peninsula, West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights.
key_individual.significance: Dayan became the global symbol of Israeli military dominance and deterrence. His aggressive operational tempo secured total victory across three fronts within 132 hours, fundamentally transforming Middle Eastern borders.
key_individual.origins: Born in 1915 on Degania Alef, the first kibbutz in Palestine, Dayan trained in British night squads during the 1936–39 Arab Revolt, lost his left eye fighting Vichy French forces in 1941, and forged an aggressive doctrine of pre-emption and deterrence as IDF Chief of Staff.

lessons.title: KT 2.2: The Six-Day War, May–June 1967
lessons.learning_objective: Explain how the crisis of May 1967 triggered the Six Day War and analyse why Israel achieved rapid victory across three fronts.
learning_objectives: Explain how Soviet false reports, Nasser's troop deployments, and the closure of the Straits of Tiran triggered the crisis of May 1967.
Describe how Israel's pre-emptive dawn airstrike destroyed the Arab air forces on 5 June 1967.
Analyse the key military campaigns across Sinai, the West Bank, and the Golan Heights that transformed the map of the Middle East.
lessons.hook_text: On the morning of 5 June 1967, nearly 200 Israeli fighter jets flew low beneath radar over the Mediterranean. Within three hours, over 300 Egyptian aircraft lay burning on the tarmac. By Saturday evening, the map of the Middle East had been changed forever.

teacher_notes.primer: This lesson covers the rapid descent into war in May 1967 and the six days of combat that radically redrew the Middle East. Pupils examine how Soviet false intelligence reports, Nasser's expulsion of UNEF peacekeepers, and the blockade of the Straits of Tiran led Israel to launch a decisive pre-emptive dawn air strike on 5 June 1967. They then study the rapid three-front campaign (Sinai, West Bank/Jerusalem, Golan Heights) that resulted in Israel quadrupling its territory in under a week.

objectives.objective: Explain the sequence of events in May 1967 that made war unavoidable (Soviet reports, UNEF, Tiran).
objectives.primer: Guide pupils through paragraph [1.1]. Stress that the USSR fed false intelligence to Egypt claiming Israeli brigades were massed on the Syrian border. Nasser responded by moving 100,000 troops into the Sinai, expelling UN peacekeepers, and closing the Straits of Tiran to Israeli ships.
objectives.question: Why did Israel regard the closure of the Straits of Tiran as an act of war (casus belli)?

objectives.objective: Describe the execution and decisive impact of Israel's pre-emptive dawn airstrike on 5 June 1967.
objectives.primer: Direct pupils to paragraph [2.1] and Source A. Emphasize that Israeli jets flew below radar detection to destroy 300+ Egyptian aircraft on the ground, securing complete air supremacy.
objectives.question: How did gaining total control of the skies in the first three hours determine the outcome of the entire ground war?

objectives.objective: Trace the three military campaigns and explain why Israel succeeded so rapidly in Sinai, the West Bank, and the Golan Heights.
objectives.primer: Lead pupils through paragraphs [3.1]–[3.2]. Contrast Israeli military coordination, training, and motivation with Egyptian panic, chaotic communications, and the lack of coordination among Arab allies.
objectives.question: What was the religious and emotional significance of Israeli forces capturing the Old City of Jerusalem and the Western Wall?

teacher_notes.hinge_question: At which exact step in May 1967 did Nasser's brinkmanship cross Israel's stated red line from diplomatic posturing into inevitable war?
teacher_notes.hinge_guidance: Strong GCSE answers pinpoint 22 May 1967, when—having already marched troops into Sinai and expelled UNEF—Nasser closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping bound for Eilat, an act Israel had publicly declared a casus belli since 1957, compounded on 30 May when King Hussein placed Jordan's army under Egyptian command. Catch pupils who claim the USSR wanted a full Arab-Israeli war in May 1967: Moscow's false 13 May warning of Israeli brigades aimed to bolster its ally Syria, not ignite a catastrophic Arab defeat.

misconceptions.misconception: Thinking Egypt, Syria, and Jordan launched a surprise attack on Israel on 5 June 1967.
misconceptions.correction: While Egypt massed troops in Sinai, expelled UNEF, and blockaded Tiran in May 1967, Israel struck first at 07:45 on 5 June 1967 with Operation Focus, destroying over 300 Egyptian aircraft on the tarmac within three hours.

misconceptions.misconception: Assuming Israel planned from day one to conquer the West Bank from Jordan even if King Hussein stayed neutral.
misconceptions.correction: Prime Minister Levi Eshkol sent urgent messages via the UN on 5 June urging King Hussein to stay out of the fighting; only after Jordanian artillery shelled West Jerusalem—misled by false Egyptian radio claims of victory—did the IDF counter-attack into East Jerusalem and the West Bank.

misconceptions.misconception: Confusing the territories won in 1948–49 with the territories occupied in June 1967.
misconceptions.correction: GCSE Exam Tip: Memorise the four territories captured in June 1967—Sinai and Gaza (from Egypt), the West Bank and East Jerusalem (from Jordan), and the Golan Heights (from Syria).

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: In mid-May 1967, President Nasser ordered 100,000 Egyptian troops into the Sinai and expelled the [UNEF (UN Emergency Force)] peacekeepers. On 22 May, Nasser announced the closure of the [Straits of Tiran] to Israeli shipping, an act Israel considered a trigger for war. Facing hostile Arab armies on three borders, the Israeli government launched a surprise [Pre-emptive Strike] on the morning of 5 June 1967. Within three hours, the Israeli Air Force achieved total [Air Supremacy] by destroying over 300 Egyptian aircraft on the ground. Israeli armoured columns quickly seized the entire Sinai Peninsula, while paratroopers captured the [West Bank] from Jordan and advanced to the [Western Wall] in the Old City of Jerusalem.

narrative_blocks.title: Soviet Warning, UNEF Expelled & Straits of Tiran Closed
paragraphs: [1.1] On **13 May 1967**, the **Soviet Union** passed a false intelligence warning to Cairo alleging that Israel had massed ten to twelve brigades on Syria’s border for an imminent invasion. Although UN observers confirmed no buildup existed, Nasser could not look weak as champion of Pan-Arabism: on 14–15 May he marched **100,000 Egyptian troops** and 1,000 tanks into the **Sinai Peninsula** and demanded the withdrawal of **United Nations Emergency Force (UNEF)** peacekeepers on 16 May.

[1.2] When UN Secretary-General U Thant withdrew UNEF without Security Council debate, Egyptian forces occupied Sharm el-Sheikh overlooking the Gulf of Aqaba. On **22 May 1967**, Nasser closed the **Straits of Tiran** to all Israeli shipping and vital oil tankers bound for Eilat—crossing the explicit red line Israel had warned since 1957 would constitute an act of war.

sources.source_context: A false Soviet warning on 13 May 1967 claimed Israel was massing troops against Syria. Nasser sent about 100,000 troops into Sinai, demanded the withdrawal of UNEF, and on 22 May closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli ships — crossing a red line Israel had declared since 1957.
sources.context: After expelling UN peacekeepers from Sinai, Nasser announced on 22 May 1967 that the Straits of Tiran were closed to Israeli shipping.
sources.model_answer: Nasser had promised to defend Syria and lead the Arab world, so reopening the Straits would have looked like surrender to Israel. Israel had warned since 1957 that closing Tiran would be an act of war, because Eilat was its only route to the Red Sea and its oil supply; Backing down would have cost each leader his credibility at home.

perspective_pair.framing_note: Read together, the two statements show how one narrow sea lane became a test of national honour and legal rights for both governments.

side_a.title: Speech at Bir Gifgafa air base, Sinai
side_a.text: Speaking to Egyptian pilots in Sinai, Nasser announced that the Gulf of Aqaba was Egyptian territorial water and that Israeli ships would no longer pass through the Straits of Tiran. He said Egypt had moved its forces to defend Syria against Israeli threats and to restore the situation before 1956. He declared that if Israel threatened war, Egypt's armed forces were ready to meet it.
side_a.provenance: Summary of Nasser's speech broadcast by Cairo Radio, 22 May 1967.

side_b.title: Prime Minister Levi Eshkol's statement to the Knesset
side_b.text: Eshkol told the Knesset that any interference with Israeli shipping in the Straits of Tiran was a serious breach of international law and an act of aggression against Israel. He reminded the maritime powers of the promises of free passage made when Israel withdrew from Sinai in 1957 and called on them to act. Israel, meanwhile, mobilised its reserves while its diplomats sought international support.
side_b.provenance: Summary of Eshkol's statement to the Knesset, 23 May 1967.

hotspots.title: Straits of Tiran: Nasser Expels UNEF & Blocks Israeli Shipping
hotspots.details: Prompted by a false Soviet intelligence report of Israeli troops massing against Syria, Nasser marched 100,000 soldiers into Sinai, expelled UNEF peacekeepers, and closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping and oil tankers bound for Eilat on 22 May 1967—crossing Israel’s stated red line for war.

hotspots.label: Sinai & Air Strikes
hotspots.title: Sinai Peninsula: Pre-Emptive Air Strikes & Armoured Sweep
hotspots.details: At 07:45 on 5 June 1967, the Israeli Air Force flew low beneath radar to destroy over 300 Egyptian aircraft and crater runways on the ground within hours. Deprived of air cover across open desert, Egyptian armies collapsed as Israeli tanks captured Gaza and all of Sinai up to the Suez Canal by 8 June.
hotspots.hinge: Why did destroying Egypt’s air force on the ground on the morning of 5 June decide the battle for Sinai almost immediately?

hotspots.label: East Jerusalem & West Bank
hotspots.title: East Jerusalem & The West Bank: Captured from Jordan
hotspots.details: Honouring his 30 May defence pact with Nasser and misled by Egyptian radio claims of victory, Jordan’s King Hussein shelled West Jerusalem on 5 June. Israeli paratroopers and armour counter-attacked, seizing East Jerusalem’s Old City (Western Wall) and the entire West Bank up to the River Jordan by 7 June.
hotspots.hinge: Why did King Hussein’s decision to honour his alliance with Egypt cost Jordan East Jerusalem and the West Bank?

hotspots.label: Golan Heights
hotspots.title: The Golan Heights: Storming the Syrian Plateau
hotspots.details: From fortified bunkers atop the steep Golan escarpment, Syrian guns had shelled Israeli settlements around the Sea of Galilee for years. On 9–10 June 1967, just before a UN ceasefire took hold, Israeli forces stormed the plateau, tripling Israeli-held territory overall while placing over one million Palestinians under occupation.

narrative_blocks.title: The Jordan Defence Pact & National Unity Cabinet
paragraphs: [2.1] On **30 May 1967**, Jordan’s **King Hussein** flew to Cairo and signed a mutual **Joint Defence Pact** with his former rival Nasser, placing Jordan’s armed forces under Egyptian command as Iraqi troops entered Jordan. Meanwhile, US President **Lyndon B. Johnson** warned Israel not to fire first, yet failed to assemble an international naval convoy to reopen the Straits of Tiran.

[2.2] Encircled by hostile armies on three fronts and convinced American diplomacy could not lift the naval blockade, Israeli civilians dug trenches in public city parks amid deep fear of destruction. On 1 June, Prime Minister Levi Eshkol formed a national unity cabinet, appointing war hero **Moshe Dayan** Minister of Defence alongside Chief of Staff Yitzhak Rabin to prepare a pre-emptive strike.

side_a.title: The Joint Defence Agreement
side_a.text: Under the agreement, Egypt and Jordan promised that an armed attack on either state would be treated as an attack on both, and that each would immediately help the other. Jordanian forces were placed under the command of an Egyptian general. Arab radio stations celebrated the pact as proof of Arab unity after years of quarrels, and presented it as a defensive shield against Israeli attack.
side_a.provenance: Summary of the Egyptian–Jordanian defence agreement and Arab press coverage, 30 May–1 June 1967.

side_b.title: Israeli view of encirclement
side_b.text: Foreign Minister Abba Eban met President Johnson on 26 May, who urged Israel not to fire first and promised to try to organise an international convoy through the Straits. After the pact, Israeli leaders believed they faced Egyptian, Jordanian, Syrian and Iraqi forces on three fronts while the convoy plan stalled. Civilians dug trenches, reserves stayed mobilised and many Israelis feared their country could be destroyed if it waited.
side_b.provenance: Summary of Israeli government records and public reaction, late May 1967; photo LBJ Presidential Library, 26 May 1967.

narrative_blocks.title: Operation Focus: Pre-Emptive Air Supremacy
paragraphs: [3.1] At 07:45 on **5 June 1967**, the Israeli Air Force launched **the pre-emptive air strike** (**Operation Focus**, or **Mivtza Moked**) against Egyptian military airfields. Flying beneath radar at treetop height across the Mediterranean under strict radio silence, nearly 200 Israeli fighter jets struck just as Egyptian morning patrols landed and senior commanders sat stuck in Cairo traffic.

[3.2] Dropping specialised runway-cratering bombs first to trap enemy aircraft on the tarmac, Israeli waves strafed parked bombers and MiG fighters with cannon fire. Within three hours, the strike wiped out the Egyptian Air Force, destroying over **300 Egyptian aircraft** on the ground—and crippling Jordanian and Syrian airbases that afternoon—to win total air supremacy across every front.

sources.context: On 5 June 1967 Israel's pre-emptive air strike destroyed over 300 Egyptian aircraft, giving Israeli ground forces air supremacy.
sources.model_answer: Israel's surprise air strike on the morning of 5 June destroyed most of the Egyptian air force on the ground within about three hours. With no enemy aircraft left to attack them, Israeli tank columns could move fast across open desert, while retreating Egyptian columns were exposed to Israeli jets; the first three hours effectively decided the war.

narrative_blocks.title: Sinai Blitzkrieg & Capture of East Jerusalem
paragraphs: [4.1] Shielded by total air supremacy between **5 and 8 June 1967**, Israeli armoured divisions led by Generals **Israel Tal**, Avraham Yoffe, and **Ariel Sharon** smashed through Egyptian fortifications in Gaza and Abu Ageila. Retreating Egyptian columns caught in the open desert were devastated from the air at the **Mitla Pass**, allowing Israeli tanks to reach the Suez Canal and Sharm el-Sheikh by 8 June.

[4.2] Meanwhile on 5 June, misled by false Cairo radio broadcasts claiming Egyptian victories, King Hussein’s artillery shelled West Jerusalem despite Israeli appeals to stay out. Israeli brigades counter-attacked into the **West Bank**, and on **7 June 1967** paratroopers stormed Jerusalem’s Old City to capture **East Jerusalem** and the **Western Wall**, driving Jordanian forces back across the River Jordan.

sources.source_context: On 5 June, believing false Egyptian claims of victory, Jordan shelled West Jerusalem despite Israeli messages urging Hussein to stay out. sources.context: Jordan entered the war on 5 June; on 7 June Israeli paratroopers captured East Jerusalem and the Old City.
sources.model_answer: For Israelis and Jews worldwide, capturing the Old City was an emotional national and religious triumph because Jews could pray at the Western Wall again after being barred under Jordanian rule since 1948. For Jordanians and Palestinians, however, 7 June meant losing East Jerusalem — including the Haram al-Sharif and al-Aqsa Mosque as well as major Christian holy sites — and placed East Jerusalem's Palestinian residents under Israeli military occupation; Control of Jerusalem therefore became one of the hardest issues in any future peace talks.

narrative_blocks.image_alt: Military campaign map of the Six-Day War Sinai penetrations on 5–6 June 1967 showing Israeli armoured divisions under Generals Tal, Yoffe, and Sharon advancing into Gaza, Rafah, and Abu Ageila
narrative_blocks.caption: Reference Map: Sinai Penetrations (5–6 June 1967) — Israeli armoured divisions led by Generals Tal, Yoffe, and Sharon broke through Gaza, Rafah, and Abu Ageila toward the Mitla Pass and Suez Canal.
narrative_blocks.content: [4.1] Shielded by total air supremacy between **5 and 8 June 1967**, Israeli armoured divisions led by Generals **Israel Tal**, Avraham Yoffe, and **Ariel Sharon** smashed through Egyptian fortifications in Gaza and Abu Ageila. Retreating Egyptian columns caught in the open desert were devastated from the air at the **Mitla Pass**, allowing Israeli tanks to reach the Suez Canal and Sharm el-Sheikh by 8 June. [4.2] Meanwhile on 5 June, misled by false Cairo radio broadcasts claiming Egyptian victories, King Hussein’s artillery shelled West Jerusalem despite Israeli appeals to stay out. Israeli brigades counter-attacked into the **West Bank**, and on **7 June 1967** paratroopers stormed Jerusalem’s Old City to capture **East Jerusalem** and the **Western Wall**, driving Jordanian forces back across the River Jordan.

narrative_blocks.title: Storming the Golan Heights & Six-Day Victory
paragraphs: [5.1] With Egypt and Jordan defeated, Defence Minister Moshe Dayan ordered a final northern offensive on **9 June 1967** against the fortified Syrian **Golan Heights**, from which Syrian artillery had shelled northern Israeli villages for years. Backed by relentless air strikes, Israeli infantry and armoured bulldozers fought uphill through concrete bunkers to capture Quneitra before a UN ceasefire took effect on **10 June 1967**.

[5.2] In just six days, Israel shattered three Arab armies and tripled the territory under its control—occupying the Sinai Peninsula, Gaza Strip, West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Golan Heights. While giving Israel deep strategic buffers, victory placed over one million Palestinians under military occupation and humiliated Arab regimes, transforming the Middle East conflict.

sources.title: Source A: Nasser and Eshkol on the Closure of the Straits of Tiran
sources.image_alt: Relief map of the Sinai Peninsula showing the Gulf of Aqaba, the Israeli port of Eilat at its northern tip and the narrow Strait of Tiran at Sharm el-Sheikh in the south.
sources.caption: The Sinai Peninsula: Israeli ships reached the port of Eilat only through the narrow Strait of Tiran at Sharm el-Sheikh, which Egypt closed to Israeli shipping on 22 May 1967.
sources.desc: Map of the Sinai Peninsula and Gulf of Aqaba with paired summaries of Nasser's announcement of 22 May 1967 and the Israeli government's response.

sources.source_context: A false Soviet warning on 13 May 1967 claimed Israel was massing troops against Syria. Nasser sent about 100,000 troops into Sinai, demanded the withdrawal of UNEF, and on 22 May closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli ships — crossing a red line Israel had declared since 1957.
sources.context: After expelling UN peacekeepers from Sinai, Nasser announced on 22 May 1967 that the Straits of Tiran were closed to Israeli shipping.
sources.model_answer: Nasser had promised to defend Syria and lead the Arab world, so reopening the Straits would have looked like surrender to Israel. Israel had warned since 1957 that closing Tiran would be an act of war, because Eilat was its only route to the Red Sea and its oil supply; Backing down would have cost each leader his credibility at home.

perspective_pair.framing_note: Read together, the two statements show how one narrow sea lane became a test of national honour and legal rights for both governments.

side_a.title: Speech at Bir Gifgafa air base, Sinai
side_a.text: Speaking to Egyptian pilots in Sinai, Nasser announced that the Gulf of Aqaba was Egyptian territorial water and that Israeli ships would no longer pass through the Straits of Tiran. He said Egypt had moved its forces to defend Syria against Israeli threats and to restore the situation before 1956. He declared that if Israel threatened war, Egypt's armed forces were ready to meet it.
side_a.provenance: Summary of Nasser's speech broadcast by Cairo Radio, 22 May 1967.

side_b.title: Prime Minister Levi Eshkol's statement to the Knesset
side_b.text: Eshkol told the Knesset that any interference with Israeli shipping in the Straits of Tiran was a serious breach of international law and an act of aggression against Israel. He reminded the maritime powers of the promises of free passage made when Israel withdrew from Sinai in 1957 and called on them to act. Israel, meanwhile, mobilised its reserves while its diplomats sought international support.
side_b.provenance: Summary of Eshkol's statement to the Knesset, 23 May 1967.

sources.image_alt: King Hussein of Jordan, President Nasser and Field Marshal Amer sit together in Cairo shortly before signing a defence pact.
sources.caption: King Hussein of Jordan (left), President Nasser and Egyptian army commander Abdel Hakim Amer in Cairo before signing the Egyptian–Jordanian defence pact, 30 May 1967.

sources.provenance: Photo: photographer not credited, Cairo, 30 May 1967 (Wikimedia Commons, public domain). Side A: summary of the terms and public statements of the Egyptian–Jordanian pact. Side B: summary of Israeli government and public reactions, late May 1967; side B photo LBJ Library, 26 May 1967.
sources.citation: Egyptian–Jordanian Joint Defence Agreement, 30 May 1967; LBJ Presidential Library photo, 26 May 1967.
sources.source_context: King Hussein had been attacked by Nasser's radio for years, but after the Samu raid and the May crisis he feared that staying out of an Arab–Israeli war would cost him his throne. On 30 May he signed a joint defence pact in Cairo; Iraqi troops soon entered Jordan. In Israel, Prime Minister Eshkol formed a national unity government on 1 June and appointed Moshe Dayan Minister of Defence.
sources.context: On 30 May 1967 King Hussein flew to Cairo and signed a defence pact with Nasser, placing Jordan's army under Egyptian command.
sources.model_answer: The pact put Jordan's army under Egyptian command, so Israel now faced hostile forces on its southern, eastern and northern borders at once. With President Johnson unable to organise a convoy to reopen the Straits, many Israeli leaders concluded that waiting made Israel weaker; the pact therefore strengthened the case for a pre-emptive strike.

perspective_pair.framing_note: The same agreement looked defensive from Cairo and Amman and threatening from Tel Aviv and Jerusalem; comparing the two views explains the speed of the final slide to war.

side_a.title: The Joint Defence Agreement
side_a.text: Under the agreement, Egypt and Jordan promised that an armed attack on either state would be treated as an attack on both, and that each would immediately help the other. Jordanian forces were placed under the command of an Egyptian general. Arab radio stations celebrated the pact as proof of Arab unity after years of quarrels, and presented it as a defensive shield against Israeli attack.
side_a.provenance: Summary of the Egyptian–Jordanian defence agreement and Arab press coverage, 30 May–1 June 1967.

side_b.title: Israeli view of encirclement
side_b.text: Foreign Minister Abba Eban met President Johnson on 26 May, who urged Israel not to fire first and promised to try to organise an international convoy through the Straits. After the pact, Israeli leaders believed they faced Egyptian, Jordanian, Syrian and Iraqi forces on three fronts while the convoy plan stalled. Civilians dug trenches, reserves stayed mobilised and many Israelis feared their country could be destroyed if it waited.
side_b.provenance: Summary of Israeli government records and public reaction, late May 1967; photo LBJ Presidential Library, 26 May 1967.

questions.question: 2. Write a narrative account analysing the key events leading up to and during the Six Day War in May–June 1967. [8 marks]
questions.prompt: Use the structure strip and causal connectives below to structure your response.
questions.model:
On 13 May 1967, a false Soviet intelligence warning alleging an Israeli troop buildup against Syria prompted Egyptian President Nasser to march 100,000 troops into Sinai and expel UNEF peacekeepers on 16 May. Escalating further, Nasser closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping on 22 May and signed a Joint Defence Pact with Jordan’s King Hussein on 30 May; when US President Lyndon B. Johnson failed to reopen Tiran by sea, Israel appointed Moshe Dayan Defence Minister to prepare a pre-emptive strike.

At 07:45 on 5 June 1967, the Israeli Air Force launched Operation Focus, flying beneath radar to crater Egyptian runways and destroy over 300 Egyptian aircraft on the ground within three hours. Shielded by total air supremacy between 5 and 8 June, Israeli armoured divisions under Tal, Yoffe, and Sharon routed Egyptian forces through the Mitla Pass to the Suez Canal, while Jordanian shelling of West Jerusalem triggered an Israeli counter-attack that captured East Jerusalem’s Old City and the West Bank by 7 June.

With Egypt and Jordan defeated, Dayan ordered a final assault on 9 June up the fortified Syrian Golan Heights, seizing Quneitra before a UN Security Council ceasefire took effect on 10 June 1967. In six days Israel tripled the territory under its control—occupying Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights—placing over one million Palestinians under military occupation.

tier_2m.title: 2/8 Simple Narrative
tier_2m.text: In May 1967, President Nasser sent Egyptian troops into Sinai, removed UN peacekeepers, and closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli ships. On 5 June 1967, Israel launched a surprise air strike that destroyed Egypt’s air force and went on to capture Sinai, the West Bank, and the Golan Heights in six days.
tier_2m.verdict: AO2 Level 1 (1 mark) • AO1 Level 1 (1 mark). Simple chronological overview with limited own knowledge beyond the stimulus bullets.

tier_5m.title: 5/8 Sequenced Account
tier_5m.text:
The crisis began in May 1967 after a false Soviet report led Nasser to march 100,000 troops into Sinai, expel UNEF peacekeepers on 16 May, and close the Straits of Tiran on 22 May, before signing a Joint Defence Pact with King Hussein of Jordan on 30 May.

Next, at 07:45 on 5 June 1967, Israel launched Operation Focus, destroying over 300 Egyptian aircraft on the ground in three hours. Israeli armoured divisions then crossed Sinai to the Suez Canal while paratroopers captured East Jerusalem and the West Bank by 7 June.

Finally, Israeli troops stormed the Syrian Golan Heights on 9 June before a UN ceasefire took effect on 10 June 1967, tripling the territory under Israeli control.
tier_5m.verdict: AO2 Level 2 (2–3 marks) • AO1 Level 2 (2–3 marks). Clear three-part chronological sequence with strong own knowledge, needing more explicit causal explanation of why US diplomatic failure and air supremacy decided each front.

tier_8m.title: 8/8 Grade 9 Exam ★
tier_8m.text:
On 13 May 1967, a false Soviet intelligence warning alleging an Israeli troop buildup against Syria prompted Egyptian President Nasser to march 100,000 troops into Sinai and expel UNEF peacekeepers on 16 May. Escalating further, Nasser closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping on 22 May and signed a Joint Defence Pact with Jordan’s King Hussein on 30 May; when US President Lyndon B. Johnson failed to reopen Tiran by sea, Israel appointed Moshe Dayan Defence Minister to prepare a pre-emptive strike.

At 07:45 on 5 June 1967, the Israeli Air Force launched Operation Focus, flying beneath radar to crater Egyptian runways and destroy over 300 Egyptian aircraft on the ground within three hours. Shielded by total air supremacy between 5 and 8 June, Israeli armoured divisions under Tal, Yoffe, and Sharon routed Egyptian forces through the Mitla Pass to the Suez Canal, while Jordanian shelling of West Jerusalem triggered an Israeli counter-attack that captured East Jerusalem’s Old City and the West Bank by 7 June.

With Egypt and Jordan defeated, Dayan ordered a final assault on 9 June up the fortified Syrian Golan Heights, seizing Quneitra before a UN Security Council ceasefire took effect on 10 June 1967. In six days Israel tripled the territory under its control—occupying Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights—placing over one million Palestinians under military occupation.
tier_8m.verdict: AO1 Level 3 (4 marks) • AO2 Level 3 (4 marks). Organised beginning–developments–outcome narrative with explicit causal links and own knowledge beyond the stimulus.

video.title: The History Channel: How the Six-Day War Changed the Map of the Middle East
video.teacher_guidance: Visual tactical recap of the morning of 5 June 1967: 200 Israeli aircraft flying under Egyptian radar to destroy airbases in 3 hours. Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–04:22 • Lesson Phase: Starter Hook (0–5m). Tone Alert: Fast-paced cartographic summary illustrating how six days of combat reshaped the geopolitical boundaries of the region.
video.viewing_task:
1. [01:05] Recall: What was the military codename of the surprise Israeli pre-emptive air strike launched at 07:45 on the morning of 5 June 1967?
  2. [02:30] Explain: Explain how the destruction of over 300 Egyptian combat aircraft on the ground in the first three hours decided the entire outcome of the Six-Day War.
  3. [03:50] Challenge: By 10 June 1967, Israel had captured territories three times its original size. How did this astonishing victory transform Israel from a vulnerable state into an occupying power with complex demographic problems?
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: the pre-emptive air strike (Mivtza Moked).
  2. Explain: Achieving total air supremacy allowed Israeli Mirages and Super Mystères to act as flying artillery with complete freedom. Israeli ground forces advancing across Sinai, the West Bank, and the Golan Heights faced zero hostile air attacks, while retreating Egyptian, Jordanian, and Syrian armor was mercilessly pulverized from the air.
  3. Challenge: While conquering the Sinai, Gaza Strip, West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Golan Heights provided unprecedented geographical buffer zones, it brought over one million disenfranchised Palestinian Arabs under Israeli military control, creating a profound, permanent dilemma between democratic principles and demographic preservation.

video.title: Real Time History: The Six-Day War Combat Timeline Across Three Fronts
video.teacher_guidance: Objective, non-partisan military analysis explaining the collapse of Egyptian forces in the Sinai passes, Jordanian artillery shelling of Tel Aviv and Israeli counter-attack, and the storming of the Golan Heights. Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–08:30 • Lesson Phase: Guided Instruction & Dual-Coding. Tone Alert: Objective, detailed military timeline breaking down operational movements across all three combat fronts.
video.viewing_task:
1. [02:10] Recall: On which three distinct geographical fronts did the Israel Defense Forces fight between 5 and 10 June 1967?
  2. [04:45] Explain: Why did Egyptian Field Marshal Abdel Hakim Amer issue a catastrophic general retreat order across the Sinai on 6 June, and what were its military consequences?
  3. [07:15] Challenge: Analyze the factors behind Israeli military dominance: how did superior pilot training, ground turnaround speed (jets refueled and rearmed in under 8 minutes), and decentralized officer initiative explain Israel's victory over numerically larger Arab armies?
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: The Southern Front in the Sinai Peninsula and Gaza against Egypt; the Eastern Front in the West Bank and Jerusalem against Jordan; and the Northern Front on the Golan Heights against Syria.
  2. Explain: Panicked by the total destruction of his air force and initial IDF breakthroughs, Amer suffered an emotional breakdown and ordered a disorderly retreat to the Suez Canal without organizing rear-guard defensive lines. Egyptian divisions abandoned their heavy equipment in panic, turning the narrow Sinai mountain passes (such as Mitla) into deadly bottlenecks where hundreds of tanks were destroyed.
  3. Challenge: Arab armies were strictly hierarchical, Soviet-trained, and politically distrustful, requiring rigid top-down orders before acting. Conversely, Israeli pilots averaged hundreds more flight hours, ground crews turned around warplanes four times faster than standard NATO times, and junior Israeli commanders were trained to exploit tactical initiative on the spot, creating irresistible operational tempo.

video.title: Unpacked (Avi Posen): The Battle for the Old City & Reunification of Jerusalem
video.teacher_guidance: Avi Posen recounts the intense urban fighting in East Jerusalem, Paratroopers reaching the Western Wall, and the profound religious and national euphoria across Israel. Recommended Watch Window: 01:15–06:40 • Lesson Phase: Cultural & Media Deconstruction. Tone Alert: Emotive mainstream Israeli educational framing; emphasizes deep ancestral connection to Jerusalem's holy sites.
video.viewing_task:
1. [02:30] Recall: Which brigade of Israeli paratroopers breached the Lions' Gate to capture the Old City of Jerusalem on 7 June 1967, and who commanded them?
  2. [04:15] Explain: Why did the capture of the Old City and the Western Wall evoke such an extraordinary outpouring of tears and euphoria across the Jewish world?
  3. [05:50] Challenge: Deconstruct the term 'reunification of Jerusalem'. How do Palestinians and international bodies view the annexation of East Jerusalem under international law, and why does this remain one of the most explosive issues in the world?
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: The 55th Paratroopers Brigade, commanded by Colonel Mordechai 'Motta' Gur.
  2. Explain: For nearly 2,000 years since the Roman destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE—and specifically during the 19 years of Jordanian rule (1948–1967) when Jews were barred from the Old City—the Western Wall was inaccessible. When battle-hardened paratroopers reached the Wall and heard the Shofar blown, it felt like the historic fulfillment of two millennia of prayer and survival.
  3. Challenge: While Israel passed legislation declaring Jerusalem 'complete and united' as its eternal capital, Palestinians view East Jerusalem as the occupied capital of their future state. Under international law (including UN Security Council Resolution 252 and the Fourth Geneva Convention), unilateral annexation of territory by war is illegal, leaving Jerusalem's sovereign status internationally contested.

video.title: BBC / ERA: Battle for the Holy City (Days That Shook the World)
video.teacher_guidance: Dramatic BBC reconstruction of urban combat in Jerusalem, King Hussein's dilemmas, and the UN ceasefire negotiations. Recommended Watch Window: 10:00–20:15 • Lesson Phase: High-Attainer Stretch & Oral History Investigation. Tone Alert: Gripping BBC documentary combining Jordanian soldier testimonies and Israeli paratrooper memories of the fierce urban struggle for Jerusalem.
video.viewing_task:
1. [11:20] Recall: What historic walled sector of Jerusalem was captured by Israeli paratroopers on 7 June 1967 following fierce fighting against Jordanian forces?
  2. [14:40] Explain: How was King Hussein of Jordan deceived by President Nasser's telephone calls claiming massive Egyptian victories into continuing artillery strikes against West Jerusalem?
  3. [18:30] Challenge: Evaluate oral testimonies from both Jordanian legionnaires and Israeli paratroopers. How do their personal memories challenge simplistic one-sided narratives of cowardice or effortless victory?
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: The Old City of Jerusalem (including the Western Wall and Temple Mount).
  2. Explain: Nasser lied to King Hussein on secure radio links, claiming Egyptian forces had destroyed 75% of the Israeli Air Force and were advancing through the Negev. Believing Israel was on the verge of destruction, Hussein rejected Israeli secret diplomatic pleas to stay out of the war, ordering his artillery to shell Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, sealing Jordan's defeat.
  3. Challenge: Far from an easy walkover, the battle of East Jerusalem resulted in severe casualties on both sides; Israeli veterans openly praised the resolute bravery of the Jordanian soldiers who fought to the death in narrow concrete bunkers. These oral accounts demonstrate that military disaster stemmed from political deception and absent air cover, not a lack of soldierly valor.

lessons.hook_text: In the summer of 1967, Israel found itself ruling over one million Palestinians. In September, Arab leaders declared the "Three Noes" in Khartoum. In November, the UN passed Resolution 242 promising "Land for Peace"—yet its ambiguous words locked the region in stalemate.

teacher_notes.primer: This lesson investigates the political and diplomatic aftermath of the 1967 Six Day War. Pupils explore how Israel administered five new territories (Sinai, Gaza, West Bank, East Jerusalem, Golan Heights) with over a million Palestinian inhabitants, sparking a second refugee crisis. They examine the hardline Arab response at the Khartoum Summit ("Three Noes") and dissect the core terms and deliberate linguistic ambiguities of UN Security Council Resolution 242 ("Land for Peace").

teacher_notes.hinge_question: How did a single missing word—'the'—in the English text of UN Security Council Resolution 242 allow both Israel and Arab states to claim the resolution backed their position?
teacher_notes.hinge_guidance: Strong GCSE answers explain 'constructive ambiguity': British drafter Lord Caradon wrote 'withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied in the recent conflict' (not 'from all the territories'), enabling Israel to argue it only needed to withdraw to 'secure and recognised boundaries' after peace treaties, while Arab governments pointed to the French text ('des territoires occupés') and the preamble banning acquisition of territory by war to demand 100% withdrawal from every inch seized in June 1967.

misconceptions.misconception: Reading the August 1967 Khartoum 'Three Noes' (no peace, no recognition, no negotiations) as a call for an immediate Arab military invasion.
misconceptions.correction: While Khartoum ruled out direct talks or recognition of Israel, Nasser and King Hussein actually used the summit to secure Gulf oil subsidies in return for ending the Yemen war and pursuing diplomatic/political recovery of lost land rather than immediate reckless war.

misconceptions.misconception: Noticing Palestinians by name inside UN Security Council Resolution 242 (November 1967).
misconceptions.correction: Resolution 242 never mentioned 'Palestinians' or Palestinian statehood, referring only to 'achieving a just settlement of the refugee problem'—a crucial omission that alienated the PLO for the next twenty-one years.

misconceptions.misconception: Treating all post-1967 Israeli settlements as identical in motive.
misconceptions.correction: Labour's Yigal Allon Plan proposed strategic farming settlements in the Jordan Valley as military security buffers while offering to return densely populated West Bank towns, whereas religious-nationalist settlers (later Gush Emunim) claimed Judea and Samaria as an ancestral biblical homeland.

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: Following the Six-Day War, Israel controlled five [Occupied Territories]: the Sinai, Gaza, West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights. Over 300,000 Palestinians were newly displaced across the River Jordan, creating a second refugee crisis. In August 1967, Arab leaders gathered at the [Khartoum Conference] in Sudan, issuing a defiant declaration known as [The Three Noes]. In November, the United Nations attempted to resolve the conflict by passing [UN Resolution 242]. This historic resolution established the formula of [Land for Peace], but deliberate wording differences between English and French allowed both sides to interpret it differently, while the growth of [Israeli Settlements] in the West Bank further complicated future peace negotiations.

narrative_blocks.title: The Capture of East Jerusalem
paragraphs: [1.1] Victory in June 1967 tripled the territory under Israeli control—occupying Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, and the Golan Heights—while displacing **300,000 refugees** into neighbouring Jordan and Syria. On **7 June 1967**, Israeli paratroopers under Colonel **Motta Gur** stormed into Jerusalem’s Old City, allowing Jewish worshippers to pray freely at the **Western Wall** for the first time since 1948.

[1.2] Weeks later, the Knesset formally annexed **East Jerusalem**, expanding municipal boundaries and declaring a united Jerusalem Israel’s eternal capital while placing over one million Palestinians across the West Bank and Gaza under military rule. However, the United Nations condemned the annexation as illegal under international law, insisting Jerusalem’s status required direct bilateral negotiations.

narrative_blocks.title: The Khartoum Summit & The "Three No’s"
paragraphs: [2.1] Stunned by their catastrophic territorial losses, eight Arab heads of state gathered in Sudan for the **Khartoum** Arab League Summit in August 1967. While moderates like Jordan's King Hussein sought diplomatic avenues to recover lost territory, hardline regimes in Syria and Algeria insisted on total military defiance and an economic oil embargo against Israel’s Western allies.

[2.2] On **1 September 1967**, the summit issued the famous **Khartoum Resolution**, adopting the uncompromising **Three Noes**: "No peace with Israel, no recognition of Israel, no negotiations with Israel." This unyielding stance hardened Israeli public opinion, convincing political leaders that Arab states remained committed to Israel’s destruction and ending immediate hopes of trading captured land for permanent peace.

sources.source_context: After their defeat, eight Arab heads of state met in Khartoum. Moderates such as King Hussein wanted diplomacy to win back land, while Syria and Algeria wanted continued confrontation. The final resolution of 1 September combined a demand for Israeli withdrawal with the famous refusals of peace, recognition and negotiation.
sources.context: At the Khartoum summit (29 August–1 September 1967) Arab leaders adopted the "Three Noes".
sources.model_answer: Israel's cabinet had secretly agreed in June 1967 to return Sinai and the Golan in exchange for peace, so the Three Noes looked like a flat rejection of any deal. Israeli leaders concluded they should hold the territories until Arab states were ready to negotiate; Arab leaders, however, saw negotiating under occupation as rewarding Israel's conquest.

narrative_blocks.content: [2.1] Stunned by their catastrophic territorial losses, eight Arab heads of state gathered in Sudan for the **Khartoum** Arab League Summit in August 1967. While moderates like Jordan's King Hussein sought diplomatic avenues to recover lost territory, hardline regimes in Syria and Algeria insisted on total military defiance and an economic oil embargo against Israel’s Western allies. [2.2] On **1 September 1967**, the summit issued the famous **Khartoum Resolution**, adopting the uncompromising **Three Noes**: "No peace with Israel, no recognition of Israel, no negotiations with Israel." This unyielding stance hardened Israeli public opinion, convincing political leaders that Arab states remained committed to Israel’s destruction and ending immediate hopes of trading captured land for permanent peace.

narrative_blocks.title: UN Resolution 242: "Land for Peace"
paragraphs: [3.1] On **22 November 1967**, the United Nations Security Council unanimously adopted **Resolution 242**, drafted by British Ambassador Lord Caradon. The resolution established the cornerstone principle of modern Middle Eastern diplomacy: "**Land for Peace**." It linked Israeli military withdrawal from captured lands to the right of every regional state to live in peace within secure and recognized boundaries.

[3.2] However, the resolution contained deliberate wording ambiguities: the English text called for withdrawal from "territories occupied" rather than all territories, allowing Israel to argue for defensible border adjustments. Furthermore, the resolution referred to Palestinian Arabs merely as a "refugee problem," ignoring their national rights to self-determination and prompting the PLO to reject the diplomatic framework completely.

perspective_pair.framing_note: Resolution 242 was accepted by Israel, Egypt and Jordan, but for different reasons; comparing their readings explains why it became both the basis of peace talks and a source of argument.

side_a.title: Israeli reading of Resolution 242
side_a.text: Israel stressed that the resolution called for withdrawal from "territories occupied", not from "the territories" or "all" of them. Israeli leaders argued this allowed new, secure borders to be agreed in negotiations, and that withdrawal could only come as part of a peace settlement in which Arab states recognised Israel. They pointed to the phrase "secure and recognized boundaries" as proof that the 1949 lines need not be restored.
side_a.provenance: Summary of Israeli government statements on Resolution 242, 1967–68.

side_b.title: Arab and Palestinian readings of Resolution 242
side_b.text: Egypt and Jordan accepted the resolution but read it, supported by the French text, as requiring Israeli withdrawal from all land taken in June 1967. They argued that acquiring territory by war was inadmissible, as the preamble stated. The PLO rejected the resolution outright because it described Palestinians only as a "refugee problem", ignoring their claim to be a people with national rights.
side_b.provenance: Summary of Egyptian, Jordanian and PLO statements, 1967–68.

narrative_blocks.title: The Bar-Lev Line on the Suez Canal
paragraphs: [4.1] Along the **Suez Canal**—which remained blocked to all international shipping by sunken vessels and naval mines from June 1967—Israeli Chief of Staff **Haim Bar-Lev** constructed a heavily fortified defensive barrier between 1968 and 1969. The **Bar-Lev Line** featured a **20-metre high artificial sand rampart** backed by concrete bunkers, minefields, and observation posts along the east bank.

[4.2] This closed waterway became the fierce battleground of the **War of Attrition** (1969–1970), as Nasser launched sustained artillery bombardments and commando raids across the canal to wear down Israeli resolve and prevent the ceasefire line becoming permanent. Holding the line bred a false sense of Israeli invincibility that proved costly in October 1973.

narrative_blocks.title: The Beginning of Israeli Settlements
paragraphs: [5.1] Following the 1967 conquest, Deputy Prime Minister **Yigal Allon** formulated the **Allon Plan**, proposing agricultural settlements along the Jordan Valley as military security buffers while returning Arab-populated central hilltops to Jordanian administrative control. The ruling Labour Party initially authorized settlements strictly on perimeter security grounds to protect the narrow coastal heartland against external ground invasion.

[5.2] However, religious-nationalist movements like Gush Emunim soon began establishing ideological **Israeli settlements** deep in the biblical heartland of the **West Bank** (Judea and Samaria). When Menachem Begin's Likud party took power in 1977, state subsidies expanded settlements dramatically, embedding hundreds of thousands of Jewish residents into occupied territories and creating severe physical obstacles to any viable two-state solution.

side_b.text: Egypt and Jordan accepted the resolution but read it, supported by the French text, as requiring Israeli withdrawal from all land taken in June 1967. They argued that acquiring territory by war was inadmissible, as the preamble stated. The PLO rejected the resolution outright because it described Palestinians only as a "refugee problem", ignoring their claim to be a people with national rights.

questions.question: 3. Explain the importance of UN Resolution 242 (November 1967) for Arab-Israeli relations after the Six Day War. [8 marks]
questions.prompt: Use the structure strip and causal connectives below to structure your response.
questions.model:
First, UN Security Council Resolution 242 (22 November 1967) was important because it established the enduring "Land for Peace" diplomatic framework for future Middle East negotiations. Passed unanimously after Arab leaders issued the Khartoum Summit’s uncompromising "Three Noes" (1 September 1967), British-drafted Resolution 242 linked Israeli military withdrawal from conquered territory to Arab recognition of every regional state’s right to live in peace within secure and recognised borders, creating the benchmark later used in Egyptian, Jordanian, and Palestinian peace talks.

Second, deliberate ambiguity in Resolution 242’s wording entrenched diplomatic deadlock with Arab states and alienated the PLO. Calling in English for withdrawal from "territories occupied" rather than "the territories" allowed Israel to argue for defensible border adjustments while building the Bar-Lev Line and Allon Plan settlements, whereas Arab governments demanded total pre-war withdrawal; meanwhile, referring to Palestinians merely as a "refugee problem" ignored Palestinian statehood, prompting the PLO to reject Resolution 242 and escalate armed struggle.

tier_2m.title: 2/8 Simple Statement
tier_2m.text: UN Resolution 242 was important because it introduced the idea of "Land for Peace", asking Israel to withdraw from captured land in return for peace with Arab states. However, Israel and the Arab states disagreed over what it meant, so no peace deal was signed.
tier_2m.verdict: AO1 Level 1 (1 mark) • AO2 Level 1 (1 mark). Valid basic point on "Land for Peace" and disagreement, lacking specific wording details or PLO reaction.

tier_5m.title: 5/8 Descriptive Analysis
tier_5m.text:
First, UN Resolution 242 in November 1967 set out the "Land for Peace" formula after the Arab League’s Khartoum "Three Noes", calling for Israeli withdrawal alongside secure and recognised borders for every state in the region.

Second, the English text called for withdrawal from "territories occupied" rather than "the territories", and referred only to a "refugee problem" without mentioning Palestinian statehood. Israel kept building the Bar-Lev Line and Allon Plan settlements while the PLO rejected Resolution 242.
tier_5m.verdict: AO1 Level 2 (2–3 marks) • AO2 Level 2 (2–3 marks). Accurate knowledge of both diplomatic principles and textual ambiguity, needing sharper analytical focus on long-term Arab-Israeli relations.

tier_8m.title: 8/8 Grade 9 Exam ★

First, UN Security Council Resolution 242 (22 November 1967) was important because it established the enduring "Land for Peace" diplomatic framework for future Middle East negotiations. Passed unanimously after Arab leaders issued the Khartoum Summit’s uncompromising "Three Noes" (1 September 1967), British-drafted Resolution 242 linked Israeli military withdrawal from conquered territory to Arab recognition of every regional state’s right to live in peace within secure and recognised borders, creating the benchmark later used in Egyptian, Jordanian, and Palestinian peace talks.

Second, deliberate ambiguity in Resolution 242’s wording entrenched diplomatic deadlock with Arab states and alienated the PLO. Calling in English for withdrawal from "territories occupied" rather than "the territories" allowed Israel to argue for defensible border adjustments while building the Bar-Lev Line and Allon Plan settlements, whereas Arab governments demanded total pre-war withdrawal; meanwhile, referring to Palestinians merely as a "refugee problem" ignored Palestinian statehood, prompting the PLO to reject Resolution 242 and escalate armed struggle.

stages.title: The Capture of East Jerusalem
stages.trigger: Israeli paratroopers capture the Old City of Jerusalem and the Western Wall; the Israeli parliament quickly annexes East Jerusalem under Israeli law.
stages.because: Jordan had opened artillery fire on West Jerusalem on the first day of the war, giving Israel the opportunity to capture the sacred holy sites.
stages.therefore: Reunited Jerusalem under Israeli control, but was condemned by the UN and became the most emotional, contested issue in the entire conflict.
stages.connective: Stunned by their catastrophic battlefield defeat, Arab leaders gathered to coordinate a response...
stages.exam_link: Q1 Consequence: Made Jerusalem the most sacred and intractable dispute between Israelis and Palestinians.
stages.question: How did annexing East Jerusalem and new refugees transform the conflict?

stages.title: The Khartoum Summit & The "Three No’s"
stages.trigger: Arab heads of state meet in Khartoum and declare the famous "Three No’s": no peace with Israel, no recognition of Israel, no negotiations with Israel.
stages.because: Defeated Arab leaders could not recognize Israel or accept the permanent loss of Arab land without being overthrown by their own people.
stages.therefore: Destroyed Israeli hopes of quickly trading captured land for permanent peace treaties, locking both sides into a bitter stalemate.
stages.connective: To break the diplomatic deadlock, the United Nations drafted a historic peace formula...
stages.exam_link: Q1 Consequence: Blocked early peace negotiations and entrenched the diplomatic stalemate after the 1967 war.
stages.question: Why did Arab leaders adopt the "Three Noes" at the Khartoum Summit in 1967?

stages.title: UN Resolution 242: "Land for Peace"
stages.trigger: The UN passes Resolution 242, establishing the principle of "Land for Peace": Israel should withdraw from occupied lands in return for Arab recognition of its right to live in peace.
stages.because: The superpowers (USA and USSR) wanted to prevent another regional war while resolving the refugee and territorial crisis.
stages.therefore: Became the basis for all future peace negotiations, but vague English phrasing ("withdrawal from territories" rather than "all territories") led to years of disagreement.
stages.connective: Expecting no quick peace deal, Israel built heavy military fortifications along the new borders...
stages.exam_link: Q1 Consequence: Established the international framework of "Land for Peace" that underpinned all subsequent peace talks (Camp David and Oslo).
stages.question: How did UN Resolution 242 define "Land for Peace", and why was it disputed?

stages.title: The Bar-Lev Line on the Suez Canal
stages.trigger: Israel builds a massive defensive barrier of giant sand walls and concrete fortresses along the entire eastern bank of the Suez Canal.
stages.because: The Sinai Desert provided Israel with strategic depth to absorb any future Egyptian attack and protect mainland Israeli cities.
stages.therefore: Created a false sense of security among Israeli commanders, who believed Egyptian forces could never cross the canal, setting the stage for surprise in 1973.
stages.connective: Alongside military forts, Israeli civilians began settling inside the captured Arab territories...
stages.exam_link: Q2 Narrative Account: Bred the military overconfidence that left Israeli forces unprepared for the surprise Egyptian canal crossing in 1973.
stages.question: How did the blocked Suez Canal and Bar-Lev Line fuel the War of Attrition?

stages.title: The Beginning of Israeli Settlements
stages.trigger: Israel begins building permanent civilian settlements in the newly captured territories: the West Bank, Golan Heights, and Gaza Strip.
stages.because: The Israeli government sought security buffer zones, while religious settlers believed the land belonged to the historic Jewish homeland.
stages.therefore: Created permanent Jewish communities inside Palestinian areas, establishing "facts on the ground" that made future territorial compromise far harder.
stages.connective: Faced with permanent occupation and defeated Arab armies, Palestinians turned to armed guerrilla warfare...
stages.exam_link: Q1 Consequence: Created permanent Jewish settlements in Palestinian territory, which became a major barrier to a two-state solution.
stages.question: How did the Allon Plan and West Bank settlements obstruct a two-state deal?
