questions.question: 3. Explain the importance of Soviet measures in Czechoslovakia (1968) for international relations. [8 marks]
questions.prompt: Write two distinct analytical paragraphs: (1) Impact on US-Soviet superpower relations (temporary chill & cancelled Johnson–Kosygin summit, yet no military clash due to Vietnam & unspoken spheres), and (2) Severe fracturing of international Communism (Romania, Yugoslavia, China, and Western European Eurocommunism).
questions.examiner_tip: Notice the stem says "international relations"—cover BOTH superpower relations with the USA AND Moscow’s damaged relations within the wider Communist world!
questions.model:
First, Soviet measures in Czechoslovakia in August 1968 were important for superpower relations because they caused only a short-lived diplomatic chill while confirming that neither superpower would risk nuclear war over the other’s sphere of influence. Although US President Lyndon B. Johnson condemned the invasion, cancelled a planned Moscow disarmament summit, and supported a UN Security Council resolution (vetoed by Moscow), Washington was bogged down with 500,000 troops in the Vietnam War and took zero military action—demonstrating tacit acceptance of the Iron Curtain that allowed détente talks to resume within two years.

Second, Moscow’s armed intervention and the Brezhnev Doctrine permanently fractured unity across the international Communist movement. Inside Eastern Europe, Nicolae Ceaușescu’s Romania refused to send troops and aligned more independently alongside Tito’s Yugoslavia, while Mao Zedong’s China denounced Soviet "social imperialism" fearing a similar Soviet strike. Simultaneously, outrage led the powerful French and Italian Communist Parties to distance themselves from Kremlin control under "Eurocommunism", eroding Moscow’s authority as leader of world communism.

tier_2m.title: 2/8 Simple Statement
tier_2m.text: Soviet measures in Czechoslovakia in 1968 were important for international relations because the USA condemned the invasion and cancelled talks, while Communist countries like China and Romania criticised Moscow too.
tier_2m.verdict: AO1 Level 1 (1 mark) • AO2 Level 1 (1 mark). Valid identification of US and Communist criticism, lacking analytical depth on Vietnam, spheres of influence, and Eurocommunism.

tier_4m.title: 4/8 Descriptive
tier_4m.text:
After Soviet-led Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia in August 1968, US President Lyndon B. Johnson condemned the invasion, cancelled a planned summit in Moscow, and backed a UN resolution that the USSR vetoed, though America was busy fighting in Vietnam.

At the same time, Romania refused to join the invasion, China and Yugoslavia criticised Brezhnev, and French and Italian Communist parties protested against Moscow.
tier_4m.verdict: AO1 Level 2 (2 marks) • AO2 Level 2 (2 marks). Accurate factual detail across both paragraphs, but describes reactions rather than explicitly explaining what they revealed and changed in international relations.

tier_8m.title: 8/8 Grade 9 Exam ★
tier_8m.text:
First, Soviet measures in Czechoslovakia in August 1968 were important for superpower relations because they caused only a short-lived diplomatic chill while confirming that neither superpower would risk nuclear war over the other’s sphere of influence. Although US President Lyndon B. Johnson condemned the invasion, cancelled a planned Moscow disarmament summit, and supported a UN Security Council resolution (vetoed by Moscow), Washington was bogged down with 500,000 troops in the Vietnam War and took zero military action—demonstrating tacit acceptance of the Iron Curtain that allowed détente talks to resume within two years.

Second, Moscow’s armed intervention and the Brezhnev Doctrine permanently fractured unity across the international Communist movement. Inside Eastern Europe, Nicolae Ceaușescu’s Romania refused to send troops and aligned more independently alongside Tito’s Yugoslavia, while Mao Zedong’s China denounced Soviet "social imperialism" fearing a similar Soviet strike. Simultaneously, outrage led the powerful French and Italian Communist Parties to distance themselves from Kremlin control under "Eurocommunism", eroding Moscow’s authority as leader of world communism.
tier_8m.verdict: AO1 Level 3 (4 marks) • AO2 Level 3 (4 marks). Two distinct, factually evidenced analytical paragraphs explaining both superpower sphere-of-influence restraint and the fracturing of global communism.

teacher_notes.hinge_question: Why did the August 1968 Warsaw Pact invasion succeed in keeping Eastern Europe obedient for twenty years under the Brezhnev Doctrine, yet permanently fracture Soviet leadership of the world Communist movement?
teacher_notes.hinge_guidance: Strong GCSE answers separate bloc control from global Communist unity: inside the Warsaw Pact, sending 500,000 troops, enforcing Gustav Husak's 'normalisation', and proclaiming the Brezhnev Doctrine deterred further satellite challenges until Gorbachev abandoned it in 1989; yet outside Soviet borders, Communist China (fearing Moscow might invoke the Brezhnev Doctrine against Beijing), Yugoslavia, Albania, Warsaw Pact member Romania (Ceausescu refused to send troops), and Western European 'Eurocommunist' parties in France and Italy openly condemned Moscow—shattering monolithic world communism while Washington's muted response (bogged down in Vietnam) cleared the path to 1970s Detente.

misconceptions.misconception: Writing that Czechoslovak soldiers and armed militias fought pitched street battles against Soviet tanks in August 1968 just like Budapest in 1956.
misconceptions.correction: Wanting to prevent a 1956-style bloodbath, Dubcek and President Svoboda ordered the Czechoslovak army to stay in barracks; citizens met the 500,000 Warsaw Pact troops with non-violent passive resistance (removing street signs, underground radio, peace marches, and student Jan Palach's January 1969 self-immolation), resulting in under 150 deaths compared with ~2,500 in Hungary.

misconceptions.misconception: Assuming every Warsaw Pact country joined the August 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia.
misconceptions.correction: Troops came from the USSR, Poland, Hungary, Bulgaria, and logistical support from East Germany—crucially, Nicolae Ceausescu's Communist Romania refused to participate and publicly denounced the invasion, winning Western trade favours.

misconceptions.misconception: Claiming the 1968 invasion plunged US–Soviet relations into a long, deep freeze that prevented arms talks.
misconceptions.correction: Although President Lyndon Johnson condemned the invasion and cancelled a planned Moscow summit while the USSR vetoed a UN resolution, America was bogged down with 500,000+ troops in Vietnam and accepted tacit spheres of influence—allowing Nixon and Brezhnev to open Detente talks within months.

source_context.Source A: Overnight on 20–21 August 1968, up to 500,000 Warsaw Pact troops and thousands of tanks rolled into Czechoslovakia in Operation Danube, seizing Prague's Ruzyn airport and deploying beneath Hradcany Castle as unarmed citizens confronted bewildered tank crews, painted swastikas on Soviet hulls, and twisted road signs. By ordering the Czechoslovak army not to open fire, Prague avoided a Budapest-scale slaughter while exposing before world cameras that Moscow lacked any local mandate. Hinge Question: Was Czechoslovak passive resistance in August 1968 a moral success that exposed Soviet aggression, or proof that unarmed protest could not stop tank divisions?
source_context.Source B: Arrested in Prague on 21 August and flown in handcuffs to the Kremlin, Alexander Dubcek was forced to sign the Moscow Protocol on 26 August 1968 reinstating censorship before being replaced in April 1969 by pro-Soviet hardliner Gustav Husak and sent to work as a minor forestry clerk in Bratislava. Avoiding another international outcry like Imre Nagy's 1958 execution, Moscow instead relied on Husak's systematic 'normalisation' purges to expel nearly a third of Party members, professors, and journalists. Hinge Question: Why was gradual bureaucratic 'normalisation' under Gustav Husak a smarter tool of Soviet control in 1969 than executing Dubcek?
source_context.Source C: First set out in Pravda on 26 September 1968 and proclaimed personally by Leonid Brezhnev to the Polish Communist Congress in Warsaw on 12 November 1968, the Brezhnev Doctrine declared that whenever internal or external forces threatened one-party Communist rule in any socialist state, all socialist states had the collective right and duty to intervene militarily. This retroactively justified invading a loyal Warsaw Pact member and locked Eastern European regimes in place until 1989. Hinge Question: How did the Brezhnev Doctrine expand Moscow's red line beyond Khrushchev's 1956 rule on Warsaw Pact membership?
source_context.Source D: Speaking from the White House on 21 August 1968, President Lyndon B. Johnson condemned the Warsaw Pact invasion as an affront to human conscience and cancelled his planned disarmament summit with Brezhnev, yet took zero military or economic countermeasures. With over half a million American troops tied down in the Vietnam War during a turbulent US election year—and recognizing an unspoken rule not to interfere inside each other's Cold War backyards—Washington prioritised avoiding superpower confrontation. Hinge Question: Why did America's involvement in the Vietnam War weaken Washington's moral and diplomatic leverage over Czechoslovakia in August 1968?
source_context.Source E: Within hours of Soviet tanks entering Prague on 21 August 1968, Western Europe's two largest Communist parties—the French PCF and Italian PCI—took the unprecedented step of publicly condemning Moscow in L'Humanite and L'Unita, launching independent 'Eurocommunism' alongside fierce denunciations from Tito's Yugoslavia, Ceausescu's Romania, and Mao's China (which fought border clashes with Soviet troops in 1969). Hinge Question: How did splitting Beijing and Western European Communists away from Moscow inadvertently give the USSR an extra incentive to seek Detente with the USA in the early 1970s?

standoff.title: Was the 1968 Invasion a Strategic Success or Costly Setback for the USSR?

side_a.label: Strategic Success for Moscow
points: Crushed the Prague Spring with minimal combat losses and restored StB control under Gustáv Husák until 1989.
The Brezhnev Doctrine deterred other Warsaw Pact states from abandoning one-party Communist rule.
Tied down in Vietnam, the USA took zero military action and resumed Détente talks within a few years.

side_b.label: Ideological Setback for Moscow
points: Proved Soviet communism in Eastern Europe relied on 500,000 invading troops rather than popular consent.
Pushed Romania (Ceaușescu), Yugoslavia (Tito), and Mao’s China further away from Moscow.
Prompted French and Italian Communist Parties to break from Kremlin authority through Eurocommunism.

narrative_blocks.title: Superpower Pressures Behind Détente
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Superpower Pressures Behind Détente
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 1: Superpower Pressures Behind Détente — Why did the USA and USSR both pursue Détente in the early 1970s?
paragraphs: [1.1] By the early **1970s**, urgent strategic and economic pressures pushed both the **USA** and the **USSR** toward **Détente**—a deliberate relaxation of Cold War tension. Since the **1962 Cuban Missile Crisis**, both superpowers feared **Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD)** and wanted to curb ruinous arms spending. Under President **Richard Nixon** and adviser **Henry Kissinger**, the **USA** was drained by the **Vietnam War**, which cost over **$150 billion**, killed **58,000** Americans, fuelled inflation, and sparked fierce domestic protests.

[1.2] Meanwhile, Soviet leader **Leonid Brezhnev** needed Western grain imports and modern industrial technology to rescue stagnant living standards across the **USSR**. Having finally achieved rough nuclear parity with Washington, Moscow also feared diplomatic isolation after its bitter **Sino-Soviet** border split—especially once Nixon visited Communist **China** in **February 1972**—giving both capitals strong incentives to negotiate.

stage_hook_map.title: Superpower Détente: Summits, SALT 1 & the Helsinki Accords
stage_hook_map.subtitle: 1972–1975 · Tap numbered pins or enlarge for Whiteboard Mode

hotspots.label: 1. Beijing Summit
hotspots.title: Beijing: Nixon–Mao Rapprochement Pressures Moscow
hotspots.details: Exploiting the bitter Sino-Soviet border split, President Richard Nixon and Henry Kissinger visited Communist China in February 1972. Fearing diplomatic encirclement by a US–Chinese alignment while needing Western grain and industrial technology, Leonid Brezhnev became eager to strike arms agreements with Washington.
hotspots.hinge: How did Nixon’s historic visit to Beijing in February 1972 strengthen America’s negotiating hand with the USSR three months later?

hotspots.label: 2. Moscow (SALT 1)
hotspots.title: Moscow Summit: SALT 1, the ABM Treaty & MIRV Loopholes
hotspots.details: At the May 1972 Moscow Summit, Nixon and Brezhnev signed SALT 1: limiting each superpower to two Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) sites, freezing ICBM and SLBM launcher totals for five years, and pledging peaceful coexistence. However, SALT 1 left multiple-warhead MIRVs unrestricted, allowing total warhead stockpiles to keep rising.
hotspots.hinge: Why was SALT 1 hailed as a diplomatic breakthrough in 1972 despite failing to stop the growth of nuclear warheads?

hotspots.label: 3. Washington Summit
hotspots.title: Washington, D.C.: Vietnam Exhaustion, Grain Trade & Summit Thaw
hotspots.details: Drained by a Vietnam War costing over $150 billion and 58,000 American lives, Washington welcomed Détente to curb military spending. Brezhnev visited the USA in June 1973 to sign agreements on trade, agriculture, and preventing nuclear war, securing vital American grain shipments to relieve Soviet food shortages.
hotspots.hinge: Why did domestic economic pressures inside both the USA and the USSR make Détente mutually attractive in the early 1970s?

hotspots.label: 4. Vladivostok Accord
hotspots.title: Vladivostok Summit: Ford & Brezhnev Agree Equal Strategic Caps
hotspots.details: Following Nixon’s Watergate resignation, President Gerald Ford met Brezhnev at Vladivostok in November 1974 to agree equal ceilings of 2,400 strategic nuclear delivery vehicles and limits on MIRV launchers. This framework paved the way for the June 1979 Vienna SALT 2 treaty—and the symbolic July 1975 Apollo–Soyuz space handshake.
hotspots.hinge: Why did negotiations to turn the 1974 Vladivostok framework into the 1979 SALT 2 treaty drag on for nearly five years?

hotspots.label: 5. Helsinki Accords
hotspots.title: Helsinki: 35 Nations Sign the Three Baskets (Borders, Trade & Rights)
hotspots.details: In August 1975, the USA, USSR, Canada, and 32 European states signed the Helsinki Accords: Basket 1 recognised post-1945 European borders (including East Germany), Basket 2 expanded trade and scientific links, and Basket 3 pledged respect for speech, religion, and movement. Dissidents soon formed Helsinki Watch and Charter 77 to hold Moscow to Basket 3.
hotspots.hinge: Why did Basket 1 initially look like a triumph for Brezhnev, yet Basket 3 prove a long-term political trap for Communist regimes?

narrative_blocks.title: The Moscow Summit & SALT 1 Agreements
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: The Moscow Summit & SALT 1 Agreements
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 2: The Moscow Summit & SALT 1 Agreements — What did Nixon and Brezhnev agree and leave out in SALT 1 in 1972?
narrative_blocks.image_alt: US President Richard Nixon and Soviet General Secretary Leonid Brezhnev seated at a white table in St Vladimir Hall in the Kremlin signing the SALT 1 agreements on 26 May 1972
narrative_blocks.caption: US President Richard Nixon and Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev signing the SALT 1 agreements in the Grand Kremlin Palace, Moscow, on 26 May 1972.
paragraphs: [2.1] On **26 May 1972**, **Nixon** and **Brezhnev** signed **SALT 1** (the **Strategic Arms Limitation Talks**) at the **Moscow Summit**—the first formal superpower nuclear arms accord. First, the **Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty** restricted each nation to just **two ABM sites** (one protecting its capital and one guarding an **ICBM** field), preserving deterrence by preventing either side from blocking nuclear retaliation. Second, a five-year **Interim Agreement** froze strategic **ICBMs** and submarine-launched **SLBMs** at existing totals.

[2.2] Third, the **Basic Principles Agreement** committed both superpowers to avoid military confrontation and pursue peaceful coexistence. However, **SALT 1** had serious loopholes: it froze launcher numbers rather than cutting arsenals and left **MIRVs**—single missiles carrying multiple independently targeted warheads—completely unrestricted, allowing warhead stockpiles to multiply throughout the **1970s**.

narrative_blocks.title: Symbolic Thaw & Space Cooperation
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Symbolic Thaw & Space Cooperation
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 3: Symbolic Thaw & Space Cooperation — In what ways did superpower cooperation deepen between 1973 and July 1975?
paragraphs: [3.1] Following the Moscow accords, summit diplomacy and commercial trade expanded rapidly between **1973** and **July 1975**. **Leonid Brezhnev** visited Washington in **June 1973** to sign agreements on trade, agriculture, and preventing nuclear war, while **Richard Nixon** returned to Moscow in **June 1974** shortly before resigning over the **Watergate** scandal and handing the presidency to **Gerald Ford**. Millions of tonnes of American grain arrived in Soviet ports, relieving acute food shortages.

[3.2] Détente reached its symbolic peak on **17 July 1975** during the joint **Apollo–Soyuz** mission, when an American **Apollo** spacecraft docked in Earth orbit with a Soviet **Soyuz** capsule. Watched live on television, US commander **Thomas Stafford** shook hands through the open docking hatch with cosmonaut **Alexei Leonov**, turning space rivalry into public partnership—even while covert **Middle East** and Third World competition persisted.

narrative_blocks.title: The Three Baskets of the Helsinki Accords
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: The Three Baskets of the Helsinki Accords
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 4: The Three Baskets of the Helsinki Accords — How did the August 1975 Helsinki Accords reward and embarrass the USSR?
narrative_blocks.image_alt: US President Gerald Ford and Secretary of State Henry Kissinger conferring across a polished conference table with Soviet General Secretary Leonid Brezhnev and Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko at the US Embassy during the Helsinki Summit, August 1975
narrative_blocks.caption: President Gerald Ford and Henry Kissinger (right) conferring with Leonid Brezhnev and Andrei Gromyko (left) during the Helsinki Summit in Finland, August 1975.
paragraphs: [4.1] In **August 1975**, **35 nations**—including US President **Gerald Ford**, **Leonid Brezhnev** for the **USSR**, Canada, and 32 European states—gathered in Finland and signed the **Helsinki Accords** across three **"Baskets"**. **Basket 1 (European Borders)** declared post-1945 frontiers inviolable and formally recognised **East Germany**, rewarding Moscow with Western acceptance of its Eastern European sphere. **Basket 2 (International Cooperation)** expanded East–West trade, industrial exchanges, and joint scientific research.

[4.2] Crucially, **Basket 3 (Human Rights)** committed every signatory state to respect freedom of speech, religion, press information, and movement across borders. Although Brezhnev assumed Basket 3 was harmless diplomatic window-dressing, brave dissidents formed **Helsinki Watch** monitoring groups inside the **USSR** and **Charter 77** in Czechoslovakia, repeatedly embarrassing Moscow before Western journalists over political arrests.

narrative_blocks.title: Carter, SALT 2 & Strained Détente
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Carter, SALT 2 & Strained Détente
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 5: Carter, SALT 2 & Strained Détente — What caused Détente and SALT 2 to falter under Jimmy Carter by 1979?
paragraphs: [5.1] Inaugurated in **January 1977**, US President **Jimmy Carter** placed **human rights** at the centre of American diplomacy, writing to Soviet dissident **Andrei Sakharov** and linking trade to Moscow’s treatment of dissidents. **Leonid Brezhnev** resented this as meddling in Soviet internal affairs, while US Senate hawks condemned Soviet-backed Communist interventions in **Angola** and **Ethiopia** alongside new Soviet **SS-20** missiles aimed at Western Europe.

[5.2] Despite mounting suspicion, **Jimmy Carter** and Brezhnev signed **SALT 2** in **Vienna** on **18 June 1979**, setting an equal cap of **2,400** strategic nuclear delivery vehicles (falling to **2,250**) and limiting **MIRV** launchers. Yet fierce US Senate criticism stalled ratification, and after Soviet troops invaded **Afghanistan** in **December 1979**, Carter withdrew **SALT 2** in **January 1980**—ending **Détente**.

stages.title: Superpower Pressures Behind Détente
stages.trigger: Vietnam War costs ($150bn+, 58,000 US dead), Soviet economic stagnation, MAD fears, and Nixon’s February 1972 visit to China push Washington and Moscow to negotiate.
stages.because: Neither superpower could afford unlimited nuclear spending while facing domestic inflation or agricultural shortages and rival threats from Beijing.
stages.therefore: Both capitals embraced Détente—managing Cold War competition through summit diplomacy and trade.
stages.connective: Those negotiations produced a landmark nuclear arms summit in Moscow in May 1972...
stages.exam_link: Q2 Narrative: Opening causes explaining why both superpowers actively needed Détente by 1970–72.
stages.question: Why did the USA and USSR both pursue Détente in the early 1970s?

stages.title: The Moscow Summit & SALT 1 Agreements
stages.trigger: On 26 May 1972 at the Moscow Summit, Nixon and Brezhnev sign the ABM Treaty (two sites each), the five-year Interim Agreement freezing ICBMs/SLBMs, and Basic Principles.
stages.because: Limiting missile shields preserved MAD stability and slowed costly new launcher construction for both economies.
stages.therefore: Formal arms control began, though leaving multi-warhead MIRVs uncapped meant nuclear warhead totals kept rising.
stages.connective: Building on Moscow’s diplomatic breakthrough, superpower trade and space cooperation expanded...
stages.exam_link: Q3 Importance: First strategic arms limit stabilising deterrence while exposing the MIRV loophole.
stages.question: What did Nixon and Brezhnev agree and leave out in SALT 1 in 1972?

stages.title: Symbolic Thaw & Space Cooperation
stages.trigger: Follow-up summits (1973–74), massive US grain exports to the USSR, and the 17 July 1975 Apollo–Soyuz orbital docking showcase superpower partnership.
stages.because: Both governments wanted visible proof that peaceful coexistence lowered nuclear danger and delivered economic benefits.
stages.therefore: Public optimism peaked in summer 1975, clearing the path for a 35-nation European security conference.
stages.connective: Two weeks after the orbital handshake, 35 leaders gathered in Finland to sign the broadest accord of the decade...
stages.exam_link: Q2 Narrative: Bridging high-water mark linking SALT 1 to the August 1975 Helsinki summit.
stages.question: In what ways did superpower cooperation deepen between 1973 and July 1975?

stages.title: The Three Baskets of the Helsinki Accords
stages.trigger: In August 1975, 35 states sign the Helsinki Accords covering Basket 1 (post-war European borders/East Germany), Basket 2 (trade/science), and Basket 3 (human rights).
stages.because: Brezhnev craved Western recognition of Eastern Europe’s 1945 borders, assuming Basket 3 human-rights clauses would prove toothless.
stages.therefore: Dissidents formed Helsinki Watch and Charter 77, turning Moscow’s own signature into a moral weapon against Communist repression.
stages.connective: Soviet crackdowns on those Helsinki dissidents soon collided with a new US president...
stages.exam_link: Q1 Consequence / Q3 Importance: Recognised Eastern Bloc borders while destabilising Soviet legitimacy via Basket 3.
stages.question: How did the August 1975 Helsinki Accords reward and embarrass the USSR?

stages.title: Carter, SALT 2 & Strained Détente
stages.trigger: After human-rights clashes and African proxy disputes, Carter and Brezhnev sign SALT 2 in Vienna (18 June 1979), capping launchers at 2,400 and limiting MIRVs.
stages.because: Both leaders still hoped to rescue strategic arms control despite growing anger from US Senate hawks over Soviet SS-20s and Angola/Ethiopia.
stages.therefore: Senate delays stalled SALT 2 until the December 1979 Soviet invasion of Afghanistan led Carter to withdraw ratification completely.
stages.connective: When Red Army paratroopers landed in Kabul at Christmas 1979, Détente collapsed overnight.
stages.exam_link: Q2 Narrative: Closing unravelling showing why Détente was already strained before Kabul fell.
stages.question: What caused Détente and SALT 2 to falter under Jimmy Carter by 1979?

sources.title: Source B: Extract from the Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty & Interim Agreement (SALT 1, 26 May 1972)
sources.text:
ABM Treaty, Article III: Each Party undertakes not to deploy ABM systems or their components except that: (a) within one ABM system deployment area having a radius of one hundred and fifty kilometres and centred on the Party’s national capital, a Party may deploy no more than one hundred ABM launchers... and (b) within one ABM system deployment area... containing ICBM silo launchers, a Party may deploy no more than one hundred ABM launchers.
Interim Agreement, Article I: The Parties undertake not to start construction of additional fixed land-based intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) launchers after July 1, 1972.
sources.content:
ABM Treaty, Article III: Each Party undertakes not to deploy ABM systems or their components except that: (a) within one ABM system deployment area having a radius of one hundred and fifty kilometres and centred on the Party’s national capital, a Party may deploy no more than one hundred ABM launchers... and (b) within one ABM system deployment area... containing ICBM silo launchers, a Party may deploy no more than one hundred ABM launchers.
Interim Agreement, Article I: The Parties undertake not to start construction of additional fixed land-based intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) launchers after July 1, 1972.
sources.provenance: Bilateral Strategic Arms Limitation Talks (SALT 1) treaties signed by Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev in Moscow, 26 May 1972 (US Department of State Treaty Series).
sources.citation: United States Treaties and Other International Agreements (23 UST 3435).
sources.model_answer: If either superpower had built a nationwide anti-missile shield, it might have felt safe launching a nuclear first strike without fearing retaliation; capping ABM sites at two guaranteed mutual vulnerability under MAD while avoiding a ruinous defensive arms race.
sources.context: Signed at the Moscow Summit on 26 May 1972 after two and a half years of complex technical negotiations.
sources.source_context: SALT 1 paired a permanent limit of two ABM defensive sites each with a five-year freeze on ICBM and SLBM missile launchers, yet said nothing about fitting multiple MIRV warheads onto each missile.

teacher_notes.source_context: SALT 1 paired a permanent limit of two ABM defensive sites each with a five-year freeze on ICBM and SLBM missile launchers, yet said nothing about fitting multiple MIRV warheads onto each missile. **Hinge Question:** Which dangerous multi-warhead weapon technology did Article I of the Interim Agreement leave completely unrestricted?
teacher_notes.hinge_question: Which dangerous multi-warhead weapon technology did Article I of the Interim Agreement leave completely unrestricted?

sources.question: Why did restricting defensive anti-missile shields to just two sites in Source B actually make nuclear war less likely under MAD?

sources.title: Source C: The Orbital Handshake During the Apollo–Soyuz Test Project (17 July 1975)
sources.image_alt: American Apollo commander Thomas Stafford reaching through the circular docking hatch in Earth orbit to shake hands with Soviet Soyuz commander Alexei Leonov on 17 July 1975
sources.caption: US astronaut Thomas P. Stafford (right, in tan flight suit) shaking hands through the orbital docking hatch with Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov during the joint Apollo–Soyuz mission, 17 July 1975.
sources.provenance: Official NASA mission photograph AST-09-564, Earth orbit, 17 July 1975 (NASA / Public Domain).
sources.citation: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), Johnson Space Center Archive.
sources.model_answer: Docking rival space capsules in orbit dramatised for global television audiences that Cold War Space Race competitors could cooperate peacefully, yet it remained largely symbolic PR that did not halt nuclear MIRV deployment or Third World proxy rivalries.
sources.context: Broadcast live around the world on 17 July 1975, two weeks before the Helsinki Summit opened in Finland.
sources.source_context: Agreed at the 1972 Moscow Summit and flown in July 1975, the Apollo–Soyuz Test Project required American and Soviet engineers to share technical specs and learn each other’s languages—marking Détente’s warmer public peak.

teacher_notes.source_context: Agreed at the 1972 Moscow Summit and flown in July 1975, the Apollo–Soyuz Test Project required American and Soviet engineers to share technical specs and learn each other’s languages—marking Détente’s warmer public peak. **Hinge Question:** Does symbolic scientific cooperation in space prove that ideological rivalry on Earth had ended by 1975?

sources.title: Source D: Extract from Principle VII & Basket III of the Helsinki Final Act (1 August 1975)
sources.text: The participating States will respect human rights and fundamental freedoms, including the freedom of thought, conscience, religion or belief, for all without distinction as to race, sex, language or religion. They will promote and encourage the effective exercise of civil, political, economic, social, cultural and other rights and freedoms... The participating States make it their aim to facilitate freer movement and contacts, individually and collectively, whether privately or officially, among persons, institutions and organisations of the participating States, and to contribute to the solution of the humanitarian problems that arise in that connection.

They will promote and encourage the effective exercise of civil, political, economic, social, cultural and other rights and freedoms... The participating States make it their aim to facilitate freer movement and contacts, individually and collectively, whether privately or officially, among persons, institutions and organisations of the participating States, and to contribute to the solution of the humanitarian problems that arise in that connection.
sources.provenance: Final Act of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), signed by 35 heads of state in Helsinki, Finland, 1 August 1975.
sources.citation: OSCE / CSCE Helsinki Final Act Archive (1 August 1975).
sources.model_answer: Brezhnev signed Basket III as the price for securing Western recognition of Eastern Europe’s post-1945 borders in Basket I, assuming human-rights language was non-binding; instead, Soviet and Eastern Bloc dissidents published the text and formed Helsinki Watch and Charter 77 to expose Communist repression.
sources.context: Published in full in Soviet state newspapers in August 1975 alongside Basket I’s border guarantees.
sources.source_context: Because Moscow wanted to boast about Basket I’s recognition of post-war borders and East Germany, Soviet newspapers printed the entire Helsinki Final Act—inadvertently handing millions of Soviet citizens the exact human-rights promises of Basket III.

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: Driven by Vietnam War costs, Soviet economic stagnation, and shared fear of [Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD)], Washington and Moscow embraced [Détente] in the early 1970s. Nixon and Brezhnev signed [SALT 1] in May 1972, though multi-warhead [MIRV] missiles remained unrestricted. In August 1975, 35 nations signed the [Helsinki Accords], recognising European borders while inspiring Basket 3 human-rights dissidents, before Senate opposition and Afghanistan doomed [SALT 2] in 1979–80.

items.question: On what night did Warsaw Pact forces launch their full-scale military invasion of Czechoslovakia?
items.explanation: Late on 20–21 August 1968, Warsaw Pact troops and tanks crossed into Czechoslovakia from multiple directions.

items.question: How did ordinary Czechoslovaks respond to Dubček’s call for peaceful passive resistance in August 1968?
items.answer: Removing street signs and running secret radio broadcasts
items.explanation: Citizens removed or repainted road signs to confuse tank columns, argued with soldiers in Russian, and broadcast from hidden studios.

items.question: What coerced agreement was an arrested Alexander Dubček forced to sign in the Kremlin on 26 August 1968?
items.explanation: Flown to Moscow under arrest, Dubček signed the Moscow Protocol restoring censorship and stationing Soviet garrisons in Czechoslovakia.

items.question: In which Soviet newspaper was the justification known as the Brezhnev Doctrine first published in September 1968?
items.explanation: Pravda published the doctrine on 26 September 1968 before Brezhnev proclaimed it formally in Warsaw in November 1968.

items.question: How did US President Lyndon B. Johnson respond to the August 1968 Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia?
items.answer: Condemned it verbally and cancelled a Moscow summit
items.explanation: Johnson protested verbally and cancelled his planned Moscow summit, yet took zero military action inside the Soviet sphere.

items.question: Roughly how many Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia in August 1968?
items.explanation: Roughly half a million troops backed by thousands of tanks rapidly overwhelmed Czechoslovakia overnight.

items.question: Approximately how many Czechoslovaks were killed during the August 1968 invasion, compared with thousands in Hungary in 1956?
items.explanation: Because Dubček ordered non-violent passive resistance rather than armed combat, fewer than 100 people died during the August invasion.

items.question: Which hardline pro-Soviet leader replaced Alexander Dubček in April 1969?
items.explanation: Moscow installed Gustáv Husák in April 1969 to dismantle all remaining Prague Spring reforms over the next twenty years.

items.question: What core rule did the 1968 Brezhnev Doctrine impose on every Warsaw Pact satellite state?
items.answer: Maintain one-party Communist rule and Warsaw Pact membership
items.explanation: The Brezhnev Doctrine declared Warsaw Pact states had a duty to intervene militarily whenever one-party socialism was threatened.

items.question: Which major Asian conflict tying down 500,000 US soldiers deterred Washington from confronting Moscow in 1968?
items.explanation: With 500,000 US troops bogged down in Vietnam and a 1968 presidential election underway, Washington avoided a European crisis.

quiz.question: Roughly how much had the Vietnam War cost the United States financially by the early 1970s?
quiz.q: Roughly how much had the Vietnam War cost the United States financially by the early 1970s?
quiz.explanation: Vietnam drained over $150 billion from the US budget alongside 58,000 American deaths, fuelling inflation and social protest.

quiz.question: Which Communist power did President Richard Nixon visit in February 1972, alarming Moscow?
quiz.q: Which Communist power did President Richard Nixon visit in February 1972, alarming Moscow?
quiz.explanation: Following the Sino-Soviet border split, Nixon’s February 1972 visit to Mao’s China made Brezhnev eager to avoid facing a US–Chinese alignment.

quiz.question: What urgent economic imports did Leonid Brezhnev need from the West in the early 1970s?
quiz.q: What urgent economic imports did Leonid Brezhnev need from the West in the early 1970s?
options: Grain imports and modern industrial technology
quiz.answer: Grain imports and modern industrial technology
quiz.a: Grain imports and modern industrial technology
quiz.explanation: Poor harvests and lagging Soviet computer and consumer industries made American grain and Western technology vital.

quiz.question: Which nuclear deterrence concept convinced both superpowers after 1962 that nuclear war was unwinnable?
quiz.q: Which nuclear deterrence concept convinced both superpowers after 1962 that nuclear war was unwinnable?
quiz.explanation: With rough nuclear parity, any nuclear first strike guaranteed devastating retaliation and mutual annihilation under MAD.

quiz.question: Where and when did Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev sign the SALT 1 agreements?
quiz.q: Where and when did Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev sign the SALT 1 agreements?
quiz.explanation: Nixon and Brezhnev signed SALT 1 in the Grand Kremlin Palace in Moscow on 26 May 1972.

quiz.question: How many Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) defensive sites was each superpower permitted under the 1972 ABM Treaty?
quiz.q: How many Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) defensive sites was each superpower permitted under the 1972 ABM Treaty?
quiz.explanation: Each side could defend only its national capital and one ICBM field, ensuring nuclear deterrence remained stable.

quiz.question: How long did SALT 1’s Interim Agreement freeze strategic ICBM and SLBM missile launchers?
quiz.q: How long did SALT 1’s Interim Agreement freeze strategic ICBM and SLBM missile launchers?
quiz.explanation: The five-year Interim Agreement froze strategic ICBM and submarine-launched SLBM totals while SALT 2 was negotiated.

quiz.question: Which multi-warhead missile technology was left completely unrestricted by SALT 1 in 1972?
quiz.q: Which multi-warhead missile technology was left completely unrestricted by SALT 1 in 1972?
quiz.explanation: Multiple Independently Targetable Re-entry Vehicles (MIRVs) allowed a single missile to carry multiple warheads, multiplying total warheads despite the launcher freeze.

quiz.question: Who succeeded Richard Nixon as US President in August 1974 after the Watergate scandal?
quiz.q: Who succeeded Richard Nixon as US President in August 1974 after the Watergate scandal?
quiz.explanation: Vice-President Gerald Ford assumed the presidency in August 1974 and continued Détente summits with Brezhnev.

quiz.question: Which joint US–Soviet space mission docked in Earth orbit on 17 July 1975?
quiz.q: Which joint US–Soviet space mission docked in Earth orbit on 17 July 1975?
quiz.explanation: An American Apollo capsule docked with a Soviet Soyuz spacecraft on 17 July 1975 in a televised symbol of Détente.

quiz.question: Which two commanders shook hands through the open orbital hatch during the July 1975 docking?
quiz.q: Which two commanders shook hands through the open orbital hatch during the July 1975 docking?
quiz.explanation: US commander Thomas Stafford and Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov shook hands in orbit live on global television.

quiz.question: When did Leonid Brezhnev travel to Washington to sign accords on trade and preventing nuclear war?
quiz.q: When did Leonid Brezhnev travel to Washington to sign accords on trade and preventing nuclear war?
quiz.explanation: Brezhnev’s June 1973 Washington summit expanded agricultural and commercial trade alongside nuclear war prevention pledges.

quiz.question: How many nations signed the Helsinki Accords in Finland in August 1975?
quiz.q: How many nations signed the Helsinki Accords in Finland in August 1975?
quiz.explanation: Thirty-five states—the USA, Canada, the USSR, and 32 European countries—signed the Helsinki Final Act on 1 August 1975.

quiz.question: What did Basket 1 of the August 1975 Helsinki Accords establish regarding Europe?
quiz.q: What did Basket 1 of the August 1975 Helsinki Accords establish regarding Europe?
options: European borders were inviolable, recognising East Germany
NATO and the Warsaw Pact were abolished
The Berlin Wall was immediately dismantled
Soviet troops withdrew from Poland and Hungary
quiz.answer: European borders were inviolable, recognising East Germany
quiz.a: European borders were inviolable, recognising East Germany
quiz.explanation: Basket 1 formally accepted Europe’s post-1945 frontiers and recognised Communist East Germany, fulfilling a long-held Soviet diplomatic goal.

quiz.question: What area did Basket 2 of the Helsinki Accords promote between East and West?
quiz.q: What area did Basket 2 of the Helsinki Accords promote between East and West?
options: Trade, industrial links, and scientific cooperation
quiz.answer: Trade, industrial links, and scientific cooperation
quiz.a: Trade, industrial links, and scientific cooperation
quiz.explanation: Basket 2 encouraged economic trade, technology sharing, and joint scientific and environmental research.

quiz.question: Why did Basket 3 of the Helsinki Accords unexpectedly embarrass the Soviet government?
quiz.q: Why did Basket 3 of the Helsinki Accords unexpectedly embarrass the Soviet government?
options: Dissidents used its human-rights pledges to expose repression
It forced Moscow to pay WWII reparations
It banned Soviet grain purchases from America
It handed East Berlin to West Germany
quiz.answer: Dissidents used its human-rights pledges to expose repression
quiz.a: Dissidents used its human-rights pledges to expose repression
quiz.explanation: Helsinki Watch groups in the USSR and Charter 77 in Czechoslovakia held Moscow publicly accountable to Basket 3’s human-rights promises.

quiz.question: Which issue did President Jimmy Carter place at the heart of US foreign policy from January 1977?
quiz.q: Which issue did President Jimmy Carter place at the heart of US foreign policy from January 1977?
quiz.explanation: Carter wrote to dissident Andrei Sakharov and linked Soviet trade to human rights, angering Brezhnev.

quiz.question: In which two African countries did Soviet-backed Communist interventions anger US Senators in the late 1970s?
quiz.q: In which two African countries did Soviet-backed Communist interventions anger US Senators in the late 1970s?
quiz.explanation: Soviet arms and Cuban troops in Angola and Ethiopia convinced US hawks that Moscow was exploiting Détente.

quiz.question: Where and when did Jimmy Carter and Leonid Brezhnev sign the SALT 2 treaty?
quiz.q: Where and when did Jimmy Carter and Leonid Brezhnev sign the SALT 2 treaty?
quiz.explanation: Carter and Brezhnev signed SALT 2 at the Hofburg Palace in Vienna on 18 June 1979, capping launchers at 2,400.

quiz.question: Why did President Carter withdraw SALT 2 from the US Senate in January 1980?
quiz.q: Why did President Carter withdraw SALT 2 from the US Senate in January 1980?
options: Soviet troops invaded Afghanistan in December 1979
Brezhnev tested an atmospheric bomb over Cuba
East Germany blockaded West Berlin again
China declared war on the USSR
quiz.answer: Soviet troops invaded Afghanistan in December 1979
quiz.a: Soviet troops invaded Afghanistan in December 1979
quiz.explanation: Following the December 1979 Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, Carter withdrew SALT 2 from Senate ratification, ending Détente.

questions.question: 2. Write a narrative account analysing the key events of détente in the 1970s. [8 marks]
questions.prompt: Write 3 chronological paragraphs (Beginning: pressures for détente & May 1972 SALT 1 -> Middle: July 1975 Apollo–Soyuz & August 1975 Helsinki Accords [own knowledge] -> Outcome: Carter’s human-rights clash, June 1979 SALT 2 & January 1980 withdrawal) linked by causal connectives.
questions.examiner_tip: Pearson Edexcel caps answers at 4/8 if you only describe SALT 1 and SALT 2. Bridge the two treaties with accurate own knowledge of the July 1975 Apollo–Soyuz mission, the August 1975 Helsinki Accords, and December 1979 Afghanistan.
questions.model:
Drained by the $150 billion Vietnam War while Leonid Brezhnev needed Western grain and feared isolation after Richard Nixon visited China in February 1972, both superpowers turned toward détente. This directly produced the May 1972 Moscow Summit, where Nixon and Brezhnev signed SALT 1—restricting each nation to two ABM sites and freezing ICBM and SLBM launchers for five years, though leaving multi-warhead MIRVs uncapped.

Building on SALT 1, expanding American grain exports and follow-up summits culminated in the televised July 1975 Apollo–Soyuz orbital handshake and the August 1975 Helsinki Accords signed by Gerald Ford, Brezhnev, and 33 other leaders. While Basket 1 recognised post-war borders and East Germany, Basket 3’s human-rights pledges unexpectedly inspired Helsinki Watch and Charter 77 dissidents to expose Soviet repression.

Consequently, superpower trust frayed from 1977 when President Jimmy Carter championed dissidents like Andrei Sakharov while US Senate hawks condemned Soviet SS-20 missiles and interventions in Angola and Ethiopia. Although Carter and Brezhnev signed SALT 2 in Vienna in June 1979 to cap strategic launchers at 2,400 and limit MIRVs, Senate opposition stalled ratification until the December 1979 Soviet invasion of Afghanistan led Carter to withdraw SALT 2 in January 1980, ending détente.

tier_2m.title: 2/8 Simple Narrative
tier_2m.text: In the 1970s the USA and USSR wanted better relations to save money and avoid nuclear war. Nixon and Brezhnev signed SALT 1 in 1972 to limit missiles, cooperated in space and at Helsinki in 1975, and signed SALT 2 in 1979 before fighting in Afghanistan ended détente.
tier_2m.verdict: AO2 Level 1 (1 mark) • AO1 Level 1 (1 mark). Basic chronological outline of the decade, but lacks specific treaty terms and analytical links explaining why détente rose and unravelled.

tier_4m.title: 4/8 Sequenced Account
tier_4m.text:
On 26 May 1972, President Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev met in Moscow and signed SALT 1. This limited each superpower to two Anti-Ballistic Missile sites and froze ICBM and SLBM missile launchers for five years, though MIRVs were not banned.

Later in the decade, President Jimmy Carter and Brezhnev met in Vienna in June 1979 and signed SALT 2, setting an equal limit of 2,400 strategic nuclear delivery vehicles and restricting MIRV launchers, though the US Senate never ratified it.
tier_4m.verdict: AO2 Level 2 (2 marks) • AO1 Level 2 (2 marks). Chronological description relying on the two stimulus points without explicit causal links or bridging own knowledge (Apollo–Soyuz, Helsinki Accords, Afghanistan), legally capping the response at 4/8 under the Pearson Edexcel mark scheme.

tier_8m.title: 8/8 Grade 9 Exam ★
tier_8m.text:
Drained by the $150 billion Vietnam War while Leonid Brezhnev needed Western grain and feared isolation after Richard Nixon visited China in February 1972, both superpowers turned toward détente. This directly produced the May 1972 Moscow Summit, where Nixon and Brezhnev signed SALT 1—restricting each nation to two ABM sites and freezing ICBM and SLBM launchers for five years, though leaving multi-warhead MIRVs uncapped.

Building on SALT 1, expanding American grain exports and follow-up summits culminated in the televised July 1975 Apollo–Soyuz orbital handshake and the August 1975 Helsinki Accords signed by Gerald Ford, Brezhnev, and 33 other leaders. While Basket 1 recognised post-war borders and East Germany, Basket 3’s human-rights pledges unexpectedly inspired Helsinki Watch and Charter 77 dissidents to expose Soviet repression.

Consequently, superpower trust frayed from 1977 when President Jimmy Carter championed dissidents like Andrei Sakharov while US Senate hawks condemned Soviet SS-20 missiles and interventions in Angola and Ethiopia. Although Carter and Brezhnev signed SALT 2 in Vienna in June 1979 to cap strategic launchers at 2,400 and limit MIRVs, Senate opposition stalled ratification until the December 1979 Soviet invasion of Afghanistan led Carter to withdraw SALT 2 in January 1980, ending détente.
tier_8m.verdict: AO1 Level 3 (4 marks) • AO2 Level 3 (4 marks). Organised beginning–developments–outcome analytical narrative linked by explicit causal connectives and deploying accurate own knowledge beyond the two stimulus bullets.

questions.question: 3. Explain the importance of SALT 1 (1972) for attempts to reduce superpower tensions in the 1970s. [8 marks]
questions.prompt: Write two distinct PEEL paragraphs explaining WHY SALT 1 mattered for attempts to reduce tensions: (1) Stabilising nuclear deterrence and unlocking 1973–75 cooperation, and (2) Leaving MIRVs uncapped so rival arms competition continued.
questions.examiner_tip: Anchor both paragraphs directly to "attempts to reduce superpower tensions in the 1970s"—explain both the diplomatic breakthrough SALT 1 unlocked and the technical limits that forced tense SALT 2 talks.
questions.model:
First, SALT 1 in May 1972 was crucially important for attempts to reduce superpower tensions because it established the first binding nuclear arms limits and unlocked wider East–West diplomacy. By restricting each superpower to just two Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) sites and freezing strategic ICBM and SLBM launchers for five years, Nixon and Brezhnev stabilised Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) and pledged peaceful coexistence under the Basic Principles Agreement. This breakthrough proved Washington and Moscow could negotiate constructively, paving the way for 1973–74 trade summits, major US grain exports, the July 1975 Apollo–Soyuz mission, and the August 1975 Helsinki Accords.

Second, SALT 1 was also important because its major technical loopholes limited how deeply tensions fell, forcing difficult follow-up negotiations throughout the 1970s. Because the five-year Interim Agreement froze missile launchers rather than warheads and left Multiple Independently Targeted Re-entry Vehicles (MIRVs) completely unrestricted, nuclear warhead stockpiles continued multiplying on both sides. Consequently, underlying strategic distrust persisted and compelled Carter and Brezhnev to spend years negotiating SALT 2 (1979).

tier_2m.title: 2/8 Simple Statement
tier_2m.text: SALT 1 in 1972 was very important for reducing superpower tensions because it was the first time the USA and USSR agreed to limit their nuclear missiles, which showed they could work together peacefully during the 1970s.
tier_2m.verdict: AO1 Level 1 (1 mark) • AO2 Level 1 (1 mark). Valid general point about nuclear arms control, but lacks specific factual evidence (ABM Treaty, five-year launcher freeze, MIRVs, follow-up summits).

tier_4m.title: 4/8 Descriptive
tier_4m.text:
At the Moscow Summit in May 1972, President Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev signed SALT 1. The ABM Treaty restricted each country to two Anti-Ballistic Missile sites and the Interim Agreement froze ICBM and SLBM missile launchers for five years.

However, SALT 1 only froze launcher numbers for five years and did not ban MIRV missiles carrying multiple warheads, so both superpowers carried on building thousands more nuclear warheads before signing SALT 2 in 1979.
tier_4m.verdict: AO1 Level 2 (2 marks) • AO2 Level 2 (2 marks). Accurate factual detail across two paragraphs, but describes events rather than explicitly explaining why SALT 1 mattered specifically for attempts to reduce superpower tensions in the 1970s.

tier_8m.title: 8/8 Grade 9 Exam ★
tier_8m.text:
First, SALT 1 in May 1972 was crucially important for attempts to reduce superpower tensions because it established the first binding nuclear arms limits and unlocked wider East–West diplomacy. By restricting each superpower to just two Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) sites and freezing strategic ICBM and SLBM launchers for five years, Nixon and Brezhnev stabilised Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) and pledged peaceful coexistence under the Basic Principles Agreement. This breakthrough proved Washington and Moscow could negotiate constructively, paving the way for 1973–74 trade summits, major US grain exports, the July 1975 Apollo–Soyuz mission, and the August 1975 Helsinki Accords.

Second, SALT 1 was also important because its major technical loopholes limited how deeply tensions fell, forcing difficult follow-up negotiations throughout the 1970s. Because the five-year Interim Agreement froze missile launchers rather than warheads and left Multiple Independently Targeted Re-entry Vehicles (MIRVs) completely unrestricted, nuclear warhead stockpiles continued multiplying on both sides. Consequently, underlying strategic distrust persisted and compelled Carter and Brezhnev to spend years negotiating SALT 2 (1979).
tier_8m.verdict: AO1 Level 3 (4 marks) • AO2 Level 3 (4 marks). Two distinct, factually evidenced analytical paragraphs directly explaining importance for the second half of the question stem.

teacher_notes.primer: This KT 3.1 enquiry examines both why Détente emerged around 1970–72 and why it remained a managed rivalry rather than genuine friendship. Stress the symmetry of pragmatic self-interest (Vietnam/inflation/China for Nixon & Kissinger; economic stagnation/grain/parity/Sino-Soviet split for Brezhnev), the MIRV loophole inside SALT 1, and the delicious historical irony of Helsinki Basket 3.

objectives.objective: Explain the converging American and Soviet pressures that produced Détente by 1972.
objectives.primer: Pair Vietnam’s $150bn+ cost and 58,000 US deaths with Soviet agricultural/tech stagnation, rough nuclear parity (MAD), and Nixon’s February 1972 triangular diplomacy in Beijing.
objectives.question: Why did rough nuclear parity make Brezhnev far more willing to sign an arms freeze in 1972 than Khrushchev had been in 1960?

objectives.objective: Distinguish the concrete terms and hidden loopholes of SALT 1 (1972) and the Helsinki Accords (1975).
objectives.primer: Make sure students separate ABM Treaty (2 defensive sites) from Interim Agreement (5-year ICBM/SLBM freeze, zero MIRV cap) and know all three Helsinki Baskets cleanly.
objectives.question: Why did capping defensive anti-missile shields in the ABM Treaty paradoxically make both superpowers feel safer?

objectives.objective: Evaluate why Détente and SALT 2 were already faltering under Jimmy Carter before December 1979.
objectives.primer: Show that Afghanistan delivered the fatal blow, but Carter’s human-rights push, Soviet SS-20s, and Angola/Ethiopia had already turned the US Senate against SALT 2.
objectives.question: Did Détente fail because Jimmy Carter emphasised human rights, or because neither superpower ever abandoned Cold War competition in the Third World?

teacher_notes.curriculum_link: Key Topic 3.1: Attempts to reduce tension (Detente), 1970–79 — economic and strategic motives for Detente, SALT 1 (May 1972), Nixon-Brezhnev summits, Apollo-Soyuz (July 1975), the three Baskets of the Helsinki Accords (Aug 1975), Jimmy Carter's human rights diplomacy, and SALT 2 (June 1979) (Edexcel Paper 2 Demand: 8m Consequences & 16m Importance).
teacher_notes.hinge_question: Did 1970s Detente genuinely end Cold War competition, or merely set safer nuclear ground rules while both superpowers competed elsewhere—and why did Helsinki Basket 3 backfire on Brezhnev?
teacher_notes.hinge_guidance: Strong GCSE answers evaluate Detente's real achievements AND built-in limits: SALT 1 (1972) capped ABMs and froze ICBM/SLBM launchers while Helsinki Basket 1 recognised post-war European borders, reducing immediate nuclear danger and saving money after Vietnam and Soviet economic stagnation; yet SALT 1 left multi-warhead MIRVs uncapped, proxy rivalries persisted in the Middle East (1973) and Africa, and Helsinki Basket 3's human-rights pledges unexpectedly empowered Charter 77 and Moscow Helsinki Group dissidents inside the Soviet bloc.

misconceptions.misconception: Writing that Detente meant the Cold War ended in the 1970s or that SALT 1 destroyed thousands of nuclear weapons.
misconceptions.correction: Detente meant a relaxation of tension, NOT disarmament or friendship: SALT 1 (1972) and SALT 2 (1979) set ceilings on missile launchers rather than scrapping warheads (which only began under Gorbachev's 1987 INF Treaty), and MIRV technology actually allowed warhead counts to keep rising.

misconceptions.misconception: Mixing up the three Baskets of the August 1975 Helsinki Accords.
misconceptions.correction: GCSE Exam Tip: Memorise the 3 Baskets cleanly—Basket 1 (European Borders: inviolability of post-1945 frontiers, a major prize for Brezhnev), Basket 2 (Cooperation: trade, science, technology), and Basket 3 (Human Rights: freedom of speech, movement, religion, which inspired Soviet-bloc dissidents).

misconceptions.misconception: Assuming SALT 2 (signed June 1979) became binding law ratified by the US Senate.
misconceptions.correction: Although Jimmy Carter and Leonid Brezhnev signed SALT 2 in Vienna on 18 June 1979, conservative Senate opposition stalled ratification, and Carter formally withdrew SALT 2 from the Senate after Soviet troops invaded Afghanistan in December 1979.

teacher_notes.send_adaptation: Pair the Why Both Superpowers Wanted Detente Concept Diagram with the Visual Story Sheet while playing Studio Audio so learners match US motives (Vietnam cost/inflation/China triangle) with Soviet motives (stagnant living standards/grain imports/Sino-Soviet split/border recognition). Map SALT 1 -> Apollo-Soyuz -> Helsinki 3 Baskets -> SALT 2 onto the Workbook Verso Spine.
teacher_notes.stretch_challenge: Assess whether the August 1975 Helsinki Final Act should be judged primarily as Leonid Brezhnev's greatest diplomatic triumph (securing Western recognition of Soviet Eastern European borders) or a Trojan horse that eroded Communist legitimacy from within.

source_context.Source A: Inaugurated in 1969 facing spiralling Vietnam War costs ($150+ billion), over 58,000 US deaths, domestic inflation, and urban anti-war protests, Republican President Richard Nixon worked with National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger to pursue pragmatic realpolitik. By visiting Mao Zedong in Beijing in February 1972 ('triangular diplomacy'), Nixon leveraged the Sino-Soviet split to make Leonid Brezhnev eager for a Moscow summit three months later. Hinge Question: Why could a lifelong anti-communist hawk like Richard Nixon negotiate Detente with Beijing and Moscow without being accused of weakness at home?
source_context.Source B: Signed by Nixon and Brezhnev in Moscow on 26 May 1972, SALT 1 combined the Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty—restricting each superpower to just two defensive anti-missile sites of 100 launchers—with a five-year Interim Agreement freezing ICBM and submarine-launched ballistic missile launchers. Paradoxically, banning nationwide missile shields stabilised peace by guaranteeing neither side could block retaliation under Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD), though MIRV multiple warheads remained unregulated. Hinge Question: Why did limiting defensive anti-missile shields in the 1972 ABM Treaty make a pre-emptive nuclear first strike less tempting?
source_context.Source C: Broadcast live to television audiences worldwide on 17 July 1975, American astronaut Thomas Stafford and Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov shook hands in Earth orbit through the docking hatch linking Apollo and Soyuz spacecraft, transforming the 1957–69 Space Race into a symbol of scientific partnership. Yet critics noted that orbital pageantry masked ongoing proxy conflicts from October 1973 in the Middle East to civil war in Angola. Hinge Question: Was the 1975 Apollo-Soyuz mission substantive superpower cooperation or symbolic theatre masking continued Cold War rivalry?
source_context.Source D: Signed on 1 August 1975 in Finland by US President Gerald Ford, Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev, Canada, and 32 European states, the Helsinki Final Act traded Basket 1 (accepting Europe's post-1945 borders, including East and West Germany) and Basket 2 (trade and science) for Basket 3 pledges to respect freedom of thought, conscience, religion, and movement. Brezhnev published the text in Pravda assuming Basket 3 was harmless paper, only for Yuri Orlov's Moscow Helsinki Group and Charter 77 in Prague to hold Communist regimes publicly to their own signatures. Hinge Question: Why did Brezhnev underestimate the long-term political danger of signing Basket 3 at Helsinki in 1975?
source_context.Source E: Photographed embracing in Vienna's Hofburg Palace on 18 June 1979, President Jimmy Carter and an ailing Leonid Brezhnev signed SALT 2 after seven years of tough bargaining to cap each side at 2,400 strategic delivery vehicles and limit MIRVed missiles. Within six months, however, rising fury over Soviet/Cuban interventions in Africa, the Iranian crisis, and December 1979's Soviet invasion of Afghanistan prompted Carter to pull SALT 2 from the US Senate, burying Detente. Hinge Question: Had Soviet troops not invaded Afghanistan in December 1979, how healthy was Detente by the time SALT 2 was signed in June 1979?

four_corners.statement: Détente in the 1970s never ended the Cold War; it merely set polite rules for continuing the nuclear arms race.
four_corners.follow_up: Point to one specific detail—such as MIRVs, Basket 3, Angola/Ethiopia, or the ABM Treaty—to justify where you stood.

standoff.title: Was Détente Genuine Peace-Making or Pragmatic Pause?

side_a.label: Genuine Breakthroughs (1972–79)
points: SALT 1’s ABM Treaty and Interim Agreement placed the first legal caps on strategic launchers.
Regular Nixon/Ford/Carter–Brezhnev summits, US grain sales, and Apollo–Soyuz built direct communication.
35 nations signed the Helsinki Accords (1975) and SALT 2 (1979) agreed equal 2,400 launcher ceilings.

side_b.label: Shallow & Fragile Pause
points: SALT 1 left multi-warhead MIRVs uncapped, allowing total nuclear warheads to surge.
Moscow deployed SS-20 missiles and backed Communist forces in Angola and Ethiopia.
Clashes over Helsinki Basket 3 human rights and Afghanistan swiftly destroyed SALT 2.

[01:20] Causal Pressures: Why did the Vietnam War and domestic inflation push President Nixon to seek Détente with the Soviet Union?
[04:30] Treaty Balance: What did Moscow gain from Basket 1 of the 1975 Helsinki Accords, and why did Basket 3 become a political problem for Brezhnev?
video.model_answer: The Vietnam War cost the USA over $150 billion and 58,000 lives, fuelling domestic protest and inflation that forced Nixon to curb arms spending. At Helsinki in 1975, Basket 1 gave Moscow formal Western recognition of post-1945 Eastern European borders and East Germany, whereas Basket 3's human-rights pledges empowered dissidents and Western critics to expose Soviet political repression.

[02:45] Arms Control Analysis: Why did the 1972 ABM Treaty and Interim Agreement fail to halt the growth of nuclear warhead stockpiles during the 1970s?
[08:10] Turning Point: Why did Détente unravel under President Jimmy Carter between 1977 and December 1979?
video.model_answer: SALT 1 froze the number of ICBM and SLBM missile launchers rather than warheads and left MIRV technology (multiple warheads on a single missile) unrestricted. Under Carter from 1977, disputes over Soviet human-rights abuses, Soviet interventions in Angola and Ethiopia, SS-20 missiles, and finally the December 1979 Soviet invasion of Afghanistan caused Carter to withdraw SALT 2.

narrative_blocks.title: Crisis in Kabul & The Soviet Invasion
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Crisis in Kabul & The Soviet Invasion
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 1: Crisis in Kabul & The Soviet Invasion — Why did Brezhnev order the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979?
paragraphs: [1.1] In **April 1978**, the **Saur Revolution** brought the pro-Soviet Communist **PDPA** under **Nur Muhammad Taraki** to power in **Afghanistan**. Radical land and secular reforms provoked fierce armed rebellion from Islamic **Mujahideen** guerrillas, and in **September 1979** Prime Minister **Hafizullah Amin** seized power and had Taraki murdered. Watching the **1979 Iranian Revolution** next door, **Leonid Brezhnev** feared Islamic fundamentalism spreading north across the border into **30 million** Muslims living in Soviet Central Asian republics.

[1.2] Suspecting the unpredictable **Amin** of secretly contacting the **USA**, **Brezhnev** invoked the **Brezhnev Doctrine** to preserve a bordering Communist state. Between **24 and 27 December 1979**, Soviet airborne forces and armoured columns invaded **Afghanistan**, storming Kabul’s presidential palace, killing Amin, and installing Moscow-backed **Babrak Karmal**—trapping the **USSR** in a costly ten-year guerrilla war.

hotspots.label: Kabul Palace Stormed
hotspots.title: Kabul & Bagram: Hafizullah Amin Killed & Babrak Karmal Installed
hotspots.details: After Hafizullah Amin seized power in Kabul from fellow Communist Nur Muhammad Taraki amid swelling Mujahideen rebellion, Brezhnev suspected Amin of contacting Washington and invoked the Brezhnev Doctrine. Between 24 and 27 December 1979, Soviet airborne troops landed at Bagram and Kabul, killed Amin, and installed Moscow loyalist Babrak Karmal.
hotspots.hinge: Why did Brezhnev expect a swift 1968-style intervention in Kabul, yet instead trap the USSR in a ten-year guerrilla war?

hotspots.label: Termez & Salang Thrust
hotspots.title: Termez, Salang Pass & Kushka: Soviet 40th Army Overland Invasion
hotspots.details: Soviet armoured divisions crossed the Amu Darya at Termez through the high-altitude Salang Tunnel toward Kabul while a western thrust from Kushka seized Herat and Kandahar. Controlling cities and highways proved far easier than subduing rugged mountain valleys, eventually costing Moscow ~15,000 Soviet lives and $8 billion a year.
hotspots.hinge: How did Afghanistan’s mountainous geography expose the limits of conventional Soviet tank and air power?

hotspots.label: Iranian Revolution
hotspots.title: Iran (1979): Fears of Islamic Fundamentalism on the Soviet Border
hotspots.details: Ayatollah Khomeini’s 1979 Islamic Revolution in neighbouring Iran alarmed both superpowers: Washington lost its key Persian Gulf ally, while the Kremlin feared militant Islamism spreading across Afghanistan into the 30 million Muslim citizens of the Turkmen, Uzbek, and Tajik Soviet republics.
hotspots.hinge: Why did the 1979 Iranian Revolution heighten security fears simultaneously in Moscow and in Washington?

hotspots.label: Peshawar & CIA Supply
hotspots.title: Peshawar & Quetta: Mujahideen Sanctuaries & CIA Operation Cyclone
hotspots.details: Under President Carter—and vastly expanded under Ronald Reagan’s Second Cold War—the CIA funnelled billions of dollars in cash, rifles, and later shoulder-fired Stinger anti-aircraft missiles through Karachi to Pakistani bases around Peshawar and Quetta, bleeding the Red Army across the frontier.
hotspots.hinge: Why was covertly arming the Mujahideen through Pakistan so effective at draining Soviet military morale and resources?

hotspots.label: Carter Doctrine (Gulf)
hotspots.title: Persian Gulf & Strait of Hormuz: The Carter Doctrine & Sanctions
hotspots.details: On 23 January 1980, President Jimmy Carter declared that the USA would use military force if necessary to defend the oil-rich Persian Gulf from outside control, backed by a Rapid Deployment Force. Carter simultaneously withdrew SALT 2 from the Senate, imposed grain and high-tech embargoes, and led a 60-nation boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics.
hotspots.hinge: Why did the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan immediately kill 1970s Détente and trigger the 1980 and 1984 Olympic boycotts?

narrative_blocks.title: The Carter Doctrine & Death of Détente
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: The Carter Doctrine & Death of Détente
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 2: The Carter Doctrine & Death of Détente — How did Jimmy Carter retaliate against the USSR in January 1980?
narrative_blocks.image_alt: Soviet airborne soldiers in combat gear walking toward a Mil Mi-8 transport helicopter marked with a red star on a stony landing strip against barren Afghan mountains in the 1980s
narrative_blocks.caption: Soviet airborne troops boarding a Mil Mi-8 transport helicopter during counter-insurgency operations in mountainous Afghanistan in the 1980s.
paragraphs: [2.1] Calling the Afghan invasion the gravest threat to peace since **1945**, US President **Jimmy Carter** buried **Détente** in **January 1980**. In his **23 January 1980** State of the Union address, he proclaimed the **Carter Doctrine**: the **USA** would use military force if necessary to block any outside power—meaning the **USSR**—from gaining control of the oil-rich **Persian Gulf**, backed by a new **Rapid Deployment Force**.

[2.2] Simultaneously, **Jimmy Carter** withdrew the **SALT 2** treaty from the US Senate, increased American defence spending by **5 per cent**, and imposed a punishing **grain embargo** alongside a ban on exporting computers and oil-drilling technology to the **USSR**. Under **CIA Operation Cyclone**, Washington also channelled money and weapons through Pakistan to arm the Afghan **Mujahideen**.

narrative_blocks.title: Tit-for-Tat Olympic Boycotts
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Tit-for-Tat Olympic Boycotts
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 3: Tit-for-Tat Olympic Boycotts — In what ways did the 1980 and 1984 Olympic boycotts deepen rivalry?
paragraphs: [3.1] Cold War confrontation immediately spilled into international sport when **Jimmy Carter** gave Moscow an ultimatum to withdraw from **Afghanistan** by **February 1980** or face an **Olympic** boycott. When **Leonid Brezhnev** refused, the **USA** led over **60 nations**—including **West Germany**, **China**, **Japan**, **Canada**, and **Kenya**—to boycott the **1980 Moscow Summer Olympics**, denying the Kremlin the global showcase it had spent billions building and prompting rival **Liberty Bell Classic** games in Philadelphia.

[3.2] Although British athletes still competed in Moscow under the neutral **Olympic** flag, Soviet leaders resented the public diplomatic humiliation. Four years later, in **May 1984**, the **USSR** cited alleged anti-Soviet hysteria and inadequate athlete security to lead **14 Eastern Bloc** allies in a retaliatory boycott of the **1984 Los Angeles Summer Olympics**, underscoring frozen superpower relations.

narrative_blocks.title: Ronald Reagan & The Second Cold War
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Ronald Reagan & The Second Cold War
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 4: Ronald Reagan & The Second Cold War — What policies launched Ronald Reagan’s Second Cold War between 1981 and 1983?
narrative_blocks.image_alt: Official White House portrait of US President Ronald Reagan in 1981
narrative_blocks.caption: Official White House portrait of US President Ronald Reagan (inaugurated January 1981), who abandoned Détente to wage the high-spending "Second Cold War".
paragraphs: [4.1] Inaugurated in **January 1981**, staunchly anti-communist US President **Ronald Reagan** dismissed **Détente** as a *"one-way street"* exploited by Moscow and ignited the **Second Cold War**. Determined to negotiate only from overwhelming strength, Reagan launched a **$1 trillion** American defence build-up across the early **1980s**, funding **100 B-1 Lancer** bombers, **Trident** nuclear submarines, stealth aircraft, the **neutron bomb**, and **Pershing II** and **Cruise** missiles deployed in Western Europe.

[4.2] Alongside military rearmament, **Ronald Reagan** sharpened ideological warfare: on **8 March 1983** he denounced the **Soviet Union** as an **"Evil Empire"** and the *"focus of evil in the modern world"*. Under the **Reagan Doctrine**, Washington openly funded and armed anti-communist guerrillas—from Nicaragua’s Contras to **Stinger** anti-aircraft missiles later supplied to Afghanistan’s **Mujahideen**—to roll back Soviet influence.

narrative_blocks.title: Star Wars (SDI) & Soviet Economic Strain
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Star Wars (SDI) & Soviet Economic Strain
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 5: Star Wars (SDI) & Soviet Economic Strain — What caused Reagan’s 1983 Strategic Defence Initiative to alarm Moscow?
paragraphs: [5.1] On **23 March 1983**, **Reagan** stunned **Moscow** by announcing the **Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI)**—nicknamed **"Star Wars"** by journalists. Rather than relying on **Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD)**, **SDI** proposed a network of orbiting space satellites armed with high-powered lasers to intercept and destroy Soviet **ICBMs** in flight before they could hit American soil, creating a nuclear shield over the **USA** while bypassing the **1972 ABM Treaty**.

[5.2] Soviet leaders—passing rapidly through elderly premiers **Yuri Andropov** and **Konstantin Chernenko** after **Brezhnev**’s death in **1982**—viewed **SDI** as an existential threat that could hand Washington a **first-strike** capability and neutralise Soviet missiles. Because the stagnant Soviet command economy lagged far behind America in microchips and supercomputers, **Moscow** knew trying to match **Star Wars** would bankrupt the **USSR**.

causal_domino_spine.title: From Kabul to ‘Star Wars’: The Second Cold War (1979–85)

stages.title: Crisis in Kabul & The Soviet Invasion
stages.trigger: Between 24 and 27 December 1979, Soviet troops invade Afghanistan, kill erratic PDPA leader Hafizullah Amin, and install Moscow loyalist Babrak Karmal.
stages.because: Brezhnev feared Mujahideen Islamic rebellion (after Iran’s 1979 Revolution) spreading into Soviet Central Asia and suspected Amin of courting the USA.
stages.therefore: The Red Army became bogged down in a ten-year guerrilla war ("the USSR’s Vietnam") that shocked Washington.
stages.connective: Outraged by Moscow’s first military invasion outside the Warsaw Pact since WWII, President Carter retaliated immediately...
stages.exam_link: Q3 Importance: Destroyed Détente overnight and trapped the USSR in a draining decade-long war.
stages.question: Why did Brezhnev order the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979?

stages.title: The Carter Doctrine & Death of Détente
stages.trigger: On 23 January 1980, Carter proclaims the Carter Doctrine defending the Persian Gulf by military force, withdraws SALT 2, halts grain/tech exports, and launches CIA Operation Cyclone.
stages.because: Washington feared Soviet forces in Afghanistan stood within striking distance of Western oil supplies in the Persian Gulf.
stages.therefore: Seven years of Détente arms control and trade vanished in weeks as US money armed the Afghan Mujahideen.
stages.connective: To punish Moscow visibly on the world stage, Carter next targeted the Kremlin’s proudest summer spectacle...
stages.exam_link: Q1 Consequence: Ended SALT 2 ratification, choked Soviet grain/tech imports, and militarised Gulf containment.
stages.question: How did Jimmy Carter retaliate against the USSR in January 1980?

stages.title: Tit-for-Tat Olympic Boycotts
stages.trigger: The USA leads over 60 nations to boycott the 1980 Moscow Olympics; in May 1984 the USSR leads 14 Eastern Bloc states to boycott the Los Angeles Olympics.
stages.because: Moscow refused Carter’s February 1980 withdrawal deadline from Afghanistan, prompting public Western protest and later Soviet payback.
stages.therefore: Even non-political cultural and sporting ties froze across East and West.
stages.connective: Meanwhile, American voters elected a new president determined to confront communism head-on...
stages.exam_link: Q1 Consequence / Q2 Narrative: Turned global sporting festivals into public Cold War propaganda clashes.
stages.question: In what ways did the 1980 and 1984 Olympic boycotts deepen rivalry?

stages.title: Ronald Reagan & The Second Cold War
stages.trigger: From January 1981, Reagan launches a $1 trillion US arms build-up (B-1 bombers, Trident, Pershing II/Cruise), backs guerrillas via the Reagan Doctrine, and calls the USSR an "Evil Empire" (8 March 1983).
stages.because: Reagan believed Détente had allowed Soviet expansionism and that only overwhelming American military and moral pressure would force Soviet retreat.
stages.therefore: Superpower rhetoric and nuclear missile deployments in Europe reached their tensest pitch since 1962.
stages.connective: Fifteen days after his "Evil Empire" speech, Reagan unveiled an ambitious new space technology...
stages.exam_link: Q2 Narrative: Escalation from Carter’s containment to Reagan’s offensive ideological and military pressure.
stages.question: What policies launched Ronald Reagan’s Second Cold War between 1981 and 1983?

stages.title: Star Wars (SDI) & Soviet Economic Strain
stages.trigger: On 23 March 1983, Reagan announces the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI / "Star Wars")—space-based lasers designed to shoot down Soviet ICBMs in flight.
stages.because: Reagan sought to render nuclear missiles obsolete and exploit America’s decisive lead in microchips and space technology.
stages.therefore: Ageing Soviet leaders knew SDI threatened to neutralise MAD and that matching US space spending would bankrupt the USSR.
stages.connective: By 1985, economic exhaustion forced a new Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, to rethink the Cold War completely.
stages.exam_link: Q3 Importance: Shifted the nuclear balance technologically and exposed terminal Soviet economic weakness.
stages.question: What caused Reagan’s 1983 Strategic Defence Initiative to alarm Moscow?

sources.title: Source B: President Jimmy Carter’s State of the Union Address Proclaiming the Carter Doctrine (23 January 1980)
sources.text:
The region which is now threatened by Soviet troops in Afghanistan is of great strategic importance: It contains more than two-thirds of the world’s exportable oil... The Soviet effort to dominate Afghanistan has brought Soviet military forces to within 300 miles of the Indian Ocean and close to the Straits of Hormuz, a waterway through which most of the world’s oil must flow.
Let our position be absolutely clear: An attempt by any outside force to gain control of the Persian Gulf region will be regarded as an assault on the vital interests of the United States of America, and such an assault will be repelled by any means necessary, including military force.
