sources.provenance: State of the Union Address delivered by President Jimmy Carter before a joint session of the US Congress, Washington, D.C., 23 January 1980.
sources.citation: Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: Jimmy Carter, 1980–81.
sources.model_answer: Whereas Brezhnev saw invading Afghanistan as a defensive move to stabilise a bordering Communist state against Islamic rebellion, Source B shows Carter viewed Red Army forces 300 miles from the Straits of Hormuz as a stepping stone to strangle two-thirds of the world’s oil.
sources.context: Delivered before Congress four weeks after Soviet paratroopers seized Kabul and killed Hafizullah Amin.
sources.source_context: Deliberately modelling his warning on the 1947 Truman Doctrine, Carter backed his speech by creating the Rapid Deployment Force, registering young Americans for a potential military draft, and halting US grain shipments to the USSR.

teacher_notes.source_context: Deliberately modelling his warning on the 1947 Truman Doctrine, Carter backed his speech by creating the Rapid Deployment Force, registering young Americans for a potential military draft, and halting US grain shipments to the USSR. **Hinge Question:** Which 1947 presidential pledge did Carter deliberately echo by promising US military containment in the Persian Gulf?
teacher_notes.hinge_question: Which 1947 presidential pledge did Carter deliberately echo by promising US military containment in the Persian Gulf?

sources.question: How does Source B show that President Carter interpreted the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan through a wider geopolitical lens than Brezhnev intended?

sources.title: Source D: Extract from President Ronald Reagan’s "Evil Empire" Speech (8 March 1983)
sources.text: During my first press conference as President, in answer to a direct question, I pointed out that, as good Marxist-Leninists, the Soviet leaders have openly and publicly declared that the only morality they recognise is that which will further their cause, which is world revolution... So, in your discussions of the nuclear freeze proposals, I urge you to beware the temptation of pride—the temptation of blithely declaring yourselves above it all and label both sides equally at fault, to ignore the facts of history and the aggressive impulses of an evil empire, to simply call the arms race a giant misunderstanding and thereby remove yourself from the struggle between right and wrong and good and evil.
sources.content: During my first press conference as President, in answer to a direct question, I pointed out that, as good Marxist-Leninists, the Soviet leaders have openly and publicly declared that the only morality they recognise is that which will further their cause, which is world revolution... So, in your discussions of the nuclear freeze proposals, I urge you to beware the temptation of pride—the temptation of blithely declaring yourselves above it all and label both sides equally at fault, to ignore the facts of history and the aggressive impulses of an evil empire, to simply call the arms race a giant misunderstanding and thereby remove yourself from the struggle between right and wrong and good and evil.
sources.provenance: Speech delivered by US President Ronald Reagan to the Annual Convention of the National Association of Evangelicals, Orlando, Florida, 8 March 1983.
sources.citation: Ronald Reagan Presidential Library & Museum, Simi Valley, California.
sources.model_answer: Under Détente, Nixon and Ford treated the USSR as a legitimate, permanent superpower partner with equal strategic interests, whereas Reagan rejected moral equivalence and nuclear-freeze compromises—framing the Cold War as a spiritual battle between good and an "evil empire".
sources.context: Spoken in Orlando, Florida as Reagan defended his $1 trillion arms build-up and European Pershing II deployments against Western peace protests.
sources.source_context: In early 1983 millions of Western protesters campaigned for a bilateral "nuclear freeze"; Reagan used moral religious language before evangelical leaders to rally support for B-1 bombers, Trident submarines, and Pershing II missiles.

teacher_notes.source_context: In early 1983 millions of Western protesters campaigned for a bilateral "nuclear freeze"; Reagan used moral religious language before evangelical leaders to rally support for B-1 bombers, Trident submarines, and Pershing II missiles. **Hinge Question:** Why was Reagan addressing this warning specifically to domestic supporters of a "nuclear freeze" in March 1983?
teacher_notes.hinge_question: Why was Reagan addressing this warning specifically to domestic supporters of a "nuclear freeze" in March 1983?

sources.question: How did Ronald Reagan’s language in Source D break sharply with the diplomatic assumptions of 1970s Détente?

sources.title: Source E: President Ronald Reagan’s Televised Oval Office Address Announcing SDI (23 March 1983)
sources.image_alt: Television broadcast frame of US President Ronald Reagan seated in the Oval Office in a dark suit and red patterned tie delivering his 23 March 1983 address announcing the Strategic Defence Initiative
sources.caption: President Ronald Reagan speaking from the Oval Office on 23 March 1983 to announce the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI / "Star Wars")—an orbital defence shield to intercept Soviet ballistic missiles.
sources.provenance: White House televised address on Peace and National Security, Oval Office, 23 March 1983 (Ronald Reagan Presidential Library / Public Domain).
sources.citation: Ronald Reagan Presidential Library, Audiovisual Collection (NARA).
sources.model_answer: Even if space lasers remained years away, SDI threatened to overturn Mutually Assured Destruction by giving America a first-strike shield, and Moscow knew its stagnant economy—lagging badly in microchips and supercomputers—could never afford a high-tech space race.
sources.context: Broadcast nationally fifteen days after Reagan’s "Evil Empire" speech, shocking both Moscow and several NATO allies.
sources.source_context: Soviet General Secretary Yuri Andropov denounced SDI as a reckless bid to disarm the USSR and breach the 1972 ABM Treaty, realising that competing with Silicon Valley computing would push the Soviet budget toward collapse.

teacher_notes.source_context: Soviet General Secretary Yuri Andropov denounced SDI as a reckless bid to disarm the USSR and breach the 1972 ABM Treaty, realising that competing with Silicon Valley computing would push the Soviet budget toward collapse. **Hinge Question:** Which 1972 SALT 1 treaty did Soviet leaders accuse Reagan of violating by proposing space-based missile defences?

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: After Soviet troops invaded Afghanistan in December 1979 to crush Islamic [Mujahideen] rebels, Jimmy Carter proclaimed the [Carter Doctrine] over the Persian Gulf and sparked tit-for-tat [Olympic Boycotts] in 1980 and 1984. From 1981, Ronald Reagan escalated the [Second Cold War] through a $1 trillion arms build-up, backing anti-communist guerrillas under the [Reagan Doctrine], and unveiling the space-based [Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI)] in March 1983.

items.question: Roughly how much had the Vietnam War cost the United States financially by the early 1970s?
items.explanation: Vietnam drained over $150 billion from the US budget alongside 58,000 American deaths, fuelling inflation and social protest.

items.question: Where and when did Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev sign the SALT 1 agreements?
items.explanation: Nixon and Brezhnev signed SALT 1 in the Grand Kremlin Palace in Moscow on 26 May 1972.

items.question: Who succeeded Richard Nixon as US President in August 1974 after the Watergate scandal?
items.explanation: Vice-President Gerald Ford assumed the presidency in August 1974 and continued Détente summits with Brezhnev.

items.question: How many nations signed the Helsinki Accords in Finland in August 1975?
items.explanation: Thirty-five states—the USA, Canada, the USSR, and 32 European countries—signed the Helsinki Final Act on 1 August 1975.

items.question: Which issue did President Jimmy Carter place at the heart of US foreign policy from January 1977?
items.explanation: Carter wrote to dissident Andrei Sakharov and linked Soviet trade to human rights, angering Brezhnev.

items.question: Which Communist power did President Richard Nixon visit in February 1972, alarming Moscow?
items.explanation: Following the Sino-Soviet border split, Nixon’s February 1972 visit to Mao’s China made Brezhnev eager to avoid facing a US–Chinese alignment.

items.question: How many Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) defensive sites was each superpower permitted under the 1972 ABM Treaty?
items.explanation: Each side could defend only its national capital and one ICBM field, ensuring nuclear deterrence remained stable.

items.question: Which joint US–Soviet space mission docked in Earth orbit on 17 July 1975?
items.explanation: An American Apollo capsule docked with a Soviet Soyuz spacecraft on 17 July 1975 in a televised symbol of Détente.

items.question: What did Basket 1 of the August 1975 Helsinki Accords establish regarding Europe?
items.answer: European borders were inviolable, recognising East Germany
items.explanation: Basket 1 formally accepted Europe’s post-1945 frontiers and recognised Communist East Germany, fulfilling a long-held Soviet diplomatic goal.

items.question: In which two African countries did Soviet-backed Communist interventions anger US Senators in the late 1970s?
items.explanation: Soviet arms and Cuban troops in Angola and Ethiopia convinced US hawks that Moscow was exploiting Détente.

quiz.question: Which April 1978 coup first brought the pro-Soviet Communist PDPA party to power in Afghanistan?
quiz.q: Which April 1978 coup first brought the pro-Soviet Communist PDPA party to power in Afghanistan?
quiz.explanation: In April 1978 the Saur Revolution installed Communist leader Nur Muhammad Taraki in Kabul, sparking fierce Islamic resistance.

quiz.question: Who overthrew and murdered Nur Muhammad Taraki in September 1979, alarming Leonid Brezhnev?
quiz.q: Who overthrew and murdered Nur Muhammad Taraki in September 1979, alarming Leonid Brezhnev?
quiz.explanation: Prime Minister Hafizullah Amin seized power in September 1979, and Brezhnev suspected him of secretly contacting the USA.

quiz.question: What were the Islamic guerrilla fighters rebelling against Communist rule in Afghanistan called?
quiz.q: What were the Islamic guerrilla fighters rebelling against Communist rule in Afghanistan called?
quiz.explanation: The Mujahideen waged holy war (jihad) from Afghanistan’s mountains against PDPA secular reforms and the invading Red Army.

quiz.question: Whom did Soviet forces install as Afghanistan’s new ruler after invading on 24–27 December 1979?
quiz.q: Whom did Soviet forces install as Afghanistan’s new ruler after invading on 24–27 December 1979?
quiz.explanation: Soviet troops stormed Kabul’s palace, killed Amin, and installed loyal Moscow ally Babrak Karmal.

quiz.question: Which vital oil-producing region did the January 1980 Carter Doctrine pledge US military force to defend?
quiz.q: Which vital oil-producing region did the January 1980 Carter Doctrine pledge US military force to defend?
quiz.explanation: On 23 January 1980 Carter warned that any outside bid to control the oil-rich Persian Gulf would be repelled by military force.

quiz.question: Which major 1979 arms treaty did Jimmy Carter withdraw from the US Senate in January 1980?
quiz.q: Which major 1979 arms treaty did Jimmy Carter withdraw from the US Senate in January 1980?
quiz.explanation: Carter shelved Senate ratification of the June 1979 Vienna SALT 2 treaty in direct retaliation for the invasion of Afghanistan.

quiz.question: What crucial agricultural export did President Carter ban selling to the Soviet Union in January 1980?
quiz.q: What crucial agricultural export did President Carter ban selling to the Soviet Union in January 1980?
quiz.explanation: Carter imposed a punishing US grain embargo alongside a ban on exporting computers and oil-drilling technology to Moscow.

quiz.question: What was the codename of the covert CIA programme channelling money and weapons to the Afghan Mujahideen?
quiz.q: What was the codename of the covert CIA programme channelling money and weapons to the Afghan Mujahideen?
quiz.explanation: Under CIA Operation Cyclone, Washington funnelled arms and funds via Pakistan to bleed Soviet forces in Afghanistan.

quiz.question: How many countries joined the US-led boycott of the 1980 Moscow Summer Olympics?
quiz.q: How many countries joined the US-led boycott of the 1980 Moscow Summer Olympics?
quiz.explanation: After Moscow ignored Carter’s February 1980 withdrawal deadline, over 60 countries boycotted the Moscow Summer Games.

quiz.question: Which alternative athletics event did the USA host in Philadelphia for boycotting athletes in 1980?
quiz.q: Which alternative athletics event did the USA host in Philadelphia for boycotting athletes in 1980?
quiz.explanation: Washington organised the rival Liberty Bell Classic in July 1980 for athletes from nations boycotting Moscow.

quiz.question: Which Summer Olympic Games did the USSR and 14 Eastern Bloc allies boycott in May 1984?
quiz.q: Which Summer Olympic Games did the USSR and 14 Eastern Bloc allies boycott in May 1984?
quiz.explanation: In May 1984 the Soviet Union led 14 Communist allies in a retaliatory boycott of the Los Angeles Summer Olympics.

quiz.question: What official excuse did Moscow give in May 1984 for refusing to send athletes to Los Angeles?
quiz.q: What official excuse did Moscow give in May 1984 for refusing to send athletes to Los Angeles?
options: Anti-Soviet hysteria and inadequate athlete security
quiz.answer: Anti-Soviet hysteria and inadequate athlete security
quiz.a: Anti-Soviet hysteria and inadequate athlete security
quiz.explanation: Moscow claimed commercialism, anti-Soviet protests, and poor security endangered Soviet athletes—masking diplomatic payback for 1980.

quiz.question: When was Republican Ronald Reagan inaugurated as President of the United States?
quiz.q: When was Republican Ronald Reagan inaugurated as President of the United States?
quiz.explanation: Elected in November 1980, Ronald Reagan took office in January 1981 promising peace through overwhelming American strength.

quiz.question: Roughly how much did Ronald Reagan commit to his massive US defence build-up in the early 1980s?
quiz.q: Roughly how much did Ronald Reagan commit to his massive US defence build-up in the early 1980s?
quiz.explanation: Reagan spent over $1 trillion across the early 1980s on B-1 bombers, Trident submarines, stealth aircraft, and Pershing II/Cruise missiles.

quiz.question: What famous phrase did Ronald Reagan use to describe the Soviet Union on 8 March 1983?
quiz.q: What famous phrase did Ronald Reagan use to describe the Soviet Union on 8 March 1983?
quiz.explanation: Addressing evangelical Christians in Orlando on 8 March 1983, Reagan called the USSR an "evil empire" and the focus of evil.

quiz.question: What policy committed the Reagan administration to arming anti-communist guerrillas in the Third World?
quiz.q: What policy committed the Reagan administration to arming anti-communist guerrillas in the Third World?
quiz.explanation: Under the Reagan Doctrine, Washington armed anti-communist insurgents such as Nicaragua’s Contras and Afghanistan’s Mujahideen (including Stinger missiles).

quiz.question: What media nickname was given to Reagan’s 23 March 1983 Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI)?
quiz.q: What media nickname was given to Reagan’s 23 March 1983 Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI)?
quiz.explanation: Journalists dubbed SDI "Star Wars" after George Lucas’s sci-fi films because it proposed orbiting laser satellites in space.

quiz.question: What was the core military purpose of the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI)?
quiz.q: What was the core military purpose of the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI)?
options: Destroy Soviet ICBMs in flight with space lasers
Place nuclear warheads on the Moon
Build underground fallout bunkers in every city
Replace NATO ground troops in West Berlin
quiz.answer: Destroy Soviet ICBMs in flight with space lasers
quiz.a: Destroy Soviet ICBMs in flight with space lasers
quiz.explanation: SDI aimed to intercept Soviet ballistic missiles from orbit before they could strike the USA, rendering Soviet ICBMs obsolete.

quiz.question: Which two elderly Soviet leaders succeeded Brezhnev briefly between 1982 and 1985?
quiz.q: Which two elderly Soviet leaders succeeded Brezhnev briefly between 1982 and 1985?
quiz.explanation: Following Brezhnev’s death in November 1982, Yuri Andropov (1982–84) and Konstantin Chernenko (1984–85) led an ageing Kremlin.

quiz.question: Why could the Soviet economy not realistically match Reagan’s SDI programme in the mid-1980s?
quiz.q: Why could the Soviet economy not realistically match Reagan’s SDI programme in the mid-1980s?
options: It lagged in microchips and faced economic bankruptcy
It lacked oil and natural gas reserves
It had disbanded all Soviet rocket scientists
The UN Security Council banned Soviet satellites
quiz.answer: It lagged in microchips and faced economic bankruptcy
quiz.a: It lagged in microchips and faced economic bankruptcy
quiz.explanation: Drained by Afghanistan and lagging far behind America in computer technology, matching SDI threatened to bankrupt the USSR.

questions.question: 1(a). Explain one consequence of the Carter Doctrine (1980). [4 marks]
questions.prompt: State one clear consequence -> support with specific January 1980 detail (Persian Gulf / Rapid Deployment Force OR sanctions / Operation Cyclone) -> explain what this led to.
questions.examiner_tip: Do not confuse Jimmy Carter’s January 1980 Gulf commitment and sanctions with Ronald Reagan’s 1983 SDI—keep your evidence anchored tightly to 1980.
questions.model: One major consequence of the Carter Doctrine in January 1980 was the militarisation of American containment across the Persian Gulf, ending 1970s détente. Pledging US military force to block Soviet expansion beyond Afghanistan toward Middle Eastern oil supplies, President Jimmy Carter created a Rapid Deployment Force and raised defence spending by 5 per cent, reviving open superpower confrontation.

tier_1m.title: 1/4 Assertion
tier_1m.text: One consequence of the Carter Doctrine in 1980 was that relations between the USA and the Soviet Union got much worse and détente ended.
tier_1m.verdict: AO2 Level 1 (1 mark) • AO1 Level 0 (0 marks). Simple assertion that relations worsened, with zero supporting knowledge of the Persian Gulf pledge, military measures, or sanctions.

tier_2m.title: 2/4 Basic Knowledge
tier_2m.text: One consequence of the Carter Doctrine in January 1980 was that President Carter warned the USSR that the USA would use military force to protect oil supplies in the Persian Gulf.
tier_2m.verdict: AO2 Level 1 (1 mark) • AO1 Level 1 (1 mark). Accurately states the content of Carter’s pledge, but needs explicit explanation of the concrete military or diplomatic consequence that followed.

tier_4m.title: 4/4 Grade 9 Exam ★
tier_4m.text: One major consequence of the Carter Doctrine in January 1980 was the militarisation of American containment across the Persian Gulf, ending 1970s détente. Pledging US military force to block Soviet expansion beyond Afghanistan toward Middle Eastern oil supplies, President Jimmy Carter created a Rapid Deployment Force and raised defence spending by 5 per cent, reviving open superpower confrontation.
tier_4m.verdict: AO2 Level 2: 2m • AO1 Level 2: 2m (Option A: 58w • Option B: 55w). Each exemplar earns full 4/4 marks in two–three crisp sentences by developing ONE focused consequence with precise factual detail—either militarised Persian Gulf containment via the Rapid Deployment Force (Option A) or economic sanctions, SALT 2 withdrawal, and CIA aid to the Mujahideen (Option B)—rather than listing multiple undeveloped consequences.

options.label: Option A (4/4): Militarised Gulf Containment
options.text: One major consequence of the Carter Doctrine in January 1980 was the militarisation of American containment across the Persian Gulf, ending 1970s détente. Pledging US military force to block Soviet expansion beyond Afghanistan toward Middle Eastern oil supplies, President Jimmy Carter created a Rapid Deployment Force and raised defence spending by 5 per cent, reviving open superpower confrontation.

Backing his warning over the Persian Gulf with action, Jimmy Carter withdrew SALT 2 from the Senate, banned US grain and computer exports to Moscow, and armed Afghan Mujahideen fighters through Pakistan under CIA Operation Cyclone.

questions.question: 2. Write a narrative account analysing the key events in the end of détente and the ‘Second Cold War’ in the years 1979–84. [8 marks]
stimulus: the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (1979)
the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI)
bullet_points: the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (1979)
the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI)
questions.prompt: Write 3 chronological paragraphs (Beginning: Dec 1979 invasion of Afghanistan & Jan 1980 Carter Doctrine/Moscow boycott -> Middle: Reagan’s 1981–83 $1trn rearmament & Evil Empire speech [own knowledge] -> Outcome: March 1983 SDI & May 1984 LA Olympic boycott).
questions.examiner_tip: Bridge 1979 and 1983–84 using own knowledge of the January 1980 Carter Doctrine, the 1980 Moscow Olympic boycott, Ronald Reagan’s $1 trillion arms build-up, and the 1984 Los Angeles boycott.
questions.model:
Détente collapsed in December 1979 when Leonid Brezhnev sent Soviet troops into Afghanistan to kill erratic Communist leader Hafizullah Amin, install Babrak Karmal, and stop Islamic Mujahideen rebellion spreading north. Viewing Red Army forces near the Persian Gulf as aggressive expansion, US President Jimmy Carter retaliated in January 1980 by proclaiming the Carter Doctrine, withdrawing SALT 2, halting grain and computer sales, arming the Mujahideen under Operation Cyclone, and leading over 60 nations to boycott the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

This breakdown escalated into the ‘Second Cold War’ once Ronald Reagan became president in January 1981. Dismissing détente as a "one-way street", Reagan launched a $1 trillion defence build-up—funding B-1 bombers, Trident submarines, and Pershing II and Cruise missiles in Western Europe—backed anti-communist guerrillas under the Reagan Doctrine, and denounced the USSR on 8 March 1983 as an "Evil Empire".

Consequently, superpower hostility peaked on 23 March 1983 when Reagan unveiled the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI), proposing orbiting space lasers to destroy Soviet ICBMs in flight. Because SDI threatened to neutralise Mutually Assured Destruction and bankrupt the computer-lagging Soviet economy, Kremlin leaders reacted furiously and led 14 Eastern Bloc allies to boycott the May 1984 Los Angeles Olympics.

tier_2m.title: 2/8 Simple Narrative
tier_2m.text: In December 1979 the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan, which made the USA angry and ended détente. Then Ronald Reagan became US President, spent huge amounts on weapons, announced his Star Wars laser shield in 1983, and both countries boycotted each other’s Olympic Games.
tier_2m.verdict: AO2 Level 1 (1 mark) • AO1 Level 1 (1 mark). Basic sequence of events from 1979 to 1984, but lacks precise historical detail and explicit causal explanation.

tier_4m.title: 4/8 Sequenced Account
tier_4m.text:
In December 1979, Soviet airborne and armoured forces invaded Afghanistan under the Brezhnev Doctrine, killing Hafizullah Amin and installing Babrak Karmal to fight Islamic Mujahideen rebels.

In March 1983, US President Ronald Reagan announced the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI), nicknamed "Star Wars", proposing orbiting laser satellites in space to shoot down Soviet ballistic missiles before they could reach America.
tier_4m.verdict: AO2 Level 2 (2 marks) • AO1 Level 2 (2 marks). Chronological description relying on the two stimulus points without explicit causal links or bridging own knowledge (Carter Doctrine, SALT 2 withdrawal, Olympic boycotts, Reagan’s $1 trillion build-up), legally capping the response at 4/8 under the Pearson Edexcel mark scheme.

tier_8m.title: 8/8 Grade 9 Exam ★
tier_8m.text:
Détente collapsed in December 1979 when Leonid Brezhnev sent Soviet troops into Afghanistan to kill erratic Communist leader Hafizullah Amin, install Babrak Karmal, and stop Islamic Mujahideen rebellion spreading north. Viewing Red Army forces near the Persian Gulf as aggressive expansion, US President Jimmy Carter retaliated in January 1980 by proclaiming the Carter Doctrine, withdrawing SALT 2, halting grain and computer sales, arming the Mujahideen under Operation Cyclone, and leading over 60 nations to boycott the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

This breakdown escalated into the ‘Second Cold War’ once Ronald Reagan became president in January 1981. Dismissing détente as a "one-way street", Reagan launched a $1 trillion defence build-up—funding B-1 bombers, Trident submarines, and Pershing II and Cruise missiles in Western Europe—backed anti-communist guerrillas under the Reagan Doctrine, and denounced the USSR on 8 March 1983 as an "Evil Empire".

Consequently, superpower hostility peaked on 23 March 1983 when Reagan unveiled the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI), proposing orbiting space lasers to destroy Soviet ICBMs in flight. Because SDI threatened to neutralise Mutually Assured Destruction and bankrupt the computer-lagging Soviet economy, Kremlin leaders reacted furiously and led 14 Eastern Bloc allies to boycott the May 1984 Los Angeles Olympics.

questions.question: 3. Explain the importance of the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI) for US-Soviet relations. [8 marks]
questions.prompt: Write two distinct PEEL paragraphs explaining WHY SDI mattered for US-Soviet relations: (1) Threatening Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) and escalating suspicion, and (2) Exposing Soviet economic/computer weakness and forcing later arms talks.
questions.examiner_tip: Focus on strategic and economic consequences rather than technical descriptions of lasers—explain both short-term Kremlin alarm (1983–84) and longer-term pressure on Soviet spending.
questions.model:
First, Ronald Reagan’s March 1983 Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI) was strategically important for US-Soviet relations because it threatened to overturn Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) and deepened distrust during the Second Cold War. By proposing orbiting space satellites armed with lasers to intercept Soviet ICBMs in flight before hitting America, SDI bypassed the spirit of the 1972 ABM Treaty and threatened to render Soviet nuclear missiles obsolete. Consequently, elderly Kremlin leaders Yuri Andropov and Konstantin Chernenko feared Washington was seeking a nuclear first-strike shield, intensifying superpower hostility between 1983 and 1985.

Second, SDI was decisively important because it exposed the severe economic and technological weakness of the USSR, shifting Cold War leverage toward Washington. Already drained by fighting Mujahideen guerrillas in Afghanistan and starved of Western technology since 1980, the stagnant Soviet command economy lagged far behind America in microchips and supercomputers. Realising that matching "Star Wars" would bankrupt the Soviet state ultimately compelled Mikhail Gorbachev from 1985 to seek summit diplomacy and deep arms reductions.

tier_2m.title: 2/8 Simple Statement
tier_2m.text: SDI was very important for US-Soviet relations because Reagan planned to put lasers in space to shoot down Soviet nuclear missiles, which frightened Soviet leaders and showed the USSR could not afford to keep up with American spending.
tier_2m.verdict: AO1 Level 1 (1 mark) • AO2 Level 1 (1 mark). Valid general point identifying space defence and cost, but lacks precise historical detail (MAD, 1972 ABM Treaty, microchip gap, Gorbachev’s shift).

tier_4m.title: 4/8 Descriptive
tier_4m.text:
On 23 March 1983, President Ronald Reagan announced the Strategic Defence Initiative, nicknamed "Star Wars". It proposed launching space satellites fitted with high-powered lasers to intercept and destroy Soviet ICBMs before they reached US soil.

At the time, the Soviet Union was ruled by elderly leaders Yuri Andropov and Konstantin Chernenko and was spending billions fighting in Afghanistan while lagging behind the USA in microchips and supercomputers.
tier_4m.verdict: AO1 Level 2 (2 marks) • AO2 Level 2 (2 marks). Accurate factual detail across two paragraphs, but describes events rather than explicitly explaining why SDI mattered specifically for US-Soviet relations.

tier_8m.title: 8/8 Grade 9 Exam ★
tier_8m.text:
First, Ronald Reagan’s March 1983 Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI) was strategically important for US-Soviet relations because it threatened to overturn Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) and deepened distrust during the Second Cold War. By proposing orbiting space satellites armed with lasers to intercept Soviet ICBMs in flight before hitting America, SDI bypassed the spirit of the 1972 ABM Treaty and threatened to render Soviet nuclear missiles obsolete. Consequently, elderly Kremlin leaders Yuri Andropov and Konstantin Chernenko feared Washington was seeking a nuclear first-strike shield, intensifying superpower hostility between 1983 and 1985.

Second, SDI was decisively important because it exposed the severe economic and technological weakness of the USSR, shifting Cold War leverage toward Washington. Already drained by fighting Mujahideen guerrillas in Afghanistan and starved of Western technology since 1980, the stagnant Soviet command economy lagged far behind America in microchips and supercomputers. Realising that matching "Star Wars" would bankrupt the Soviet state ultimately compelled Mikhail Gorbachev from 1985 to seek summit diplomacy and deep arms reductions.
tier_8m.verdict: AO1 Level 3 (4 marks) • AO2 Level 3 (4 marks). Two distinct, factually evidenced analytical paragraphs directly explaining importance for the second half of the question stem.

teacher_notes.primer: This KT 3.2 enquiry bridges the collapse of Détente in December 1979 and the high-stakes confrontation of the early 1980s. Emphasise two nuances: (1) the "Second Cold War" began under Democrat Jimmy Carter in January 1980 (Carter Doctrine, SALT 2 withdrawal, grain embargo, Operation Cyclone, Moscow boycott) before Ronald Reagan dramatically escalated it from 1981, and (2) SDI mattered far more for its economic/psychological impact on Moscow than its unbuilt 1983 hardware.

teacher_notes.curriculum_link: Key Topic 3.2: Flashpoints & the Second Cold War, 1979–85 — Saur Revolution & Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (Dec 1979), the Carter Doctrine (Jan 1980), SALT 2 withdrawal, grain embargo & 1980/1984 Olympic boycotts, Ronald Reagan's 'Evil Empire' & defence build-up, and the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI / 'Star Wars', March 1983) (Edexcel Paper 2 Demand: 8m Analytical Narrative & 16m Importance).
teacher_notes.hinge_question: Why did Ronald Reagan's March 1983 announcement of the Strategic Defence Initiative ('Star Wars') alarm Kremlin leaders so deeply when orbital laser shields did not even exist yet?
teacher_notes.hinge_guidance: Strong GCSE answers connect technology and economics: first, SDI threatened to overturn the 1972 ABM Treaty and MAD by giving America a theoretical shield from behind which it could strike first with impunity; second, aged Soviet leaders knew their stagnant command economy—already bleeding $3–8 billion a year in Afghanistan and lagging far behind Silicon Valley microchips and computers—could not afford another trillion-dollar space arms race without bankrupting consumer living standards. Also remind pupils that the 'Second Cold War' started under Jimmy Carter in January 1980 (Carter Doctrine, grain embargo, CIA Operation Cyclone aid to Mujahideen, Moscow Olympic boycott), before Reagan escalated it from 1981.

misconceptions.misconception: Thinking Leonid Brezhnev invaded Afghanistan in December 1979 aiming to conquer Persian Gulf oilfields.
misconceptions.correction: While Washington feared a Soviet push toward Persian Gulf oil (sparking the January 1980 Carter Doctrine), Brezhnev invaded defensively under the Brezhnev Doctrine after Hafizullah Amin murdered Taraki—fearing an Islamic Mujahideen victory on the USSR's border (especially after Iran's 1979 Islamic Revolution) would spread unrest into Soviet Central Asian republics.

misconceptions.misconception: Attributing every measure of the early 1980s 'Second Cold War' solely to Ronald Reagan after January 1981.
misconceptions.correction: GCSE Exam Tip: Give Jimmy Carter his exact January 1980 turning-point credit—shelving SALT 2, proclaiming the Carter Doctrine (Rapid Deployment Force for the Persian Gulf), banning US grain and high-tech exports, covertly arming the Mujahideen, and leading the 60+ nation boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

misconceptions.misconception: Writing that America actually built and deployed working 'Star Wars' laser satellites in space during the 1980s.
misconceptions.correction: SDI (announced 23 March 1983) remained an ambitious research programme plagued by technical hurdles, yet Soviet fear of American computing superiority gave Reagan decisive psychological and economic leverage at later summits with Gorbachev.

source_context.Source A: Entering the White House in January 1977 hoping to slash nuclear stockpiles and champion human rights, President Jimmy Carter admitted after Soviet paratroopers seized Kabul and killed Hafizullah Amin in late December 1979 that the invasion changed his view of Soviet intentions more dramatically in one week than the previous two and a half years. Within weeks Carter shelved SALT 2, embargoed US grain shipments, boosted defence spending, and authorised covert CIA aid to Afghan Mujahideen fighters. Hinge Question: Why did December 1979 transform Jimmy Carter overnight from an advocate of arms reductions into the architect of the Second Cold War?
source_context.Source B: Addressing Congress on 23 January 1980, President Carter declared the Carter Doctrine: any outside attempt to gain control of the Persian Gulf region—containing two-thirds of the world's exportable oil just 300 miles south of Soviet-occupied Afghanistan—would be repelled by any means necessary, including US military force via a new Rapid Deployment Force. Extending Truman's 1947 containment principle to the Persian Gulf, the speech formally buried 1970s Detente. Hinge Question: Why did Washington interpret Moscow's defensive intervention in Kabul as a direct strategic threat to Western oil supplies in the Straits of Hormuz?
source_context.Source C: After Soviet troops remained in Afghanistan past Carter's February 1980 deadline, the United States led over sixty nations—including West Germany, Japan, Canada, China, and many Islamic states—in boycotting the July–August 1980 Moscow Summer Olympics, spoiling Brezhnev's showcase of Communist prestige. Several NATO allies such as Britain and France still let athletes compete under the Olympic flag, and in 1984 Moscow retaliated by leading fourteen Eastern Bloc states in boycotting the Los Angeles Games. Hinge Question: What did the 1980 and 1984 Olympic boycotts achieve symbolically, and why did they fail to force Soviet troops out of Afghanistan?
source_context.Source D: Speaking to the National Association of Evangelicals in Orlando on 8 March 1983, President Ronald Reagan urged Western voters to reject 'nuclear freeze' campaigns and branded the Soviet Union an 'Evil Empire' and 'the focus of evil in the modern world', pairing moral confrontation with a $1 trillion defence build-up (B-1 bombers, Trident submarines, Pershing II and Cruise missiles in Europe, and the Reagan Doctrine). In Moscow, elderly KGB-trained leader Yuri Andropov feared Washington might actually be preparing a nuclear first strike (exemplified by the November 1983 Able Archer scare). Hinge Question: Was Reagan's 'Evil Empire' rhetoric reckless provocation that risked nuclear miscalculation, or deliberate pressure designed to force Moscow to negotiate from weakness?
source_context.Source E: Speaking live from the Oval Office on 23 March 1983—fifteen days after his 'Evil Empire' speech—President Reagan unveiled the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI), calling on US scientists to develop space- and ground-based laser and particle-beam interceptors to render nuclear ballistic missiles 'impotent and obsolete'. Because matching SDI required advanced microcomputers the stagnant Soviet command economy lacked, 'Star Wars' became Moscow's central obsession at the 1985–86 summits. Hinge Question: How did announcing SDI shift the Cold War competition onto technological terrain where the Soviet command economy simply could not compete?

narrative_blocks.title: Soviet Crisis & Exhaustion by 1985
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Soviet Crisis & Exhaustion by 1985
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 1: Soviet Crisis & Exhaustion by 1985 — Why was the Soviet Union facing severe internal crisis by March 1985?
paragraphs: [1.1] When 54-year-old **Mikhail Gorbachev** became General Secretary in **March 1985** after three elderly, ailing leaders (**Leonid Brezhnev**, **Yuri Andropov**, and **Konstantin Chernenko**) died in quick succession, the **Soviet Union** faced acute systemic crisis. Central planning bred industrial stagnation, falling oil revenues, rusting factories, and chronic urban food queues, while military spending swallowed roughly **25% of Soviet GDP** as Moscow struggled to match **Ronald Reagan**’s computerised **Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI)**.

[1.2] Abroad, the unwinnable war in **Afghanistan** bled the Soviet treasury of **$8 billion** every year and cost **15,000** Soviet soldiers’ lives. Worse still, the **April 1986 Chernobyl** nuclear power-plant explosion in Ukraine spread radioactive fallout across Europe and exposed Soviet technological decay and official cover-ups, convincing Gorbachev that survival required urgent reform.

narrative_blocks.title: Gorbachev’s Perestroika, Glasnost & Reform
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Gorbachev’s Perestroika, Glasnost & Reform
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 2: Gorbachev’s Perestroika, Glasnost & Reform — How did Gorbachev try to reform communism through Perestroika and Glasnost?
narrative_blocks.image_alt: Soviet General Secretary Mikhail Gorbachev speaking earnestly behind podium microphones in October 1986
narrative_blocks.caption: Soviet General Secretary Mikhail Gorbachev speaking at an international press conference in October 1986 as he promoted Perestroika, Glasnost, and diplomatic "New Thinking".
paragraphs: [2.1] Crucially, **Gorbachev** remained a committed Marxist-Leninist whose **‘New Thinking’** aimed to rescue and modernise **communism**, not abolish it. Under **Perestroika** (*economic restructuring*), Moscow relaxed rigid state production quotas, legalised small private and cooperative businesses in **1987–88**, welcomed joint ventures with Western firms, and sought deep cuts in nuclear weapons spending so money could rebuild civilian living standards.

[2.2] Alongside economic reform, Gorbachev launched **Glasnost** (*political openness*) to overcome entrenched party corruption and win public backing against conservative officials. State censorship loosened so newspapers and television could openly investigate Stalinist terror, economic waste, and **Chernobyl**; prominent exiled dissident physicist **Andrei Sakharov** was freed in **December 1986**, and **1989** brought multi-candidate elections to a new **Congress of People’s Deputies**.

narrative_blocks.title: Geneva, Reykjavik & Early Summit Diplomacy
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Geneva, Reykjavik & Early Summit Diplomacy
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 3: Geneva, Reykjavik & Early Summit Diplomacy — What did Reagan and Gorbachev achieve at Geneva and Reykjavik by October 1986?
paragraphs: [3.1] Because **Perestroika** required slashing crippling defence budgets, **Gorbachev** urgently pursued arms-control talks with US President **Ronald Reagan**. Meeting face-to-face for the first time at the **Geneva Summit** in **November 1985**, the two leaders stepped away from stiff advisers for private fireside conversations, forged warm personal rapport, and signed a landmark joint declaration stating that *"a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought"*.

[3.2] Eleven months later, at the **Reykjavik Summit** in Iceland in **October 1986**, Gorbachev stunned Washington by proposing a **50% cut** in strategic arsenals and eventually abolishing all ballistic nuclear missiles within ten years—provided Reagan confined **SDI** research strictly to the laboratory. Reagan refused to scrap **SDI**, causing **Reykjavik** to collapse without a treaty, yet both sides now trusted that sweeping disarmament was achievable.

narrative_blocks.title: The INF Treaty & Disarmament Breakthrough
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: The INF Treaty & Disarmament Breakthrough
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 4: The INF Treaty & Disarmament Breakthrough — What caused the December 1987 INF Treaty to mark a historic breakthrough?
narrative_blocks.image_alt: President Ronald Reagan and General Secretary Mikhail Gorbachev laughing together in tan armchairs beside a roaring stone fireplace at the Geneva Summit in November 1985
narrative_blocks.caption: Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev in fireside conversation at Villa Fleur d’Eau during the Geneva Summit (November 1985), establishing the personal trust that paved the way for the 1987 INF Treaty.
paragraphs: [4.1] In **June 1987**, speaking before West Berlin’s **Brandenburg Gate**, **Reagan** publicly challenged Moscow to prove its reformist sincerity: *"Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!"* Meanwhile, Soviet scientists quietly advised **Gorbachev** that America’s **SDI** laser shield was technologically unproven and far cheaper to counter than to match, persuading him in **February 1987** to uncouple missile cuts from **SDI**.

[4.2] Consequently, at the **Washington Summit** on **8 December 1987**, Reagan and Gorbachev signed the **Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces** (**INF Treaty**). Unlike **SALT 1**, which merely capped warhead growth, the **INF Treaty** eliminated an entire category of land-based nuclear and conventional missiles with ranges of **500 to 5,500 km**—destroying over **2,600** Soviet **SS-20** and US **Pershing II** and **Cruise** missiles under intrusive on-site inspections.

narrative_blocks.title: Leaving Afghanistan, UN Cuts & The Malta Summit
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Leaving Afghanistan, UN Cuts & The Malta Summit
narrative_blocks.act_title: Stage 5: Leaving Afghanistan, UN Cuts & The Malta Summit — In what ways did Soviet policy between 1988 and December 1989 end rivalry?
paragraphs: [5.1] Superpower reconciliation accelerated throughout **1988**. Visiting the **Moscow Summit** in **May–June 1988**, **Reagan** strolled across **Red Square** with **Gorbachev** and told reporters he no longer considered the **Soviet** Union an *"Evil Empire"* because it belonged to *"another time, another era"*. Addressing the **United Nations** on **7 December 1988**, Gorbachev announced unilateral cuts of **500,000 Red Army** troops and formally abandoned the **1968 Brezhnev Doctrine**, promising that **Soviet** tanks would never again crush Eastern European political choices.

[5.2] True to his word, Gorbachev completed the full withdrawal of **Soviet** forces from **Afghanistan** in **February 1989**, removing a major barrier to Western trust. Finally, aboard storm-tossed warships at the **Malta Summit** in **December 1989**, Gorbachev and new US President **George H. W. Bush** declared the Cold War officially over.

causal_domino_spine.title: From Soviet Stagnation to Ending Superpower Confrontation (1985–89)

stages.title: Soviet Crisis & Exhaustion by 1985
stages.trigger: Mikhail Gorbachev inherits stagnant Soviet industry, urban food queues, 25% of GDP absorbed by defence against SDI, the $8bn/year Afghan war, and the April 1986 Chernobyl disaster.
stages.because: Decades of central planning and geriatric rule under Brezhnev, Andropov, and Chernenko left the USSR unable to match American computer technology or feed its citizens adequately.
stages.therefore: Gorbachev concluded that the Soviet system faced collapse unless Moscow reformed at home and halted the arms race abroad.
stages.connective: To rescue Soviet socialism from within, Gorbachev launched twin domestic reforms...
stages.exam_link: Q3 Importance: Explains why economic exhaustion and SDI forced Moscow toward summit concessions.
stages.question: Why was the Soviet Union facing severe internal crisis by March 1985?

stages.title: Gorbachev’s Perestroika, Glasnost & Reform
stages.trigger: Gorbachev introduces Perestroika (economic restructuring and cooperative enterprise) alongside Glasnost (ending censorship, freeing Andrei Sakharov, and contesting elections).
stages.because: He believed openness and decentralised incentives would revitalise Communist productivity while freeing funds from military waste.
stages.therefore: Domestic reform required urgent international disarmament with Washington to slash Soviet military spending.
stages.connective: Seeking breathing space to pay for Perestroika, Gorbachev sat down directly with Ronald Reagan...
stages.exam_link: Q1 Consequence: Opened public criticism inside the USSR and drove Gorbachev to seek arms cuts.
stages.question: How did Gorbachev try to reform communism through Perestroika and Glasnost?

stages.title: Geneva, Reykjavik & Early Summit Diplomacy
stages.trigger: Reagan and Gorbachev establish fireside rapport at Geneva (November 1985) and nearly agree to abolish ballistic missiles at Reykjavik (October 1986) before stalling over SDI.
stages.because: Although Reagan refused to confine SDI research to the laboratory, both leaders genuinely wanted to prevent nuclear catastrophe.
stages.therefore: Personal trust replaced "Second Cold War" hostility, laying the blueprint for verifiable missile reductions.
stages.connective: Once Soviet physicists advised that SDI could be countered cheaply, Gorbachev broke the deadlock...
stages.exam_link: Q2 Narrative: Crucial bridge showing how Geneva and Reykjavik built trust despite no formal treaty.
stages.question: What did Reagan and Gorbachev achieve at Geneva and Reykjavik by October 1986?

stages.title: The INF Treaty & Disarmament Breakthrough
stages.trigger: Following Reagan’s June 1987 Brandenburg Gate speech, Reagan and Gorbachev sign the INF Treaty in Washington on 8 December 1987.
stages.because: Gorbachev uncoupled intermediate missile talks from SDI so the USSR could reduce European nuclear tension and cut military expenditure.
stages.therefore: For the first time in the Cold War, both superpowers physically destroyed an entire class of missiles (500–5,500 km) under mutual on-site inspections.
stages.connective: Armed with genuine nuclear verification, Gorbachev dismantled the remaining pillars of Soviet confrontation...
stages.exam_link: Q3 Importance: Eliminated over 2,600 SS-20, Pershing II, and Cruise missiles and proved mutual verification worked.
stages.question: What caused the December 1987 INF Treaty to mark a historic breakthrough?

stages.title: Leaving Afghanistan, UN Cuts & The Malta Summit
stages.actor: Gorbachev, Reagan & George H. W. Bush
stages.trigger: After the May 1988 Moscow Summit, Gorbachev announces 500,000 troop cuts and ends the Brezhnev Doctrine at the UN (Dec 1988), exits Afghanistan (Feb 1989), and meets Bush at Malta (Dec 1989).
stages.because: Moscow could no longer bankroll foreign occupations or coerce Eastern Europe while restructuring its domestic economy.
stages.therefore: Superpower ideological confrontation ended peacefully, unleashing dramatic revolutions across Eastern Europe.
stages.connective: Without Red Army tanks propping them up, Communist regimes across the Warsaw Pact immediately began to topple.
stages.exam_link: Q2 Narrative: Culmination of "New Thinking" ending the Afghan war, the Brezhnev Doctrine, and superpower rivalry.
stages.question: In what ways did Soviet policy between 1988 and December 1989 end rivalry?

sources.title: Source A: Soviet Soldiers and Armoured Column Withdrawing from Afghanistan (1988–89)
sources.image_alt: Soviet soldiers in field caps standing in formation before BTR armoured personnel carriers and main battle tanks during the military withdrawal from Afghanistan, 1988–89
sources.caption: Soviet troops and armoured vehicles assembling during the phased withdrawal from Afghanistan (May 1988 – February 1989) ordered by Mikhail Gorbachev.
sources.provenance: Soviet military press photograph by Mikhail Evstafiev documenting the 40th Army withdrawal from Afghanistan, 1988–89 (CC BY-SA 3.0).
sources.citation: RIA Novosti / Mikhail Evstafiev Documentary Collection.
sources.model_answer: Gorbachev called Afghanistan a "bleeding wound" that drained $8 billion a year and 15,000 Soviet lives needed for domestic economic restructuring, while pulling out by February 1989 removed the exact grievance that had destroyed Détente in 1979.
sources.context: Photographed during the final Soviet withdrawal across the Hairatan Friendship Bridge completed on 15 February 1989.
sources.source_context: Following the April 1988 Geneva Accords, Gorbachev withdrew all Soviet forces from Afghanistan by 15 February 1989, ending a nine-year war against US-armed Mujahideen fighters.

teacher_notes.source_context: Following the April 1988 Geneva Accords, Gorbachev withdrew all Soviet forces from Afghanistan by 15 February 1989, ending a nine-year war against US-armed Mujahideen fighters. **Hinge Question:** Which December 1979 decision by Leonid Brezhnev was Gorbachev reversing here?
teacher_notes.hinge_question: Which December 1979 decision by Leonid Brezhnev was Gorbachev reversing here?

sources.question: Why was the military withdrawal shown in Source A vital both for Gorbachev’s domestic Perestroika and for improving relations with the USA?

sources.title: Source B: Joint US–Soviet Statement at the Close of the Geneva Summit (21 November 1985)
sources.text: The sides, having discussed key security issues, and conscious of the special responsibility of the USSR and the US for maintaining peace, have agreed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. Recognising that any conflict between the USSR and the US could have catastrophic consequences, they emphasised the importance of preventing any war between them, whether nuclear or conventional. They will not seek to achieve military superiority.
sources.content: The sides, having discussed key security issues, and conscious of the special responsibility of the USSR and the US for maintaining peace, have agreed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. Recognising that any conflict between the USSR and the US could have catastrophic consequences, they emphasised the importance of preventing any war between them, whether nuclear or conventional. They will not seek to achieve military superiority.
sources.provenance: Official Joint Soviet–United States Statement issued by Mikhail Gorbachev and Ronald Reagan at Geneva, Switzerland, 21 November 1985.
sources.citation: Ronald Reagan Presidential Library, Public Papers of the Presidents (1985).
sources.model_answer: Just two years after Reagan branded the USSR an "Evil Empire" and launched SDI to regain strategic advantage, both leaders publicly renounced "military superiority" and agreed nuclear war could never be won, reopening regular summit diplomacy.
sources.context: Issued jointly at Geneva on 21 November 1985 after the first US–Soviet summit in six years (since Vienna in June 1979).
sources.source_context: Although Reagan refused to give up SDI at Geneva, five hours of private fireside talks convinced both Reagan and Gorbachev that the other genuinely feared nuclear miscalculation.

teacher_notes.source_context: Although Reagan refused to give up SDI at Geneva, five hours of private fireside talks convinced both Reagan and Gorbachev that the other genuinely feared nuclear miscalculation. **Hinge Question:** Even though Geneva produced no formal arms treaty, why do historians view this November 1985 summit as a turning point?
teacher_notes.hinge_question: Even though Geneva produced no formal arms treaty, why do historians view this November 1985 summit as a turning point?

sources.question: Why did the wording of Source B mark such a dramatic shift from the "Second Cold War" rhetoric of 1981–84?

sources.title: Source C: President Ronald Reagan Speaking at the Brandenburg Gate, West Berlin (12 June 1987)
sources.image_alt: President Ronald Reagan speaking behind bulletproof glass at a podium draped in black-red-gold banners in front of the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin, flanked by US and West German flags, 12 June 1987
sources.caption: President Ronald Reagan speaking before the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin on 12 June 1987 alongside West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, challenging Mikhail Gorbachev to "tear down this wall!"
sources.provenance: White House Photographic Office photograph, Brandenburg Gate, West Berlin, 12 June 1987 (Ronald Reagan Presidential Library / Public Domain).
sources.citation: Ronald Reagan Presidential Library & Museum / NARA.
sources.model_answer: Standing directly before the sealed concrete divide of Berlin, Reagan used maximum global media symbolism to challenge Gorbachev to prove that Soviet "openness" and "New Thinking" meant real freedom for Europeans rather than mere propaganda.
sources.context: Delivered on 12 June 1987 during Berlin’s 750th anniversary celebrations while US–Soviet negotiators drafted the INF Treaty.
sources.source_context: Senior US diplomats feared Reagan’s blunt challenge at the Brandenburg Gate would offend Gorbachev and derail arms talks, yet six months later Gorbachev travelled to Washington to sign the INF Treaty.

teacher_notes.source_context: Senior US diplomats feared Reagan’s blunt challenge at the Brandenburg Gate would offend Gorbachev and derail arms talks, yet six months later Gorbachev travelled to Washington to sign the INF Treaty. **Hinge Question:** Why had cautious State Department diplomats tried to cut the line "tear down this wall" from Reagan’s draft speech?
teacher_notes.hinge_question: Why had cautious State Department diplomats tried to cut the line "tear down this wall" from Reagan’s draft speech?

sources.question: Why did President Reagan choose the Brandenburg Gate (Source C) in June 1987 to test the sincerity of Gorbachev’s Glasnost?

sources.title: Source D: Gorbachev and Reagan Signing the INF Treaty at the White House (8 December 1987)
sources.image_alt: Mikhail Gorbachev on the left and Ronald Reagan on the right seated at a wooden table signing the bound INF Treaty volumes beneath US and Soviet flags in the East Room of the White House, 8 December 1987
sources.caption: General Secretary Mikhail Gorbachev and President Ronald Reagan signing the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty in the East Room of the White House, 8 December 1987.
sources.provenance: Official White House photograph, East Room, Washington D.C., 8 December 1987 (Ronald Reagan Presidential Library / Public Domain).
sources.citation: Ronald Reagan Presidential Library & Museum (NARA).
sources.model_answer: Whereas the 1972 SALT 1 agreement merely froze limits on certain launchers while warhead totals kept rising, the 1987 INF Treaty physically abolished an entire class of missiles (500–5,500 km range) and allowed American and Soviet inspectors onto each other’s bases.
sources.context: Signed at the Washington Summit on 8 December 1987, leading to the verified destruction of 2,692 Soviet and American missiles by June 1991.
sources.source_context: Reagan delighted Gorbachev at the signing ceremony by quoting the Russian proverb "Trust, but verify" ("Doveryai, no proveryai"), ushering in unprecedented mutual on-site weapons inspections.

teacher_notes.source_context: Reagan delighted Gorbachev at the signing ceremony by quoting the Russian proverb "Trust, but verify" ("Doveryai, no proveryai"), ushering in unprecedented mutual on-site weapons inspections. **Hinge Question:** What Russian proverb did Reagan repeatedly quote during the INF negotiations—"Doveryai, no proveryai"?
teacher_notes.hinge_question: What Russian proverb did Reagan repeatedly quote during the INF negotiations—"Doveryai, no proveryai"?

sources.question: How did the INF Treaty signed in Source D go far beyond earlier 1970s Détente agreements such as SALT 1?

sources.title: Source E: Mikhail Gorbachev’s Address to the United Nations General Assembly (7 December 1988)
sources.text: It is obvious to everyone that force and the threat of force neither can nor should be instruments of foreign policy... Freedom of choice is a universal principle that knows no exceptions... Today I can report to you that the Soviet Union has taken a decision to reduce its armed forces. Within the next two years their numerical strength will be reduced by 500,000 men, and the volume of conventional armaments will also be substantially cut.
sources.content: It is obvious to everyone that force and the threat of force neither can nor should be instruments of foreign policy... Freedom of choice is a universal principle that knows no exceptions... Today I can report to you that the Soviet Union has taken a decision to reduce its armed forces. Within the next two years their numerical strength will be reduced by 500,000 men, and the volume of conventional armaments will also be substantially cut.
sources.provenance: Speech delivered by Soviet General Secretary Mikhail Gorbachev to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, 7 December 1988.
sources.citation: United Nations Official Records, 43rd Session / CWIHP Archive.
sources.model_answer: By declaring that "freedom of choice... knows no exceptions" and renouncing military force while cutting 500,000 Red Army troops, Gorbachev signalled that Moscow had buried the 1968 Brezhnev Doctrine and would not send tanks if Eastern Europeans rejected Communist rule.
sources.context: Delivered in New York on 7 December 1988, stunning Western governments with unilateral conventional troop and tank withdrawals from Eastern Europe.
sources.source_context: Gorbachev’s December 1988 UN address dismantled the military threat that had kept Communist regimes in power across Eastern Europe since 1945–48 and crushed uprisings in 1956 and 1968.

teacher_notes.source_context: Gorbachev’s December 1988 UN address dismantled the military threat that had kept Communist regimes in power across Eastern Europe since 1945–48 and crushed uprisings in 1956 and 1968. **Hinge Question:** Why did reform movements in Poland and Hungary immediately test Gorbachev’s promise within months of this speech?

items.question: Which April 1978 coup first brought the pro-Soviet Communist PDPA party to power in Afghanistan?
items.explanation: In April 1978 the Saur Revolution installed Communist leader Nur Muhammad Taraki in Kabul, sparking fierce Islamic resistance.

items.question: Which vital oil-producing region did the January 1980 Carter Doctrine pledge US military force to defend?
items.explanation: On 23 January 1980 Carter warned that any outside bid to control the oil-rich Persian Gulf would be repelled by military force.

items.question: How many countries joined the US-led boycott of the 1980 Moscow Summer Olympics?
items.explanation: After Moscow ignored Carter’s February 1980 withdrawal deadline, over 60 countries boycotted the Moscow Summer Games.

items.question: When was Republican Ronald Reagan inaugurated as President of the United States?
items.explanation: Elected in November 1980, Ronald Reagan took office in January 1981 promising peace through overwhelming American strength.

items.question: What media nickname was given to Reagan’s 23 March 1983 Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI)?
items.explanation: Journalists dubbed SDI "Star Wars" after George Lucas’s sci-fi films because it proposed orbiting laser satellites in space.

items.question: Who overthrew and murdered Nur Muhammad Taraki in September 1979, alarming Leonid Brezhnev?
items.explanation: Prime Minister Hafizullah Amin seized power in September 1979, and Brezhnev suspected him of secretly contacting the USA.

items.question: Which major 1979 arms treaty did Jimmy Carter withdraw from the US Senate in January 1980?
items.explanation: Carter shelved Senate ratification of the June 1979 Vienna SALT 2 treaty in direct retaliation for the invasion of Afghanistan.

items.question: Which alternative athletics event did the USA host in Philadelphia for boycotting athletes in 1980?
items.explanation: Washington organised the rival Liberty Bell Classic in July 1980 for athletes from nations boycotting Moscow.

items.question: Roughly how much did Ronald Reagan commit to his massive US defence build-up in the early 1980s?
items.explanation: Reagan spent over $1 trillion across the early 1980s on B-1 bombers, Trident submarines, stealth aircraft, and Pershing II/Cruise missiles.

items.question: What was the core military purpose of the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI)?
items.answer: Destroy Soviet ICBMs in flight with space lasers
items.explanation: SDI aimed to intercept Soviet ballistic missiles from orbit before they could strike the USA, rendering Soviet ICBMs obsolete.

quiz.question: Roughly what proportion of Soviet GDP was consumed by military spending by 1985?

quiz.explanation: Trying to match US nuclear and computer spending drained roughly a quarter of Soviet GDP while civilian shops suffered acute shortages.

quiz.question: Roughly how much money did the war in Afghanistan cost the Soviet Union each year during the 1980s?
quiz.q: Roughly how much money did the war in Afghanistan cost the Soviet Union each year during the 1980s?
quiz.explanation: Fighting US-backed Mujahideen guerrillas in Afghanistan cost Moscow roughly $8 billion annually and claimed 15,000 Soviet soldiers’ lives.

quiz.question: Which April 1986 catastrophe in Ukraine exposed Soviet technological decay and official state cover-ups?

quiz.explanation: The explosion at the Chernobyl nuclear plant in April 1986 spread radiation across Europe and reinforced Gorbachev’s case for openness.

quiz.question: Which Russian term described Gorbachev’s policy of "political openness" and relaxed state censorship?
quiz.q: Which Russian term described Gorbachev’s policy of "political openness" and relaxed state censorship?

quiz.question: Which prominent exiled Soviet dissident physicist did Gorbachev release under Glasnost in December 1986?
quiz.q: Which prominent exiled Soviet dissident physicist did Gorbachev release under Glasnost in December 1986?

quiz.question: Why did the October 1986 Reykjavik Summit collapse without a signed disarmament treaty?

questions.question: 2. Write a narrative account analysing the key events in how Reagan and Gorbachev reduced superpower tensions in the years 1985–89. [8 marks]
stimulus: Gorbachev’s ‘new thinking’
Reagan and the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI)
bullet_points: Gorbachev’s ‘new thinking’
Reagan and the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI)
questions.prompt: Write 3 chronological paragraphs (Beginning: Soviet crisis, ‘new thinking’ & Nov 1985 Geneva Summit -> Middle: Oct 1986 Reykjavik SDI clash & Dec 1987 INF Treaty [own knowledge] -> Outcome: 1988 Moscow/UN speech, Feb 1989 Afghan exit & Dec 1989 Malta Summit).
questions.examiner_tip: Use Reykjavik (October 1986) to connect both stimulus points, then bring in the December 1987 INF Treaty, Gorbachev’s December 1988 UN speech, and the December 1989 Malta Summit as own knowledge.
questions.model:
Inheriting economic stagnation, the $8 billion-a-year Afghan war, and military costs absorbing 25% of Soviet GDP in March 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev launched ‘new thinking’—perestroika and glasnost—requiring urgent arms reductions. This directly led to the November 1985 Geneva Summit, where Ronald Reagan and Gorbachev built warm fireside trust and signed a joint statement declaring that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought".

At the October 1986 Reykjavik Summit, Gorbachev proposed sweeping ballistic missile abolition provided Reagan confined SDI to the laboratory, causing talks to collapse when Reagan refused to scrap SDI. However, once Soviet scientists advised in February 1987 that SDI was unproven and cheaper to counter than match, Gorbachev uncoupled disarmament from SDI—producing the December 1987 Washington Summit and the INF Treaty eliminating over 2,600 missiles (500–5,500 km range) under on-site inspections.

Consequently, reconciliation accelerated across 1988–89. After Reagan walked Red Square at the May 1988 Moscow Summit and dropped his "Evil Empire" label, Gorbachev used his December 1988 UN speech to cut 500,000 troops and abandon the Brezhnev Doctrine, withdrew all Soviet forces from Afghanistan in February 1989, and joined President George H. W. Bush at Malta in December 1989 to declare the Cold War over.

tier_2m.title: 2/8 Simple Narrative
tier_2m.text: When Gorbachev became Soviet leader in 1985 he introduced ‘new thinking’ because the Soviet economy was struggling. Although he and Reagan argued over Reagan’s SDI space shield at first, they later signed a nuclear missile treaty in 1987 and ended Cold War tensions by 1989.
tier_2m.verdict: AO2 Level 1 (1 mark) • AO1 Level 1 (1 mark). Basic story outlining reform, disagreement over SDI, and a 1987 treaty, but lacks named summits, specific terms, and analytical links.

tier_4m.title: 4/8 Sequenced Account
tier_4m.text:
In March 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev launched ‘new thinking’, introducing perestroika to restructure the stagnant Soviet economy and glasnost to allow greater political openness while seeking cuts in military spending.

Meanwhile, President Ronald Reagan insisted on keeping the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI) space laser programme, refusing Gorbachev’s demand to confine SDI research to laboratories before eventually negotiating nuclear reductions.
tier_4m.verdict: AO2 Level 2 (2 marks) • AO1 Level 2 (2 marks). Chronological description relying on the two stimulus points without explicit causal links or bridging own knowledge (Geneva, Reykjavik, the December 1987 INF Treaty, Afghanistan withdrawal, Malta), legally capping the response at 4/8 under the Pearson Edexcel mark scheme.

Consequently, reconciliation accelerated across 1988–89. questions.question: 3. Explain the importance of Reagan and Gorbachev for reducing superpower tensions in the years 1985–89. [8 marks]
questions.prompt: Write two distinct PEEL paragraphs explaining WHY both Reagan and Gorbachev were important for reducing tensions: (1) Personal summit rapport and pragmatic compromise delivering the 1987 INF Treaty, and (2) Ending ideological hostility and foreign military intervention by 1988–89.
questions.examiner_tip: Balance BOTH leaders in your explanation: show how Gorbachev’s reformist courage interacted with Reagan’s shift from "Evil Empire" pressure to warm summit partnership.
questions.model:
First, Reagan and Gorbachev were vitally important for reducing superpower tensions because their personal summit rapport and pragmatic compromises broke the nuclear deadlock of the Second Cold War. Stepping away from advisers for fireside talks at Geneva (November 1985), both leaders agreed nuclear war must never be fought, while their ambitious proposals at Reykjavik (October 1986) proved deep cuts were possible despite Reagan refusing to scrap SDI. When Gorbachev pragmatically uncoupled disarmament from SDI and Reagan welcomed verifiable cuts, they signed the December 1987 INF Treaty—destroying over 2,600 SS-20, Pershing II, and Cruise missiles under intrusive on-site inspections.

Second, both leaders were decisive because they dismantled the ideological hostility and military interventions that had sustained East–West confrontation. Determined to fund domestic perestroika rather than spend 25% of GDP on defence, Gorbachev cut 500,000 Red Army troops and abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine at the UN in December 1988 before withdrawing all Soviet troops from Afghanistan in February 1989. Crucially, Reagan matched Soviet reform with diplomatic warmth at the May 1988 Moscow Summit by renouncing his "Evil Empire" label, enabling George H. W. Bush and Gorbachev to declare the Cold War over at Malta in December 1989.

tier_2m.title: 2/8 Simple Statement
tier_2m.text: Reagan and Gorbachev were very important for reducing tensions between 1985 and 1989 because they got on well personally at summits, trusted each other, and agreed to destroy nuclear missiles instead of threatening war.
tier_2m.verdict: AO1 Level 1 (1 mark) • AO2 Level 1 (1 mark). Valid general point about personal trust and missile cuts, but lacks named summits, treaties, or policy details.

tier_4m.title: 4/8 Descriptive
tier_4m.text:
Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev met at four summits between 1985 and 1988: Geneva in 1985, Reykjavik in 1986, Washington in December 1987 where they signed the INF Treaty destroying missiles of 500–5,500 km range, and Moscow in May 1988.

During the same years, Gorbachev introduced perestroika and glasnost inside the USSR, announced cuts of 500,000 troops at the United Nations in December 1988, and withdrew Soviet soldiers from Afghanistan in February 1989.
tier_4m.verdict: AO1 Level 2 (2 marks) • AO2 Level 2 (2 marks). Accurate factual detail across two paragraphs, but describes events rather than explicitly explaining why Reagan and Gorbachev mattered specifically for reducing superpower tensions.

teacher_notes.primer: This enquiry bridges the "Second Cold War" (Lesson 10) and the 1989 revolutions (Lesson 12). Ensure pupils grasp two core Edexcel distinctions: (1) Gorbachev introduced Perestroika and Glasnost to SAVE and modernise Soviet communism—not to destroy it; and (2) Reagan’s role combined early 1981–84 economic/technological pressure (SDI exposing Soviet exhaustion) with pragmatic 1985–88 summit flexibility once Gorbachev offered verifiable cuts.

teacher_notes.hinge_question: Why did the October 1986 Reykjavik Summit—which broke up without an agreement over SDI—actually pave the way for the historic December 1987 INF Treaty?
teacher_notes.hinge_guidance: Strong GCSE answers explain that at Reykjavik Gorbachev and Reagan stunned aides by coming within a hair's breadth of abolishing all ballistic missiles before Gorbachev insisted Reagan confine SDI to the laboratory for ten years and Reagan refused; yet Reykjavik built deep personal trust, proved sweeping nuclear abolition was negotiable, and once Soviet scientists advised Gorbachev that SDI was too technically flawed and easily overwhelmed to justify blocking a deal, Gorbachev untied the INF package—leading directly to the December 1987 Washington INF Treaty eliminating an entire class of nuclear missiles (500–5,500 km range) with on-site inspections.

misconceptions.misconception: Believing Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in March 1985 intending to destroy communism and break up the USSR.
misconceptions.correction: Gorbachev was a committed Leninist reformer: Perestroika (economic restructuring), Glasnost (openness), ending the Afghan war, and cutting nuclear arms aimed to rescue and modernise Soviet socialism by shifting scarce roubles from missiles to consumer goods and technology.

misconceptions.misconception: Confusing Perestroika with Glasnost in Paper 2 answers.
misconceptions.correction: GCSE Exam Tip: Perestroika = economic restructuring (allowing small private cooperatives, enterprise incentives, foreign investment, cutting military waste); Glasnost = political openness (relaxing censorship, exposing corruption and Stalinist crimes—dramatically accelerated after the April 1986 Chernobyl nuclear cover-up).

misconceptions.misconception: Treating the December 1987 INF Treaty as just another missile freeze like 1972's SALT 1.
misconceptions.correction: Unlike SALT 1 and 2 (which only capped launcher ceilings), the 1987 Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty was the first agreement actually to scrap and physically destroy an entire category of existing US and Soviet nuclear missiles (2,692 Pershing II, Cruise, and SS-20 missiles) verified by mutual on-site inspections.

teacher_notes.send_adaptation: Project the Brezhnev Stagnation to New Thinking Concept Diagram alongside the Visual Story Sheet while playing Studio Audio. Have learners map the five summits cleanly onto the Workbook Verso Spine using brief memory hooks: Geneva 1985 (Fireside rapport), Reykjavik 1986 (SDI deadlock), Washington 1987 (INF signed), Moscow 1988 ('Evil Empire' dropped), Malta 1989 (Bush & Gorbachev declare Cold War over).
teacher_notes.stretch_challenge: Assess whether the end of superpower confrontation between 1985 and 1989 owed more to Ronald Reagan's 'peace through strength' pressure (SDI and defence spending) or to Mikhail Gorbachev's courage in abandoning decades of Soviet orthodoxy.

source_context.Source A: Completed on 15 February 1989 across the Hairatan Friendship Bridge, Mikhail Gorbachev's phased withdrawal of the Soviet 40th Army ended a nine-year war in Afghanistan that had killed ~15,000 Soviet troops and drained billions of roubles a year—what Gorbachev called the USSR's 'bleeding wound'. Leaving Afghanistan removed a major obstacle to US–Soviet trust while signalling unmistakably to Eastern European Communist leaders that Moscow would no longer prop up unpopular regimes by military force. Hinge Question: Why was withdrawing Soviet troops from Afghanistan essential to both halves of Gorbachev's domestic and foreign 'New Thinking'?
source_context.Source B: Issued at the close of their first face-to-face summit in Geneva on 21 November 1985—after Reagan and Gorbachev stepped away from advisers for private fireside chats—this joint statement famously declared that 'a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought' and pledged 50% strategic arms cuts in principle. Although no binding treaty was signed at Geneva, personal chemistry between the two leaders broke the icy deadlock of the Second Cold War. Hinge Question: Why did establishing personal trust at Geneva in November 1985 matter so much even without a formal arms treaty?
source_context.Source C: Speaking before West Berlin's Brandenburg Gate on 12 June 1987 alongside Chancellor Helmut Kohl, President Reagan directly challenged the Soviet leader's reformist credentials: 'Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!' Delivered six months before the Washington INF Summit, Reagan combined public moral pressure over European division with active private arms-control diplomacy. Hinge Question: How did Reagan manage to challenge Soviet rule at the Brandenburg Gate in June 1987 without derailing the INF Treaty negotiations signed that December?
source_context.Source D: Signed by Reagan and Gorbachev in the White House East Room on 8 December 1987, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty eliminated all land-based nuclear and conventional missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 km—leading to the verified destruction of 2,692 Soviet SS-20 and US Pershing II/Cruise missiles with unprecedented on-site inspections ('trust, but verify'). Gorbachev broke the Reykjavik deadlock after Soviet scientists confirmed SDI was far less realistic than feared and Soviet economic restructuring urgently needed defence cuts. Hinge Question: Why is the December 1987 INF Treaty widely judged a far deeper breakthrough than SALT 1 in 1972?
source_context.Source E: Addressing a stunned UN General Assembly in New York on 7 December 1988, Mikhail Gorbachev announced unilateral cuts of 500,000 Soviet troops and withdrawing 50,000 soldiers and 5,000 tanks from Eastern Europe, declaring that force could no longer be an instrument of foreign policy and 'freedom of choice is a universal principle that knows no exceptions'. In a single speech, Gorbachev publicly buried the 1968 Brezhnev Doctrine. Hinge Question: Once Gorbachev promised 'universal freedom of choice' and tank withdrawals at the UN in December 1988, could Eastern Europe's Communist dictatorships survive?

side_a.label: Gorbachev’s ‘New Thinking’
points: Proposed bold 50% strategic cuts at Reykjavik and dropped the SDI precondition in February 1987.
Accepted intrusive on-site inspections under the December 1987 INF Treaty.
Unilaterally cut 500,000 troops at the UN (1988), withdrew from Afghanistan (1989), and ended the Brezhnev Doctrine.

side_b.label: Reagan’s Strength & Flexibility
points: Launched the $1 trillion defence build-up and SDI (1983), exposing Soviet economic and computer exhaustion.
Refused to trade away SDI at Reykjavik (1986), negotiating from technological strength.
Pivoted warmly from "Evil Empire" rhetoric to personal trust at Geneva, Washington, and Moscow.

video.title: Perestroika & Glasnost (The End of the Soviet Union) | Simple History
video.teacher_guidance: Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–06:30 | Lesson Phase: Starter Hook | Tone Alert: Visual explanation of Soviet economic stagnation in 1985, the 1986 Chernobyl disaster, and Gorbachev's twin domestic reforms of Perestroika and Glasnost.
video.viewing_task:
[01:15] Domestic Crisis: What economic and technological problems convinced Mikhail Gorbachev that the USSR urgently needed reform in 1985–86?
[04:10] Reform Aims: Distinguish clearly between Perestroika and Glasnost—and explain why Gorbachev introduced them to save communism rather than end it.
video.model_answer: By 1985–86 the USSR suffered industrial stagnation, food shortages, heavy military spending (~25% of GDP), the costly Afghan war, and the April 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster. Perestroika restructured the economy by allowing small private cooperatives and lower arms spending, while Glasnost relaxed state censorship so public scrutiny could overcome corrupt Communist Party hardliners.

video.title: The Cold War: Strategic Defence Initiative and the Summits 1985–1988 | I'm Stuck — GCSE Revision
video.teacher_guidance: Recommended Watch Window: 02:30–10:05 | Lesson Phase: Enquiry Depth | Tone Alert: Step-by-step GCSE revision sequence tracing Geneva (1985), Reykjavik (1986), Washington and the INF Treaty (Dec 1987), Moscow (1988), and Malta (1989).
video.viewing_task:
[03:40] Summit Comparison: Why did the October 1986 Reykjavik Summit break down without a treaty despite personal rapport built at Geneva in 1985?
[06:50] Breakthrough: Why was the December 1987 INF Treaty in Washington a far deeper disarmament milestone than SALT 1?
video.model_answer: At Reykjavik, Gorbachev offered 50% strategic cuts only if Reagan restricted SDI ('Star Wars') to laboratory research, which Reagan refused. Once Gorbachev uncoupled missile talks from SDI in 1987, the Washington INF Treaty eliminated an entire class of land-based nuclear and conventional missiles (ranges 500–5,500 km, over 2,600 SS-20, Pershing II, and Cruise missiles) verified by on-site inspections.
