lessons.subtitle: People-Power on the Pnyx, Ostrakon Shards & Kleroterion Juries, Sparta's Agoge Barracks, and Girls' & Women's Lives
lessons.enquiryQuestion: How different was daily life in democratic Athens and warrior Sparta?
lessons.enquiry_question: How different was daily life in democratic Athens and warrior Sparta?
lessons.prologue: Climb the windy Pnyx hill in Athens to vote by raising your hand, or march barefoot at age seven into Sparta's tough agoge barracks! Compare pottery ostraka and marble jury machines with bronze helmets — and discover a big surprise about Spartan girls and women.
lessons.blurb: Climb the windy Pnyx hill in Athens to vote by raising your hand, or march barefoot at age seven into Sparta's tough agoge barracks! Compare pottery ostraka and marble jury machines with bronze helmets — and discover a big surprise about Spartan girls and women.

teacher_notes.primer: This second Key Stage 2 enquiry builds civic comparison skills by contrasting sea-trading democratic Athens with land-locked military Sparta (c. 508–430 BC). Primary pupils investigate how Athenian direct democracy worked on the Pnyx hill, through pottery ostrakon ballots and the marble kleroterion jury machine — while critically spotting who was excluded (women, enslaved people, and foreign-born metics). Pupils then contrast Sparta's two kings, elders, helot farmworkers, and age-7 agoge barracks, uncovering the striking historical twist that Spartan girls trained outdoors and Spartan women owned land and spoke far more freely than Athenian women!

objectives.objective: Explain how direct democracy worked in Athens from c. 508 BC — and identify which residents were excluded from voting.
objectives.primer: Investigate Assembly debates on the Pnyx, pottery ostrakon banishment votes, the marble kleroterion, and excluded women, enslaved people, and metics.
objectives.question: Why was Athens's 'people-power' revolutionary in 508 BC, yet unfair to more than half the city's adults?

objectives.objective: Describe how land-locked Sparta was ruled by two kings and elders and how boys were trained in the agoge from age seven.
objectives.primer: Examine Sparta's mountain valley, helot farm labour, full-time warrior citizens, and harsh barefoot agoge barracks.
objectives.question: Why did Sparta turn every citizen boy into a full-time soldier starting at just seven years old?

objectives.objective: Compare growing up as a boy or girl in Athens versus Sparta to reach an evidenced historical judgement.
objectives.primer: Contrast Athenian boys' schooling and Athenian women's indoor lives with Spartan girls' athletics and Spartan women's land ownership.
objectives.question: Why might an Ancient Greek boy choose Athens, while an Ancient Greek girl might prefer growing up in Sparta?

source_context.Source A: Elected general year after year by Athens’s citizen Assembly, Pericles championed direct democracy and introduced daily pay so poorer rowers and cobblers could serve on juries! **Hinge Question:** Why did Pericles’s sculptor show him wearing a soldier’s helmet tilted calmly back rather than wearing a royal gold crown?
source_context.Source B: Dug up in the Agora of Athens and dated to 461 BC, this everyday clay pot shard has "Cimon son of Miltiades" scratched into its surface. **Hinge Question:** Why did Athenians scratch names onto cheap broken pot shards to banish ambitious politicians for ten years?
source_context.Source C: Athenians worried rich people might bribe judges if they knew who would sit on the jury — so each morning they slotted citizens’ bronze tickets into a marble kleroterion! **Hinge Question:** How did picking 500 jurors at random on the morning of a trial stop wealthy people from cheating or bribing the court?
source_context.Source D: While citizen farmers in Athens fought only when wars broke out, Spartan men trained full-time from age seven to fight inside a bronze-armoured shield wall! **Hinge Question:** What must it have felt like — for sight, hearing, and breathing — fighting inside a heavy bronze helmet like Source D?

vocab.definition: Rule by the people (from Greek demokratia = people-power), invented in Athens around 508 BC so male citizens voted directly on laws.
A broken pottery shard scratched with a politician's name by Athenian voters to banish dangerous leaders from the city for ten years.
A slotted marble machine in Athens that used falling black and white balls to pick 500 courtroom jurors fairly by chance.

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: Around 508 BC, Athens created direct [Democracy], where male citizens debated on the Pnyx, scratched a pottery [Ostrakon] to banish bossy leaders, and picked juries randomly with a marble [Kleroterion] — though women, enslaved people, and foreign [Metics] could not vote. Rival Sparta sent seven-year-old boys into tough [Agoge] barracks instead!

narrative_blocks.title: c. 508–430 BC: People-Power on the Pnyx & Who Was Left Out
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.1] Around **508 BC**, citizens in sea-trading **Athens** invented **demokratia** [dem-oh-KRAH-tee-uh], meaning people-power! Instead of obeying kings, adult male citizens climbed the rocky **Pnyx** [puh-NIKS] hill every few days. Thousands debated war and taxes before raising hands to vote on every law. Voters even scratched bossy leaders' names onto broken pottery **ostrakon** [OS-truh-kon] shards to banish them for ten years.

[2.2] Athens also slotted bronze name-tickets into a marble **kleroterion** [kler-oh-TEER-ee-on] machine. Falling balls picked five hundred jurors fairly by chance! Yet **direct democracy** shut out **women**, **enslaved people**, and foreign **metics**.

Voters even scratched bossy leaders' names onto broken pottery **ostrakon** [OS-truh-kon] shards to banish them for ten years.

[2.2] Athens also slotted bronze name-tickets into a marble **kleroterion** [kler-oh-TEER-ee-on] machine. Falling balls picked five hundred jurors fairly by chance! Yet **direct democracy** shut out **women**, **enslaved people**, and foreign **metics**.

narrative_blocks.title: Two Kings & Tough Barracks: Growing Up Inside Warrior Sparta
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.3] Far inland beneath snowy Mount Taygetos lay rival **Sparta**. Spartans cared little for speeches, silver coins, or theatres. Instead, citizens prized strict discipline and quiet obedience. **Two kings** led Sparta's army beside a council of older nobles. Conquered farmworkers called **helots** grew crops so Spartan men trained full-time.

[2.4] At **seven years old**, boys left home for harsh barracks called the **agoge** [uh-GOH-gay]. Barefoot in winter, they slept on river reeds and ate dark broth! Hungry boys even sneaked extra food to practise stealth.

sources.question: Why does Pericles wear a raised soldier’s helmet instead of a king’s crown in Source A?
sources.model_answer: Democratic Athens had no kings! Citizens elected Pericles as both a persuasive Assembly speaker and an army general, so the tilted helmet showed civic duty rather than royal rule.

narrative_blocks.title: Boys, Girls & Women: Comparing Daily Life in Athens and Sparta
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.5] Childhood felt wildly different depending on whether you grew up in Athens or Sparta! Wealthy **Athenian boys** paid tutors to teach reading, geometry, poetry, music, and graceful sport. **Athenian girls**, however, rarely went to school, learning spinning, weaving, and housework indoors under male guardians.

[2.6] In **Sparta**, girls trained outdoors at running, wrestling, and throwing the javelin! Because Spartan husbands lived away in army barracks, **Spartan women** ran farms and owned land themselves. Athenians gasped to hear confident Spartan women speaking openly in public! Spartans believed strong mothers raised the bravest soldiers.

tasks.title: 1. Primary Evidence Detective
tasks.question: Why does Pericles wear a raised soldier’s helmet instead of a king’s crown in Source A?
tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, Pericles wears a raised soldier’s helmet rather than a king’s crown because Athens...
hints: Remember how democratic Athens was governed around 430 BC compared with kingdoms.
Explain that citizens elected Pericles as an army general (strategos) and Assembly speaker.
Show why a tilted hoplite helmet symbolised elected civic duty rather than royal power.
tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, Pericles wears a raised soldier’s helmet rather than a king’s crown because Athens was a democracy with zero kings! Citizens voted each year to elect Pericles as an army general (strategos) and listened to his speeches on the Pnyx hill, so the helmet showed civic service.

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain how Athenian democracy differed from modern British democracy — especially regarding who could vote!
tasks.starter: Although Athens gave us the word democracy around 508 BC, voting there worked very differently from today because...
hints: Explain that Athens used direct democracy — adult male citizens climbed the Pnyx hill to vote on every law themselves.
List the huge groups shut out of voting in Athens: all women, enslaved people, and foreign-born metics.
Contrast this with modern Britain, where both women and men vote as equals to elect Members of Parliament!
tasks.model_answer: Although Athens gave us the word democracy around 508 BC, voting there worked very differently from today because Athenians practised direct democracy, meaning adult male citizens gathered on the Pnyx hill to vote in person on every single law and war decision. However, Athenian democracy excluded most of the city's population: women, enslaved people, and foreign-born traders called metics had zero right to vote! Today, adult women and men vote equally to elect representatives.

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did democratic Athens and warrior Sparta govern their cities differently, and whose lives were freer in each polis?
tasks.starter: Choosing whether to grow up in Ancient Athens or Ancient Sparta depends hugely on whether you were a boy or a girl...
hints: Weigh up the best and worst parts of Athens (schooling, poetry, and Pnyx voting for men — yet women and enslaved people excluded).
Weigh up the best and worst parts of Sparta (harsh age-7 agoge barracks and helot labour — yet outdoor athletics and land rights for women).
Reach a clear historian's verdict showing why a citizen boy might pick Athens while a girl might prefer Sparta!
tasks.model_answer: Choosing whether to grow up in Ancient Athens or Ancient Sparta depends hugely on whether you were a boy or a girl! A citizen boy would probably pick Athens, where he studied reading, music, and poetry instead of leaving home at seven for Sparta's freezing barefoot agoge barracks, and grew up to vote freely on the Pnyx hill. However, a girl might strongly prefer Sparta! While Athenian girls stayed mostly indoors weaving and could never vote or own property, Spartan girls trained outdoors in athletics and grew into confident Spartan women who ran estates, owned land, and spoke freely in public.

quiz.question: Around 508 BC, what bold new system of government did Athens invent, meaning "people-power"?
quiz.q: Around 508 BC, what bold new system of government did Athens invent, meaning "people-power"?
quiz.explanation: Combining demos (people) and kratos (power), Athenian demokratia let adult male citizens vote directly on laws.

quiz.question: Which rocky hillside in Athens did thousands of male citizens climb every few days to debate and vote?
quiz.q: Which rocky hillside in Athens did thousands of male citizens climb every few days to debate and vote?
quiz.explanation: Adult male Athenian citizens gathered outdoors on the rocky Pnyx hill to debate war, taxes, and laws before voting by hand.

quiz.question: For how many years was an overly bossy Athenian politician banished if citizens voted him out on pottery ostrakon shards?
quiz.q: For how many years was an overly bossy Athenian politician banished if citizens voted him out on pottery ostrakon shards?
quiz.explanation: Scratching a leader’s name onto enough broken ostrakon pot shards banished him from Athens for ten years to protect democracy.

quiz.question: Why did Athenians use a slotted marble kleroterion machine with falling balls to choose 500 court jurors?
quiz.q: Why did Athenians use a slotted marble kleroterion machine with falling balls to choose 500 court jurors?
options: To pick jurors randomly on the morning of a trial so nobody could bribe them
To count silver coins collected at the harbour gate
To measure olive oil poured into clay storage jars
To time footraces during religious festivals
quiz.answer: To pick jurors randomly on the morning of a trial so nobody could bribe them
quiz.a: To pick jurors randomly on the morning of a trial so nobody could bribe them
quiz.explanation: Picking 500 jurors by pure chance right before a trial stopped wealthy defendants from bribing judges.

quiz.question: Which three large groups living in Athens were completely shut out from voting in its direct democracy?
quiz.q: Which three large groups living in Athens were completely shut out from voting in its direct democracy?
options: Women, enslaved people, and foreign-born metics
quiz.answer: Women, enslaved people, and foreign-born metics
quiz.a: Women, enslaved people, and foreign-born metics
quiz.explanation: Only adult male Athenian citizens could vote; women, enslaved people, and foreign-born residents called metics were excluded.

quiz.question: How was inland Sparta’s government led differently from democratic Athens?
quiz.q: How was inland Sparta’s government led differently from democratic Athens?
options: By lottery tickets drawn every morning
By two kings alongside a council of older nobles
quiz.answer: By two kings alongside a council of older nobles
quiz.a: By two kings alongside a council of older nobles
quiz.explanation: Two warrior kings led Sparta’s army alongside a strict council of older nobles.

quiz.question: Who were the "helots" in Ancient Sparta?
quiz.q: Who were the "helots" in Ancient Sparta?
options: Conquered local farmworkers forced to grow food for Sparta
quiz.answer: Conquered local farmworkers forced to grow food for Sparta
quiz.a: Conquered local farmworkers forced to grow food for Sparta
quiz.explanation: Conquered helots worked the fields around Sparta so male Spartan citizens could train full-time as soldiers.

quiz.question: At what young age did Spartan boys leave their families to enter the tough agoge army barracks?
quiz.q: At what young age did Spartan boys leave their families to enter the tough agoge army barracks?
quiz.explanation: At just seven years old, Spartan boys left home to live and train inside the harsh agoge military barracks.

quiz.question: What tough conditions did Spartan boys endure inside the agoge barracks?
quiz.q: What tough conditions did Spartan boys endure inside the agoge barracks?
options: Sleeping on feather beds and eating sweet honey cakes
Going barefoot in winter, sleeping on river reeds, and eating plain dark broth
Sailing wooden merchant ships to Egypt every summer
Carving marble statues on the Acropolis
quiz.answer: Going barefoot in winter, sleeping on river reeds, and eating plain dark broth
quiz.a: Going barefoot in winter, sleeping on river reeds, and eating plain dark broth
quiz.explanation: Spartan boys trained barefoot in winter, slept on rough river reeds, and ate plain dark broth to build endurance.

quiz.question: According to Source A, which elected Athenian general paid poorer citizens a daily wage so they could serve on juries?
quiz.q: According to Source A, which elected Athenian general paid poorer citizens a daily wage so they could serve on juries?
quiz.explanation: Pericles championed Athenian democracy and introduced daily jury pay so poorer rowers and cobblers could take part.

quiz.question: What subjects did wealthy Athenian boys study with private tutors?
quiz.q: What subjects did wealthy Athenian boys study with private tutors?
options: Reading, geometry, poetry, music, and athletics
quiz.answer: Reading, geometry, poetry, music, and athletics
quiz.a: Reading, geometry, poetry, music, and athletics
quiz.explanation: Wealthy Athenian families paid tutors to teach boys reading, geometry, poetry, music, and graceful athletics.

quiz.question: How were most girls raised in classical Athens compared with boys?
quiz.q: How were most girls raised in classical Athens compared with boys?
options: They stayed mostly indoors learning spinning, weaving, and household skills
They entered army barracks at age seven
They voted on laws every week on the Pnyx hill
They captained wooden warships at sea
quiz.answer: They stayed mostly indoors learning spinning, weaving, and household skills
quiz.a: They stayed mostly indoors learning spinning, weaving, and household skills
quiz.explanation: Athenian girls rarely attended school, instead learning spinning, weaving, and running a household indoors under male guardians.

quiz.question: Which outdoor sports did Spartan girls practise to grow strong and athletic?
quiz.q: Which outdoor sports did Spartan girls practise to grow strong and athletic?
options: Running, wrestling, and throwing the javelin

quiz.question: Why did Spartan women enjoy far greater freedom to run farms and own land than Athenian women?
quiz.q: Why did Spartan women enjoy far greater freedom to run farms and own land than Athenian women?
options: Athens had no farms or countryside at all
Spartan women were allowed to vote on the Pnyx hill
Spartan husbands spent years away in army barracks, so women managed estates
Greek gods forbade men in Sparta from speaking
quiz.answer: Spartan husbands spent years away in army barracks, so women managed estates
quiz.a: Spartan husbands spent years away in army barracks, so women managed estates
quiz.explanation: With Spartan men living in military barracks or away on campaign, Spartan women ran farms, owned land, and spoke openly in public.

Narrow eye slits and covered ears made it hot, dark, and hard to hear inside

lessons.prologue: Gaze up at snowy Mount Olympus where Zeus hurls thunderbolts, climb misty Delphi to hear the Oracle's riddles, and spot Heracles battling the Hydra on clay vases! Then race down Olympia's dusty track in 776 BC under the Sacred Truce.
lessons.blurb: Gaze up at snowy Mount Olympus where Zeus hurls thunderbolts, climb misty Delphi to hear the Oracle's riddles, and spot Heracles battling the Hydra on clay vases! Then race down Olympia's dusty track in 776 BC under the Sacred Truce.

teacher_notes.primer: This third Key Stage 2 enquiry explores how shared religion, mythology, and pan-Hellenic festivals shaped everyday Greek culture (776–400 BC). Primary pupils meet the Twelve Olympians on Mount Olympus (Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Hermes), discover why marble temples like the Parthenon housed sacred statues while sacrifices happened outdoors, and visit the Oracle at Delphi. Pupils read Greek myths directly off black-figure and red-figure clay vases (Heracles and the Hydra, Odysseus, Medusa) before investigating the Ancient Olympic Games held every four years at Olympia from 776 BC under the Sacred Truce (Ekecheiria).

items.question: Why did Ancient Greece split into independent poleis, and what were the two main town spaces inside a polis?
items.answer: Steep mountains and Aegean islands divided cities; each polis had a high Acropolis and an open Agora marketplace
items.explanation: Even while governing themselves separately, Greek city-states shared similar hill fortresses and bustling marketplaces.

items.question: What united proud Hellenes across rival city-states around 800–500 BC?
items.answer: A shared Greek language, the 24-letter Greek alphabet adapted from Phoenicians, shared gods, and sea trade
items.explanation: Speaking and writing Greek while worshipping the same gods bound distant islanders and mainlanders together.

items.question: Where did adult male Athenian citizens gather to debate and vote in their direct democracy, and who was shut out?
items.answer: On the rocky Pnyx hill; women, enslaved people, and foreign-born metics were excluded from voting
items.explanation: Invented around 508 BC, Athenian demokratia gave male citizens direct votes while barring more than half the population.

items.question: In Athens, what was the difference between a pottery 'ostrakon' and a marble 'kleroterion'?
items.answer: An ostrakon potsherd banished bossy leaders for ten years; a kleroterion machine picked 500 jurors fairly by chance
items.explanation: Both clever inventions stopped ambitious or wealthy citizens from seizing unfair control in Athens.

items.question: What was Sparta's 'agoge', and how did Spartan women have more freedom than Athenian women?
items.answer: Sparta's harsh military barracks for boys from age 7; Spartan women trained outdoors as girls, owned land, and spoke freely
items.explanation: Because Spartan husbands lived in barracks, Spartan women managed estates and owned property unlike secluded Athenian women.

narrative_blocks.title: Twelve Gods on Snowy Mount Olympus & Gleaming Marble Temples
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.1] Religion shaped every single day in Ancient Greece! Greeks believed twelve immortal gods ruled from snowy **Mount Olympus**, Greece's tallest peak. **Zeus** hurled thunderbolts beside queen **Hera**, while **Poseidon** shook the seas. Wise **Athena** guarded Athens, twins **Apollo** and **Artemis** loved music and hunting, and **Hermes** wore winged sandals.

[3.2] Cities built marble homes for their gods, like Athens's **Parthenon**. Inside stood a tall gold-and-ivory statue of **Athena**. Crowds worshipped outdoors at stone **altars**, pouring wine and roasting meat so sweet smoke rose skyward!

narrative_blocks.title: Riddles at Mountain Delphi & Hero Myths on Painted Clay Vases
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.3] Before wars or sea trips, leaders climbed mountain **Delphi** to ask Apollo's **Oracle**. Inside the temple, a priestess called the **Pythia** [PITH-ee-uh] spoke mysterious riddles from Apollo! Generals studied every clue carefully before marching their armies out. Storytellers also chanted exciting **myths** about brave heroes and fierce monsters.

[3.4] Families loved hearing how strong **Heracles** [HER-uh-kleez] fought the many-headed **Hydra**. Clever **Odysseus** [oh-DISS-ee-us] outwitted giants, and Perseus faced snake-haired **Medusa**. Potters painted those tales onto glossy **black-figure** and **red-figure** clay vases. Every painted jar turned Greek supper tables into lively storybooks!

narrative_blocks.title: 776 BC at Olympia: The Sacred Truce, Chariots & Olive Crowns
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.5] Religion also inspired the world's most famous sports festival! Every four summers from **776 BC**, Greeks met at **Olympia** for **Zeus** at the **Ancient Olympic Games**. Messengers first announced a **Sacred Truce** called **Ekecheiria** [ek-eh-KY-ree-uh]. Fighting paused across Greece so athletes and crowds travelled safely.

[3.6] Athletes swore beside Zeus's smoky altar never to cheat. Crowds cheered the barefoot **stadion** sprint, **discus**, **javelin**, **wrestling**, and **chariot racing**! Champions won no gold medals at Olympia. Instead, winners wore a wild-olive crown called a **kotinos** [KOT-ih-nos] that brought glory home.

tasks.title: 1. Primary Evidence Detective
tasks.question: Why can’t historians be certain whether Source A shows Zeus or Poseidon?
tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, historians cannot be certain whether this bronze statue is Zeus or Poseidon because...
hints: Compare how Greek sculptors pictured the bearded Olympian brothers Zeus and Poseidon.
Look closely at the statue’s empty raised right hand poised to hurl something.
Explain what missing bronze object vanished in the Cape Artemision shipwreck!
tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, historians cannot be certain whether this bronze statue is Zeus or Poseidon because both Olympian brothers were sculpted as muscular, bearded rulers. Since the weapon once held in his raised right hand — either Zeus’s thunderbolt or Poseidon’s three-pronged trident — was lost under the sea, the mystery remains!

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Compare the Ancient Olympic Games of 776 BC at Olympia with our modern Olympic Games today!
tasks.starter: Although our modern Olympics were inspired by Ancient Greece, the Games starting in 776 BC had big similarities and differences...
hints: List events we still recognise from Olympia: the stadion sprint, discus, javelin, wrestling, and four-yearly summer timing.
Explain key differences: held ALWAYS at Olympia as a religious festival for Zeus under the Sacred Truce (Ekecheiria).
Contrast ancient winners' wild-olive kotinos wreaths (and male-only Greek competitors) with today's worldwide gold, silver, and bronze medals!
tasks.model_answer: Although our modern Olympics were inspired by Ancient Greece, the Games starting in 776 BC had big similarities and differences. Just like today, athletes met every four years to compete in sprinting (the stadion), throwing the discus and javelin, and wrestling. However, the Ancient Olympics never moved to new countries — they were always held at Olympia as a sacred religious festival for Zeus, protected by the Sacred Truce (Ekecheiria) that paused Greek wars, and champions won a wild-olive kotinos wreath rather than gold medals!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did belief in the Olympian gods inspire Greek temples, hero myths, and the Ancient Olympic Games?
tasks.starter: Religion was never separate from everyday life in Ancient Greece — instead, honouring the gods shaped almost everything Greeks did...
hints: Explain how belief in the twelve gods of Mount Olympus shaped hilltop temples like Athens's Parthenon and outdoor sacrifices.
Show how Apollo's Oracle at Delphi guided big decisions, while hero myths filled painted clay vases.
Prove that religion even shaped sport and peace through Zeus's 776 BC Olympic Games and the Sacred Truce at Olympia!
tasks.model_answer: Religion was never separate from everyday life in Ancient Greece — instead, honouring the gods shaped almost everything Greeks did! Belief in the twelve Olympians on snowy Mount Olympus inspired cities to crown their hills with marble temples like Athena's Parthenon and gather around outdoor altars. Before wars or voyages, leaders climbed mountain Delphi to ask Apollo's Oracle for guidance, while potters painted myths of Heracles and the Hydra onto everyday clay vases. Most remarkably, honouring Zeus at Olympia from 776 BC paused wars under the Sacred Truce for the Ancient Olympic Games!

quiz.question: Which Greek god shook the seas with his trident, and which wise goddess protected Athens?
quiz.q: Which Greek god shook the seas with his trident, and which wise goddess protected Athens?
options: Apollo shook the seas; Artemis protected Athens
Poseidon shook the seas; Athena protected Athens
Hermes shook the seas; Hera protected Athens
Heracles shook the seas; Medusa protected Athens
quiz.answer: Poseidon shook the seas; Athena protected Athens
quiz.a: Poseidon shook the seas; Athena protected Athens
quiz.explanation: Sea-god Poseidon ruled the waves while wise warrior goddess Athena guarded craftworkers and the city of Athens.

quiz.question: What stood inside the inner hall of Athens’s gleaming marble Parthenon temple?
quiz.q: What stood inside the inner hall of Athens’s gleaming marble Parthenon temple?
options: A giant gold-and-ivory statue of goddess Athena
quiz.answer: A giant gold-and-ivory statue of goddess Athena
quiz.a: A giant gold-and-ivory statue of goddess Athena
quiz.explanation: Inside the Parthenon stood sculptor Phidias’s dazzling twelve-metre statue of Athena made with gold plates and carved ivory.

quiz.question: Where did ordinary Greek crowds gather to pour wine and roast offerings for the gods?
quiz.q: Where did ordinary Greek crowds gather to pour wine and roast offerings for the gods?
quiz.explanation: Temples were sacred homes for a god’s statue, so crowds worshipped outside around open-air stone altars where smoke rose skyward.

quiz.question: Which swift messenger god wore winged sandals in Greek belief?
quiz.q: Which swift messenger god wore winged sandals in Greek belief?
quiz.explanation: Winged-sandalled Hermes sped between Mount Olympus and mortals as the swift messenger of the gods.

quiz.question: Why did Greek kings and generals climb mountain Delphi before starting wars or voyages?
quiz.q: Why did Greek kings and generals climb mountain Delphi before starting wars or voyages?
options: To mine gold for new shields
To question Apollo’s Oracle for divine guidance
To watch chariot races at Olympia
To hide inside Mycenae’s Lion Gate
quiz.answer: To question Apollo’s Oracle for divine guidance
quiz.a: To question Apollo’s Oracle for divine guidance
quiz.explanation: Anxious leaders travelled high up to Delphi to ask Apollo’s Oracle for advice before big decisions.

quiz.question: What was the title of the priestess at Delphi who spoke mysterious riddles from Apollo?
quiz.q: What was the title of the priestess at Delphi who spoke mysterious riddles from Apollo?
quiz.explanation: Seated inside Apollo’s mountain temple at Delphi, the priestess known as the Pythia chanted riddles generals tried to decode.

quiz.question: In Greek myth, which multi-headed swamp monster did strong hero Heracles battle on Source C?
quiz.q: In Greek myth, which multi-headed swamp monster did strong hero Heracles battle on Source C?
quiz.explanation: Source C shows Heracles fighting the terrifying many-headed Hydra monster painted in black silhouette on a clay jar.

quiz.question: Which snake-haired monster did hero Perseus face in Greek mythology?
quiz.q: Which snake-haired monster did hero Perseus face in Greek mythology?
quiz.explanation: Greek storytellers told how brave Perseus outwitted snake-haired Medusa, while Odysseus outsmarted giants.

quiz.question: What were the two famous styles of glossy painted Greek myth pottery called?
quiz.q: What were the two famous styles of glossy painted Greek myth pottery called?
quiz.explanation: Greek potters painted gods and heroes onto glossy black-figure and red-figure clay vases that survived for millennia.

quiz.question: In which year were the earliest recorded Ancient Olympic Games held at Olympia in honour of Zeus?
quiz.q: In which year were the earliest recorded Ancient Olympic Games held at Olympia in honour of Zeus?
quiz.explanation: Every four summers starting in 776 BC, Greeks gathered at Olympia to honour sky-king Zeus with athletic contests.

quiz.question: What did the Olympic Sacred Truce (Ekecheiria) do before every Olympic festival?
quiz.q: What did the Olympic Sacred Truce (Ekecheiria) do before every Olympic festival?
options: Awarded silver coins to every runner
Paused wars so athletes and visitors could travel safely
quiz.answer: Paused wars so athletes and visitors could travel safely
quiz.a: Paused wars so athletes and visitors could travel safely
quiz.explanation: Heralds proclaimed the Sacred Truce (Ekecheiria) across Greece so rival cities paused fighting while travellers journeyed to Olympia.

quiz.question: Which barefoot sprint at Olympia gave English our modern word "stadium"?
quiz.q: Which barefoot sprint at Olympia gave English our modern word "stadium"?
quiz.explanation: Runners raced barefoot down a packed-earth track called the stadion — giving us our modern word "stadium"!

quiz.question: What prize was placed on an Olympic champion’s head instead of a gold medal?
quiz.q: What prize was placed on an Olympic champion’s head instead of a gold medal?
options: A woven crown of wild olive leaves called a kotinos
quiz.answer: A woven crown of wild olive leaves called a kotinos
quiz.a: A woven crown of wild olive leaves called a kotinos
quiz.explanation: Victorious athletes at Olympia won a sacred wild-olive wreath called a kotinos and brought lasting honour to their home polis.

quiz.question: Alongside the stadion sprint, which other events thrilled crowds at the Ancient Olympics?
quiz.q: Alongside the stadion sprint, which other events thrilled crowds at the Ancient Olympics?
options: Discus, javelin, wrestling, and chariot racing
quiz.answer: Discus, javelin, wrestling, and chariot racing
quiz.a: Discus, javelin, wrestling, and chariot racing
quiz.explanation: Ancient Olympic crowds cheered the barefoot sprint, discus, javelin, wrestling, and thunderous horse-drawn chariot races.

lessons.prologue: In 490 BC, the gigantic Persian Empire sailed across the Aegean to crush tiny Greece! Lock bronze shields in the Marathon phalanx, guard the narrow cliffs of Thermopylae alongside King Leonidas, and ram enemy warships with wooden triremes in the Strait of Salamis.
lessons.blurb: In 490 BC, the gigantic Persian Empire sailed across the Aegean to crush tiny Greece! Lock bronze shields in the Marathon phalanx, guard the narrow cliffs of Thermopylae alongside King Leonidas, and ram enemy warships with wooden triremes in the Strait of Salamis.

teacher_notes.primer: This fourth Key Stage 2 enquiry explores one of history’s most dramatic turning points: the Greco-Persian Wars (490–479 BC). Primary pupils investigate why Darius I and Xerxes of the Achaemenid Persian Empire invaded mainland Greece, and analyse how outnumbered Greek poleis triumphed through citizen hoplite phalanx teamwork at Marathon (490 BC), King Leonidas’s delaying stand at the mountain pass of Thermopylae (480 BC), and Admiral Themistocles’s naval trap using 170-oar wooden triremes inside the narrow Strait of Salamis (480 BC).

objectives.objective: Explain why the Persian Empire invaded Greece in 490 BC and how the Athenian phalanx won at Marathon.
objectives.primer: Contrast vast Achaemenid Persia under Darius I with citizen hoplites locking shields at Marathon and Pheidippides’s famous run.
objectives.question: How did heavy bronze shields and tight phalanx teamwork help outnumbered Athenians win at Marathon?

objectives.objective: Analyse how Spartan King Leonidas and Greek allies used mountain geography at Thermopylae in 480 BC.
objectives.primer: Trace Xerxes’s 480 BC invasion, the Persian Immortals, and 300 Spartans plus Greek allies holding the narrow coastal pass.
objectives.question: Why did holding the narrow pass of Thermopylae for three days give the rest of Greece precious time to prepare?

objectives.objective: Explain how Themistocles and 170-oar wooden triremes defeated Persia’s fleet in the Strait of Salamis.
objectives.primer: Examine triple-banked oars, bronze waterline rams, and how narrow sea channels trapped Xerxes’s crowded ships.
objectives.question: Why were smaller, nimbler Greek triremes far deadlier than giant Persian ships inside a narrow sea strait?

source_context.Source A: Greek citizen-soldiers called hoplites bought their own bronze helmets, shin guards, spears, and heavy round shields, locking them edge-to-edge in a tight phalanx. **Hinge Question:** Why did each hoplite’s round shield protect both his own left side and his neighbour’s right side in the phalanx?
source_context.Source B: King Darius I and King Xerxes commanded an elite guard of 10,000 soldiers nicknamed the "Immortals" because whenever one fell, another stepped into place at once. **Hinge Question:** How does the colourful woven clothing of the Persian Immortals in Source B differ from the heavy bronze armour of Greek hoplites?
source_context.Source C: Unearthed on the hilltop of Sparta, this marble warrior wears a cheek-guarded helmet with a tall crest — recalling King Leonidas and the 300 Spartans at Thermopylae in 480 BC. **Hinge Question:** Why was a narrow mountain pass squeezed between cliffs and sea the cleverest place for Leonidas’s small force to block Xerxes’s huge army?
source_context.Source D: When Athens struck rich silver in its mines, Themistocles persuaded citizens to spend the silver building 200 fast wooden triremes instead of sharing out pocket money! **Hinge Question:** How did Themistocles use geography to turn Persia’s huge number of ships into a weakness inside the narrow Strait of Salamis?

items.question: What was a Greek "polis", and why did mountains and sea divide Greece into separate city-states?
items.answer: An independent Greek city-state; steep mountains and islands separated communities so each ruled itself
items.explanation: From Enquiry 1: Greece’s rugged mountains and Aegean islands encouraged proud self-governing poleis like Athens and Sparta.

items.question: In ancient Athens, what was the difference between the high rocky Acropolis and the busy Agora below?
items.answer: The Acropolis was the sacred hilltop fortress of temples, while the Agora was the open marketplace and meeting square
items.explanation: From Enquiry 1: Citizens worshipped Athena up on the Acropolis and shopped, chatted, and debated down in the Agora.

items.question: In Athenian democracy, what were an "ostrakon" pottery shard and a stone "kleroterion" machine used for?
items.answer: An ostrakon voted to banish a dangerous leader for ten years; a kleroterion picked citizen jurors randomly
items.explanation: From Enquiry 2: Athenians scratched names onto broken ostraka on the Pnyx and used bronze-and-stone kleroteria for fair juries.

items.question: What was the tough training school entered by Spartan boys at age seven called?
items.explanation: From Enquiry 2: Sparta’s strict agoge trained boys in marching, athletics, endurance, and discipline to build a fearless army.

items.question: When did the Ancient Olympic Games begin at Olympia, and what did the Sacred Truce guarantee?
items.answer: 776 BC; the Sacred Truce paused wars so athletes and spectators could travel safely to Olympia
items.explanation: From Enquiry 3: Held every four years to honour Zeus, the Olympics united rival Greek city-states under a peaceful truce.

vocab.definition: Many different lands and peoples ruled together by one powerful king or emperor, such as Achaemenid Persia.
A heavily armed Greek citizen-soldier carrying a round bronze-faced shield, crested helmet, and long thrusting spear.
A tight shoulder-to-shoulder battle block of Greek hoplites locking shields together behind a forest of spears.
A fast ancient Greek wooden warship powered by 170 oarsmen on three levels and armed with a bronze ram.
A narrow channel of sea squeezed between two coasts or islands, such as the Strait of Salamis.

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: When the vast Persian [Empire] invaded Greece, each citizen [Hoplite] locked his round bronze shield into a tight [Phalanx] at Marathon. Ten years later at sea, fast wooden [Trireme] warships trapped and rammed Persia’s crowded fleet inside the narrow [Strait] of Salamis.

narrative_blocks.title: 490 BC: Darius Invades, the Hoplite Phalanx & Marathon
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] East across the sea lay the **Persian Empire**, ruled by **King Darius I**. In **490 BC**, Darius sent ships to punish **Athens** for helping rebel towns. Persian archers landed on the plain of **Marathon**, north of Athens. Citizen **hoplites** [HOP-lyts] locked bronze shields and spears in a tight **phalanx** [FAL-anks].

[4.2] Charging fast, the Greek phalanx smashed through the Persian lines! Legend says **Pheidippides** [fy-DIP-ih-deez] ran twenty-six miles to Athens, cried "Joy, we win!", and fell. His run inspired our **marathon**, and Athens raised a grassy **burial mound**.
narrative_blocks.content:
[4.1] East across the sea lay the **Persian Empire**, ruled by **King Darius I**. In **490 BC**, Darius sent ships to punish **Athens** for helping rebel towns. Persian archers landed on the plain of **Marathon**, north of Athens. Citizen **hoplites** [HOP-lyts] locked bronze shields and spears in a tight **phalanx** [FAL-anks].

[4.2] Charging fast, the Greek phalanx smashed through the Persian lines! Legend says **Pheidippides** [fy-DIP-ih-deez] ran twenty-six miles to Athens, cried "Joy, we win!", and fell. His run inspired our **marathon**, and Athens raised a grassy **burial mound**.

narrative_blocks.caption: The nine-metre-high Athenian burial mound on the plain of Marathon, raised to honour the 192 Athenians who fell in 490 BC.
narrative_blocks.image_caption: The nine-metre-high Athenian burial mound on the plain of Marathon, raised to honour the 192 Athenians who fell in 490 BC.

narrative_blocks.title: 480 BC: King Xerxes & the Brave Stand at Thermopylae
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.3] Ten years later, in **480 BC**, Darius's son **King Xerxes** led a bigger invasion. Huge armies with elite **Persian Immortals** marched south to conquer Greece. Rival Greeks united at last to defend their homeland. **Spartan King Leonidas** marched north to guard the narrow pass of **Thermopylae** [ther-MOP-ih-lee].

[4.4] Steep cliffs rose on one side while deep sea waves crashed below. For three days, **three hundred Spartans** and allies blocked thousands of soldiers. When a traitor showed Xerxes a **mountain path**, Leonidas stayed fighting so allies escaped.

narrative_blocks.title: 480–479 BC: Wooden Triremes & Victory in the Strait of Salamis
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.5] Persian troops marched on and burned empty Athens after families sailed to safety. Clever Admiral **Themistocles** [thuh-MIS-tuh-kleez] trusted Athens's fast wooden warships, called **triremes** [TRY-reemz]. Each sleek trireme used **170 oarsmen** seated on three wooden levels. Painted eyes gleamed above a heavy **bronze ram** at the waterline.

[4.6] Themistocles sent a trick message to lure Xerxes's fleet into the narrow **Strait of Salamis**. Crowded Persian ships crashed together while nimble Greek triremes rammed their hulls. After Salamis in **480 BC** and Plataea in **479 BC**, Greece stayed free!

tasks.title: 1. Primary Evidence Detective
tasks.question: Look closely at the warriors on Source A. What armour and weapons made a phalanx so tough?
tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, round bronze shields, helmets, and spears made a Greek phalanx tough by...
hints: List the protective bronze armour worn on the warriors’ heads, chests, and shins.
Notice how their large round shields overlap shoulder-to-shoulder.
Explain how locking shields into a tight phalanx wall protected every neighbour in line.
tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, round bronze shields, helmets, and spears made a Greek phalanx tough by locking hoplite warriors shoulder-to-shoulder into one moving bronze wall. Each soldier’s shield protected both himself and his neighbour while rows of long iron-tipped spears thrust forward together.

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain how clever use of geography helped the Greeks at both Thermopylae and Salamis in 480 BC.
tasks.starter: Even though King Xerxes brought far more soldiers and ships in 480 BC, the Greeks used geography cleverly...
hints: Explain how steep cliffs and the sea at Thermopylae let King Leonidas block thousands of Persians in a narrow gap.
Explain how Admiral Themistocles lured Persia’s giant fleet into the narrow Strait of Salamis.
Explain why Persia’s huge numbers actually turned into a clumsy traffic jam inside the narrow sea strait!
tasks.model_answer: Even though King Xerxes brought far more soldiers and ships in 480 BC, the Greeks used geography cleverly on land and sea. At Thermopylae, King Leonidas chose a narrow road squeezed between steep cliffs and waves so Xerxes’s vast army could only attack a few soldiers wide. At sea, Admiral Themistocles lured Persia’s giant fleet into the narrow Strait of Salamis, where Persia’s crowded ships jammed together in a tangle while nimble 170-oar Greek triremes rammed their hulls!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did tiny, rival Greek city-states unite to defeat the mighty Persian Empire between 490 and 479 BC?
tasks.starter: Tiny Greek city-states defeated the mighty Persian Empire through three vital strengths: teamwork, weaponry, and clever tactics...
hints: Explain how citizen hoplites won on land at Marathon (490 BC) using bronze armour and the tight phalanx.
Explain how rival poleis united in 480 BC as Sparta led at Thermopylae and Athens led at sea.
Judge which turning point mattered most — Marathon’s confidence boost, Thermopylae’s delay, or Themistocles’s triremes at Salamis!
tasks.model_answer: Tiny Greek city-states defeated the mighty Persian Empire through three vital strengths: teamwork, weaponry, and clever tactics. First, at Marathon in 490 BC, heavily armoured citizen hoplites locked bronze shields into a charging phalanx to beat Darius I’s archers. Second, when Xerxes returned in 480 BC, rival poleis like Sparta and Athens united, as King Leonidas’s brave stand at narrow Thermopylae bought precious time. Most decisive of all, Admiral Themistocles’s 170-oar wooden triremes trapped and sank Xerxes’s fleet inside the narrow Strait of Salamis!

quiz.question: Which Persian king sent warships across the Aegean Sea in 490 BC to punish Athens at Marathon?
quiz.q: Which Persian king sent warships across the Aegean Sea in 490 BC to punish Athens at Marathon?
quiz.explanation: In 490 BC, King Darius I of the Persian Empire sent troops to Marathon to punish Athens for aiding rebel Greek towns.

quiz.question: What was a Greek citizen-soldier armed with a round bronze shield, helmet, and long spear called?
quiz.q: What was a Greek citizen-soldier armed with a round bronze shield, helmet, and long spear called?
quiz.explanation: Greek citizen-soldiers were called hoplites, named after their heavy bronze equipment and round shields.

quiz.question: How did Greek hoplites fight together inside a tight "phalanx" formation?
quiz.q: How did Greek hoplites fight together inside a tight "phalanx" formation?
options: By riding camels in wide circles
By locking round shields edge-to-edge with rows of spears pointing forward
By hiding individually behind olive trees
By firing iron cannons from stone castles
quiz.answer: By locking round shields edge-to-edge with rows of spears pointing forward
quiz.a: By locking round shields edge-to-edge with rows of spears pointing forward
quiz.explanation: Locking heavy shields shoulder-to-shoulder turned a Greek phalanx into a tough wall of bronze and spears.

quiz.question: According to Greek legend, who ran 26 miles from Marathon to Athens to announce victory in 490 BC?
quiz.q: According to Greek legend, who ran 26 miles from Marathon to Athens to announce victory in 490 BC?
quiz.explanation: Legend tells how runner Pheidippides raced 26 miles from Marathon to Athens shouting "Joy, we win!" — inspiring our modern marathon.

quiz.question: What monument still rises on the plain of Marathon to honour the Athenians who fell in 490 BC?
quiz.q: What monument still rises on the plain of Marathon to honour the Athenians who fell in 490 BC?
quiz.explanation: Athenians heaped a tall grassy burial mound over their fallen citizen-soldiers right on the plain of Marathon.

quiz.question: Who led the massive second Persian invasion of Greece in 480 BC, ten years after Marathon?
quiz.q: Who led the massive second Persian invasion of Greece in 480 BC, ten years after Marathon?
options: King Xerxes, son of Darius I
quiz.answer: King Xerxes, son of Darius I
quiz.a: King Xerxes, son of Darius I
quiz.explanation: In 480 BC, Darius’s son King Xerxes marched a huge army south to conquer Greece’s independent city-states.

quiz.question: Why were Persia’s 10,000 elite royal guards in Source B nicknamed the "Immortals"?
quiz.q: Why were Persia’s 10,000 elite royal guards in Source B nicknamed the "Immortals"?
options: Whenever one soldier fell, another stepped forward immediately to keep their number at 10,000
They never slept or ate food on campaign
They rode winged horses into battle
quiz.answer: Whenever one soldier fell, another stepped forward immediately to keep their number at 10,000
quiz.a: Whenever one soldier fell, another stepped forward immediately to keep their number at 10,000
quiz.explanation: Replacing every fallen guard straight away made Persia’s elite 10,000-strong force seem never-ending.

quiz.question: Which Spartan king led 300 Spartans and Greek allies at the narrow pass of Thermopylae in 480 BC?
quiz.q: Which Spartan king led 300 Spartans and Greek allies at the narrow pass of Thermopylae in 480 BC?
quiz.explanation: Spartan King Leonidas led 300 Spartans alongside brave Greek allies to block the narrow coastal pass of Thermopylae.

quiz.question: Why was the narrow pass of Thermopylae such a clever place for a small Greek force to block a huge army?
quiz.q: Why was the narrow pass of Thermopylae such a clever place for a small Greek force to block a huge army?
options: Thick snowstorms hid the entire Persian camp
A wide desert stretched for miles on every side
Wooden drawbridges lifted across a deep moat
Steep cliffs on one side and deep sea waves below stopped Persia using its huge numbers at once
quiz.answer: Steep cliffs on one side and deep sea waves below stopped Persia using its huge numbers at once
quiz.a: Steep cliffs on one side and deep sea waves below stopped Persia using its huge numbers at once
quiz.explanation: Squeezed between sheer mountain cliffs and the sea, only a narrow front of Persian troops could fight the Greek shield wall at one time.

quiz.question: How did King Xerxes’s soldiers finally get behind Leonidas’s defenders after three days at Thermopylae?
quiz.q: How did King Xerxes’s soldiers finally get behind Leonidas’s defenders after three days at Thermopylae?
options: A traitor showed the Persians a hidden mountain path around the pass
Persian ships tunnelled right underneath the cliffs
The Spartans ran out of drinking water on the first hour
Giant wooden trebuchets knocked the mountain flat
quiz.answer: A traitor showed the Persians a hidden mountain path around the pass
quiz.a: A traitor showed the Persians a hidden mountain path around the pass
quiz.explanation: After three fierce days, a local traitor guided Persian soldiers along a hidden mountain path behind Leonidas’s position.

quiz.question: What were Athens’s fast wooden warships with three banks of oars called?
quiz.q: What were Athens’s fast wooden warships with three banks of oars called?
quiz.explanation: Sleek Greek warships powered by three tiers of oars were called triremes.

quiz.question: How many oarsmen rowed a Greek trireme, and what weapon sat at its waterline prow?
quiz.q: How many oarsmen rowed a Greek trireme, and what weapon sat at its waterline prow?
options: 170 oarsmen and a heavy bronze ram
quiz.answer: 170 oarsmen and a heavy bronze ram
quiz.a: 170 oarsmen and a heavy bronze ram
quiz.explanation: Powered by 170 rowers, each nimble trireme steered a heavy underwater bronze ram straight into enemy wooden hulls.

quiz.question: Which clever Athenian admiral persuaded citizens to build 200 triremes and set a trap at Salamis?
quiz.q: Which clever Athenian admiral persuaded citizens to build 200 triremes and set a trap at Salamis?
quiz.explanation: Admiral Themistocles convinced Athens to spend silver-mine riches on triremes and lured Xerxes’s fleet into a narrow channel.

quiz.question: Why did Persia’s much larger fleet lose inside the narrow Strait of Salamis in 480 BC?
quiz.q: Why did Persia’s much larger fleet lose inside the narrow Strait of Salamis in 480 BC?
options: Crowded Persian ships jammed together in the tight water while nimble Greek triremes rammed them
A sudden volcano sank only the Persian ships
Persian sailors forgot to bring wooden oars
Icebergs blocked the Aegean Sea in summer
quiz.answer: Crowded Persian ships jammed together in the tight water while nimble Greek triremes rammed them
quiz.a: Crowded Persian ships jammed together in the tight water while nimble Greek triremes rammed them
quiz.explanation: Lured into the narrow Strait of Salamis by Themistocles’s trick message, Persia’s huge ships collided and could not manoeuvre.

quiz.question: After Salamis in 480 BC, which final Greek victory in 479 BC kept Greece’s city-states independent and free?
quiz.q: After Salamis in 480 BC, which final Greek victory in 479 BC kept Greece’s city-states independent and free?
quiz.explanation: Following naval victory at Salamis (480 BC) and land victory at Plataea (479 BC), Greece remained independent.

lessons.prologue: Test the crystal-clear acoustics of Epidaurus’s 14,000-seat stone theatre, debate big questions barefoot alongside Socrates in Athens, observe patients on Kos with Hippocrates, and shout "Eureka!" with Archimedes as Greek thinkers change human knowledge forever!
lessons.blurb: Test the crystal-clear acoustics of Epidaurus’s 14,000-seat stone theatre, debate big questions barefoot alongside Socrates in Athens, observe patients on Kos with Hippocrates, and shout "Eureka!" with Archimedes as Greek thinkers change human knowledge forever!

teacher_notes.primer: This fifth Key Stage 2 enquiry explores the intellectual flowering of Classical and Hellenistic Greece. Primary pupils examine open-air hillside amphitheatres such as Epidaurus (tragedies, comedies, and expressive masks), meet Athens’s great philosophers ("lovers of wisdom": Socrates, Plato’s Academy, and Aristotle’s natural classification), contrast Hippocrates’s clinical observation on Kos with earlier supernatural explanations of illness, and trace breakthroughs in geometry and physics by Pythagoras, Euclid, and Archimedes.

objectives.objective: Describe how open-air Greek amphitheatres like Epidaurus staged tragedies and comedies using masks and acoustics.
objectives.primer: Explore 14,000-seat stone hillside bowls, festivals of Dionysus, acoustic design, and expressive tragic and comic masks.
objectives.question: How could 14,000 spectators hear and see every emotion clearly without microphones or electric spotlights?

objectives.objective: Explain what "philosopher" means and how Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle shaped careful thinking and science.
objectives.primer: Trace Socrates’s brave questioning in the Agora, Plato’s Academy, and Aristotle classifying plants, animals, and nature.
objectives.question: Why did Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle encourage people to test ideas using questions, logic, and evidence?

objectives.objective: Assess the significance of Hippocrates in medicine and Pythagoras, Euclid, and Archimedes in maths and levers.
objectives.primer: Contrast blaming angry gods with Hippocrates observing symptoms on Kos, alongside geometry and Archimedes’s "Eureka!".
objectives.question: Why do modern doctors and mathematicians still build upon discoveries made in Ancient Greece?

source_context.Source A: Only three main male actors spoke roles in most Greek plays, swapping lightweight masks backstage to play kings, queens, or comic servants before 14,000 spectators! **Hinge Question:** Why did Greek actors wear bold masks with exaggerated faces and wide mouths inside giant open-air hillside theatres?
source_context.Source B: Unlike statues of handsome athletes, Socrates was carved with a snub nose and tangled beard — matching a humble thinker who cared about truth rather than wealth. **Hinge Question:** Why did Socrates believe asking careful questions was a better way to teach people than simply telling them what to think?
source_context.Source C: Aristotle spent years wading beside Greek lagoons with fishermen to study octopuses, seashells, and dolphins first-hand, sorting over 500 living species into groups! **Hinge Question:** How did Aristotle’s habit of observing real plants and animals closely help launch modern science?
source_context.Source D: Before Hippocrates taught on the island of Kos, many people blamed fevers on curses from angry gods; he insisted every illness has a natural physical cause! **Hinge Question:** Why was recording a patient’s daily temperature, breathing, and diet a giant leap forward for medicine?

items.explanation: From Enquiry 1: Acropolis means "high city", offering every polis both strong defence and a proud religious heart.

items.question: Contrast Athens and Sparta: how did Athenian citizens make laws compared with how Sparta trained boys?
items.answer: Athenian male citizens voted directly on the Pnyx, whereas Sparta trained boys from age seven in the tough military agoge
items.explanation: From Enquiry 2: Athens prized open citizen debate and juries, while Sparta focused on warrior obedience and strength.

items.question: What prize did Olympic champions win at Olympia in 776 BC, and which chief god did the festival honour?
items.answer: A woven crown of sacred wild olive leaves, won in honour of Zeus
items.explanation: From Enquiry 3: Winning glory for your home polis before Zeus mattered far more to athletes than gold coins!

items.question: How did outnumbered Athenian citizen hoplites defeat King Darius I’s Persian army at Marathon in 490 BC?
items.answer: By locking heavy bronze shields and long spears together in a tight phalanx and charging at a run
items.explanation: From Enquiry 4: Phalanx teamwork let Athens win at Marathon, inspiring Pheidippides’s famous twenty-six-mile run.

items.question: How did King Leonidas at Thermopylae and Admiral Themistocles at Salamis work to save Greece in 480 BC?
items.answer: Leonidas delayed Xerxes’s army in a narrow mountain pass, while Themistocles’s 170-oar triremes sank Persia’s fleet in a narrow strait
items.explanation: From Enquiry 4: Both commanders used Greece’s narrow cliffs and sea channels to beat a much larger invading force.

Meanwhile, each questioning [Philosopher] in Athens debated truth, while Greek mathematicians explored shapes and triangles through [Geometry].

narrative_blocks.title: c. 460–330 BC: Hillside Amphitheatres, Masks, Tragedies & Comedies
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.1] After defeating Persia, Greece entered a golden age of drama and bold ideas. Builders carved curved stone **amphitheatres** into sunny hillsides, like **Epidaurus** [ep-ih-DAW-rus]. Its stone rows seated **14,000 spectators** under open blue skies. Clever curved steps carried even a quiet whisper right to the back row!

[5.2] At festivals for **Dionysus** [dy-uh-NY-sus], male actors staged sad **tragedies** and funny **comedies**. Performers wore bold **theatre masks** with wide mouths so distant crowds saw every face. Poor citizens even got coin tokens so everyone could watch and debate fairness.

narrative_blocks.title: c. 430–322 BC: Athens’s Philosophers — Socrates, Plato & Aristotle
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.3] In busy Athens, thinkers called **philosophers**, or **"lovers of wisdom"**, asked how people should live. Barefoot **Socrates** [SOK-ruh-teez] walked through the **Agora** every day. He asked sharp questions so citizens tested their own beliefs. In **399 BC**, angry jurors condemned Socrates, yet he drank poison rather than stop.

[5.4] His pupil **Plato** opened a shady garden school in Athens called the **Academy**. Next, **Aristotle** [AR-ih-stot-ul] studied nature by observing, measuring, and sorting real facts. Grouping hundreds of plants and animals built roots for **science** at his **Lyceum** school.

narrative_blocks.title: c. 420–212 BC: Hippocrates on Kos, Geometry & Archimedes’s "Eureka!"
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.5] For centuries, sick people blamed illnesses on angry gods and begged for magic cures. On the island of **Kos**, doctor **Hippocrates** [hip-OK-ruh-teez] taught a wiser method. Doctors checked natural **symptoms** closely and kept careful bedside notes. He prescribed clean food, fresh air, and rest under the ethical **Hippocratic Oath**.

[5.6] Greek **mathematicians** also unlocked rules of shapes and machines we still use today. **Pythagoras** studied right-angled triangles, while **Euclid** [YOO-klid] wrote a clear **geometry** guide. Later, **Archimedes** [ar-kih-MEE-deez] mastered levers and shouted **"Eureka!"** after solving a bath puzzle!

tasks.title: 1. Primary Evidence Detective
tasks.question: Inspect Source A. Mention two clever reasons Greek actors wore masks like these on stage.
tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, Greek actors wore expressive terracotta masks with wide open mouths for two clever reasons...
hints: Imagine sitting right at the top row of a 14,000-seat open-air hillside theatre.
Explain how bold, exaggerated mouths and eyebrows showed tragic or comic feelings from far away.
Describe how swapping lightweight masks backstage let three male actors play many characters.
tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, Greek actors wore expressive terracotta masks with wide open mouths for two clever reasons. First, bold expressions let spectators sitting at the back of huge 14,000-seat hillside theatres see tragic or comic emotions clearly; second, swapping masks let just three actors play many male and female roles!

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain how Hippocrates of Kos changed medicine compared with older beliefs about angry gods.
tasks.starter: Before Hippocrates taught doctors on the island of Kos, many people misunderstood illness because...
hints: Describe how people previously blamed fevers and sickness on curses or angry Olympian gods.
Explain how Hippocrates on Kos taught doctors to check symptoms, fresh air, clean diet, and rest.
Explain why the Hippocratic Oath still matters to hospital doctors and patients in our world today!
tasks.model_answer: Before Hippocrates taught doctors on the island of Kos, many people misunderstood illness because they blamed fevers on angry gods and begged temple priests for magic cures. Hippocrates transformed medicine by insisting every sickness has a natural cause inside the body. He trained physicians to observe a patient’s daily symptoms carefully and prescribe clean diet, fresh air, and quiet rest. Even today, new doctors honour his Hippocratic Oath by promising to put patient safety and care first!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did Ancient Greek playwrights, philosophers, doctors, and mathematicians transform human knowledge?
tasks.starter: Ancient Greek thinkers transformed human knowledge across philosophy, medicine, and mathematics...
hints: Explain what Socrates, Plato’s Academy, and Aristotle achieved as "lovers of wisdom" and early scientists.
Compare Hippocrates’s clinical medicine on Kos with Pythagoras, Euclid, and Archimedes in geometry and levers.
Reach your own reasoned judgment on which breakthrough matters most, showing how they actually supported one another!
tasks.model_answer: Ancient Greek thinkers transformed human knowledge across philosophy, medicine, and mathematics. In Athens, philosophers ("lovers of wisdom") led by Socrates, Plato at the Academy, and Aristotle taught people to ask sharp questions and classify plants and animals scientifically. On Kos, Hippocrates saved lives by observing natural symptoms, while Pythagoras, Euclid, and Archimedes unlocked geometry and levers. Overall, philosophy’s habit of testing ideas with reason and evidence mattered most because it powered both Greek medicine and Greek mathematics!

options: Tragedies were serious plays about pride and fate, while comedies were funny plays teasing leaders
Tragedies used puppets, while comedies used chariots
Tragedies lasted ten seconds, while comedies lasted three weeks
Tragedies were silent dances, while comedies were flute solos
quiz.answer: Tragedies were serious plays about pride and fate, while comedies were funny plays teasing leaders

teacher_notes.primer: This capstone Key Stage 2 enquiry traces how Greek ideas spread across the ancient world and live on today. Primary pupils follow Alexander the Great of Macedon (taught by Aristotle, riding Bucephalus) from 336 to 323 BC across Egypt, Persia, and north-west India, explore Hellenistic Alexandria’s Great Library and Pharos Lighthouse, note Rome’s conquest of Greece in 146 BC alongside Roman admiration for Greek teachers and art, and evaluate Ancient Greece’s everyday legacy in Britain and the modern world: democracy and juries, Greek-rooted English words, Doric/Ionic/Corinthian columns, geometry, and the 1896 Athens Modern Olympic Games.

items.question: In ancient Athens, where did male citizens gather outdoors to vote on laws by raising hands?
items.answer: On the rocky hillside of the Pnyx
items.explanation: From Enquiries 1–2: Six thousand citizens met on the Pnyx near the Acropolis to debate and vote directly.

items.question: Why did rival Greek poleis pause their wars every four years starting in 776 BC?
items.answer: To honour the Olympic Sacred Truce so athletes and visitors could travel safely to Olympia for Zeus’s festival
items.explanation: From Enquiry 3: Shared Greek language, gods, and the Olympic Games linked rival city-states together.

items.question: Name one land battle and one sea battle where outnumbered Greeks defeated the Persian Empire.
items.answer: Marathon (490 BC) or Thermopylae (480 BC) on land, and the Strait of Salamis (480 BC) at sea
items.explanation: From Enquiry 4: Hoplite phalanxes and 170-oar wooden triremes saved Greek independence against Darius I and Xerxes.

items.question: How did the hillside stone bowl at Epidaurus and wide-mouthed masks help 14,000 theatre spectators?
items.answer: Curved acoustics carried quiet stage voices to the top row, while bold masks showed tragic or comic faces from afar
items.explanation: From Enquiry 5: Open-air Greek amphitheatres turned tragedies and comedies into shared civic festivals.

items.question: How did Socrates in Athens and Hippocrates on Kos encourage people to search for truth?
items.answer: Socrates asked sharp questions to test beliefs, while Hippocrates observed natural patient symptoms instead of blaming angry gods
items.explanation: From Enquiry 5: Greek philosophers, doctors, and mathematicians championed careful observation, reason, and evidence.

narrative_blocks.title: 336–323 BC: Young King Alexander, Bucephalus & a Vast Empire
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.1] North of the old city-states lay mountainous **Macedon** [MASS-ih-don]. There, young prince **Alexander** learned science and poetry from **Aristotle**. As a boy, he tamed a wild black warhorse named **Bucephalus** [byoo-SEF-uh-lus] in the sun. Crowned king in **336 BC** aged twenty, **Alexander the Great** united Greece and marched east.

[6.2] Over eleven years, unbeaten Alexander led armies across **Egypt**, **Persia**, and north-west **India**. Before dying aged **thirty-two** in **323 BC**, he founded cities named **Alexandria**. Blending Greek speech with eastern customs shaped the lively **Hellenistic** [hel-uh-NIS-tik] world.

narrative_blocks.title: 323–146 BC: Alexandria’s Great Library, Pharos & Conquering Rome
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.3] Egypt's busy port of **Alexandria** shone with its tall **Pharos Lighthouse**. Inside the **Great Library**, scholars gathered hundreds of thousands of papyrus scrolls. Thinkers from distant lands studied stars, maps, and Euclid's **geometry** in Greek.

[6.4] Meanwhile, a strong new power rose west across the sea in Italy: the **Roman Republic**. In **146 BC**, tough Roman legions conquered mainland Greece and its old city-states. Yet Romans admired Greece deeply, copying marble statues and hiring **Greek teachers**. Educated Romans also read Homer and matched Roman gods to Olympians.

narrative_blocks.title: 1896 & Today: Democracy, Words, Columns & the Modern Olympics
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.5] Over two thousand years have passed, yet Ancient Greece's rich **legacy** still shapes our lives. When citizens vote in elections or sit on courtroom **juries**, they echo Athenian **democracy**. Everyday English words come straight from Greek, including **school**, **dinosaur**, **planet**, **music**, **theatre**, and **history**!

[6.6] Grand museums and town halls still copy **Doric**, **Ionic**, and leafy **Corinthian** stone **columns**. In **1896**, athletes met inside Athens's white marble **Panathenaic** [pan-ath-uh-NAY-ik] **Stadium**. Fourteen nations launched the **Modern Olympic Games** there. Today, Greek curiosity still inspires classrooms worldwide!

tasks.title: 1. Primary Evidence Detective
tasks.question: Look closely at Source A. Why did minting coins like this help unite Alexander’s vast empire?
tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, minting silver coins of Alexander wearing Heracles’s lion skin helped unite his empire by...
hints: Spot the fierce lion-scalp headdress linking Alexander to legendary hero Heracles.
Explain how stamping his heroic image onto millions of coins spread royal propaganda.
Show how sharing one trusted silver coin and Greek script made trade easier from Egypt to Asia.
tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, minting silver coins of Alexander wearing Heracles’s lion skin helped unite his empire by advertising his unbeaten heroic strength across Egypt, Persia, and Greece. Sharing one trusted silver currency stamped with Greek letters also let merchants and soldiers trade smoothly across thousands of miles.

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain how Alexander the Great and the Romans both helped Greek ideas spread across the world.
tasks.starter: Greek ideas did not stay trapped inside tiny Aegean city-states because both Alexander and Rome spread them...
hints: Explain how Aristotle’s pupil Alexander marched across Egypt, Persia, and India, founding cities named Alexandria.
Describe how Alexandria’s Great Library and Pharos Lighthouse made Hellenistic Greek learning famous.
Explain the fascinating twist of 146 BC — Rome conquered Greece with armies, yet Greek art and teachers won over Rome!
tasks.model_answer: Greek ideas did not stay trapped inside tiny Aegean city-states because both Alexander and Rome spread them far and wide. First, between 336 and 323 BC, Aristotle’s pupil Alexander the Great marched across Egypt, Persia, and north-west India, founding cities named Alexandria — including Egypt’s port with its Pharos Lighthouse and Great Library — to create a blended Hellenistic world. Later, when Roman legions conquered Greece in 146 BC, admiring Romans copied Greek marble statues and hired Greek teachers, carrying Greek learning across Europe!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did Alexander the Great spread Greek culture, and what is Ancient Greece’s lasting legacy in our world today?
tasks.starter: More than two thousand years on, Ancient Greece leaves an extraordinary legacy across our daily lives...
hints: Mention Athenian democracy and juries alongside Greek-rooted English words like school, dinosaur, planet, theatre, and history.
Mention Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian columns, Euclid’s geometry, Hippocrates’s medicine, and the 1896 Modern Olympics.
Weigh these gifts carefully and justify which single Greek legacy makes the biggest difference to human life today!
tasks.model_answer: More than two thousand years on, Ancient Greece leaves an extraordinary legacy across our daily lives. Every school day we speak Greek-rooted words like school, dinosaur, planet, music, theatre, and history, while studying Euclid’s geometry! Our grand buildings display Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian columns, doctors honour Hippocrates, and athletes compete in the Modern Olympic Games revived at Athens in 1896. Above all, Greece’s greatest legacy is democracy, juries, and free questioning — giving ordinary citizens a voice in shaping fair laws!
