banner.caption: Re-enactors clashing with spears, swords, chainmail, and painted shields beneath battle banners to recreate the fierce struggle at the Battle of Hastings in October 1066.

key_individuals.name: King Raedwald of East Anglia & Edith Pretty
key_individuals.role: 7th-Century Anglo-Saxon Overlord & The Landowner Who Uncovered His Ship Burial
key_individuals.origins: Raedwald ruled the Kingdom of East Anglia in the early AD 600s as Bretwalda ("overlord"); over 1,300 years later, Suffolk landowner Edith Pretty asked self-taught archaeologist Basil Brown to excavate the mysterious grassy mounds on her Sutton Hoo estate.
key_individuals.significance: Together across thirteen centuries, Raedwald's royal funeral and Edith Pretty's 1939 excavation revealed the dazzling 27-metre Sutton Hoo ship burial — proving forever that the early Anglo-Saxon era was a "Golden Age" of artistry and trade rather than a backward "Dark Age."
achievements: Buried around AD 625 inside Mound 1 with an iconic iron-and-bronze face-mask helmet, gold-and-garnet shoulder clasps, Sri Lankan garnets, Byzantine silver, and Frankish gold coins.
Included both pagan warrior treasures and two Christian silver baptismal spoons ("Saulos" and "Paulos"), matching Bede's account that Raedwald kept both pagan and Christian altars.
Generously donated in full to the public by Edith Pretty in 1939 — the greatest single gift of British archaeological treasure ever made by a living donor.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Acidic Suffolk sand rotted every oak plank and bone to dark stains, yet Basil Brown's careful trowel-work uncovered the iron ship rivets and intact royal burial chamber just weeks before World War II began.

key_individuals.name: The Venerable Bede
key_individuals.role: Northumbrian Monk, Scientist & "Father of English History" at Jarrow Monastery
key_individuals.origins: Entered the twin Northumbrian monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow at age seven and spent his whole life praying, teaching, studying astronomy and tides, and writing inside one of Europe's finest libraries.
key_individuals.significance: Completed his History of the English Church and People in AD 731 — our richest written primary source for Anglo-Saxon migration, kingdoms, and Christian conversion — and popularised counting historical years using Anno Domini ("AD").
achievements: Authored over forty Latin books on history, scripture, poetry, calendar science, and how the Moon pulls ocean tides.
Carefully named his eyewitness informants and copied papal letters rather than inventing legends, earning respect across medieval Europe.
Popularised the BC / AD dating system across western Christendom that historians still use on timelines today.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Although Bede rarely travelled beyond Tyne and Wear in northern England, correspondents from Canterbury to Rome sent documents to Jarrow so he could write the history of the whole island.

key_individuals.name: King Alfred the Great
key_individuals.role: King of Wessex (AD 871–899) Who Saved Anglo-Saxon England, Built 33 Burhs & Championed Learning
key_individuals.origins: Youngest of five sons of King Aethelwulf of Wessex; visited Rome as a boy and inherited the West Saxon throne in AD 871 at the height of the Great Heathen Army's invasions.
key_individuals.significance: Regrouped in the Somerset marshes at Athelney after Guthrum's Twelfth Night attack in AD 878, triumphed at the Battle of Edington, negotiated the Danelaw peace treaty, fortified Wessex with 33 walled burhs, and revived English literacy.
achievements: Defeated Guthrum's shield wall at Edington (May AD 878), stood as godfather at Guthrum's Christian baptism, and recaptured London in AD 886.
Engineered 33 fortified burhs (such as Wareham and Wallingford) so no Wessex family lived over 20 miles from safety, supported by taller 60-oar warships.
Translated vital Latin books into Old English, commissioned crystal reading pointers like the Alfred Jewel, and launched the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Out of dozens of monarchs across more than a thousand years, Alfred of Wessex is the ONLY ruler in British history given the title "the Great."

key_individuals.name: Aethelflaed, Lady of the Mercians
key_individuals.role: Warrior Ruler of Mercia, Fort-Builder & Architect of the Danelaw Reconquest
key_individuals.origins: Eldest daughter of King Alfred the Great, educated at Wessex's royal court and married to Lord Aethelred of Mercia to seal the alliance between Wessex and western Mercia.
key_individuals.significance: After her husband fell ill and died in AD 911, Mercian nobles chose Aethelflaed to govern in her own right as "Lady of the Mercians" — planning campaigns with her brother King Edward the Elder and raising her nephew Athelstan.
achievements: Constructed ten strategic Mercian burhs, including Tamworth, Stafford, Bridgnorth, Chester, and Warwick, to guard river crossings and borders.
Stormed Viking-held Derby in AD 917 and won the peaceful surrender of Viking Leicester in AD 918 without losing a single soldier.
Received promises of allegiance from the leaders of Viking York shortly before her death at Tamworth in June AD 918.
key_individuals.key_distinction: One of the most successful military and political female rulers anywhere in early medieval Europe, directly paving the way for a united England.

key_individuals.name: King Athelstan
key_individuals.role: Grandson of Alfred & First True "King of All England" (Reigned AD 924–939)
key_individuals.origins: Grandson of King Alfred the Great, raised in the household of his aunt Aethelflaed in Mercia, which made him trusted by both West Saxons in the south and Mercians in the Midlands.
key_individuals.significance: Captured the Viking kingdom of York in AD 927 and crushed a combined Viking, Scottish, and Strathclyde invasion at the Battle of Brunanburh in AD 937 — uniting Wessex, Mercia, and Northumbria into one Kingdom of England.
achievements: Accepted the submission of northern rulers at Eamont Bridge in AD 927 and styled himself "Rex totius Britanniae" ("King of all Britain") on charters and coins.
Issued detailed royal law codes protecting trade, standardising silver coinage across burhs, and aiding the poor.
Pictured around AD 934 presenting a book to St Cuthbert (Corpus Christi MS 183) — the earliest surviving lifetime portrait of an English monarch.
key_individuals.key_distinction: While Alfred the Great saved southern Wessex, his grandson Athelstan was the first ruler in history to govern one united Kingdom of England from the Channel to Northumbria.

key_individuals.name: King Cnut & Queen Emma
key_individuals.role: Rulers of England, Denmark & Norway's Peaceful 11th-Century North Sea Empire
key_individuals.origins: Cnut was a young Danish Viking prince who won the English throne in AD 1016; Emma of Normandy was a skilled diplomat who had previously been queen to Anglo-Saxon King Aethelred and married Cnut in AD 1017.
key_individuals.significance: Ended decades of devastating Viking raids and Danegeld silver demands, uniting England, Denmark, and Norway into a prosperous North Sea Empire while respecting Anglo-Saxon laws and Christian monasteries.
achievements: Divided England into four great earldoms (Wessex, Mercia, East Anglia, and Northumbria) and issued Cnut's Winchester law code treating Danes and English equally.
Generously patronised English churches and shrines, famously pictured together gifting a golden cross to Winchester's New Minster around AD 1031.
Sent Cnut's famous AD 1027 open letter from Rome vowing before God to rule all his realms justly and protect English pilgrims and merchants.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Famous legend remembers Cnut sitting by the incoming tide — not because he foolishly thought he could stop the waves, but to teach flattering courtiers that even a mighty king obeys God's power!

guided_reading.book_title: History of the English Church and People (Book II, Ch. 13, AD 731)
guided_reading.author: Venerable Bede (Public Domain translation by A. M. Sellar, 1907)
guided_reading.provenance_note: From Venerable Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation II.13 (AD 731), translated by A. M. Sellar (London: George Bell, 1907 — Public Domain), lightly trimmed for KS2 oral reading.
guided_reading.author_context: Writing at Jarrow Monastery in AD 731, the monk Bede preserved the most famous picture in early English literature: a tiny sparrow flying through a warm, firelit Anglo-Saxon mead hall.
guided_reading.cover_caption: Reconstructed rectangular Anglo-Saxon timber hall with steep thatched roof at West Stow in Suffolk, built over 5th-century post-holes.

vocabVault.def: A grand rectangular timber hall with a roaring central fire where a warrior king feasted with his followers.
The Old English word for an Anglo-Saxon king who protected his people and shared gold rings.
The wise Northumbrian monk at Jarrow called the 'Father of English History' for his AD 731 book.
A wild, howling storm of freezing wind, rain, and swirling winter snow.

guided_reading.extract:
One winter night in Northumbria, King Edwin met his wise nobles inside a smoky timber mead hall. Together they talked about human life and new teachings. Up stood an old warrior who shared a picture everyone knew by heart.

Picture this, O King, as you sit at supper with your captains in winter! A bright fire blazes on the central hearth, warming the wooden hall from end to end. Outside the thick doors, icy tempests of rain and snow howl across the dark land.

All at once, one tiny sparrow darts quickly in through one open door! Straight across the warm firelight it flutters, then slips out through the far door. While it stays indoors, no winter frost can touch its small wings.

Yet that bright flash of warmth passes in the blink of an eye! Out from winter into winter the little bird vanishes back into the dark. Our short life on earth shines just like that, so wise teachings are well worth following!

parent_discussion.question: What sensory details inside an Anglo-Saxon timber mead hall make the room feel cosy compared to the night outside?
parent_discussion.answer: A bright fire blazes on the central hearth warming the timber hall while the king dines with his captains, safe from howling rain and snow.

parent_discussion.question: Why did King Edwin's wise noble compare a person's life to a tiny sparrow flying through two doors of a hall?
parent_discussion.answer: Just like the sparrow enjoys a brief warm moment by the fire between dark winter storms, human life is short and precious.

parent_discussion.question: Why was the timber mead hall the beating heart of every early Anglo-Saxon kingdom?
parent_discussion.answer: Inside the mead hall, a cyning shared food, honey mead, and gold rings to bind loyal warriors together and held council on big decisions.

story_check.question: Who wrote down the famous story of the winter sparrow in AD 731 at Jarrow Monastery?
story_check.feedback: Spot on! Venerable Bede recorded the parable of the sparrow in his AD 731 History of the English Church and People.

story_check.question: Which small bird flew out of the snowstorm through the warm timber mead hall?
story_check.feedback: Correct! The sparrow fluttered through one door into the firelight and straight out the opposite door.

story_check.question: Where was the roaring fire placed inside an Anglo-Saxon king's timber mead hall?
options: On top of the thatched roof
On a central hearth in the middle of the hall
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Just like Bede wrote, a bright fire blazed on the central hearth to warm the whole timber hall.

monday_cold_call.question: In Bede's AD 731 story, what flew through King Edwin's warm winter mead hall, and what was the warrior comparing it to?
monday_cold_call.answer: A tiny sparrow flew out of a winter snowstorm through the firelit mead hall and back into the dark, which the noble compared to a human life.

guided_reading.hinge_question: Why do you think Anglo-Saxon kings built grand timber mead halls beside rivers rather than moving into cold, roofless Roman stone ruins?

guided_reading.book_title: Beowulf — The Royal Ship-Burial & Boar-Crested Helmets
guided_reading.author: Anonymous Anglo-Saxon Poet (trans. Francis B. Gummere, 1909 — Public Domain)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Public-domain verse lines from Beowulf (lines 32–42, 303–306), translated in alliterative metre by Francis B. Gummere (1909), paired with the 1939 Sutton Hoo Mound 1 excavation.
guided_reading.author_context: For centuries, historians thought the glittering ship-burials in the Old English poem Beowulf were pure legend—until Basil Brown dug Mound 1 at Sutton Hoo in 1939!
guided_reading.cover_caption: Reconstruction of the iron-and-gilt-bronze Sutton Hoo helmet from Mound 1 in Suffolk, inlaid with red garnets and stamped warrior panels.

vocabVault.def: The Suffolk burial mounds where diggers in 1939 uncovered a 27-metre Anglo-Saxon royal ship burial.
The oldest surviving epic poem in Old English, chanted aloud in mead halls to the music of a harp.
The powerful 7th-century ruler of East Anglia most likely honoured inside Mound 1 at Sutton Hoo.
Glowing dark-red gemstones traded all the way from India and Sri Lanka to decorate Sutton Hoo gold.

guided_reading.extract:
Long before books were printed, Anglo-Saxon poets strummed wooden lyres in firelit halls and chanted the epic poem Beowulf. Listen to how the poet described burying a mighty king inside a treasure-packed ship:
There at the harbour stood the ring-prowed ship,
Icy and eager to sail, a royal vessel!
They laid their beloved lord deep in its bosom,
The famous giver of gold rings beside the mast.
From distant lands came heaps of shining treasure;
Never heard I of a ship more richly loaded
With battle-weapons, mail-coats, and gleaming swords!
Elsewhere in the poem, warriors marched wearing helmets just like the one later dug up in Suffolk:
Boar-figures shone above their cheek-guards,
Adorned with bright gold, gleaming and fire-hardened,
Standing fierce guard over those brave warriors' lives!
In summer 1939 at Sutton Hoo, Edith Pretty and Basil Brown brushed away Suffolk sand. Beneath Mound 1 lay iron ship rivets, red Indian garnets, and King Raedwald's gleaming helmet, proving the poet described real life!

parent_discussion.question: Which treasures placed beside the mast in the poem Beowulf match real objects found in Mound 1 at Sutton Hoo?
parent_discussion.answer: Battle-weapons, mail-coats, gleaming swords, gold treasures from distant lands (like Indian garnets and Byzantine spoons), and gilded helmets with boar figures!

parent_discussion.question: Notice the rhythm and repeated starting sounds in lines like 'laid their beloved lord'. Why were Old English poems written like that?
parent_discussion.answer: Strong beats and matching starting letters (alliteration) helped bards remember thousands of lines by heart while chanting to a harp.

parent_discussion.question: Why did Edith Pretty and Basil Brown's 1939 dig at Sutton Hoo completely transform how historians viewed the 'Dark Ages'?
parent_discussion.answer: Finding dazzling goldwork, red Sri Lankan garnets, and a 27-metre ship proved Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were artistic, wealthy, and connected across continents.

story_check.question: What is the name of the famous Old English epic poem that describes a royal ship burial packed with weapons and gold?
story_check.feedback: Spot on! Beowulf opens with a royal ship burial loaded with weapons and distant treasures—just like Sutton Hoo.

story_check.question: Who teamed up in Suffolk in 1939 to excavate the ghost ship inside Mound 1 at Sutton Hoo?
options: Edith Pretty and archaeologist Basil Brown
story_check.feedback: Correct! Landowner Edith Pretty asked local archaeologist Basil Brown to dig Mound 1, revealing iron rivets from a 27-metre ship.

story_check.question: Where had the glowing red garnet gemstones on Sutton Hoo's sword fittings and helmet eyebrows travelled from?
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Scientific tests proved those glowing red garnets came thousands of miles from India and Sri Lanka.

monday_cold_call.question: How did the 1939 Sutton Hoo ship burial prove that scenes in the Old English poem Beowulf were based on real customs?
monday_cold_call.answer: Sutton Hoo's 27-metre ship, distant treasures, swords, and gilded boar-crested helmet matched the royal ship burial and helmets described in Beowulf.

guided_reading.hinge_question: Why would a 7th-century king like Raedwald be buried with BOTH pagan war gear and Christian silver spoons inside the same ship?

guided_reading.book_title: Letters on the Viking Raid at Lindisfarne & Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (AD 793)
guided_reading.author: Alcuin of York & Chronicler (translated from Latin & Old English)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Adapted for KS2 oral reading from Alcuin of York, Epistola 16 to King Ethelred of Northumbria (summer AD 793) and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for AD 793 (Public Domain).
guided_reading.author_context: On 8 June AD 793, shallow-draught Viking longships stormed Holy Island at Lindisfarne—prompting Northumbrian scholar Alcuin to write one of history's most shocked letters!
guided_reading.cover_caption: Carved sandstone grave marker from Lindisfarne Priory showing seven armed Viking raiders marching with raised battle-axes and swords.

vocabVault.def: Holy Island off the Northumberland coast, where Viking longships launched their famous AD 793 raid.
A famous Northumbrian scholar and teacher who wrote horrified letters when news of Lindisfarne arrived.
How shallowly a ship's hull sits in water—letting Viking longships glide straight onto sandy beaches.
A peaceful Christian community where monks prayed, painted vellum Gospels, and guarded silver treasures.

guided_reading.extract:
In the year AD 793, frightening signs shook the people of Northumbria! Monks wrote of wild whirlwinds, bright lightning, and fiery dragons flashing across the sky. Soon after, on 8 June, sleek Viking longships glided onto Holy Island at Lindisfarne!

When news of the raid crossed the sea, scholar Alcuin grabbed his quill pen in horror. With a heavy heart, he wrote a warning letter to Northumbria's King Ethelred.

For nearly three hundred and fifty years, our people have lived in this lovely land! Never before has such terror struck Britain from a pagan seafaring folk. Nobody ever dreamed that raiders could sail straight across the open North Sea!

Look at Saint Cuthbert's church, stained with priests' blood and stripped of silver treasures! Britain's holiest island has fallen prey to fierce raiders. Guard your coasts well, O King, for everyone fears this storm is only the beginning!

parent_discussion.question: Why did Alcuin say nobody in Britain had ever thought a raid like 8 June AD 793 was even possible?
parent_discussion.answer: For centuries people thought the stormy open North Sea acted like a wall—not realising clinker-built Viking longships could cross open ocean and beach straight onto islands.

parent_discussion.question: Why were isolated island monasteries like Lindisfarne 'soft targets' for early Viking summer raiders?
parent_discussion.answer: Coastal monasteries sat right beside the sea, held silver chalices and jewel-covered Gospel books, and were lived in by unarmed monks.

parent_discussion.question: Alcuin feared in AD 793 that this raid was 'only the beginning'. How did events in AD 865 prove him right?
parent_discussion.answer: Summer raids grew larger until the Great Heathen Army landed in AD 865 to stay all winter, conquering York (Jorvik), East Anglia, and Mercia!

story_check.question: On what exact date did Viking longships launch their shocking raid on Holy Island at Lindisfarne?
story_check.feedback: Spot on! 8 June AD 793 at Lindisfarne marks the dramatic opening of the Viking Age in Britain.

story_check.question: Which Northumbrian scholar wrote a heartbroken letter crying 'Never before has such terror appeared in Britain'?
story_check.feedback: Correct! Alcuin of York wept over St Cuthbert's church at Lindisfarne and warned King Ethelred that worse raids might follow.

story_check.question: What clever ship-building feature let Viking longships land directly on Lindisfarne's beach and row up shallow rivers?
options: A flat, flexible clinker-built oak hull with only a 1-metre shallow draught
Solid stone anchors permanently fixed to the keel
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Overlapping oak planks gave longships a light, shallow draught of around one metre—no harbour needed!

monday_cold_call.question: Where did Vikings strike on 8 June AD 793, and why did scholar Alcuin say everyone in Britain was so shocked?
monday_cold_call.answer: Vikings raided the monastery on Holy Island at Lindisfarne, and Alcuin wrote that nobody had ever believed raiders could strike straight across the open North Sea.

guided_reading.hinge_question: Since monks wrote all the chronicles in AD 793 while Vikings wrote none, do we hear both sides of the story equally?

guided_reading.book_title: Mist Over Athelney: How Alfred Saved Wessex (AD 878)
guided_reading.author: The History Revision Hub (from Bishop Asser & the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original true historical story grounded in Bishop Asser's Life of King Alfred (AD 893), the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (AD 878–896), and the Ashmolean Museum's Alfred Jewel.
guided_reading.author_context: By winter AD 878, Viking armies had conquered every Anglo-Saxon kingdom except Wessex—forcing young King Alfred to hide inside freezing Somerset marshes and plan a comeback!
guided_reading.cover_caption: Historical engraving of the gold-and-crystal Alfred Jewel found near Athelney in Somerset, inscribed 'AELFRED MEC HEHT GEWYRCAN' ('Alfred ordered me to be made').

vocabVault.def: The remote island hidden deep inside misty Somerset marshes where King Alfred sheltered in early AD 878.
The Viking warlord defeated by Alfred at Edington who accepted Christian baptism and ruled the Danelaw.
Thirty-three fortified walled towns built across Wessex by King Alfred so no village lay far from safety.
Northern and eastern England where Viking laws and settlers ruled east of Roman Watling Street.

guided_reading.extract:
Right after Christmas in January AD 878, Viking leader Guthrum struck Chippenham by surprise! Every other Saxon kingdom had fallen, and now Wessex stood close to ruin. Young King Alfred fled into freezing Somerset marshes with a small loyal band.

Deep among tall reeds on tiny Athelney island, Alfred built a hidden fort and planned ahead. Brave riders slipped out through thick mist to call loyal farmers across three counties.

In May AD 878, Alfred rode to Egbert's Stone, where thousands of Wessex men cheered him! Locking round shields tightly at the Battle of Edington, Alfred's army smashed Guthrum's host. Surrounded in camp, Guthrum agreed to Christian baptism and a peace border for the Danelaw.

Never again would Wessex be caught off guard! Alfred ringed his land with thirty-three walled burhs and built fast sixty-oar warships. Loving wisdom too, he turned Latin books into Old English and sent bishops crystal pointers marked with his own royal name!

parent_discussion.question: Why was hiding on Athelney inside the Somerset marshes such a smart survival move by King Alfred in January AD 878?
parent_discussion.answer: Guthrum's large Viking army could not march horses or heavy carts through deep marshes and mist, giving Alfred safe time to rally Wessex farmers.

parent_discussion.question: How did Alfred's network of thirty-three fortified burhs make sure no Viking surprise attack like Chippenham could ever succeed again?
parent_discussion.answer: Every Wessex village lay within twenty miles (one day's walk) of a guarded earth-and-timber walled burh where families and cattle could shelter.

parent_discussion.question: Why is Alfred the ONLY ruler in British history given the title 'the Great'—was it just because he won battles?
parent_discussion.answer: No—besides saving Wessex at Edington and building burhs and warships, he made peace with Guthrum, opened schools, and translated books into Old English.

story_check.question: Where did King Alfred hide during winter AD 878 after Guthrum's surprise attack on Chippenham?
options: On Athelney inside the misty Somerset marshes
story_check.feedback: Spot on! Hidden among marshes and reeds at Athelney in Somerset, Alfred planned his spring comeback.

story_check.question: At which decisive battle in May AD 878 did Alfred's shield wall defeat Viking leader Guthrum?
story_check.feedback: Correct! Victory at the Battle of Edington saved Wessex and led to Guthrum's baptism and the Danelaw treaty.

story_check.question: What did King Alfred build thirty-three of across Wessex so no village lay more than twenty miles from safety?
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Walled burhs like Wareham and Wallingford protected Wessex families and grew into busy market towns.

monday_cold_call.question: How did King Alfred save Wessex in AD 878, and what two smart defences did he build afterwards?
monday_cold_call.answer: After regrouping in the Athelney marshes, Alfred defeated Guthrum at Edington in AD 878, then built 33 fortified walled burhs and 60-oar coastal warships.

guided_reading.hinge_question: Which did more to earn Alfred his title 'the Great': his sword at Edington, his walled burhs, or his Old English books and schools?

guided_reading.book_title: Risala — Eyewitness Journey from Baghdad to the Northern Rivers (AD 922)
guided_reading.author: Ahmad ibn Fadlan (adapted for KS2 from AD 922 Arabic travel journal)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Adapted into age-appropriate KS2 oral sentences from Ahmad ibn Fadlan's Risala (AD 921–922 diplomatic account for the Caliph of Baghdad), paired with Coppergate silver dirhams.
guided_reading.author_context: How did Arabic silver coins from sunny Baghdad end up buried under rainy Coppergate in Viking York? In AD 922, Arab diplomat Ahmad ibn Fadlan met Viking river-traders face to face!
guided_reading.cover_caption: An Islamic silver dirham coin stamped in Arabic script, traded by Viking river-merchants and buried in hoards across northern England.

vocabVault.def: An observant diplomat sent north from Baghdad in AD 921–922 who wrote a famous eyewitness description of Viking traders.
A pure silver coin minted in Islamic cities like Baghdad and Samarkand, prized by Viking merchants.
The bustling Viking trading city of York, where wet peat beneath Coppergate saved 40,000 everyday finds.
Glowing golden fossilised tree resin from the Baltic Sea, carved into beads and rings in Jorvik workshops.

guided_reading.extract:
In May AD 922, diplomat Ahmad ibn Fadlan rode far north from sunny Baghdad. Beside a wide river, he watched tall wooden ships pull onto the muddy bank. Stepping ashore came Viking traders called the Rus, and Ibn Fadlan stared in awe!

I have watched these Rus pitch camp on their trading trips, he wrote in his book! Never have I met taller or stronger people, for they stand like date-palm trees!

Every man carries a sharp axe, a broad patterned sword, and a belt knife at all times. Around their necks shine strings of green glass beads prized above almost everything. Rich traders gladly pay one silver dirham coin for each bead to gift their wives!

Once their boats tie up, merchants lay out bread, meat, and onions. Eagerly they hope for rich buyers bringing bags of pure Arabic silver dirhams for warm northern furs! Many of those gleaming Baghdad coins travelled all the way back to busy workshops in Jorvik.

parent_discussion.question: Which striking physical details stood out to Arab diplomat Ahmad ibn Fadlan the moment he saw Viking merchants?
parent_discussion.answer: He marvelled that they stood 'as tall as date-palm trees', never put down their axe, patterned sword, and knife, and wore prized glass bead necklaces.

parent_discussion.question: What goods did Viking river-merchants swap with buyers from Baghdad and Samarkand?
parent_discussion.answer: Vikings traded warm northern furs (and walrus ivory or amber) in exchange for bags of pure Islamic silver dirham coins and prized beads.

parent_discussion.question: How do Ibn Fadlan's AD 922 journal and the 40,000 Coppergate finds in York change the stereotype that Vikings were ONLY violent raiders?
parent_discussion.answer: Both sources prove Vikings were also long-distance international merchants, skilled comb- and shoe-makers, and navigators linking York to Baghdad and Byzantium.

story_check.question: From which great Islamic capital city had diplomat Ahmad ibn Fadlan travelled before meeting Viking river-traders in AD 922?
story_check.feedback: Spot on! Sent north by the Caliph of Baghdad, Ibn Fadlan left us a vivid eyewitness picture of Viking river-merchants.

story_check.question: What trees from his homeland did Ibn Fadlan compare the tall Viking traders to?
story_check.feedback: Correct! 'They stand as tall as date-palm trees,' marvelled Ibn Fadlan in his AD 922 journal.

story_check.question: Why have archaeologists dug up thousands of Arabic silver dirham coins in Viking hoards and under Coppergate in Jorvik (York)?
options: Viking merchants sailed eastern rivers trading furs for Islamic silver dirhams and brought them home to Britain
Romans minted Arabic coins on Hadrian's Wall
Stone Age hunters dropped them on Doggerland
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Viking river-traders connected northern England all the way to the Silk Roads and Islamic mints.

monday_cold_call.question: Who met Viking river-merchants in AD 922, and how did Islamic silver dirhams reach Viking Jorvik (York)?
monday_cold_call.answer: Arab diplomat Ahmad ibn Fadlan from Baghdad met them, recording how Vikings traded northern furs along eastern rivers for silver dirham coins that travelled back to Jorvik.

guided_reading.hinge_question: What surprises you more about Viking Jorvik: silk from Byzantium, a cowrie shell from the Red Sea, or silver coins from Baghdad?

guided_reading.book_title: The Battle of Maldon (Old English Poem, AD 991)
guided_reading.author: Anonymous Old English Poet (Public Domain verse translation)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Public-domain verse lines from the late-10th-century Old English poem The Battle of Maldon (lines 45–48, 312–319, trans. R. K. Gordon, 1926), bridging to Stamford Bridge and Hastings (1066).
guided_reading.author_context: After Aethelflaed and King Athelstan united one Kingdom of England, fresh Viking fleets demanded Danegeld silver in AD 991—inspiring Old English poetry's bravest shield-wall speech!
guided_reading.cover_caption: Historical re-enactment of a tightly locked early medieval shield wall with iron helmets, mail coats, spears, and battle banners.

vocabVault.def: King Alfred's grandson who captured York in AD 927 to become the first true King of All England.
Huge payments of silver ('Dane-gold') paid from AD 991 to persuade raiding Danish fleets to sail away.
A tight battle line where warriors locked round wooden shields edge to edge to block enemy spears.
Treasure or silver demanded by an invading army as the price for peace.

guided_reading.extract:
By AD 927, bold Aethelflaed and King Athelstan had united one Kingdom of England. Yet in August AD 991, ninety-three Viking ships anchored off Maldon in Essex demanding bags of Danegeld silver! Tall Saxon leader Byrhtnoth raised his round shield on the shore. Fiercely he shouted back words made famous in the Old English poem The Battle of Maldon:
Hear you, sea-rover, what this folk replies?
Spear-points alone will we pay you for tribute,
Sharp-edged darts and tried ancient swords,
War-gear that brings you small profit in battle!
When Byrhtnoth fell fighting, old warrior Byrhtwold lifted his ash spear and spoke famous brave lines:
Mind must be firmer, heart must be bolder,
Courage the greater as our strength grows less!
Here lies our lord cut down in the dust.
Here will I stand fast right beside my friend!
In 1066, King Harold's tired shield wall showed that same brave spirit. His men beat Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge before falling to Duke William at Hastings!

parent_discussion.question: Instead of handing over silver Danegeld coins, what 'tribute' did Byrhtnoth promise the Viking messenger across the river?
parent_discussion.answer: He answered fiercely that his people would pay only with sharp spear-points and ancient swords!

parent_discussion.question: Read Byrhtwold's famous chant ('Mind must be firmer, heart must be bolder...') out loud together. Why did those words inspire warriors when a battle went badly?
parent_discussion.answer: They reminded tired warriors never to run away, urging their minds and courage to grow stronger even as their physical strength grew weaker.

parent_discussion.question: Why was King Harold Godwinson's Saxon shield wall so exhausted by the time it faced Duke William at Hastings on 14 October 1066?
parent_discussion.answer: Harold had just marched 185 miles north to defeat Viking King Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge on 25 September, then marched 250 miles straight back south!

story_check.question: What do historians call the huge silver payments demanded by Danish fleets from AD 991 onwards?
story_check.feedback: Spot on! King Aethelred paid huge sums of silver Danegeld, though raiders kept coming back until King Cnut took the crown in AD 1016.

story_check.question: Complete old warrior Byrhtwold's famous Old English battle line: 'Mind must be firmer, heart must be bolder, courage the greater as...'
story_check.feedback: Correct! 'Courage the greater as our strength grows less!' became the most famous expression of Anglo-Saxon loyalty.

story_check.question: Which two dramatic battles in September and October 1066 ended both the Viking Age and Anglo-Saxon rule in England?
options: Stamford Bridge (25 September 1066) and Hastings (14 October 1066)
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Harold crushed Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge, then fell nineteen days later against Duke William at Hastings.

monday_cold_call.question: In The Battle of Maldon, what did Byrhtnoth refuse to pay the Vikings, and what two 1066 battles ended Anglo-Saxon rule?
monday_cold_call.answer: Byrhtnoth refused to pay silver tribute (Danegeld), promising spear-points instead, and in 1066 Stamford Bridge and the Battle of Hastings ended the Viking and Anglo-Saxon eras.

guided_reading.hinge_question: If Duke William's ships had landed three weeks later—or if Harald Hardrada had never invaded the north—would England still be Anglo-Saxon today?

lessons.prologue: In AD 762, one hundred thousand builders raised a dazzling circular capital beside the River Tigris! Step through Baghdad’s four great gates, explore the Green Dome Palace at the City of Peace, and discover why this Silk Road crossroads dwarfed Anglo-Saxon towns in Britain.
lessons.blurb: In AD 762, one hundred thousand builders raised a dazzling circular capital beside the River Tigris! Step through Baghdad’s four great gates, explore the Green Dome Palace at the City of Peace, and discover why this Silk Road crossroads dwarfed Anglo-Saxon towns in Britain.

teacher_notes.primer: This opening Key Stage 2 enquiry introduces the rapid spread of early Islam from Arabia before focusing on Abbasid Caliph al-Mansur’s decision to found Baghdad in AD 762. Primary pupils investigate why the fertile bend between the Tigris and Euphrates was a Silk Road crossroads, how 100,000 bricklayers built the 2km circular Round City (Madinat al-Salam), and how Baghdad’s nearly one million citizens around AD 900 contrasted starkly with Anglo-Saxon Britain’s small timber towns of 5,000–10,000 people.

items.question: On a history timeline, did AD 762 happen before or after the Romans left Britain around AD 410?
items.answer: After the Romans left Britain (more than 350 years later)
items.explanation: AD dates count upwards from AD 1, so AD 762 came three and a half centuries after Roman rule ended in Britain.

items.question: Why did so many ancient and medieval rulers choose to build capital cities beside major rivers?
items.answer: Rivers provided fresh drinking water, watered farm crops, and carried heavy trading boats
items.explanation: Before railways or lorries, river boats and canals were the fastest way to move food, bricks, and trade goods.

items.question: What was the famous network of overland trade routes linking China, Central Asia, Persia, and the Mediterranean called?
items.explanation: Caravans of camels and horses carried silk, spices, paper, glass, and ideas thousands of kilometres across Asia.

items.question: Which people ruled small kingdoms of wooden halls and farming villages across England around AD 900?
items.answer: The Anglo-Saxons (alongside Viking settlers in northern and eastern England)
items.explanation: Around AD 900, Anglo-Saxon Britain had small fortified *burh* towns of wooden houses rather than giant stone or brick cities.

items.question: What do historians mean when they call a group of many lands governed by one supreme ruler an "empire"?
items.answer: A large collection of countries, peoples, and cities united under a single ruler or government
items.explanation: In the early Islamic world, this vast empire was called a Caliphate and was led by a ruler known as a Caliph.

vocab.definition: The supreme political and spiritual leader who ruled the early Islamic Empire (the Caliphate).
The ruling family who took charge of the Islamic Empire in AD 750 and built Baghdad as their capital.
Human-made waterways dug between rivers to irrigate green farmlands and carry trading boats.
Arabic for "City of Peace", the official name Caliph al-Mansur gave to the Round City of Baghdad in AD 762.
Relating to the farming kingdoms and small timber towns of early medieval Britain between c. AD 410 and 1066.

narrative_blocks.title: AD 610–762: Rapid Spread of Early Islam & Choosing the River Tigris
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.1] Beginning in **Arabia**, the faith of **Islam** spread swiftly across wide lands. In **AD 750**, the **Abbasid** [uh-BASS-id] family took charge of this empire, led by a **Caliph**. In **AD 762**, **Caliph al-Mansur** [al-man-SOOR] searched for a safe central spot for his **capital**. He chose a fertile green bend on the **River Tigris**.

[1.2] Deep **canals** linked the Tigris straight to the **River Euphrates**. Fresh water fed lush date palms and golden wheat fields. Round woven-reed **quffa** [KOOF-uh] boats brought silk and spices, while Silk Road camel caravans met there.
narrative_blocks.content:
[1.1] Beginning in **Arabia**, the faith of **Islam** spread swiftly across wide lands. In **AD 750**, the **Abbasid** [uh-BASS-id] family took charge of this empire, led by a **Caliph**. In **AD 762**, **Caliph al-Mansur** [al-man-SOOR] searched for a safe central spot for his **capital**. He chose a fertile green bend on the **River Tigris**.

[1.2] Deep **canals** linked the Tigris straight to the **River Euphrates**. Fresh water fed lush date palms and golden wheat fields. Round woven-reed **quffa** [KOOF-uh] boats brought silk and spices, while Silk Road camel caravans met there.

narrative_blocks.caption: Traditional round woven-reed quffa river boats on the River Tigris in Baghdad — a river craft used in Iraq since ancient times.

narrative_blocks.title: AD 762–766: 100,000 Builders & the Round City of Peace
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.3] Al-Mansur gathered **100,000 bricklayers** and diggers to raise the circular **Round City** of **Baghdad**. Architects first traced a circle **two kilometres** wide in flaming cotton seeds! Builders then baked millions of mud bricks for thick **double walls** and a deep moat. Al-Mansur named his capital **Madinat al-Salam** [mah-DEE-nat al-sah-LAHM], meaning **City of Peace**.

[1.4] Four guarded iron gates pierced the walls, named **Kufa**, **Basra**, **Khorasan**, and **Syria**. Straight market streets led towards the open centre. Right at the heart stood the **Great Mosque** beside the **Green Dome Palace**.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 900: One Million Citizens vs Anglo-Saxon Britain
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.5] Busy markets, bathhouses, and gardens soon spread beyond the Round City walls. By **AD 900**, bustling **Baghdad** was home to nearly **one million people**! Families strolled down **paved streets** beside cool **canals** and studied inside grand **libraries**.

[1.6] Meanwhile, towns in **Anglo-Saxon Britain** around **AD 900** looked tiny by comparison. Even major English towns like **London** or **Winchester** held only **5,000 to 10,000 people**. Most British families lived in smoky **timber huts** with thatched roofs. Muddy village lanes showed how huge Baghdad truly was!

tasks.title: 1. Primary Evidence Detective
tasks.question: Look closely at Source A. What does this building show about early Islamic wealth and skill?
tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, the golden dome and geometric tilework of the Dome of the Rock reveal early Islamic...
hints: Describe the shining golden dome and colourful geometric patterns covering the octagonal walls.
Notice the early date (AD 691) — decades before Baghdad was even built!
Explain what raising such a monument proves about early Islamic wealth, maths, and engineering.
tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, the golden dome and geometric tilework of the Dome of the Rock reveal early Islamic wealth, mathematical precision, and engineering skill as early as AD 691. Long before Baghdad was founded, master builders and mosaic artists could raise towering gilded domes and intricate symmetries.

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain why Caliph al-Mansur chose the River Tigris in AD 762 and built Baghdad as a circle.
tasks.starter: In AD 762, Caliph al-Mansur chose a fertile bend on the River Tigris for his circular capital because...
hints: Explain how canals joined the Tigris and Euphrates rivers to water crops and welcome Silk Road boats.
Describe the two-kilometre double brick walls, four gates, and central Great Mosque and Green Dome Palace.
Explain what placing the palace and mosque in the exact centre of Madinat al-Salam symbolised to visitors!
tasks.model_answer: In AD 762, Caliph al-Mansur chose a fertile bend on the River Tigris for his circular capital because deep canals connected it straight to the River Euphrates, watering orchards and linking river boats with Silk Road camel caravans. Using 100,000 builders, he raised the two-kilometre double brick walls of Madinat al-Salam (the City of Peace) pierced by four gates pointing across the empire. Placing the Great Mosque and Green Dome Palace at the exact centre showed that faith and the Caliph’s peaceful rule anchored the whole world!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: Why did Caliph al-Mansur build the Round City of Baghdad, and how did it compare with Britain around AD 900?
tasks.starter: By AD 900, Baghdad had grown into the bustling Crossroads of the World because...
hints: Explain how geography (Tigris, Euphrates canals, and Silk Road caravans) brought wealth to Caliph al-Mansur’s capital.
Describe how 100,000 builders constructed the safe circular Round City (Madinat al-Salam) in AD 762.
Compare Baghdad’s nearly one million residents, paved streets, and libraries with small Anglo-Saxon timber towns of 5,000–10,000 people.
tasks.model_answer: By AD 900, Baghdad had grown into the bustling Crossroads of the World because Caliph al-Mansur placed his AD 762 capital where Tigris and Euphrates canals met overland Silk Road caravans and sea ships from Asia and Africa. Protected by the double brick walls and four gates of Madinat al-Salam, trade and gold dinars funded paved streets, bathhouses, and grand libraries for nearly one million people. In contrast, divided Anglo-Saxon Britain had far smaller local trade networks, with towns of just 5,000 to 10,000 people living in thatched timber huts.

lessons.title: Enquiry 2: Paper & The House of Wisdom (c. AD 800–1000)
lessons.subtitle: Harun al-Rashid, Al-Ma’mun, Samarkand Paper-Making, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, Fatima al-Fihri & Queen Zubayda
lessons.enquiryQuestion: How did cheap paper and Baghdad’s House of Wisdom save world knowledge?
lessons.enquiry_question: How did cheap paper and Baghdad’s House of Wisdom save world knowledge?
lessons.prologue: Step inside Baghdad’s legendary House of Wisdom, where Muslim, Christian, and Jewish translators worked side by side! Discover how cheap rag paper from Samarkand filled over a hundred bookshops, while Fatima al-Fihri and Queen Zubayda funded learning and desert wells.
lessons.blurb: Step inside Baghdad’s legendary House of Wisdom, where Muslim, Christian, and Jewish translators worked side by side! Discover how cheap rag paper from Samarkand filled over a hundred bookshops, while Fatima al-Fihri and Queen Zubayda funded learning and desert wells.

teacher_notes.primer: This second Key Stage 2 enquiry explores how Baghdad’s House of Wisdom (*Bayt al-Hikma*) under Caliphs Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma’mun united technological innovation with cultural exchange. Primary pupils trace how rag paper-making arrived from China via Samarkand to create over 100 bookshops (while Europe still scraped expensive calfskin parchment), how Muslim, Christian, and Jewish translators like Hunayn ibn Ishaq rescued and tested Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit texts, and how women patrons Fatima al-Fihri (al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, AD 859) and Queen Zubayda (Hajj road wells) shaped the Golden Age.

objectives.primer: Compare cotton-and-linen rag paper mills and Baghdad’s 100+ bookshops with costly calfskin parchment.

objectives.question: Why was testing and correcting ancient books even more important than simply translating their words?

source_context.Source A: Once Islamic craftworkers learned paper-making via Samarkand, smooth rag paper replaced costly animal-skin parchment for sacred texts, poetry, and science books. **Hinge Question:** Why did switching from calfskin parchment to cotton-and-rag paper let Baghdad open over 100 bookshops?
source_context.Source B: Inside Baghdad’s House of Wisdom, Christian physician Hunayn ibn Ishaq worked beside Muslim and Jewish scholars to translate Greek medical books into clear Arabic. **Hinge Question:** What does Caliph al-Ma’mun hiring Christian, Jewish, and Muslim translators side by side reveal about Baghdad’s House of Wisdom?
source_context.Source C: Positioned halfway between China and Persia along the Silk Roads, Samarkand became famous in the AD 750s for fine rag paper that inspired Baghdad’s paper mills. **Hinge Question:** How did Silk Road cities like Samarkand carry life-changing inventions as well as luxury silk and spices?
source_context.Source D: Building on Greek star lists translated into Arabic, astronomer al-Sufi checked the night sky himself to fix star positions and note the Andromeda Galaxy! **Hinge Question:** How does Source D prove Golden Age scholars tested and improved ancient Greek books rather than just copying them?

items.question: In what year did Abbasid Caliph al-Mansur found Baghdad, and beside which major river did he build it?
items.answer: AD 762, on a fertile bend of the River Tigris (linked by canals to the River Euphrates)
items.explanation: Deep canals connected the Tigris and Euphrates, watering crops and linking river boats to Silk Road caravans.

items.question: How many workers built the two-kilometre Round City of Baghdad, and what did Madinat al-Salam mean?
items.answer: 100,000 workers built it, and Madinat al-Salam meant the "City of Peace"
items.explanation: Bricklayers baked millions of mud bricks to raise thick double walls and a deep moat around the circular city.

items.question: Name two of the Round City’s four gates and the two grand buildings right in the middle.
items.answer: Any two of Kufa, Basra, Khorasan, or Syria (towards Damascus); the Great Mosque and Green Dome Palace stood in the centre
items.explanation: Straight covered streets led from the four outer gates into the central park around the palace and mosque.

items.question: Around AD 900, how did Baghdad’s population compare with major towns in Anglo-Saxon Britain like London or Winchester?
items.answer: Baghdad had nearly one million people, while big Anglo-Saxon towns held only 5,000 to 10,000 people
items.explanation: Most families in Anglo-Saxon Britain lived in thatched timber huts, while Baghdad boasted paved streets, canals, and libraries.

items.question: What were round woven-reed quffa boats and Abbasid gold dinars used for in Baghdad?
items.answer: Quffa boats carried goods along the River Tigris, and pure gold dinars paid merchants across long-distance trade routes
items.explanation: Reliable river transport and trusted gold coins helped turn Baghdad into the Crossroads of the World.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 786–833: Harun al-Rashid, Al-Ma’mun & the Paper Revolution
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.1] Under **Caliph Harun al-Rashid** and his son **Caliph al-Ma'mun** [al-mah-MOON], Baghdad drew thinkers from afar. Together they expanded a royal library into the **House of Wisdom**, or **Bayt al-Hikma** [bayt al-HIK-mah]. Via the Silk Road city of **Samarkand**, craftworkers learned Chinese **paper-making**. Watermills beat old cotton and linen rags into smooth, cheap paper.

[2.2] Across **Europe**, scribes still scraped costly **calfskin parchment** from whole cattle herds! Cheap rag paper transformed Baghdad's **book markets**. Soon over **100 bookshops** buzzed in the **Paper Sellers' Market** with poetry and star charts.

[2.2] Across **Europe**, scribes still scraped costly **calfskin parchment** from whole cattle herds! Cheap rag paper transformed Baghdad's **book markets**. Soon over **100 bookshops** buzzed in the **Paper Sellers' Market** with poetry and star charts.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 830–900: The Translation Movement & Hunayn ibn Ishaq
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.3] Al-Ma'mun sent messengers to buy rare ancient scrolls from Greece, Persia, and India. Inside the House of Wisdom, the **Translation Movement** rescued fragile books before they crumbled. **Muslim**, **Christian**, and **Jewish** scholars worked together turning **Greek**, **Persian**, and **Sanskrit** texts into **Arabic**.

[2.4] Their star translator was **Hunayn ibn Ishaq** [hoo-NAYN ib-in is-HAHK], a gifted Christian doctor. Stories say al-Ma'mun paid him the weight of every finished book in gold! Baghdad's scholars never copied old writers blindly. Instead, they tested every claim and fixed mistakes.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 800–900: Visionary Women Patrons — Fatima al-Fihri & Queen Zubayda
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.5] Generous women also shaped the **Islamic Golden Age** as visionary **patrons** funding public works. In **AD 859**, **Fatima al-Fihri** spent her family wealth in **Fez**, Morocco. She founded **al-Qarawiyyin** [al-kah-rah-wee-YEEN], a grand mosque and teaching college. Students still gather there today to study maths, star maps, and law!

[2.6] Earlier in Baghdad, **Queen Zubayda** [zoo-BAY-dah], wife of Harun al-Rashid, planned a desert water lifeline. Thirsty pilgrims walking the hot **Hajj road** to **Mecca** needed water. Zubayda paid masons to dig stone **wells** and pools that saved thousands!

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain why learning paper-making via Samarkand was such a turning point for Baghdad and the world.
tasks.starter: Learning the secret of paper-making via Samarkand changed Baghdad and world learning forever because...
hints: Explain how Baghdad watermills beat cotton and linen rags into smooth, affordable sheets of paper.

tasks.model_answer: Learning the secret of paper-making via Samarkand changed Baghdad and world learning forever because watermills could beat old cotton and linen rags into smooth, cheap writing sheets. Meanwhile, scribes in Europe still scraped expensive calfskin parchment, needing whole herds of cattle for a single large book! Affordable paper sparked over 100 bustling bookshops in Baghdad’s Paper Sellers’ Market and let the House of Wisdom copy and share science, history, and poetry across three continents.

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did cheap paper and Baghdad’s House of Wisdom rescue and expand world knowledge?
tasks.starter: Rescuing and spreading Golden Age knowledge took an extraordinary team effort across the Islamic world...
hints: Explain how Caliphs Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma’mun funded the House of Wisdom and gathered rare scrolls.
Explain how multi-faith translators like Hunayn ibn Ishaq turned Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit books into Arabic.
Show why patrons like Fatima al-Fihri (al-Qarawiyyin, AD 859) and Queen Zubayda (Hajj wells) were equally vital!
tasks.model_answer: Rescuing and spreading Golden Age knowledge took an extraordinary team effort across the Islamic world. Caliphs Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma’mun provided royal funding to expand the House of Wisdom and send messengers for rare scrolls. Yet without skilled Muslim, Christian, and Jewish translators like Hunayn ibn Ishaq, those Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit books could never have been read, tested, and improved in Arabic on cheap rag paper. Equally important, visionary women patrons like Fatima al-Fihri — who founded al-Qarawiyyin in Fez in AD 859 — and Queen Zubayda kept students learning and travellers safe!

lessons.prologue: Every time you write zero, solve algebra, snap a photo, or visit a hospital, you use breakthroughs from the Islamic Golden Age! Meet al-Khwarizmi, astrolabe maker Mariam al-Asturlabi, light detective Ibn al-Haytham, and master surgeon al-Zahrawi.
lessons.blurb: Every time you write zero, solve algebra, snap a photo, or visit a hospital, you use breakthroughs from the Islamic Golden Age! Meet al-Khwarizmi, astrolabe maker Mariam al-Asturlabi, light detective Ibn al-Haytham, and master surgeon al-Zahrawi.

teacher_notes.primer: This third Key Stage 2 enquiry celebrates scientific, mathematical, engineering, and medical breakthroughs across the Islamic Golden Age (c. AD 820–1050 and al-Jazari’s mechanical legacy). Primary pupils investigate Muhammad al-Khwarizmi (0–9 numerals, zero/*sifr*, algebra, algorithm), Mariam al-Asturlabi’s brass astrolabes, al-Jazari’s Elephant Water Clock, Ibn al-Haytham’s pinhole *camera obscura* experiments proving how vision works, free *bimaristan* hospitals, al-Razi’s clean-air meat test and measles vs smallpox research, and al-Zahrawi’s 200 surgical tools and dissolving catgut stitches.

objectives.objective: Explain how al-Khwarizmi’s Hindu-Arabic numerals (0–9), algebra, and Mariam al-Asturlabi’s astrolabes still shape modern life.
objectives.primer: Explore zero (*sifr*), *al-Jabr* (algebra), algorithms, brass astrolabes, and al-Jazari’s Elephant Water Clock.
objectives.question: Where do we still use al-Khwarizmi’s numbers and algorithms every single day at school and home?

objectives.objective: Describe how Ibn al-Haytham used a dark pinhole room (camera obscura) to prove how human eyes see light.
objectives.primer: Contrast ancient Greek eye-ray myths with Ibn al-Haytham’s experimental proof that light travels in straight lines into our eyes.
objectives.question: Why do historians call Ibn al-Haytham a pioneer of testing ideas with real experiments?

objectives.objective: Explain why medieval Islamic bimaristan hospitals, al-Razi, and al-Zahrawi were centuries ahead of healthcare in Europe.
objectives.primer: Examine free clean wards, pharmacies, al-Razi’s fresh-meat air test and measles discovery, and al-Zahrawi’s 200 surgical tools.
objectives.question: What features of a medieval bimaristan would you still recognise inside a modern hospital today?

items.question: Why did Abbasid Caliph al-Mansur build the Round City of Baghdad (Madinat al-Salam) on the River Tigris in AD 762?
items.answer: Canals linked the Tigris and Euphrates for fertile farming and boat trade right where Silk Road routes met
items.explanation: 100,000 workers raised a circular brick capital with four gates and the Great Mosque and Green Dome Palace at its heart.

items.question: How did Baghdad around AD 900 contrast with towns in Anglo-Saxon Britain?
items.answer: Baghdad had nearly one million people with paved streets and libraries, while Anglo-Saxon towns held 5,000–10,000 in timber huts
items.explanation: Baghdad was the largest city in the western world at a time when British settlements were much smaller farming towns.

items.question: Through which Silk Road city did paper-making reach Baghdad, and how did rag paper beat European parchment?
items.answer: Via Samarkand; cotton-and-rag paper was smooth and cheap compared with costly scraped calfskin parchment
items.explanation: Affordable rag paper sparked over 100 bustling bookshops in Baghdad’s Paper Sellers’ Market.

items.question: Which faiths worked together in the House of Wisdom’s Translation Movement, led by medical translator Hunayn ibn Ishaq?
items.answer: Muslim, Christian, and Jewish scholars worked side by side translating Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit books into Arabic
items.explanation: Hunayn ibn Ishaq was a Christian physician whose clear Arabic medical translations were prized by Caliph al-Ma’mun.

items.question: How did women patrons Fatima al-Fihri (AD 859) and Queen Zubayda leave lasting legacies?
items.answer: Fatima al-Fihri founded al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, and Queen Zubayda funded stone wells along the desert Hajj road to Mecca
items.explanation: Both women used their wealth to support education, travellers, and public welfare across the Islamic world.

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: In Baghdad, al-Khwarizmi’s book al-Jabr gave us [Algebra], while his own name inspired the computer word [Algorithm]. Makers like Mariam al-Asturlabi crafted the brass [Astrolabe] to map the stars, and Ibn al-Haytham used a pinhole [Camera Obscura] to test how light enters our eyes. Meanwhile, sick patients received free care inside a clean [Bimaristan].

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 820–1206: Zero, Algebra, Astrolabes & the Elephant Clock
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.1] In **Baghdad's** House of Wisdom, **Muhammad al-Khwarizmi** [al-kwah-RIZ-mee] championed **Hindu-Arabic numerals** from **0 to 9**. Using **zero**, called **sifr** [SIF-er], made big sums far easier than clumsy Roman numerals! His **maths** book **al-Jabr** gave us **algebra**, and his own name gave us **algorithm**.

[3.2] Makers like **Mariam al-Asturlabi** [al-as-toor-LAH-bee] crafted brass **astrolabes** to map bright stars. Travellers held them up to check prayer times, sail seas, and find **Mecca**. Engineer **al-Jazari** [al-jah-ZAH-ree] also built **clocks** like his **Elephant Water Clock**. Hidden floats clashed brass cymbals every half hour to advance **science**!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 965–1040: Ibn al-Haytham’s Light Proof & Free Bimaristans
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.3] Ancient Greek writers once claimed invisible rays shot out of human eyes to see! Scientist **Ibn al-Haytham** [IB-in al-HAY-thum] doubted that story and tested **light** carefully. Inside a dark room with a tiny hole, he built a pinhole **camera obscura**. He proved light travels in **straight lines** into our eyes, inspiring modern cameras!

[3.4] Islamic cities also built free teaching hospitals called **bimaristans** [bee-MAH-rih-stahnz] for rich and poor alike. Each **bimaristan** had **clean wards**, cool fountains, and a stocked **pharmacy**. Recovering patients even got clean clothes and pocket money to rest at home!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 900–1013: Master Doctors Al-Razi & Al-Zahrawi
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.5] Before building Baghdad's hospital, chief doctor **al-Razi** [al-RAH-zee] hung fresh meat across town. He picked the spot where meat rotted slowest because the air was cleanest! Careful bedside notes helped al-Razi tell **measles** apart from **smallpox**. Trained nurses served healthy meals to help **sick people** recover.

[3.6] In Spain around **AD 1000**, royal surgeon **al-Zahrawi** [al-zah-RAH-wee] wrote an illustrated medical guide. He drew over **200 surgical tools**, including forceps, scalpels, and delicate bone saws. He also discovered **catgut stitches** that dissolved **safely** inside wounds as patients began to **heal**!

tasks.question: Explain how Ibn al-Haytham and doctor al-Razi used clever experiments instead of guesswork.
tasks.starter: Both Ibn al-Haytham and Baghdad doctor al-Razi proved the power of real scientific testing because...
hints: Describe how Ibn al-Haytham used a dark pinhole room (camera obscura) to prove light enters our eyes in straight lines.
Describe how al-Razi hung fresh meat around Baghdad to pick the cleanest-air hospital site.
Add how al-Razi’s careful bedside notes made him the first doctor to tell measles apart from smallpox!
tasks.model_answer: Both Ibn al-Haytham and Baghdad doctor al-Razi proved the power of real scientific testing because neither scholar accepted old claims without evidence. When ancient Greek books claimed rays shot out of human eyes, Ibn al-Haytham built a pitch-dark pinhole camera obscura and proved light actually travels in straight lines into our eyes! Similarly, al-Razi hung fresh meat across Baghdad to build his bimaristan where meat rotted slowest in clean air, and kept detailed bedside notes to distinguish measles from smallpox.

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did Golden Age mathematicians, astronomers, engineers, and doctors change world science forever?
tasks.starter: Although maths, optics, and medicine all transformed human life, I think the biggest Golden Age breakthrough was...
hints: Compare al-Khwarizmi’s 0–9 numerals, zero (sifr), algebra, and algorithms with Mariam al-Asturlabi’s astrolabes.
Weigh up Ibn al-Haytham’s pinhole camera obscura light proof and free bimaristan hospitals.
Reach a clear judgement explaining how your chosen breakthrough connects to the other two in modern life!
tasks.model_answer: Although maths, optics, and medicine all transformed human life, I think al-Khwarizmi’s mathematics changed our modern world the most because every other science depends on it! His Hindu-Arabic numerals (0–9 including zero, sifr), algebra, and step-by-step algorithms power modern computers, engineering, and hospital machines alike. Even so, Ibn al-Haytham’s pinhole camera obscura gave us eyeglasses and cameras, while free bimaristans, al-Razi’s clinical notes, and al-Zahrawi’s 200 surgical tools and dissolving catgut stitches created the blueprint for modern healthcare!

quiz.question: Which number system (including zero, called sifr) did Baghdad mathematician Muhammad al-Khwarizmi champion?
quiz.q: Which number system (including zero, called sifr) did Baghdad mathematician Muhammad al-Khwarizmi champion?
quiz.explanation: Al-Khwarizmi championed Hindu-Arabic numerals from 0 to 9, including zero (sifr), making big calculations clear and fast.

quiz.question: Which two modern words come from al-Khwarizmi’s book al-Jabr and his own name?
quiz.q: Which two modern words come from al-Khwarizmi’s book al-Jabr and his own name?
quiz.explanation: His book al-Jabr gave us "algebra", and the Latin form of al-Khwarizmi’s name gave us "algorithm".

quiz.question: Who was Mariam al-Asturlabi, and what precision brass instrument did she craft?
quiz.q: Who was Mariam al-Asturlabi, and what precision brass instrument did she craft?
options: A weaver who made silk carpets
A potter who glazed blue bowls
A skilled woman astronomer-maker who crafted brass astrolabes
A captain who sailed Viking longships
quiz.answer: A skilled woman astronomer-maker who crafted brass astrolabes
quiz.a: A skilled woman astronomer-maker who crafted brass astrolabes
quiz.explanation: Tenth-century craftworker Mariam al-Asturlabi made intricate brass astrolabes used to map stars, check prayer times, and navigate.

quiz.question: How often did master engineer al-Jazari’s mechanical Elephant Water Clock strike brass cymbals?
quiz.q: How often did master engineer al-Jazari’s mechanical Elephant Water Clock strike brass cymbals?
quiz.explanation: Hidden water floats inside al-Jazari’s Elephant Water Clock made figures whirl and clash cymbals every half hour!

quiz.question: What did the Arabic word "sifr" refer to in Golden Age mathematics?
quiz.q: What did the Arabic word "sifr" refer to in Golden Age mathematics?
quiz.explanation: Sifr meant zero (empty), giving English both "zero" and "cipher".

quiz.question: What wrong ancient Greek idea about human eyesight did scientist Ibn al-Haytham challenge?
quiz.q: What wrong ancient Greek idea about human eyesight did scientist Ibn al-Haytham challenge?
options: That people could see through solid brick walls
That invisible rays shot out of human eyes to touch objects
That human eyes glowed bright green in the dark
That sunlight travelled in zig-zag circles
quiz.answer: That invisible rays shot out of human eyes to touch objects
quiz.a: That invisible rays shot out of human eyes to touch objects
quiz.explanation: For centuries ancient writers claimed rays beamed out of our eyes, until Ibn al-Haytham tested light experimentally.

quiz.question: What did Ibn al-Haytham prove inside his dark-room pinhole "camera obscura"?
quiz.q: What did Ibn al-Haytham prove inside his dark-room pinhole "camera obscura"?
options: That sound travels faster than lightning
That light travels in straight lines directly into our eyes
That glass mirrors block every shadow
quiz.answer: That light travels in straight lines directly into our eyes
quiz.a: That light travels in straight lines directly into our eyes
quiz.explanation: Inside a pitch-dark room with a tiny pinhole, Ibn al-Haytham proved light travels in straight lines into the eye.

quiz.question: What was a "bimaristan" in Baghdad and other Golden Age Islamic cities?
quiz.q: What was a "bimaristan" in Baghdad and other Golden Age Islamic cities?
options: A free teaching hospital welcoming both rich and poor patients
quiz.answer: A free teaching hospital welcoming both rich and poor patients
quiz.a: A free teaching hospital welcoming both rich and poor patients
quiz.explanation: Islamic bimaristans were clean, free teaching hospitals where rich and poor citizens alike received medical care.

quiz.question: How did a bimaristan care for recovering patients even as they left to go home?
quiz.q: How did a bimaristan care for recovering patients even as they left to go home?
options: Patients received clean clothes and pocket money to rest at home while recovering
Patients had to build a brick wall to pay their bill
Only royal princes were allowed inside the wards
Patients were told to sleep outdoors on river reeds
quiz.answer: Patients received clean clothes and pocket money to rest at home while recovering
quiz.a: Patients received clean clothes and pocket money to rest at home while recovering
quiz.explanation: Bimaristans featured separate clean wards, cooling fountains, an inspected pharmacy, and recovery money for poorer patients.

quiz.question: Which modern inventions owe a debt to Ibn al-Haytham’s pinhole camera obscura and optics experiments?
quiz.q: Which modern inventions owe a debt to Ibn al-Haytham’s pinhole camera obscura and optics experiments?
quiz.explanation: Understanding how light enters lenses in straight lines paved the way for spectacles, microscopes, and modern cameras.

quiz.question: Why did chief doctor al-Razi hang pieces of fresh meat across different parts of Baghdad?
quiz.q: Why did chief doctor al-Razi hang pieces of fresh meat across different parts of Baghdad?
options: To dry spiced meat for Silk Road caravans
To find where meat rotted slowest so he could build the hospital in the cleanest air
To test which district had the hottest ovens
quiz.answer: To find where meat rotted slowest so he could build the hospital in the cleanest air
quiz.a: To find where meat rotted slowest so he could build the hospital in the cleanest air
quiz.explanation: Al-Razi cleverly picked the neighbourhood where fresh meat stayed fresh longest, proving the air there was cleanest for patients!

quiz.question: Which two dangerous childhood illnesses was Baghdad doctor al-Razi the first to tell apart clearly?
quiz.q: Which two dangerous childhood illnesses was Baghdad doctor al-Razi the first to tell apart clearly?
quiz.explanation: By keeping careful bedside notes on patient rashes and fevers, al-Razi wrote the first medical guide distinguishing measles from smallpox.

quiz.question: Around AD 1000 in Spain, how many surgical tools did royal surgeon al-Zahrawi draw in his medical guide?
quiz.q: Around AD 1000 in Spain, how many surgical tools did royal surgeon al-Zahrawi draw in his medical guide?
options: Over 200 surgical tools, including forceps, scalpels, and bone saws
quiz.answer: Over 200 surgical tools, including forceps, scalpels, and bone saws
quiz.a: Over 200 surgical tools, including forceps, scalpels, and bone saws
quiz.explanation: Al-Zahrawi illustrated over 200 precision surgical tools in Source C so trainee surgeons could recognise and use each safely.

quiz.question: What clever discovery did surgeon al-Zahrawi make using natural catgut thread?
quiz.q: What clever discovery did surgeon al-Zahrawi make using natural catgut thread?
options: Internal stitches that dissolved safely inside the body as wounds healed
Ropes for stitching wooden dhow hulls
quiz.answer: Internal stitches that dissolved safely inside the body as wounds healed
quiz.a: Internal stitches that dissolved safely inside the body as wounds healed
quiz.explanation: Al-Zahrawi discovered that natural catgut stitches dissolved harmlessly inside the body without needing a second cut!

quiz.question: Inspect Source D from AD 1224. Who worked inside a bimaristan’s pharmacy?
quiz.q: Inspect Source D from AD 1224. Who worked inside a bimaristan’s pharmacy?
options: Trained pharmacists measuring herbal syrups and remedies in clean jars
quiz.answer: Trained pharmacists measuring herbal syrups and remedies in clean jars
quiz.a: Trained pharmacists measuring herbal syrups and remedies in clean jars
quiz.explanation: Inspected hospital pharmacies employed trained pharmacists who measured exact doses of syrups and herbal medicines.

lessons.enquiry_question: How did Baghdad’s traders connect the world all the way to Britain?
lessons.prologue: Follow camel caravans resting inside walled Silk Road caravanserais, hoist triangular sails aboard an Indian Ocean dhow from Basra, cash an early paper cheque, and uncover Baghdad silver dirhams buried in Viking York!
lessons.blurb: Follow camel caravans resting inside walled Silk Road caravanserais, hoist triangular sails aboard an Indian Ocean dhow from Basra, cash an early paper cheque, and uncover Baghdad silver dirhams buried in Viking York!

teacher_notes.primer: This fourth Key Stage 2 enquiry explores Baghdad's global trade networks between c. AD 850 and 1000. Primary pupils trace overland Silk Road camel caravans stopping every 30 km at fortified caravanserais, maritime dhow voyages from Basra across the Indian Ocean using astrolabes, and early paper cheques (sakk). Crucially, pupils connect Baghdad directly to British history through Abbasid silver dirham hoards found around Viking Jorvik (York) and Anglo-Saxon King Offa of Mercia's gold imitation dinar.

objectives.objective: Describe what goods entered Baghdad's covered bazaars and how caravanserais protected Silk Road camel caravans.
objectives.primer: Explore Chinese silk and porcelain, Indian pepper and cardamom, Persian rugs, blown glass, and roadside caravanserais every 30 km.
objectives.question: Why did building fortified brick caravanserais a day’s camel march apart help Silk Road trade flourish?

objectives.objective: Explain how wooden dhow ships, brass astrolabes, and paper sakk cheques transformed sea trade and banking.
objectives.primer: Trace maritime routes from Basra across the Indian Ocean and see why merchants preferred signed paper sakk notes to heavy gold sacks.
objectives.question: How did stitched wooden dhow ships and paper sakk cheques make long-distance trade faster and safer?

objectives.objective: Use coin evidence from Viking Jorvik (York) and King Offa of Mercia to prove Baghdad’s links with Britain.
objectives.primer: Examine Abbasid silver dirham hoards across Scandinavia and Yorkshire alongside Offa’s AD 774 gold imitation dinar.
objectives.question: How did silver coins minted in the Islamic world end up buried under Viking fields near York?

source_context.Source A: Arab shipbuilders stitched flexible wooden hull planks with coconut-husk rope and raised triangular sails to ride Indian Ocean winds from Basra to India and China. **Hinge Question:** Why were stitched wooden planks and triangular sails so useful for captains crossing stormy Indian Ocean waters?
source_context.Source B: Trusted from Central Asia to Northern Europe for their pure silver weight, thousands of Abbasid dirhams travelled up Russian rivers into Viking Scandinavia and Jorvik. **Hinge Question:** Why have archaeologists dug up thousands of Arabic silver dirhams in Viking Jorvik and Scandinavia when Vikings could not read Arabic?
source_context.Source C: Spices like pepper, cardamom, cinnamon, and star anise grew in tropical India and Southeast Asia, making them worth high sums in Baghdad’s markets. **Hinge Question:** Why were tiny, lightweight sacks of pepper, cardamom, and cinnamon worth so much silver in Baghdad’s bazaars?
source_context.Source D: Baghdad did not only buy foreign goods; skilled Iraqi and Persian workshops blew and carved clear glass flasks, glazed lustre bowls, and silk cloth sold as far as China! **Hinge Question:** What does Source D prove about whether Baghdad only bought goods from abroad or also made luxury crafts to sell?

items.question: In AD 762, which Abbasid caliph founded the Round City of Baghdad beside the River Tigris?
items.explanation: Caliph al-Mansur chose a fertile bend on the River Tigris linked by canals to the Euphrates to build his circular City of Peace.

items.question: Which famous library and translation academy stood at the heart of Golden Age Baghdad?
items.explanation: Expanded by Caliphs Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma’mun, the House of Wisdom gathered scholars and manuscripts from across the known world.

items.question: Via which Central Asian city did cotton-and-rag paper-making reach Baghdad, and who was Baghdad’s star medical translator?
items.answer: Paper-making arrived via Samarkand, and Christian scholar Hunayn ibn Ishaq led medical translations into Arabic
items.explanation: Cheap Samarkand paper sparked over 100 Baghdad bookshops while Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated Greek medical works accurately.

items.question: Which House of Wisdom mathematician championed zero (0–9) and gave us the words "algebra" and "algorithm"?
items.explanation: His book Kitab al-Jabr gave us algebra, while the Latin spelling of al-Khwarizmi gave us algorithm!

items.question: What was a bimaristan in Golden Age Baghdad, and who had to pay to be treated there?
items.answer: A clean teaching hospital with separate wards and a pharmacy where rich and poor patients were treated free of charge
items.explanation: Doctors like al-Razi ran free bimaristan wards funded by charitable endowments long before modern hospitals existed in Europe.

vocab.definition: A bustling covered market street (also called a souk) lined with stalls selling silk, spices, carpets, and glass.
A walled roadside inn with courtyard wells built every thirty kilometres so Silk Road camel caravans could rest safely.
A wooden Arab sailing ship built from stitched planks and rigged with triangular sails for crossing the Indian Ocean.
A signed paper payment note from Abbasid bankers that merchants cashed in distant cities — origin of our word cheque.
A pure silver coin stamped with Arabic script, traded from Baghdad all the way to Viking Scandinavia and Jorvik (York).

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: Shoppers in Baghdad’s shaded [Bazaar] bought Chinese silk and Indian pepper brought overland by camels resting at each [Caravanserai]. Sea captains sailed wooden [Dhow] ships from Basra, bankers wrote paper [Sakk] cheques, and pure silver [Dirham] coins even reached Viking York!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 850–1000: Covered Bazaars, Silk Caravans & Roadside Caravanserais
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] **Baghdad** sat where Asia, Africa, and Europe met, making its **markets** world famous. Shaded **bazaars**, or **souks**, smelled of Indian pepper, cardamom, and sweet cinnamon. Stalls gleamed with Chinese silk, white porcelain, Persian rugs, and blown glass. Long **caravans** of two-humped **camels** crossed hot **Silk Road** desert **trails**.

[4.2] Every **thirty kilometres** along the road stood a **walled** **inn** called a **caravanserai** [kar-uh-VAN-suh-ry]. Locked brick gates kept traders safe from desert bandits at night. Tired camels drank cool well water while merchants shared spiced stews by firelight!
narrative_blocks.content:
[4.1] **Baghdad** sat where Asia, Africa, and Europe met, making its **markets** world famous. Shaded **bazaars**, or **souks**, smelled of Indian pepper, cardamom, and sweet cinnamon. Stalls gleamed with Chinese silk, white porcelain, Persian rugs, and blown glass. Long **caravans** of two-humped **camels** crossed hot **Silk Road** desert **trails**.

[4.2] Every **thirty kilometres** along the road stood a **walled** **inn** called a **caravanserai** [kar-uh-VAN-suh-ry]. Locked brick gates kept traders safe from desert bandits at night. Tired camels drank cool well water while merchants shared spiced stews by firelight!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 850–1000: Indian Ocean Dhow Ships & Paper Sakk Cheques
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.3] River boats also carried crates south down the Tigris to the busy sea port of **Basra**. Sailors loaded wooden **dhow** [DOW] ships built from planks stitched tightly with coconut rope! Tall triangular sails caught ocean winds across the **Indian Ocean** towards India and China. Captains steered safely at night by checking star heights with brass **astrolabes**.

[4.4] Carrying heavy coin sacks on **long-distance trade** risked bandit or pirate attacks. Clever Baghdad bankers solved this by writing signed paper slips called a **sakk** [SAHK]. Merchants cashed them safely afar, giving English our word **cheque**!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 774–1000: Viking Silver Dirhams in Jorvik & King Offa’s Gold Coin
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.5] Silver **trade coins** struck for **Baghdad's** caliphs even reached snowy **Scandinavia** and **Britain**! Pure Abbasid silver **dirhams** [DEER-hamz] with Arabic script flowed north up Russian rivers. **Vikings** prized this trusted silver for buying furs and swords. They even buried shining dirham hoards near **Jorvik** [YOR-vik], modern **York**!

[4.6] Even earlier, in **Anglo-Saxon Britain**, **King Offa of Mercia** admired Islamic gold coins. Around **AD 774**, Offa minted a famous gold coin copying an Abbasid Arabic **dinar**. Swirling Arabic letters beside Offa's name prove how far Baghdad's trade reached!
