tasks.title: 1. Primary Evidence Detective
tasks.question: Inspect Source A. What do the green jade tiles and eyes reveal about King Pakal’s status?
tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, the mosaic green jade tiles and shell-and-obsidian eyes on King Pakal’s mask show...
hints: Describe the 200+ fitted green jadeite tiles and lifelike shell-and-obsidian eyes.
Explain why the Maya prized green jade above gold (linking green to maize, water, and life breath).
Connect this AD 683 funerary mask in Palenque to Pakal’s sacred status as a K’uhul Ajaw.
tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, the mosaic green jade tiles and shell-and-obsidian eyes on King Pakal’s mask show he was revered as a sacred K’uhul Ajaw ("holy lord"). Because green jade symbolised sprouting maize, water, and eternal breath, fitting over 200 jade pieces honoured Pakal’s journey into the afterlife beneath Palenque.

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain why historians compare the Classic Maya to Ancient Greece rather than one single empire.
tasks.starter: Historians compare the Classic Maya world to Ancient Greece instead of one united empire because...
hints: Explain that the Maya lived in over forty independent city-states such as Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, and Copán.
Describe how each city-state obeyed its own K'uhul Ajaw ("holy lord"), laws, and army.
Explain how sharing Maya beliefs and jade symbols while fighting rival neighbours made city-states both similar and competitive!
tasks.model_answer: Historians compare the Classic Maya world to Ancient Greece instead of one united empire because no single emperor ever ruled every Maya city at once. Instead, over forty independent city-states — including fierce rivals like Tikal and Calakmul alongside Palenque, Copán, and Yaxchilán — governed their own farmland and armies under a sacred K'uhul Ajaw. Even though they shared Maya gods, step-pyramids, and trade goods, rival city-states constantly formed alliances and competed for royal glory!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: Were the Classic Maya ruled as one empire, and what reveals the power of their kings and queens?
tasks.starter: Archaeological discoveries across Mesoamerica reveal that Classic Maya kings and royal women held extraordinary power...
hints: Explain how a K'uhul Ajaw was seen as a sacred link to the gods, using King Pakal’s tomb under the Temple of the Inscriptions.
Use Lady Sak K'uk' at Palenque and Lady Six Sky at Naranjo to prove royal women also ruled and led.
Combine stone stelae, jade masks, and Bonampak murals to show how archaeology lets us check royal claims!
tasks.model_answer: Archaeological discoveries across Mesoamerica reveal that Classic Maya kings and royal women held extraordinary sacred and political power. Every K'uhul Ajaw was honoured as a holy messenger to the gods, proven by King Pakal’s sixty-eight-year reign and his green jade mosaic mask sealed beneath Palenque’s Temple of the Inscriptions. Carved limestone stelae also prove royal women shaped kingdoms directly: Lady Sak K'uk' crowned young Pakal, while Lady Six Sky rebuilt Naranjo and stood victorious on royal monuments alongside vivid palace ceremonies like those painted at Bonampak!

lessons.prologue: Centuries before Europe used the number zero, Maya scholars wrote huge sums using just a shell, a pebble dot, and a bar! Climb Copán’s 2,200-glyph stairway, unfold painted fig-bark codices, and track Venus from El Caracol’s stone observatory.
lessons.blurb: Centuries before Europe used the number zero, Maya scholars wrote huge sums using just a shell, a pebble dot, and a bar! Climb Copán’s 2,200-glyph stairway, unfold painted fig-bark codices, and track Venus from El Caracol’s stone observatory.

teacher_notes.primer: This third Key Stage 2 enquiry explores the intellectual achievements of Classic Maya scribes, mathematicians, and astronomers (c. AD 300–900). Primary pupils examine Mesoamerica’s fullest writing system (over 800 word and syllable glyphs carved on stelae and Copán’s 63-step Hieroglyphic Stairway, and painted with turkey-quill brushes onto accordion-folded fig-bark codices like the Dresden Codex). Pupils then master Maya base-20 place-value maths (shell = 0, dot = 1, bar = 5) and trace naked-eye astronomy at Chichén Itzá’s El Caracol observatory linking the 260-day Tzolk'in and 365-day Haab' calendars every 52 years.

source_context.Source A: One of just four surviving pre-Spanish Maya bark-paper books, the Dresden Codex predicts solar eclipses and tracks the planet Venus to within two hours over five hundred years! **Hinge Question:** How can you spot ones, fives, and zeros on the painted columns of Source A?
source_context.Source B: Maya readers read glyph blocks in paired columns from left to right and top to bottom, sounding out exact Mayan words carved over a thousand years ago. **Hinge Question:** Why did mixing whole-word signs with syllable sound signs let Maya scribes write anything they spoke?
source_context.Source C: Opened flat, the Madrid Codex stretches over six metres long, yet its clever accordion folds let a Maya priest tuck the whole almanac under one arm! **Hinge Question:** Why was an accordion-folded bark-paper codex so practical for Maya priests comparing calendar tables?
source_context.Source D: Royal Maya scribes were high-ranking artists (often princes and princesses!) who signed fine cacao-drinking vases with bands of painted glyphs around the rim. **Hinge Question:** What does finding neat bands of hieroglyphs painted on palace cups tell us about Maya scribes?

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 300–900: Maya Hieroglyphs, Stone Stelae & Bark-Paper Codices
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.1] Across ancient America, **Maya** scholars created the fullest system of **hieroglyphic writing**. Skilled **scribes** mastered over **800** carved or painted **glyphs** for words and syllables. Mixing word signs with sound signs let writers spell any Mayan sentence. Carvers chiselled royal births and victories onto tall limestone **stelae**.

[3.2] At **Copán**, masons carved over two thousand glyphs onto the 63-step **Hieroglyphic Stairway**! Scribes also beat inner **fig-tree bark** into sheets coated with white lime paste. Using **turkey-quill brushes**, they painted accordion-folded books called **codices**, like the **Dresden Codex**.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 350–900: Shell, Dot & Bar — Inventing Place-Value Zero
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.3] Clever **Maya** mathematicians made history by inventing **place-value zero** all on their own! Rome and Britain still used clumsy Roman numerals without any zero. Meanwhile, Maya scholars used **base-20**, matching ten fingers and ten toes, with three clear symbols.

[3.4] A carved **shell** meant **zero**, a **pebble dot** meant **one**, and a **wooden bar** equalled **five**. Scribes stacked numbers upward in vertical columns of ones, twenties, and four hundreds on bark paper. Market traders tallied cacao beans swiftly. Architects also measured giant stone pyramids accurately!

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 600–900: El Caracol Observatory & Two Interlocking Calendars
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.5] Without glass telescopes, **Maya** **astronomers** tracked stars, planets, and eclipses with sharp care. At **Chichén Itzá** [chee-CHEN eet-SAH], priests climbed the round stone tower of **El Caracol**. Narrow windows inside its thick dome lined up with bright **Venus**. Watching the sky helped scholars link two interlocking **calendars** like cogwheels.

[3.6] The **260-day** sacred **Tzolk'in** [TSOHL-keen] calendar guided holy festivals and lucky names. Alongside it turned the **365-day** solar **Haab'** [HAHB], guiding maize planting and harvest. Every **52 years**, both calendars clicked back to the exact same starting day!

tasks.question: Explain how Maya base-20 maths worked and why inventing place-value zero mattered so much.
tasks.starter: Maya mathematicians achieved one of world history’s greatest breakthroughs because...

tasks.model_answer: Maya mathematicians achieved one of world history’s greatest breakthroughs because they independently invented place-value zero long before Europe used it! Stacking numbers vertically in columns of ones, twenties, and four hundreds let market traders tally thousands of cacao beans and helped astronomers calculate sky cycles across centuries!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: Why do historians celebrate Maya scribes, mathematicians, and astronomers as world pioneers?
tasks.starter: Historians consider Maya scribes, mathematicians, and astronomers among the cleverest scholars in world history because...
hints: Explain their achievement in writing first (over 800 glyphs on Copán’s stairway and painted bark-paper codices).
Explain their achievement in maths next (inventing place-value zero with shell, dot, and bar in base-20).

tasks.model_answer: Historians consider Maya scribes, mathematicians, and astronomers among the cleverest scholars in world history because they excelled in writing, maths, and sky science all at once! First, scribes created ancient America’s fullest hieroglyphic writing system, using over 800 glyphs on monuments like Copán’s Hieroglyphic Stairway and in folding bark-paper codices. Second, mathematicians independently invented place-value zero in base-20 using just shells, dots, and bars. Finally, sighting Venus from towers like El Caracol without glass telescopes, astronomers predicted eclipses and meshed the 260-day Tzolk'in and 365-day Haab' calendars every 52 years!

lessons.prologue: Wake before dawn to hear maize dough grinding on volcanic stone metates, spend dried chocolate beans as cash in a bustling plaza market, and dive hip-first after a four-kilogram rubber ball in Pok-ta-Pok!
lessons.blurb: Wake before dawn to hear maize dough grinding on volcanic stone metates, spend dried chocolate beans as cash in a bustling plaza market, and dive hip-first after a four-kilogram rubber ball in Pok-ta-Pok!

teacher_notes.primer: This Key Stage 2 enquiry steps inside everyday Classic Maya life (c. AD 600–900). Primary pupils discover how soaking maize in limewater (nixtamal) and grinding it on volcanic stone metates nourished whole cities with tortillas and tamales, how bitter chilli-spiced cacao worked as both a royal drink and everyday market currency, how human porters and canoes traded razor-sharp obsidian and green jade without pack horses, and how athletes played the sacred rubber-ball game Pok-ta-Pok using padded hips.

objectives.objective: Explain how Maya cooks prepared nutritious maize dough on stone metates and brewed frothy spiced cacao.
objectives.primer: Explore limewater soaking (nixtamal), three-legged volcanic metates, flat tortillas, steamed tamales, and chilli-spiced royal chocolate.
objectives.question: How was a royal Maya cacao drink very different from hot chocolate today?

objectives.objective: Describe how Maya traders moved obsidian, jade, and quetzal feathers without horses or wheeled carts, using cacao beans as money.
objectives.primer: Investigate plaza markets (10 cacao beans for a rabbit, 100 for a turkey!), forehead-strap porters, and long-distance river canoes.
objectives.question: How did Maya merchants carry heavy volcanic obsidian and salt across Mesoamerica without pack animals?

objectives.objective: Infer how and why the Maya played the sacred rubber-ball game Pok-ta-Pok from ballcourt rings and player figurines.
objectives.primer: Examine stone ballcourts at Copán and Chichén Itzá, four-kilogram rubber balls, padded hip yokes, and high stone rings.
objectives.question: Why was Pok-ta-Pok both an exciting athletic contest and a sacred ceremony for the Maya?

items.question: Which three companion crops — known as the "Three Sisters" — did Maya farmers grow together?
items.answer: Maize (sweetcorn), climbing beans, and broad-leaved squash
items.explanation: Tall maize stalks supported climbing beans, beans enriched the soil, and wide squash leaves shaded damp earth.

items.question: In northern Yucatán where few surface rivers flowed, where did Maya cities collect fresh underground drinking water?
items.answer: From deep natural limestone sinkholes called cenotes (and plastered stone reservoirs)
items.explanation: Collapsed limestone cave roofs created cool, water-filled cenotes that supplied Yucatán cities year-round.

items.question: Were Classic Maya cities united under one single emperor, or ruled as independent rival city-states led by a holy lord (K'uhul Ajaw)?
items.answer: Independent rival city-states such as Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, and Copán, each ruled by a K'uhul Ajaw
items.explanation: Like Ancient Greek poleis, Maya city-states shared culture and writing while competing fiercely in war and alliances.

items.question: What dazzling treasure covered the face of King Pakal inside his tomb beneath Palenque's Temple of the Inscriptions?
items.answer: A life-sized green jade mosaic funerary mask with shell and obsidian eyes
items.explanation: Green jade symbolised breath, maize, and eternal life to Maya rulers like King K'inich Janaab' Pakal.

items.question: In Maya base-20 mathematics, what number values did a shell, a pebble dot, and a wooden bar stand for?
items.explanation: Maya mathematicians independently invented place-value zero and tracked planets in bark-paper books like the Dresden Codex.

vocab.definition: A flat or slightly curved volcanic grinding stone used with a rolling stone pin to crush soaked maize into fresh dough.
Tropical tree pods whose roasted seeds made frothy spiced royal chocolate drinks and worked as everyday Maya market money.
Shiny black volcanic glass traded from highland mountains and chipped into blades sharper than modern steel.
Tough, lustrous green stone prized above gold by Maya rulers for royal masks, beads, and polished earflares.
The fast sacred Maya ballgame where players bounced a heavy solid rubber ball off padded hips inside stone ballcourts.

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: Before dawn, Maya cooks ground soaked maize dough on a volcanic stone [Metate] to bake warm tortillas. In busy markets, shoppers spent dried [Cacao] beans as money, while highland porters traded black volcanic [Obsidian] blades and royal green [Jade]. Crowds then cheered beside stone courts as padded athletes played [Pok-ta-Pok]!

narrative_blocks.title: AD 600–900: Limewater Maize, Stone Metates & Frothy Cacao
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] Every **Maya** morning began before dawn with the crunch of grinding stones. Cooks soaked dried **maize** kernels overnight in **limewater** to soften tough skins. This clever **nixtamal** soaking unlocked vital nutrients that kept families strong. Kneeling at a volcanic stone **metate** [meh-TAH-tay], cooks crushed corn into smooth dough.

[4.2] Families baked flat **tortillas** on clay griddles or steamed **tamales** in husks. Growers also picked ripe **cacao** [kuh-KOW] pods and roasted the bitter seeds inside. Servers poured cacao from tall vases, whipping frothy drinks spiced with **chilli** and **honey**!

narrative_blocks.title: AD 600–900: Cacao Bean Money, Obsidian Blades & Jade Trade
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.3] Busy **Maya** plazas hummed with shaded markets where dried **cacao beans** worked as cash. Ten cacao beans bought a plump rabbit, while one hundred bought a turkey! Cheats sometimes filled empty bean shells with wet clay. Sharp-eyed market judges checked beans carefully.

[4.4] Mesoamerica had no pack horses, oxen, or wheeled carts for heavy loads. Strong human **porters** carried heavy packs along stone causeways using forehead straps. Dugout **canoes** paddled salt, cotton, and **quetzal** feathers, while highland merchants traded black **obsidian** blades and green **jade**.

narrative_blocks.title: AD 600–900: Roaring Stone Ballcourts & Sacred Pok-ta-Pok
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.5] Beside tall pyramids stood sloping limestone **ballcourts** for sacred **Pok-ta-Pok** [pok-tah-POK] matches. Carved scarlet macaw heads watched two **Maya** teams chase a solid **rubber ball**. Weighing up to four kilograms, that fast bouncing ball could easily bruise ribs!

[4.6] Athletes strapped thick leather-and-wood **hip yokes** tightly around their waists for safety. Touching the ball with hands or feet broke strict ballcourt rules. Players dived low to bounce the ball off padded hips towards high stone rings. Every match honoured the gods of sun and rain!

tasks.title: 1. Primary Evidence Detective
tasks.question: Look closely at Source A. Mention two ways the Classic Maya used cacao beans.
tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, Classic Maya people used valuable cacao beans in two special ways: first...
hints: Give Use 1 (Market Currency): dried cacao beans spent like coins (e.g. 10 for a rabbit, 100 for a turkey).
Give Use 2 (Royal Drink): roasted cacao ground and poured into frothy, bitter chocolate spiced with chilli.
Explain why cacao pods growing only in damp lowlands made every bean valuable.
tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, Classic Maya people used valuable cacao beans in two special ways: first, families spent dried cacao beans as everyday market money — ten beans bought a rabbit and one hundred bought a turkey! Second, nobles and kings roasted cacao beans into frothy, chilli-spiced chocolate drinks for palace feasts and rituals.

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain how Maya traders moved goods across Mesoamerica without horses, carts, or metal coins.
tasks.starter: Even without pack horses, wheeled carts, or metal coins, Maya trade thrived across Mesoamerica because...
hints: Explain how human porters with forehead straps and river canoes carried salt, feathers, jade, and black obsidian.
Describe how dried cacao beans worked as everyday money in city markets (10 for a rabbit, 100 for a turkey!).
Mention how sneaky cheats tried faking cacao beans with clay — and why obsidian was so vital without iron tools!
tasks.model_answer: Even without pack horses, wheeled carts, or metal coins, Maya trade thrived across Mesoamerica because strong human porters carried heavy packs on woven forehead straps along stone causeways, while wooden canoes paddled rivers and coasts. Highland traders brought razor-sharp black volcanic obsidian blades — vital because the Maya did not forge iron — alongside green jade for nobles. In bustling markets, dried cacao beans worked as everyday money, with ten beans buying a rabbit and market judges checking for clay-stuffed fakes!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: What did Classic Maya people eat, trade, and play in everyday life between AD 600 and 900?
tasks.starter: Everyday food, bustling trade, and sacred Pok-ta-Pok prove the Classic Maya were remarkably clever because...
hints: Explain how nixtamal limewater soaking and stone metates turned maize into healthy tortillas and tamales.
Show how long-distance canoe and porter trade connected highlands (obsidian, jade) with lowlands (cacao, salt).
Conclude by explaining how even sport (Pok-ta-Pok) linked athletic skill directly to honouring Maya gods!
tasks.model_answer: Everyday food, bustling trade, and sacred Pok-ta-Pok prove the Classic Maya were remarkably clever because cooks used nixtamal limewater soaking and stone metates to unlock vital nutrients from maize dough. Across hundreds of miles without horses, canoe crews and porters linked highland obsidian and green jade with lowland salt and cacao-bean money. Finally, roaring stone ballcourts show how Pok-ta-Pok blended athletic skill in padded hip yokes with deep religious devotion to the gods of sun and rain!

quiz.question: Why did Maya cooks soak dried maize kernels overnight in warm limewater (nixtamal)?
quiz.q: Why did Maya cooks soak dried maize kernels overnight in warm limewater (nixtamal)?
options: To turn the kernels into hard stone beads
To freeze the corn for winter travel
To soften tough skins and unlock vital nutrients for dough
To dye woven cotton robes bright blue
quiz.answer: To soften tough skins and unlock vital nutrients for dough
quiz.a: To soften tough skins and unlock vital nutrients for dough
quiz.explanation: Nixtamal soaking in limewater loosened tough corn skins and unlocked extra vitamins that kept families healthy.

quiz.question: What volcanic stone grinding tool did Maya cooks use every morning to crush soaked maize?
quiz.q: What volcanic stone grinding tool did Maya cooks use every morning to crush soaked maize?
quiz.explanation: Kneeling at a three-legged volcanic stone metate, cooks crushed wet maize into smooth dough.

quiz.question: Which everyday foods did Maya families make from fresh maize dough?
quiz.q: Which everyday foods did Maya families make from fresh maize dough?
options: Flat tortillas baked on clay griddles and steamed tamales in husks
Boiled rice noodles and barley cakes
Fried potato crisps and cheese pies
quiz.answer: Flat tortillas baked on clay griddles and steamed tamales in husks
quiz.a: Flat tortillas baked on clay griddles and steamed tamales in husks
quiz.explanation: Maize dough was patted into flat tortillas on clay griddles or steamed inside husks as tasty tamales!

quiz.question: How did royal Maya servers prepare and flavour frothy cacao drinks?
quiz.q: How did royal Maya servers prepare and flavour frothy cacao drinks?
options: Boiled with cow's milk and white cane sugar
Mixed with ice cubes and lemon juice
Poured from tall vases for foam and spiced with chilli and honey
quiz.answer: Poured from tall vases for foam and spiced with chilli and honey
quiz.a: Poured from tall vases for foam and spiced with chilli and honey
quiz.explanation: Royal servers poured roasted cacao from tall cylinder vases to whip thick foam spiced with chilli and wild honey!

quiz.question: How did scientists prove tall painted Maya cylinder vases once held cacao drinks?
quiz.q: How did scientists prove tall painted Maya cylinder vases once held cacao drinks?
options: They tested dried chemical traces of cacao and chilli trapped inside the clay walls
They found printed paper labels glued to the base
Modern kings still drank from the exact same cups
They guessed from the size of the handles
quiz.answer: They tested dried chemical traces of cacao and chilli trapped inside the clay walls
quiz.a: They tested dried chemical traces of cacao and chilli trapped inside the clay walls
quiz.explanation: Chemical tests on ancient residues inside Maya cylinder vases revealed real traces of cacao and chilli!

quiz.question: What everyday item worked as cash money in bustling Classic Maya plaza markets?
quiz.q: What everyday item worked as cash money in bustling Classic Maya plaza markets?
quiz.explanation: Dried cacao beans were valuable enough to spend like coins in every Maya marketplace!

quiz.question: In a Maya market, how many dried cacao beans bought a rabbit, and how many bought a turkey?
quiz.q: In a Maya market, how many dried cacao beans bought a rabbit, and how many bought a turkey?

quiz.a: Ten cacao beans bought a rabbit, while one hundred bought a turkey
quiz.explanation: Ten cacao beans bought a plump rabbit, while one hundred cacao beans bought a turkey!

quiz.question: Why did sharp-eyed Maya market judges sometimes squeeze cacao beans during trades?
quiz.q: Why did sharp-eyed Maya market judges sometimes squeeze cacao beans during trades?
options: To check cheats had not filled empty bean shells with clay
To make hot chocolate right on the floor
To plant trees in the middle of the plaza
quiz.answer: To check cheats had not filled empty bean shells with clay
quiz.a: To check cheats had not filled empty bean shells with clay
quiz.explanation: Sneaky cheats sometimes hollowed out cacao shells and stuffed them with clay, so market judges checked beans!

quiz.question: How did Maya merchants move heavy goods across Mesoamerica without horses, oxen, or wheeled carts?
quiz.q: How did Maya merchants move heavy goods across Mesoamerica without horses, oxen, or wheeled carts?

On steam trains through mountain tunnels
Carried by human porters with forehead straps and paddled in dugout canoes

quiz.a: Carried by human porters with forehead straps and paddled in dugout canoes
quiz.explanation: Porters walked stone causeways using forehead straps while dugout canoes paddled rivers and coasts.

quiz.question: Which two highland treasures did merchants carry down into lowland rainforest cities?
quiz.q: Which two highland treasures did merchants carry down into lowland rainforest cities?

quiz.question: What was the fast sacred team ballgame played inside sloping limestone Maya ballcourts?
quiz.q: What was the fast sacred team ballgame played inside sloping limestone Maya ballcourts?
quiz.explanation: Crowds gathered beside sloping stone ballcourts to watch athletes play sacred Pok-ta-Pok!

quiz.question: Roughly how heavy was the solid bouncing rubber ball used in Pok-ta-Pok?
quiz.q: Roughly how heavy was the solid bouncing rubber ball used in Pok-ta-Pok?
quiz.explanation: Made from tree rubber latex, the solid bouncing ball weighed up to four kilograms and could bruise ribs!

quiz.question: Why did Pok-ta-Pok athletes strap thick leather-and-wood hip yokes around their waists?
quiz.q: Why did Pok-ta-Pok athletes strap thick leather-and-wood hip yokes around their waists?
options: To carry snacks during long matches
To hold iron swords and shields
To protect their ribs and bounce the heavy rubber ball without hands or feet
quiz.answer: To protect their ribs and bounce the heavy rubber ball without hands or feet
quiz.a: To protect their ribs and bounce the heavy rubber ball without hands or feet
quiz.explanation: Touching the ball with hands or feet broke the rules, so players slammed it off padded hip yokes!

quiz.question: Why was scoring through Chichén Itzá's carved stone ballcourt ring so difficult?
quiz.q: Why was scoring through Chichén Itzá's carved stone ballcourt ring so difficult?
options: Players were blindfolded throughout the match
The court was flooded waist-deep in water
The narrow stone hoop hung high up a sheer vertical wall
Matches were only played at midnight without torches
quiz.answer: The narrow stone hoop hung high up a sheer vertical wall
quiz.a: The narrow stone hoop hung high up a sheer vertical wall
quiz.explanation: Knocking a heavy rubber ball off padded hips through a narrow hoop high up a vertical stone wall took immense skill!

quiz.question: What deeper meaning did fierce Pok-ta-Pok matches hold for Maya watchers?
quiz.q: What deeper meaning did fierce Pok-ta-Pok matches hold for Maya watchers?
options: Every match was a sacred ceremony honouring the gods of sun and rain
Winners were chosen to sail across the Atlantic Ocean
It was only a playground game for five-year-olds
It decided how many coins to mint in iron furnaces
quiz.answer: Every match was a sacred ceremony honouring the gods of sun and rain
quiz.a: Every match was a sacred ceremony honouring the gods of sun and rain
quiz.explanation: Built right beside step-pyramids, Pok-ta-Pok courts linked athletic skill to honouring Maya gods.

teacher_notes.primer: This Key Stage 2 enquiry explores how sacred stories and astronomy shaped Maya art, caves, and pyramids (c. AD 600–1200). Primary pupils read the K'iche' Maya Popol Vuh creation account (mud and wood people failing before gods kneaded yellow and white maize dough, plus the Hero Twins outwitting the lords of Xibalba), meet the Maize God, long-nosed rain god Chaac in sacred cenotes, and feathered serpent Kukulkan, and marvel at Chichén Itzá’s El Castillo (4 × 91 steps + top platform = 365 solar days, casting an equinox serpent shadow).

objectives.objective: Retell key episodes from the sacred Maya book Popol Vuh, including maize-dough humans and the Hero Twins in Xibalba.
objectives.primer: Compare the gods’ failed attempts with mud and wood against living maize dough, and trace the Hero Twins’ Pok-ta-Pok match in Xibalba.
objectives.question: Why does shaping the first humans from maize dough make such sense for Maya farming communities?

objectives.objective: Explain how and why Maya communities honoured the Maize God, rain god Chaac, and feathered serpent Kukulkan.
objectives.primer: Inspect carved Chaac rain masks at Kabah, sacred caves and cenotes as portals to Xibalba, copal incense, and turquoise Maya Blue.
objectives.question: Why were deep limestone caves and cenotes treated as sacred places to pray to Chaac?

objectives.objective: Show how Maya builders combined religion and solar astronomy at Chichén Itzá’s El Castillo pyramid.
objectives.primer: Count 4 staircases × 91 steps + 1 top temple platform = 365 days, and observe the spring and autumn equinox serpent shadow.
objectives.question: How did Maya architects turn El Castillo into a giant stone 365-day calendar?

source_context.Source A: Too heavy to wear during a fast match, polished greenstone yokes were worn in sacred rituals linking Pok-ta-Pok to the rebirth of the Maize God. **Hinge Question:** Why did Maya believers carve the Maize God onto a ceremonial Pok-ta-Pok hip yoke?
source_context.Source B: Priests burned fragrant pine-tree resin called copal inside tall clay censers like Source B so sweet white smoke rose towards the gods on pyramid tops. **Hinge Question:** Why did Maya priests burn sweet-smelling copal tree resin inside temple censers during prayers?
source_context.Source C: Maya citizens believed their K'uhul Ajaw acted as a living bridge between humans on Earth and powerful gods in the sky and watery underworld. **Hinge Question:** Why did a Maya king wear carved green jade over his heart when leading religious ceremonies?
source_context.Source D: By heating blue indigo plant leaves with special white clay, Maya makers invented "Maya Blue" — a sacred colour linked to rain god Chaac that never faded! **Hinge Question:** Why did Maya artists paint offerings to the rain god Chaac in bright turquoise Maya Blue?

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: In the sacred Maya book [Popol Vuh], the gods kneaded maize dough to make humans, and the Hero Twins outsmarted the lords of [Xibalba]. Farmers prayed in caves to long-nosed rain god [Chaac] and built El Castillo at Chichén Itzá for feathered serpent [Kukulkan]. Every spring and autumn [Equinox], sunlit triangles slither down its steps like a giant snake!

narrative_blocks.title: AD 600–900: Maize-Dough Humans, Xibalba & Rain God Chaac
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.1] Sacred **Maya** stories survived in a creation book called the **Popol Vuh** [poh-POHL VOO]. First, the gods shaped mud humans, yet they crumbled in rain. Next, wooden people walked, yet forgot to thank their makers! Finally, the gods kneaded yellow and white **maize dough** into grateful humans.

[5.2] In another tale, the **Hero Twins** beat the lords of **Xibalba** [shee-bal-BAH] at Pok-ta-Pok! Their win helped the **Maize God** rise like sprouting corn. Priests entered deep caves and **cenotes** — seen as doorways to Xibalba — burning **copal** resin for rain god **Chaac** [CHAHK].
narrative_blocks.content:
[5.1] Sacred **Maya** stories survived in a creation book called the **Popol Vuh** [poh-POHL VOO]. First, the gods shaped mud humans, yet they crumbled in rain. Next, wooden people walked, yet forgot to thank their makers! Finally, the gods kneaded yellow and white **maize dough** into grateful humans.

[5.2] In another tale, the **Hero Twins** beat the lords of **Xibalba** [shee-bal-BAH] at Pok-ta-Pok! Their win helped the **Maize God** rise like sprouting corn. Priests entered deep caves and **cenotes** — seen as doorways to Xibalba — burning **copal** resin for rain god **Chaac** [CHAHK].
narrative_blocks.image_alt: Wall of repeating carved stone masks with hooked noses representing the Maya rain god Chaac at Kabah in Yucatán
narrative_blocks.caption: Carved stone masks of long-nosed rain god Chaac covering the palace wall at Kabah in dry northern Yucatán.
narrative_blocks.image_caption: Carved stone masks of long-nosed rain god Chaac covering the palace wall at Kabah in dry northern Yucatán.

narrative_blocks.title: AD 800–1100: El Castillo — A 365-Day Calendar Carved in Stone
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.3] Every **Maya** temple linked Earth, sky, and the calendar together. At northern **Chichén Itzá**, royal builders raised a great step-pyramid nicknamed **El Castillo**. Dedicated to the feathered serpent god **Kukulkan** [koo-kool-KAHN], its four steep staircases hold ninety-one stone steps each.

[5.4] Multiply ninety-one steps by four sides and add one top platform: **365**! Clever Maya architects carved a giant stone calendar matching every day of the solar year. Priests climbed those steep stairs to watch the stars. From the top, they announced maize planting dates across the plaza.
narrative_blocks.content:
[5.3] Every **Maya** temple linked Earth, sky, and the calendar together. At northern **Chichén Itzá**, royal builders raised a great step-pyramid nicknamed **El Castillo**. Dedicated to the feathered serpent god **Kukulkan** [koo-kool-KAHN], its four steep staircases hold ninety-one stone steps each.

[5.4] Multiply ninety-one steps by four sides and add one top platform: **365**! Clever Maya architects carved a giant stone calendar matching every day of the solar year. Priests climbed those steep stairs to watch the stars. From the top, they announced maize planting dates across the plaza.

narrative_blocks.title: Spring & Autumn Equinox: Kukulkan’s Sunlit Serpent Descends
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.5] Twice each year, on the spring and autumn **equinox**, day and night last equal hours. As afternoon sunlight strikes **El Castillo**'s nine terraces, a **serpent shadow** appears. Seven sunlit triangles ripple slowly down the northern staircase wall.

[5.6] At the bottom waits a carved stone head of **Kukulkan** with open jaws! Watchers gasped in awe as the sunlit snake seemed to glide down to Earth. Makers also heated indigo leaves with white clay for unfading **Maya Blue** gifts. Those festivals celebrated spring rains and autumn **maize** harvests!

tasks.title: 1. Primary Evidence Detective
tasks.question: Look at the carved face on Source A. How does it connect Pok-ta-Pok to Maya beliefs?
tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, carving the Maize God onto a stone Pok-ta-Pok ballgame yoke connects the game to...
hints: Look closely at the Maize God’s face carved into the heavy polished greenstone hip yoke.
Recall the Popol Vuh myth of the Hero Twins playing ball against the underworld lords of Xibalba.
Explain how Pok-ta-Pok honoured the Maize God rising anew like sprouting green corn.
tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, carving the Maize God onto a stone Pok-ta-Pok ballgame yoke connects the game to the sacred Popol Vuh creation story. Rather than being just entertainment, bouncing the rubber ball honoured the Hero Twins defeating underworld lords so the Maize God could rise anew like sprouting corn!

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain how Chichén Itzá’s El Castillo pyramid blended Maya religion with clever solar astronomy.
tasks.starter: At Chichén Itzá, Maya architects proved they were master astronomers as well as temple builders because...
hints: Show the step maths on El Castillo: four staircases of 91 steps plus one top platform equals 365 solar days!
Describe what afternoon sunlight casts down the staircase every spring and autumn equinox.
Explain why seeing Kukulkan’s sunlit serpent descend in spring and autumn mattered so much to Maya maize farmers!
tasks.model_answer: At Chichén Itzá, Maya architects proved they were master astronomers as well as temple builders because El Castillo has four staircases of 91 steps plus one top platform — adding up to all 365 days of the solar year! Better still, every spring and autumn equinox, afternoon sunlight hits its nine terraces to cast seven bright triangles down the balustrade into Kukulkan’s carved stone serpent head, signalling spring rains for planting maize and autumn harvest!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: What did the Maya believe about creation and the gods, and how did beliefs shape Chichén Itzá?
tasks.starter: Sacred beliefs about maize, rain caves, and sky gods shaped almost everything the Maya built and made...
hints: Start with the Popol Vuh story of maize-dough humans and the Hero Twins outsmarting the lords of Xibalba.
Explain why caves and cenotes saw offerings of Maya Blue and copal incense for long-nosed rain god Chaac.
Finish with El Castillo at Chichén Itzá to show how religion drove world-class Maya maths and architecture!
tasks.model_answer: Sacred beliefs about maize, rain caves, and sky gods shaped almost everything the Maya built and made. Because the Popol Vuh taught that gods kneaded humans from yellow and white maize dough, protecting the corn harvest was a sacred duty. Families honoured the Maize God in Pok-ta-Pok and entered caves and cenotes — seen as doorways to Xibalba — to offer Maya Blue gifts to rain god Chaac. Finally, at Chichén Itzá, devotion to Kukulkan inspired El Castillo’s astonishing 365-step equinox calendar pyramid!

quiz.q: What is the name of the sacred creation book preserving ancient Maya stories of the gods?
quiz.explanation: Sacred K'iche' Maya stories of creation and the Hero Twins survived in the Popol Vuh!

quiz.question: In the Popol Vuh, what happened when the gods first tried making humans out of mud and wood?
quiz.q: In the Popol Vuh, what happened when the gods first tried making humans out of mud and wood?
options: Mud people crumbled in rain, and wooden people forgot to thank their makers
Mud people flew to the moon, and wooden people built iron ships
They swam across the ocean to Britain
quiz.answer: Mud people crumbled in rain, and wooden people forgot to thank their makers
quiz.a: Mud people crumbled in rain, and wooden people forgot to thank their makers
quiz.explanation: Mud humans washed away and wooden humans forgot the gods, so the gods tried a third sacred ingredient!

quiz.question: Which sacred food did the Maya gods finally knead to create grateful human beings?
quiz.q: Which sacred food did the Maya gods finally knead to create grateful human beings?
quiz.explanation: Because maize fed every Maya town, the Popol Vuh taught that gods shaped humans from yellow and white maize dough!

quiz.question: What did the Maya call the watery underworld where the Hero Twins beat dark lords at Pok-ta-Pok?
quiz.q: What did the Maya call the watery underworld where the Hero Twins beat dark lords at Pok-ta-Pok?
quiz.explanation: The Hero Twins outwitted the lords of Xibalba, helping the Maize God rise again like sprouting corn!

quiz.question: Why did Maya priests enter deep limestone caves and cenotes burning sweet copal resin?
quiz.q: Why did Maya priests enter deep limestone caves and cenotes burning sweet copal resin?
options: To mine coal for factory engines
Caves and cenotes were seen as doorways to Xibalba where priests prayed to rain god Chaac
To hide wheeled carts from rival kings
To store winter snow for royal kitchens
quiz.answer: Caves and cenotes were seen as doorways to Xibalba where priests prayed to rain god Chaac
quiz.a: Caves and cenotes were seen as doorways to Xibalba where priests prayed to rain god Chaac
quiz.explanation: Priests burned fragrant copal tree resin in caves and cenotes to carry prayers to long-nosed rain god Chaac.

quiz.question: Which feathered serpent god was honoured at Chichén Itzá's central step-pyramid, El Castillo?
quiz.q: Which feathered serpent god was honoured at Chichén Itzá's central step-pyramid, El Castillo?
quiz.explanation: Builders at Chichén Itzá dedicated El Castillo to the mighty feathered serpent god Kukulkan!

quiz.question: How many steps sit on each of El Castillo's four staircases, and what do they total with the top platform?
quiz.q: How many steps sit on each of El Castillo's four staircases, and what do they total with the top platform?
options: Four staircases of ninety-one stone steps plus one top platform equal 365
Four staircases of fifty steps plus one top platform equal 201
Four staircases of ten steps plus one top platform equal 41
Four staircases of twenty steps plus one top platform equal 81
quiz.answer: Four staircases of ninety-one stone steps plus one top platform equal 365
quiz.a: Four staircases of ninety-one stone steps plus one top platform equal 365
quiz.explanation: Ninety-one steps times four sides equals 364, plus the top temple platform makes all 365 days of the solar year!

quiz.question: Why did Maya builders design El Castillo's steps to add up to 365?
quiz.q: Why did Maya builders design El Castillo's steps to add up to 365?
options: Because 365 kings lived inside the pyramid
To measure 365 miles to the sea
To turn the pyramid into a giant stone calendar matching the solar year
quiz.answer: To turn the pyramid into a giant stone calendar matching the solar year
quiz.a: To turn the pyramid into a giant stone calendar matching the solar year
quiz.explanation: El Castillo blended sacred temple design with solar astronomy to mark all 365 days of the year.

quiz.question: Which long-nosed Maya god controlled life-giving rain, thunder, and lightning?
quiz.q: Which long-nosed Maya god controlled life-giving rain, thunder, and lightning?
quiz.explanation: Farmers across dry Yucatán prayed eagerly to long-nosed rain god Chaac so maize fields would flourish.

quiz.question: Why did Maya priests climb steep temple pyramids like El Castillo throughout the year?
quiz.q: Why did Maya priests climb steep temple pyramids like El Castillo throughout the year?
options: To watch the stars, lead offerings, and announce maize planting dates
To dry fishing nets in the wind
To ring giant iron church bells
quiz.answer: To watch the stars, lead offerings, and announce maize planting dates
quiz.a: To watch the stars, lead offerings, and announce maize planting dates
quiz.explanation: From high temple tops, priests read the sky and guided farming communities through planting and harvest rituals.

quiz.question: What happens across the world twice each year on the spring and autumn equinox?
quiz.q: What happens across the world twice each year on the spring and autumn equinox?
options: Day and night last equal hours
The sun disappears for a whole week
Winter snow falls in every rainforest
quiz.answer: Day and night last equal hours
quiz.a: Day and night last equal hours
quiz.explanation: Twice a year on the spring and autumn equinox, daytime and nighttime are equal in length.

quiz.question: What dramatic sight ripples down El Castillo's northern staircase every spring and autumn equinox?
quiz.q: What dramatic sight ripples down El Castillo's northern staircase every spring and autumn equinox?
options: A waterfall pumped from a cenote
A giant shadow shaped like a canoe
Seven sunlit triangles forming a serpent shadow that meets Kukulkan's carved stone head
Red fireworks launched from the roof
quiz.answer: Seven sunlit triangles forming a serpent shadow that meets Kukulkan's carved stone head
quiz.a: Seven sunlit triangles forming a serpent shadow that meets Kukulkan's carved stone head
quiz.explanation: Afternoon sun hits El Castillo's nine terraces to cast seven sunlit triangles slithering into Kukulkan's stone jaws!

quiz.question: How did spring and autumn equinox shadows help Maya maize farmers?
quiz.q: How did spring and autumn equinox shadows help Maya maize farmers?
options: They melted iron ore into ploughs
They frightened birds away from cobs
They cooled down hot summer plazas
Spring promised Chaac's rains for planting maize, while autumn marked harvest time
quiz.answer: Spring promised Chaac's rains for planting maize, while autumn marked harvest time
quiz.a: Spring promised Chaac's rains for planting maize, while autumn marked harvest time
quiz.explanation: Kukulkan's equinox shadow signalled spring rains for planting corn and autumn celebrations for harvest!

quiz.question: How did Maya craftworkers make their famous unfading turquoise "Maya Blue" pigment?
quiz.q: How did Maya craftworkers make their famous unfading turquoise "Maya Blue" pigment?
options: By heating indigo plant leaves with special white clay
By mixing copper rust with milk
quiz.answer: By heating indigo plant leaves with special white clay
quiz.a: By heating indigo plant leaves with special white clay
quiz.explanation: Heating blue indigo leaves with white clay created weatherproof turquoise Maya Blue honouring rain god Chaac!

quiz.question: Why has turquoise Maya Blue paint survived on clay figures for more than a thousand years?
quiz.q: Why has turquoise Maya Blue paint survived on clay figures for more than a thousand years?
options: Heating blue indigo leaves with white clay kept the turquoise pigment bright in damp tropical air
Archaeologists repainted every statue last week
The figures were sealed inside glass jars
It was made from modern plastic paint
quiz.answer: Heating blue indigo leaves with white clay kept the turquoise pigment bright in damp tropical air
quiz.a: Heating blue indigo leaves with white clay kept the turquoise pigment bright in damp tropical air
quiz.explanation: Clever Maya chemistry locked indigo dye inside clay crystals so Maya Blue stayed bright even in damp jungles!

lessons.title: Enquiry 6: The AD 900 Mystery & Seven Million Living Maya
lessons.subtitle: Drought, Deforestation & Warfare in the South, Thriving Northern Tulum, and Seven Million Maya Today
lessons.enquiryQuestion: Why did southern Maya cities empty—and why didn’t the Maya vanish?
lessons.enquiry_question: Why did southern Maya cities empty—and why didn’t the Maya vanish?
lessons.prologue: Around AD 900, jungle vines crept silently over southern pyramids at Tikal and Palenque — sparking wild rumours that the Maya vanished! Become a history detective testing lake-mud drought clues, northern coastal cities like Tulum, and over seven million living Maya people today.
lessons.blurb: Around AD 900, jungle vines crept silently over southern pyramids at Tikal and Palenque — sparking wild rumours that the Maya vanished! Become a history detective testing lake-mud drought clues, northern coastal cities like Tulum, and over seven million living Maya people today.

teacher_notes.primer: This capstone Key Stage 2 enquiry trains primary pupils in multi-causal historical explanation while dismantling the popular misconception that the Maya "mysteriously vanished." Pupils weigh three linked pressures behind the c. AD 800–950 abandonment of southern lowland cities like Tikal, Palenque, and Copán (lake-core shell evidence of severe multi-year droughts, deforestation from farming and burning lime plaster causing soil erosion, and non-stop royal warfare blocking trade), before tracing Postclassic flourishing in northern cities like Chichén Itzá, Uxmal, and coastal Tulum, courageous resistance to 16th-century Spanish conquest, and over seven million Maya people speaking 30+ Mayan languages today.

objectives.objective: Explain how severe droughts, deforestation, and rival warfare combined to empty southern Maya cities between AD 800 and 950.
objectives.primer: Connect lake-bed shell clues of multi-year drought with tree-felling for lime plaster and intensifying royal wars at Tikal, Palenque, and Copán.
objectives.question: Why do historians blame a chain of linked causes around AD 900 rather than just one single disaster?

objectives.objective: Prove that Maya civilisation continued flourishing after AD 900 in northern Yucatán cities like Chichén Itzá, Uxmal, and coastal Tulum.
objectives.primer: Follow families migrating north towards reliable cenote groundwater and booming Caribbean sea-canoe trade at walled cliffside Tulum.

items.question: Around AD 750–900, how did great stone Maya cities like Tikal compare with Anglo-Saxon towns in Britain?
items.answer: Maya cities held tens of thousands of people with tall stone pyramids and astronomy, while most Anglo-Saxons lived in smaller timber villages and burhs
items.explanation: Comparing Mesoamerica and Britain around AD 900 shows two resourceful worlds solving very different geographical challenges!

items.question: What did Maya scribes carve onto Copán’s 63-step stairway and paint onto folding fig-bark codices?
items.answer: Over 800 Maya hieroglyphic signs (glyphs) recording royal history, maths, and astronomy
items.explanation: Classic Maya scribes created the most complete writing system anywhere in the ancient Americas.

items.question: Why was black volcanic obsidian so valuable across Maya cities, and how did it reach lowland rainforests?
items.answer: It chipped into razor-sharp blades without iron, carried down from highland mountains by porters and river canoes
items.explanation: Long-distance trade linked volcanic highlands, tropical lowlands, and salt-producing northern coasts.

items.question: In the sacred K'iche' Maya Popol Vuh, why did the gods choose yellow and white maize dough to make humans?
items.answer: Mud people crumbled and wooden people forgot the gods, whereas living maize nourished grateful, speaking humans
items.explanation: Maize stood at the heart of both everyday Maya meals and sacred creation beliefs.

items.question: How did Chichén Itzá’s builders design El Castillo to honour Kukulkan and track the 365-day solar year?
items.answer: Four staircases of 91 steps plus 1 top platform equal 365 days, casting a sunlit serpent shadow every spring and autumn equinox
items.explanation: Architecture and astronomy worked together so crowds could watch Kukulkan’s shadow signal spring rains and autumn harvest.

narrative_blocks.title: AD 800–950: Empty Plazas in the South — Testing Linked Clues
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.1] Around **AD 900**, big changes struck southern **Maya** cities between **AD 800 and 950**. Royal scribes stopped carving dates at **Tikal**, **Palenque**, and **Copán**. Farming families packed their metates and walked away into the forest. Explorers once wondered if one sudden disaster had wiped everyone out!

[6.2] Lake-bed snail shells prove a severe multi-year **drought** dried up stone reservoirs. Heavy **deforestation** to burn pyramid lime plaster let fertile hillside soil wash away. Fierce royal **warfare** also blocked trade, giving historians a **multi-causal** answer of three linked causes!

narrative_blocks.title: AD 850–1500: Rival Warfare & Thriving Northern Sea Cities
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.3] As southern harvests shrank and wars raged, hungry families lost trust in southern kings. Crucially, the **Maya** people never vanished when southern plazas fell quiet after **AD 900**! Thousands moved north towards Yucatán cities with deep **cenotes**, like **Chichén Itzá** and **Uxmal**.

[6.4] During this vibrant **Postclassic** era from **AD 950 to 1520**, northern towns boomed for centuries. Stone temples rose beside busy coastal harbours and salt flats. Along the Caribbean coast, walled cliffside **Tulum** welcomed giant sea canoes. Merchants traded salt, honey, cotton, and bright feathers!

narrative_blocks.title: AD 1500s–Today: Shattering the Myth — Seven Million Living Maya!
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.5] Across the **1500s**, Spanish invaders arrived bringing steel swords, warhorses, and deadly Old World diseases. Spanish friars burned precious bark-paper books, leaving just four ancient Maya codices surviving. Even so, independent island Maya towns bravely resisted foreign conquest right until **1697**!

[6.6] Today, over **seven million** **Maya** people live proudly across Mexico and Central America. Families speak more than thirty **Mayan languages** and farm golden maize. Skilled weavers craft bright **huipil** [wee-PEEL] blouses on backstrap looms. Modern Maya scholars also read ancient stone glyphs aloud once again!

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Give a multi-causal explanation for why southern cities like Tikal and Palenque were abandoned around AD 900.
tasks.starter: Historians do not blame just one single event for the AD 900 abandonment of Tikal and Palenque; instead...
hints: Describe the lake-core shell evidence proving severe multi-year droughts dried up southern stone reservoirs.
Explain how deforestation for burning white lime plaster eroded soil while non-stop warfare blocked trade.
Explain how all three causes made citizens lose trust in kings (K'uhul Ajaw) who promised Chaac’s rain!
tasks.model_answer: Historians do not blame just one single event for the AD 900 abandonment of Tikal and Palenque; instead, they give a multi-causal explanation showing how three problems snowballed together. Snail shells in lake mud prove severe multi-year droughts emptied southern reservoirs, while deforestation to burn white pyramid plaster let thin hillside soil wash away. As harvests failed, non-stop royal warfare blocked trade routes, causing hungry families to lose trust in their kings and walk away towards northern water sources!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: Why were southern Maya cities abandoned around AD 900, and why is the "vanished Maya" story a myth?
tasks.starter: Weighing archaeological and living evidence proves that the "vanished Maya" story is a complete myth...
hints: Explain what actually changed around AD 900: drought, deforestation, and war emptied southern cities like Tikal.
Show what continued: Postclassic northern cities like Chichén Itzá, Uxmal, and coastal Tulum boomed for centuries.
Conclude with living proof today — over seven million Maya speakers, farmers, weavers, and scholars!
tasks.model_answer: Weighing archaeological and living evidence proves that the "vanished Maya" story is a complete myth! What really ended around AD 900 was royal rule in southern rainforest cities like Tikal, Palenque, and Copán after multi-year droughts, deforestation, and warfare pushed families out. Farther north, Maya civilisation flourished for centuries around deep cenotes at Chichén Itzá and Uxmal and along Caribbean sea-trade routes at cliffside Tulum. Best of all, over seven million Maya people still speak Mayan languages, farm maize, and weave vibrant huipil cloth today!

key_individuals.name: King K'inich Janaab' Pakal of Palenque (AD 603–683)
key_individuals.role: K'uhul Ajaw of Palenque & Builder of the Temple of the Inscriptions
key_individuals.origins: Born in AD 603 in the lush rainforest foothills of Chiapas, Mexico; crowned holy lord (K'uhul Ajaw) of war-torn Palenque aged just twelve with the support of his mother, Lady Sak K'uk'.
key_individuals.significance: Ruled for nearly sixty-eight years — one of the longest reigns in world history — turning Palenque into a jewel of white stucco palaces, aqueducts, and carved Maya hieroglyphs.
achievements: Rebuilt Palenque’s royal Palace and commissioned its famous four-storey stone astronomical and watch tower.
Raised the nine-tiered Temple of the Inscriptions, carved with 617 hieroglyphic blocks recording royal history and gods.
Buried in AD 683 inside a hidden stone crypt wearing a dazzling mosaic funerary mask made from over 200 pieces of green jade!
key_individuals.key_distinction: Archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier spent four years clearing a secret rubble-filled staircase inside Pakal’s pyramid before opening his untouched jade-filled tomb in 1952!

key_individuals.name: Lady Six Sky & Royal Maya Queens (7th–8th Century AD)
key_individuals.role: Warrior-Queen Regents, Dynasty Builders & Sacred Ceremony Leaders
key_individuals.origins: Royal daughters and queens of powerful Classic Maya dynasties — including Lady Six Sky (Wak Chanil Ajaw) of Dos Pilas and Naranjo, Lady Sak K'uk' of Palenque, and Lady K'ab'al Xook of Yaxchilán.
key_individuals.significance: Carved stone stelae and lintels prove royal Maya women wielded real political, military, and religious authority — ruling cities, forging alliances, and leading sacred calendar rituals.
achievements: Lady Six Sky arrived at crisis-hit Naranjo in AD 682, restored its royal line, and was carved standing triumphantly on stone stelae like a warrior-king!
Lady Sak K'uk' governed Palenque and placed the royal jade crown onto her twelve-year-old son Pakal in AD 615.
Royal queens hosted ambassadors, commissioned world-famous carved limestone lintels, and wove sacred ceremonial textiles.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Shatters the assumption that only men led ancient city-states — Maya stone monuments proudly name and picture powerful ruling queens!

key_individuals.name: Jasaw Chan K'awiil I of Tikal (r. AD 682–734)
key_individuals.role: Restorer of Tikal’s Power & Patron of the Great Plaza Pyramids
key_individuals.origins: Twenty-sixth dynastic ruler of Tikal in the tropical Petén rainforest of Guatemala, taking the throne after rival superpower Calakmul had overshadowed Tikal for more than a century.
key_individuals.significance: Defeated Tikal’s arch-rival Calakmul in AD 695 and launched a golden age of monumental limestone building that shaped Tikal’s iconic rainforest skyline.
achievements: Led Tikal’s army to decisive victory over King Yuknoom Yich'aak K'ahk' of Calakmul in August AD 695, restoring Tikal’s independence.
Planned Tikal’s twin Great Plaza masterpieces: 47-metre Temple I (Temple of the Great Jaguar) and Temple II facing his queen.
Expanded stone causeways (sacbeob), plastered reservoirs, and long-distance trade in highland obsidian, jade, and cacao.
key_individuals.key_distinction: His soaring limestone tomb-pyramid, Temple I, still pierces the emerald rainforest canopy 47 metres above Tikal’s Great Plaza today!

key_individuals.name: Classic Maya Scribes & Astronomers (c. AD 300–900)
key_individuals.role: Keepers of Glyphs, Base-20 Zero, Bark-Paper Codices & Star Tables
key_individuals.origins: Highly trained male and female court artists, mathematicians, and sky-watchers known in Mayan as aj tz'ib ("he or she of the writing"), working in royal workshops and observatories.
key_individuals.significance: Created the most complete writing system in the ancient Americas, independently invented place-value zero, and predicted solar eclipses and Venus cycles without glass telescopes.
achievements: Mastered over 800 syllable and word glyphs carved onto stone stelae and painted with fine brushes onto accordion-folded fig-bark codices.
Calculated vast numbers in base-20 maths using just three clear symbols: a shell for zero (0), a dot for one (1), and a bar for five (5).
Meshed the 260-day sacred Tzolk'in and 365-day solar Haab' calendars while tracking Venus within hours across 500 years in the Dresden Codex!
key_individuals.key_distinction: Invented a working symbol for place-value zero centuries before zero spread across medieval Europe!

key_individuals.name: Frederick Catherwood & Maya Rediscovery (1799–1854)
key_individuals.role: London-Born Architect-Artist Who Introduced Maya Cities to the Wider World
key_individuals.origins: Born in Hoxton, London, in 1799; trained as an architect and archaeological draughtsman before travelling across dense Central American rainforests with American writer John Lloyd Stephens.
key_individuals.significance: Between 1839 and 1842, Catherwood and Stephens documented forty-four Maya sites — proving right away that these stone cities were built by Indigenous Maya ancestors, not lost Old World travellers!
achievements: Used a camera lucida prism amidst biting insects, heat, and rainforest vines to draw millimetre-accurate views of Copán, Palenque, Uxmal, and Chichén Itzá.
Published Views of Ancient Monuments in Central America (1844), thrilling readers worldwide with detailed colour plates of stelae and step-pyramids.
Preserved vital visual records of carved glyph blocks and stucco reliefs before later weather or looting could damage them.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Insisted in the 1840s that Indigenous Maya builders created every pyramid and glyph — paving the way for modern glyph decipherment!

key_individuals.name: Living Maya Weavers, Farmers & Scholars Today
key_individuals.lifespan: Over Seven Million Maya People Today
key_individuals.role: Contemporary Guardians of Mayan Languages, Maize Farming, Weaving & History
key_individuals.origins: More than seven million Indigenous Maya citizens — including K'iche', Kaqchikel, Mam, Q'eqchi', Tzotzil, Tzeltal, and Yucatec Maya communities — living across southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, and El Salvador.
key_individuals.significance: Living proof that Maya civilisation never vanished: families sustain millennia-old traditions while leading modern schools, archaeology projects, literature, and environmental protection.
achievements: Speak more than thirty vibrant Mayan languages at home, in markets like Chichicastenango, and in bilingual classrooms.
Weave intricate patterned huipil textiles on traditional backstrap looms whose colours and symbols honour each community’s heritage.
Collaborate as epigraphers, archaeologists, and teachers decoding ancient stone inscriptions and protecting rainforest heritage sites.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Every woven huipil, spoken Mayan greeting, and thriving maize milpa proves Maya culture is a living story, not a vanished past!

guided_reading.book_title: Cool Sinkholes and Three Sisters: Farming the Maya Rainforest
guided_reading.author: The History Revision Hub Narrative Archive
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original historical micro-story grounded in Mesoamerican agronomy and archaeological surveys of Yucatán limestone cenotes, Tikal's plastered reservoirs, and Classic Maya 'Three Sisters' (milpa) companion farming.
guided_reading.author_context: How could millions of Classic Maya people thrive in cities where porous limestone left zero surface rivers—and without a single iron plough, ox, or wheeled cart? Read aloud to discover their water and farming secrets!
guided_reading.cover_caption: Deep natural limestone cenote sinkhole in northern Yucatán ringed by green rainforest trees above calm freshwater.

vocabVault.def: The region stretching across southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, and El Salvador where Maya cities thrived.
A deep natural sinkhole where porous limestone collapsed to reveal cool underground freshwater all year round.
Clever companion farming planting maize, climbing beans, and wide-leaved squash together in the same earth mound.
A bottle-shaped underground cistern cut into limestone and lined with waterproof plaster to store monsoon rain.

guided_reading.extract: Morning mist drifted through green Yucatán trees around AD 700 as bright quetzal birds called high above. Under the forest lay a puzzle. Porous white limestone soaked up rain like a dry sponge, leaving almost no rivers! Yet right nearby stood white Maya pyramids and busy markets. Down a rocky path, families carried clay jars to the rim of a deep cliff pool called a cenote. Where old cave roofs had fallen in, cool fresh water shone deep below all year round! South at Tikal, builders coated wide plazas and underground chultuns with smooth plaster to catch monsoon rain. In sunny clearings, farmers worked without iron ploughs or oxen. Poking holes with wooden sticks, they planted the Three Sisters together in one earth mound! Tall maize stalks held up climbing bean vines. Bean roots fed the soil, while wide squash leaves shaded damp ground—feeding stone cities while Anglo-Saxon Britain farmed round wooden halls!

parent_discussion.question: Why couldn't northern Yucatán families simply scoop water from rivers like people along Egypt's Nile or Baghdad's Tigris?
parent_discussion.answer: Yucatán sat on porous limestone rock that soaked rainwater straight underground, leaving almost no surface rivers.

parent_discussion.question: Explain how each of the 'Three Sisters' crops—maize, beans, and squash—helped the other two grow stronger.
parent_discussion.answer: Maize stalks gave poles for beans to climb, bean roots added richness back into the soil, and broad squash leaves shaded damp earth and blocked weeds!

parent_discussion.question: Why does comparing Tikal or Uxmal with AD 900 Anglo-Saxon Britain challenge old assumptions about technology?
parent_discussion.answer: Even without iron ploughs, horses, or wheels, Maya engineers and farmers supported towering stone cities and star observatories!

guided_reading.book_title: Forty-Five Hidden Steps: Finding King Pakal's Jade Mask
guided_reading.author: The History Revision Hub Narrative Archive
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original historical micro-story grounded in archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier's 1949–1952 excavation reports from the Temple of the Inscriptions at Palenque, Chiapas, Mexico.
guided_reading.author_context: Until 1952, experts insisted Maya pyramids were only solid stone bases for high temples—never royal tombs like Egypt's pyramids! Read aloud to join Alberto Ruz Lhuillier as he lifts a mysterious stone floor slab at Palenque!
guided_reading.cover_caption: Life-sized green jade mosaic funerary mask, beaded jade collars, and shell-and-obsidian eyes from King Pakal's tomb at Palenque.

vocabVault.def: The sacred Maya title meaning 'lord' or ruler—each independent Maya city-state obeyed its own K'uhul Ajaw.
Palenque's famous ruler K'inich Janaab' Pakal, crowned aged twelve in AD 615, who reigned for sixty-eight peaceful years.
A jewel-like Classic Maya city-state in southern Mexico famed for white stucco palaces and carved inscriptions.
Tough, luminous green stone prized by the Maya even higher than gold because its colour matched sprouting maize and life.

guided_reading.extract: High atop Palenque's stepped Temple of the Inscriptions in 1949, digger Alberto Ruz Lhuillier knelt in the shade. Every textbook claimed Maya pyramids were solid stone mounds, unlike Egypt's hollow tombs. Why, then, did one wide floor slab have two neat rows of round stone plugs? Lifting the heavy slab with ropes, Ruz gasped aloud! Below lay a narrow stone stairway packed tight with wet rocks and clay. For four hot summers, Mexican workers cleared bucket after bucket down forty-five steep steps inside the pyramid. At last, on 15 June 1952, workers pried open a stone door at the very bottom. Shining his torch inside, Ruz stepped into a cool vault sealed since AD 683! Under a five-tonne carved stone lid rested Palenque's great Ajaw, King Pakal. Over his face shone a life-sized green jade mosaic mask, gazing out through white shell and black glass eyes. After twelve centuries in the dark, Pakal's secret tomb amazed the whole world!

parent_discussion.question: What tiny clue on the top temple floor made Alberto Ruz Lhuillier suspect something lay hidden inside Palenque's pyramid?
parent_discussion.answer: One large stone floor slab had two neat rows of removable stone plugs sealing finger-holes used to lower it into place!

parent_discussion.question: Why did Maya rulers like King Pakal prize glowing green jade even more than shiny yellow gold?
parent_discussion.answer: Vibrant green jade matched young maize shoots, rainforest leaves, and fresh water—symbolising breath, life, and rebirth.

parent_discussion.question: Why did clearing just forty-five stairs take Ruz and his team four whole summers of hard work?
parent_discussion.answer: Maya builders had packed the entire hidden staircase tightly with heavy stones and wet lime mortar to stop tomb robbers entering.

story_check.question: How old was K'inich Janaab' Pakal when his mother helped crown him ruler of Palenque in AD 615?
story_check.feedback: Spot on! Crowned aged twelve, Pakal the Great ruled Palenque for sixty-eight remarkable years until AD 683.

story_check.question: What did Alberto Ruz Lhuillier's 1952 discovery prove for the first time?
options: That Maya builders used iron steam cranes
That some Classic Maya step-pyramids also held deep royal tombs inside
That Egyptians had sailed across the Atlantic to build Palenque
That Palenque had no written hieroglyphs
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Finding Pakal's vault overturned the old textbook claim that American pyramids were never tombs.

story_check.question: What materials formed the lifelike eyes of King Pakal's green jade mosaic mask?
options: White shell and shiny black volcanic obsidian
story_check.feedback: Well remembered! White shell whites and dark volcanic obsidian pupils gave the jade mask a startlingly lifelike gaze.

monday_cold_call.question: What clue led Alberto Ruz Lhuillier down 45 hidden stairs at Palenque in 1949–1952, and what shone over King Pakal's face inside?
monday_cold_call.answer: Stone plugs in a temple floor slab hid the rubble-packed stairs, leading to King Pakal's AD 683 tomb and his green jade mosaic mask.
