items.question: What cone-roofed homes made of wattle-and-daub and thatch did Iron Age Britons live in before the Romans arrived?
items.explanation: Iron Age families cooked, slept, and wove wool around a central fire inside circular thatched roundhouses.

items.question: Why did Julius Caesar sail to Britain twice in 55 BC and 54 BC without staying permanently?
items.answer: He won battles and tribute promises, then returned to Gaul rather than conquering the island
items.explanation: Caesar raided south-east Britain in 55 BC and 54 BC, leaving full conquest until nearly a century later.

items.question: Which Roman Emperor launched the permanent invasion of Britain in AD 43 with four legions and war elephants?
items.explanation: In AD 43, Emperor Claudius sent General Aulus Plautius with 40,000 troops and arrived with elephants at Camulodunum (Colchester).

items.question: What was the tortoise-like shield formation called when Roman legionaries locked rectangular shields overhead and in front?
items.explanation: Locking scutum shields together formed a protective shell against enemy spears, stones, and arrows.

items.question: Why did Roman soldiers become such tough, disciplined fighters compared with part-time tribal warriors?
items.answer: They were full-time professional soldiers who trained daily and marched up to 20 miles carrying heavy kit
items.explanation: Legionaries served for 25 years, wearing iron strip armour (lorica segmentata) and carrying throwing spears (pila) and short swords (gladii).

items.question: Which warrior queen of the Iceni tribe led a massive rebellion against Roman rule in AD 60–61?
items.explanation: After Romans seized Iceni lands and mistreated her daughters following King Prasutagus's death, Boudicca led a huge uprising.

items.question: Name the three Roman towns burned to the ground by Boudicca's rebel army in AD 60–61.
items.explanation: Archaeologists still find a dark red layer of burnt clay and ash beneath Colchester, London, and St Albans from Boudicca's revolt.

items.question: Along which Roman road line did Governor Suetonius Paulinus defeat Boudicca's much larger army using narrow ground and discipline?
items.explanation: Choosing a narrow funnel backed by woods, 10,000 disciplined Roman troops held firm with shield walls and javelins against Boudicca's host.

current_items.question: In what year did Emperor Hadrian visit Britain and order a stone wall across the north?
current_items.answer: AD 122
current_items.explanation: Emperor Hadrian inspected Britain in AD 122 and ordered his legions to build a sea-to-sea frontier wall.

current_items.question: How many modern miles long was Hadrian's Wall from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway?
current_items.answer: 73 miles (80 Roman miles)
current_items.explanation: Hadrian's Wall ran for 80 Roman miles — about 73 modern miles — from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth.

current_items.question: What natural condition preserved wooden ink letters underground at Vindolanda Fort?
current_items.answer: Wet, oxygen-free mud
current_items.explanation: Waterlogged, oxygen-free soil stopped bacteria from rotting the wafer-thin wooden tablets.

current_items.question: Who wrote the famous AD 100 birthday party invitation found at Vindolanda?
current_items.answer: Claudia Severa
current_items.explanation: Claudia Severa's greeting to Sulpicia Lepidina contains the oldest known Latin handwriting by a woman.

current_items.question: From which three continents did auxiliary troops come to guard Hadrian's Wall?
current_items.answer: Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa
current_items.explanation: Regiments included European Batavians, Syrian archers from the Middle East, and Aurelian Moors from North Africa.

vocab.definition: The guarded border line at the edge of an empire separating Roman land from unconquered territory beyond.
A small stone fortlet and guarded gateway built at every single Roman mile along Hadrian's Wall.
A communal Roman stone toilet block flushed clean by flowing rainwater and drainage channels.
Kept safe from rotting or crumbling over hundreds of years, such as wooden letters trapped in oxygen-free mud.
A non-citizen soldier recruited from across the Roman Empire who earned Roman citizenship after 25 years of service.

lessons.vocab_cloze_text: In AD 122, Emperor Hadrian built a 73-mile stone [Frontier] across northern Britain. Patrols checked traders at every guarded [Milecastle], while large forts like Housesteads kept troops healthy with a stone [Latrine]. Nearby at Vindolanda, wet mud [Preserved] wooden ink letters, and tombstones show that [Auxiliary] soldiers came from Europe, Syria, and North Africa.

narrative_blocks.title: 73 Miles of Stone From Sea to Sea (AD 122)
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] In **AD 122**, **Emperor Hadrian** visited Britain and ordered a stone **frontier** wall across the north. **Hadrian's Wall** ran **73 miles** (**80 Roman miles**) from **Wallsend** on the River Tyne to **Bowness-on-Solway**, dividing Roman Britain from **Caledonia** [kal-ih-DOH-nee-uh] (modern Scotland).

[4.2] At every Roman mile stood a guarded stone gatehouse called a **milecastle** to stop cattle raids and collect border **taxes**. Backed by **16** large forts like **Housesteads**, soldiers even used communal stone **latrines** flushed clean by rainwater channels!
narrative_blocks.content:

[4.2] At every Roman mile stood a guarded stone gatehouse called a **milecastle** to stop cattle raids and collect border **taxes**. Backed by **16** large forts like **Housesteads**, soldiers even used communal stone **latrines** flushed clean by rainwater channels!

narrative_blocks.title: Postcards in the Mud: The Vindolanda Tablets
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.3] Just south of the Wall stood **Vindolanda Fort** [vin-doh-LAN-duh]. There, wet, **oxygen-free mud** **preserved** hundreds of thin **wooden ink tablets** from around **AD 100** without rotting.

[4.4] On one tablet, **Claudia Severa** [KLAW-dee-uh seh-VAIR-uh] invited her friend **Sulpicia Lepidina** to a **birthday party** on 11 September — the oldest surviving **Latin handwriting by a woman**! Another tablet lists a parcel for a chilly soldier: **woollen socks**, two pairs of **sandals**, and two pairs of **underpants**.

sources.source_context: Preserved for nearly 2,000 years in wet, oxygen-free mud at Vindolanda, thin wooden ink letters reveal warm friendships and parcels of socks sent to chilly soldiers. **Hinge Question:** How do personal letters like Claudia Severa's party invitation change our picture of life on a Roman frontier?
sources.text:
Vindolanda wooden ink letters (c. AD 100): "On 11 September, sister, for my birthday, I warmly ask that you come to us, to make the day happier... Farewell, my dearest soul." "I have sent you woollen socks, sandals, and underpants."

In plain words: One wooden letter invites Claudia Severa's best friend to her birthday party on 11 September. Another letter lists a cosy parcel of warm socks, sandals, and underpants for a cold soldier!

narrative_blocks.title: Soldiers & Families From Across the Roman Empire
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.5] **Auxiliary** regiments from **three continents** — Europe, the Middle East, and **North Africa** — guarded Hadrian's Wall. **Batavian** soldiers from Europe, **Syrian archers**, and North African **Aurelian Moors** at **Burgh-by-Sands** all patrolled the windy northern border.

[4.6] Busy civilian towns called **vici** [WEE-kee] grew outside fort gates where families and shopkeepers lived. At **Arbeia Fort** [ar-BAY-uh] (South Shields), carved tombstones honour **Barates** [ba-RAH-teez] from **Syria**, his British **Catuvellauni** wife **Regina**, and young **Victor** from **Mauretania** in North Africa.

sources.question: Read the two Arbeia Fort tombstone inscriptions in Source D. What do Barates, Regina, and Victor prove about Roman Britain?
sources.model_answer: The tombstones prove Roman Britain brought people together from three continents: Barates travelled from Syria and married Regina from southern Britain, while Victor came from Mauretania in North Africa.
sources.source_context: Arbeia guarded sea supplies for Hadrian's Wall, and tombstones outside the fort prove people from Syria, North Africa, and southern Britain lived side by side. **Hinge Question:** Why are carved Roman tombstones at forts like Arbeia such valuable clues about who lived in Roman Britain?
sources.text:
Carved Roman tombstones at Arbeia Fort: "Regina, freedwoman and wife of Barates of Palmyra [in Syria], a woman of the Catuvellaunian tribe, died aged 30." — "Victor, of the Moorish nation [North Africa], aged 20, freedman of Numerianus."

In plain words: These stone memorials show that people from across the world lived beside Hadrian's Wall. Barates came from Syria and married British-born Regina, while young Victor came from North Africa!

tasks.title: 1. Primary Evidence Detective
tasks.question: Look closely at Source A. How did building Milecastle 39 along steep crags help Roman soldiers control the northern border?
tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, guarded stone Milecastles along the high crags helped Roman soldiers...
hints: Point out how the thick stone walls sit right on top of high, steep rocky cliffs.
Explain how height gave Roman sentries a clear view for miles north into Caledonia.
Mention how guarded milecastle gates controlled travellers, stopped raids, and collected taxes.
tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, guarded stone Milecastles along the high crags helped Roman soldiers spot raiders for miles across the northern hills. Built every Roman mile along Hadrian’s Wall, strong gatehouses like Milecastle 39 forced travellers and merchants through controlled doorways where troops prevented raids and collected border taxes.

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Why did Emperor Hadrian order a 73-mile stone wall with milecastle gates and 16 forts across northern Britain in AD 122?
tasks.starter: Emperor Hadrian ordered his legions to build a 73-mile stone wall across northern Britain in AD 122 because...
hints: Describe where the Wall ran (73 miles from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway) separating Roman Britain from Caledonia.
Explain the two main jobs of the guarded milecastle gates: stopping northern raids and collecting taxes from traders.
Explain why having gates every Roman mile proves the Wall was designed as a controlled border checkpoint rather than a sealed barrier.
tasks.model_answer: Emperor Hadrian ordered his legions to build a 73-mile stone wall across northern Britain in AD 122 because he wanted to protect Roman Britain from raids out of Caledonia and control everyone crossing the border. Stretching from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway, the Wall had a guarded milecastle gate every Roman mile, two watchtowers in between, and 16 forts like Housesteads behind it. Rather than blocking people completely, milecastle gates let peaceful farmers and merchants pass through once soldiers checked their goods and collected Roman taxes.

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: Why did Emperor Hadrian build a 73-mile stone wall across northern Britain, and who guarded it?
tasks.starter: Archaeological clues from Vindolanda and Arbeia prove that Rome's northern frontier was home to a remarkably diverse community because...
hints: Name auxiliary troops from across the Empire: European Batavians, Syrian archers, and North African Aurelian Moors at Burgh-by-Sands.
Use the Arbeia Fort tombstones of Syrian trader Barates, his British wife Regina, and North African freedman Victor as solid proof.
Conclude how women, children, traders, and freed people in the vici towns show the frontier was far more than an all-male army camp.
tasks.model_answer: Archaeological clues from Vindolanda and Arbeia prove that Rome's northern frontier was home to a remarkably diverse community drawn from three continents — Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa. Auxiliary regiments included Batavians from the Netherlands, Syrian archers, and North African Aurelian Moors at Burgh-by-Sands. Outside the forts in busy vici towns, families and merchants settled too: Vindolanda's wooden letters reveal commanders' wives like Claudia Severa, while carved tombstones at Arbeia honour Barates from Syria, his British wife Regina from the Catuvellauni tribe, and Victor, a freedman from Mauretania in North Africa.

quiz.explanation: Claudia Severa's wooden letter warmly invited her friend Lepidina to visit for her birthday on 11 September.

quiz.question: From which three continents were auxiliary soldiers recruited to guard Hadrian's Wall?
quiz.q: From which three continents were auxiliary soldiers recruited to guard Hadrian's Wall?
options: Europe, the Middle East (Asia), and North Africa
North America, South America, and Europe
quiz.answer: Europe, the Middle East (Asia), and North Africa
quiz.a: Europe, the Middle East (Asia), and North Africa
quiz.explanation: Auxiliary regiments came from across Europe (Batavians), the Middle East (Syrian archers), and North Africa (Aurelian Moors).

quiz.question: Where did the Aurelian Moors who guarded Hadrian's Wall at Burgh-by-Sands come from?
quiz.q: Where did the Aurelian Moors who guarded Hadrian's Wall at Burgh-by-Sands come from?
quiz.explanation: The Numerus Maurorum Aurelianorum (Aurelian Moors) stationed at Burgh-by-Sands came from North Africa.

quiz.question: What did Romans call the bustling civilian settlements where families and traders lived outside fort gates?
quiz.q: What did Romans call the bustling civilian settlements where families and traders lived outside fort gates?
quiz.explanation: Busy civilian towns called vici (singular: vicus) grew outside frontier forts to house families, shopkeepers, and craftspeople.

quiz.question: At Arbeia Fort (South Shields), where had the trader Barates and the young freedman Victor originally come from?
quiz.q: At Arbeia Fort (South Shields), where had the trader Barates and the young freedman Victor originally come from?
options: Both came from Rome in Italy
Both came from the Iceni tribe in Norfolk
Barates came from Syria and Victor came from Mauretania in North Africa
Barates came from Caledonia and Victor came from Ireland
quiz.answer: Barates came from Syria and Victor came from Mauretania in North Africa
quiz.a: Barates came from Syria and Victor came from Mauretania in North Africa
quiz.explanation: Carved tombstones at Arbeia show Barates came from Palmyra in Syria (marrying British freedwoman Regina) and Victor came from Mauretania in North Africa.

quiz.question: Which British tribe had Regina (wife of Syrian trader Barates at Arbeia Fort) been born into?
quiz.q: Which British tribe had Regina (wife of Syrian trader Barates at Arbeia Fort) been born into?
quiz.explanation: Regina's carved tombstone at South Shields records that she came from the southern British Catuvellauni tribe.

lessons.subtitle: Straight Stone Highways, Aquae Sulis Steam Baths, Hypocaust Heating & Mosaics
lessons.enquiryQuestion: How did Roman roads, baths, and towns change life in Britain?
lessons.enquiry_question: How did Roman roads, baths, and towns change life in Britain?
lessons.prologue: Roman engineers laid 10,000 miles of straight stone roads, piped fresh water into steaming bathhouses like Aquae Sulis, and heated dolphin-mosaic villas from underneath! Yet out in the countryside, did life really change for everyone?
lessons.blurb: Roman engineers laid 10,000 miles of straight stone roads, piped fresh water into steaming bathhouses like Aquae Sulis, and heated dolphin-mosaic villas from underneath! Yet out in the countryside, did life really change for everyone?

teacher_notes.primer: This Change & Continuity enquiry explores the urban and technological revolution of Roman Britain alongside deep rural continuity. Pupils examine groma-surveyed cambered stone highways, planned towns with forums, basilicas, and amphitheatres (Caerleon), aqueduct water engineering, Aquae Sulis bathhouses, and hypocaust pilae heating. Crucially, Act 3 balances elite villas like Fishbourne Palace and imported Mediterranean foods (grapes, cherries, walnuts, garum) against archaeological reality: roughly 90% of Britons remained rural farmers living in thatched roundhouses while paying Roman taxes.

objectives.objective: Explain how Roman engineers built 10,000 miles of straight, cambered stone roads and planned market towns.
objectives.primer: Show how the groma, layered gravel/stone, cambered surfaces, and drainage ditches linked forums, basilicas, and amphitheatres.
objectives.question: Why were cambered stone highways and central town forums such a dramatic change from Iron Age Britain?

objectives.objective: Describe how aqueducts, public bathhouses (Aquae Sulis), strigils, and hypocaust underfloor heating worked.
objectives.primer: Trace fresh water through aqueducts and lead pipes, and hot furnace air through hypocaust pilae pillars.
objectives.question: How did Roman engineering bring running water and underfloor central heating into British towns?

objectives.objective: Compare the luxury of mosaic villas like Fishbourne Palace with continuity in countryside roundhouses.
objectives.primer: Weigh change for wealthy Romano-British elites against continuity for nearly nine out of ten rural farmers.
objectives.question: Did Roman towns and villas change everyday life for everyone in Britain equally?

source_context.Source B: Major Roman towns and fortress settlements built oval stone amphitheatres where up to 6,000 spectators cheered gladiator bouts and parades. **Hinge Question:** Why did Roman governors and wealthy town leaders pay for free gladiator shows inside stone amphitheatres?
source_context.Source C: Public bathhouses like Aquae Sulis and wealthy villas used hypocaust heating: enslaved workers stoked a wood furnace so hot air flowed between brick tile stacks under the floor. **Hinge Question:** Who did the hard, smoky work needed to keep luxurious Roman bathhouses and villa floors warm?
source_context.Source D: Wealthy leaders decorated stone villas like Fishbourne Palace with mosaic floors, while almost nine out of ten country Britons kept living in thatched roundhouses. **Hinge Question:** Does a grand mosaic floor at Fishbourne Palace prove that EVERY family in Roman Britain lived in luxury?

items.question: How did people travel between Iron Age villages and hillforts before Roman engineers arrived?
items.explanation: Without paved highways, heavy wooden carts often sank into thick winter mud.

items.question: Which Roman Emperor sent four legions to conquer southern Britain in AD 43?
items.explanation: Emperor Claudius launched the permanent conquest of Britain in AD 43.

items.question: What defensive formation saw Roman legionaries lock rectangular shields above their heads and in front?
items.explanation: Locked scutum shields protected advancing Roman troops from stones and spears.

items.question: Why did Queen Boudicca and the Iceni tribe rebel against Rome in AD 60–61?
items.answer: Romans broke promises after King Prasutagus died, seizing Iceni wealth and mistreating Boudicca and her daughters
items.explanation: Boudicca burned Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium before being defeated at Watling Street.

items.question: In what year did Emperor Hadrian order a 73-mile stone wall across northern Britain?
items.explanation: Begun in AD 122, Hadrian's Wall stretched 73 miles from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway.

items.question: What were the fortified stone gatehouses placed at every Roman mile along Hadrian's Wall called?
items.explanation: Soldiers stationed at milecastles stopped northern raids and collected border taxes from traders.

items.question: What preserved Claudia Severa's birthday invitation and the woollen socks letter at Vindolanda Fort?
items.explanation: Waterlogged, oxygen-free mud prevented the thin wooden ink tablets from rotting away.

items.question: What do the tombstones of Barates, Regina, and Victor at Arbeia Fort prove about Roman Britain?
items.answer: People from Syria, North Africa, and British tribes lived side by side on the frontier
items.explanation: Auxiliary soldiers and traders brought families and traditions from three continents to Roman Britain.

current_items.question: What sighting tool did Roman surveyors use to build 10,000 miles of straight stone roads?
current_items.answer: A groma
current_items.explanation: Surveyors lined up hanging plumb-weights on a wooden groma cross to plot dead-straight highways.

current_items.question: What was the central open marketplace at the heart of every Roman town called?
current_items.answer: The forum
current_items.explanation: Townspeople met in the forum to shop, trade, hear announcements, and visit the basilica town hall.

current_items.question: What Roman name was given to the famous spring-fed bathhouse town of modern Bath?
current_items.answer: Aquae Sulis
current_items.explanation: Aquae Sulis combined Roman engineering with sacred hot springs dedicated to the goddess Sulis Minerva.

current_items.question: What did Romans call their underfloor central heating system supported by brick pilae stacks?
current_items.answer: A hypocaust
current_items.explanation: Hot air from a wood furnace circulated beneath floors raised on brick pilae pillars.

current_items.question: Roughly how many Britons out of ten carried on farming in countryside roundhouses during Roman rule?
current_items.answer: Almost nine out of ten Britons
current_items.explanation: While rich elites built mosaic villas, nearly 90% of Britons lived in rural farming settlements.

narrative_blocks.title: Straight Stone Roads & Bustling Market Forums
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.1] Before Rome arrived, Britons travelled slowly along muddy dirt tracks. Roman surveyors used a wooden sighting **groma** [GROH-muh] to lay **10,000 miles** of dead-straight stone roads. Gently curved (**cambered**) paving stones and deep **side ditches** drained rainwater so carts rolled smoothly in all weathers.

[5.2] Where major highways met, Romans built walled grid towns around an open market **forum** and a **basilica** [buh-SIL-ih-kuh] town hall. Nearby, oval stone **amphitheatres** like **Caerleon** [kar-LEE-on] in South Wales seated cheering crowds for **gladiator** shows.

[5.1] Before Rome arrived, Britons travelled slowly along muddy dirt tracks. Roman surveyors used a wooden sighting **groma** [GROH-muh] to lay **10,000 miles** of dead-straight stone roads. Gently curved (**cambered**) paving stones and deep **side ditches** drained rainwater so carts rolled smoothly in all weathers.

[5.2] Where major highways met, Romans built walled grid towns around an open market **forum** and a **basilica** [buh-SIL-ih-kuh] town hall. Nearby, oval stone **amphitheatres** like **Caerleon** [kar-LEE-on] in South Wales seated cheering crowds for **gladiator** shows.

narrative_blocks.title: Aqueducts, Steam Baths & Underfloor Heating
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.3] Stone **aqueducts** and underground **lead pipes** carried fresh spring water into **Roman** towns, fountains, sewers, and **bathhouses** like **Aquae Sulis** [AK-wee SOO-lis] (**Bath**). Townsfolk visited the noisy public baths daily to exercise, chat, and wash.

[5.4] Bathhouses and rich homes used **hypocaust** [HY-poh-kawst] underfloor heating. Enslaved workers stoked a wood furnace so hot air blew between brick **pilae** [PEE-ly] stacks. Bathers rubbed on **olive oil**, then scraped oil and dirt off with a curved bronze **strigil** [STRIJ-il].

narrative_blocks.title: Dolphin Mosaics vs Countryside Roundhouses
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.5] In peaceful southern Britain, wealthy leaders built grand stone country **villas** like **Fishbourne Palace** in Sussex. Craftspeople pressed thousands of tiny coloured stone **tesserae** [TESS-er-ee] cubes into wet mortar to make **mosaic** floors. Rich diners tasted new foods like **grapes**, **cherries**, **walnuts**, and salty **garum** [GA-rum] fish sauce.

[5.6] Yet life did not change equally for rural **British** farmers. Across the countryside, almost **nine out of ten Britons** kept farming in smoky **thatched roundhouses** and speaking Celtic while paying **Roman taxes**.

tasks.title: 1. Primary Evidence Detective
tasks.question: Look closely at the stone road in Source A. How was a Roman highway better than muddy Iron Age tracks?
tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, gently curved stone highways with side ditches beat muddy tracks because...
hints: Describe the tightly fitted stone slabs running straight across the hills.
Explain how the gently curved (cambered) middle let rainwater run off into side ditches.
Show why firm dry roads helped marching legions, messengers, and merchant carts.
tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, gently curved stone highways with side ditches beat muddy tracks because heavy British rain drained straight off the cambered stone surface. Instead of wagon wheels sinking into boggy ruts, Roman legions, imperial messengers, and trade carts could travel swiftly between towns in every season.

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: How did Roman engineers build roads and water systems that transformed travel and hygiene in British towns?
tasks.starter: Roman engineers transformed travel and town hygiene across Britain by building...
hints: Explain how surveyors used a groma to lay 10,000 miles of straight, cambered stone roads with side ditches.
Describe how stone aqueducts and lead pipes carried fresh spring water into fountains, sewers, and bathhouses like Aquae Sulis.
Link faster all-weather roads to both military control (moving legions fast) and booming trade in town forums.
tasks.model_answer: Roman engineers transformed travel and town hygiene across Britain by building 10,000 miles of stone highways and clever water networks. Using a groma sighting tool, soldiers built dead-straight roads with cambered surfaces and side ditches so rainwater ran off, letting legions and merchant carts reach town forums in all weathers. Meanwhile, stone aqueducts and underground lead pipes carried clean spring water into street fountains, flushing sewers, and steaming public bathhouses like Aquae Sulis, where bathers scraped off olive oil and dirt with a curved bronze strigil.

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did Roman roads, bathhouses, and stone towns transform everyday life in Britain?
tasks.starter: Roman rule brought dramatic changes to Britain's towns and wealthy homes, yet everyday life did not change equally for everyone because...
hints: Describe the big changes in towns and rich villas: 10,000 miles of stone roads, forums, Aquae Sulis baths, hypocaust heating, mosaics, and new foods.
Explain the big continuity: almost nine out of ten Britons carried on farming in countryside thatched roundhouses and speaking Celtic.
Explain how even countryside farmers in roundhouses still felt Roman rule through Roman roads and paying Roman taxes.
tasks.model_answer: Roman rule brought dramatic changes to Britain's towns and wealthy homes, yet everyday life did not change equally for everyone. For town-dwellers and rich tribal leaders in villas like Fishbourne Palace, life was transformed by 10,000 miles of stone roads, bustling forums, aqueduct water, steaming bathhouses like Aquae Sulis, hypocaust heating, dolphin mosaics, and foods like cherries and garum. However, almost nine out of ten ordinary Britons carried on farming in the countryside inside thatched timber roundhouses and speaking Celtic languages — though even they had to grow extra grain to pay Roman taxes!

quiz.question: What wooden sighting tool did Roman surveyors use to line up dead-straight highways?
quiz.q: What wooden sighting tool did Roman surveyors use to line up dead-straight highways?
quiz.explanation: Roman surveyors used a wooden sighting cross with hanging weights called a groma to plot dead-straight roads.

quiz.question: Roughly how many miles of stone highways did the Romans build across Britain?
quiz.q: Roughly how many miles of stone highways did the Romans build across Britain?
quiz.explanation: Roman engineers and legionaries laid around 10,000 miles of layered stone highways across Britain.

quiz.question: Why were Roman road surfaces cambered (gently curved) with deep ditches along both sides?
quiz.q: Why were Roman road surfaces cambered (gently curved) with deep ditches along both sides?
options: To trap enemy chariots in puddles
To stop horses galloping too quickly
So rainwater drained off and carts could move in all weathers
To grow cabbages along the middle of the road
quiz.answer: So rainwater drained off and carts could move in all weathers
quiz.a: So rainwater drained off and carts could move in all weathers
quiz.explanation: A gently curved (cambered) stone surface and side ditches drained rainwater away so roads did not turn to mud.

quiz.question: What stood at the centre of a planned Roman town as an open marketplace, alongside a basilica town hall?
quiz.q: What stood at the centre of a planned Roman town as an open marketplace, alongside a basilica town hall?
quiz.explanation: Every planned Roman town had a central open marketplace called a forum bordered by shops and a basilica town hall.

quiz.question: What crowds cheered inside oval stone amphitheatres like Caerleon in South Wales?
quiz.q: What crowds cheered inside oval stone amphitheatres like Caerleon in South Wales?
quiz.explanation: Oval stone amphitheatres like Caerleon held thousands of townspeople and soldiers cheering gladiator bouts.

quiz.question: How did Roman engineers bring fresh spring water into town fountains, sewers, and bathhouses?
quiz.q: How did Roman engineers bring fresh spring water into town fountains, sewers, and bathhouses?
options: Through stone aqueducts and underground lead pipes
In leather buckets carried on donkeys
By melting snow on rooftops only
Through hollow tree trunks floated down rivers
quiz.answer: Through stone aqueducts and underground lead pipes
quiz.a: Through stone aqueducts and underground lead pipes
quiz.explanation: Stone aqueduct channels and underground lead pipes carried clean spring water straight into Roman towns.

quiz.question: What was the Roman name for the famous hot-spring bathhouse town known today as Bath?
quiz.q: What was the Roman name for the famous hot-spring bathhouse town known today as Bath?
quiz.explanation: The Romans built a magnificent temple and steaming bath complex called Aquae Sulis around the hot springs at Bath.

quiz.question: How did a Roman hypocaust warm bathhouses and wealthy villa rooms?
quiz.q: How did a Roman hypocaust warm bathhouses and wealthy villa rooms?
options: Bonfires were lit right in the middle of mosaic carpets
Glass mirrors reflected sunshine onto stone walls
Hot air from a wood furnace blew under floors raised on stacks of brick tiles (pilae)
Boiling water was poured over woollen curtains
quiz.answer: Hot air from a wood furnace blew under floors raised on stacks of brick tiles (pilae)
quiz.a: Hot air from a wood furnace blew under floors raised on stacks of brick tiles (pilae)
quiz.explanation: In a hypocaust, enslaved workers fed a furnace so hot air circulated beneath raised floors supported on brick pilae stacks.

quiz.question: Instead of soap, what tool did Roman bathers use to scrape perfumed olive oil and dirt from their skin?
quiz.q: Instead of soap, what tool did Roman bathers use to scrape perfumed olive oil and dirt from their skin?
options: A sea sponge on a spear
quiz.explanation: Bathers rubbed olive oil onto their skin in the hot room and scraped oil, sweat, and dirt away with a curved bronze strigil.

quiz.question: Who did the hot, smoky work of stoking wood furnaces to keep Roman hypocaust floors warm?
quiz.q: Who did the hot, smoky work of stoking wood furnaces to keep Roman hypocaust floors warm?
quiz.explanation: Enslaved workers kept wood furnaces roaring so hot air flowed between the brick pilae stacks underneath.

quiz.question: What were the thousands of tiny coloured stone cubes pressed into mortar to make a Roman mosaic floor called?
quiz.q: What were the thousands of tiny coloured stone cubes pressed into mortar to make a Roman mosaic floor called?
quiz.explanation: Craftspeople cut thousands of tiny coloured stone and tile cubes called tesserae to create detailed mosaic pictures.

quiz.question: Which grand Roman villa palace in Sussex is famous for its mosaic of Cupid riding a dolphin?
quiz.q: Which grand Roman villa palace in Sussex is famous for its mosaic of Cupid riding a dolphin?
quiz.explanation: Fishbourne Roman Palace in Sussex features magnificent mosaic floors including Cupid riding a dolphin (c. AD 160).

quiz.question: Along with grapes, cherries, and walnuts, what was garum — a popular flavouring brought by the Romans?
quiz.q: Along with grapes, cherries, and walnuts, what was garum — a popular flavouring brought by the Romans?
quiz.explanation: Garum was a pungent, salty fermented fish sauce used by Romans to flavour rich banquet dishes.

quiz.question: How did almost nine out of ten ordinary Britons continue to live during the Roman period?
quiz.q: How did almost nine out of ten ordinary Britons continue to live during the Roman period?
options: Inside marble palaces with swimming pools
Farming in the countryside in thatched roundhouses while paying Roman taxes
Sailing cargo ships back and forth to Italy
quiz.answer: Farming in the countryside in thatched roundhouses while paying Roman taxes
quiz.a: Farming in the countryside in thatched roundhouses while paying Roman taxes
quiz.explanation: Almost nine out of ten Britons carried on farming in rural thatched roundhouses and speaking Celtic while paying Roman taxes.

quiz.question: Which everyday language did most countryside farming families in Britain keep speaking under Roman rule?
quiz.q: Which everyday language did most countryside farming families in Britain keep speaking under Roman rule?
quiz.explanation: While towns and officials used Latin, most rural farming families kept speaking Celtic in their roundhouses.

lessons.subtitle: Emperor Honorius's Reply, Buried Silver Hoards & Roman Clues All Around Us Today
lessons.enquiryQuestion: Why did the Romans leave Britain, and what did they leave behind?
lessons.enquiry_question: Why did the Romans leave Britain, and what did they leave behind?
lessons.prologue: By AD 410, raiders struck every coast and Emperor Honorius told Britain's towns they must defend themselves! Families buried chests of glittering silver underground as bathhouses crumbled — yet from London and straight A-roads to our ABC alphabet, July, apples, and rabbits, Roman clues still surround us every single day.
lessons.blurb: By AD 410, raiders struck every coast and Emperor Honorius told Britain's towns they must defend themselves! Families buried chests of glittering silver underground as bathhouses crumbled — yet from London and straight A-roads to our ABC alphabet, July, apples, and rabbits, Roman clues still surround us every single day.

teacher_notes.primer: This capstone enquiry brings 367 years of Roman rule in Britain to a close around AD 410 and evaluates Rome's enduring legacy. Pupils examine why legions were withdrawn (Picts, Scotti, Angles, and Saxons raiding Britain while Visigoths attacked Italy, leading to Emperor Honorius's AD 410 rescript recorded by Zosimus), what archaeological silver hoards (Hoxne and Mildenhall) and decaying bathhouses reveal about post-Roman uncertainty, and how Roman place-names (Londinium, castra/-chester), highways, the Latin ABC alphabet, Roman numerals, the 12-month calendar, Christianity, and introduced plants and animals still shape modern Britain.

objectives.objective: Explain why Roman legions left Britain by AD 410 and why Emperor Honorius told British towns to defend themselves.
objectives.primer: Connect coastal raids by Picts, Scotti, Angles, and Saxons with the wider crisis in Italy as Visigoths threatened Rome.
objectives.question: Why could Emperor Honorius spare no soldiers for Britain in AD 410?

objectives.objective: Analyse what buried treasures like the Hoxne Hoard and Mildenhall Treasure reveal about life as Roman rule ended.
objectives.primer: Explore why new coins stopped arriving, bathhouses fell into ruin, and rich families buried silver chests they never recovered.
objectives.question: Why did wealthy families bury silver hoards in Suffolk fields around AD 407–410?

objectives.objective: Evaluate the most significant parts of Rome's lasting legacy in modern Britain.
objectives.primer: Survey London, -chester/-caster fort towns, straight A-roads, the Latin alphabet, Roman numerals, calendar months, Christianity, and food/wildlife.
objectives.question: Which Roman legacies can we still spot in our towns, classrooms, and kitchens every day?

source_context.Source A: By AD 410, Visigoth armies were attacking Italy while Picts, Scotti, Angles, and Saxons raided Britain, leaving Emperor Honorius no spare legions to send. **Hinge Question:** Did the Romans leave Britain in AD 410 because Britain defeated them, or because Rome itself was in danger?
source_context.Source B: Packed inside an oak chest with gold bracelets, silver spoons, and over 15,000 coins, the Hoxne Hoard was buried after AD 407 and found in 1992 by a Suffolk farmer. **Hinge Question:** What does the fact that nobody ever came back to dig up the Hoxne Hoard suggest about Britain around AD 410?
source_context.Source C: Found in Suffolk in 1942 alongside 33 silver spoons and bowls, the Great Dish of the Mildenhall Treasure shows both rich villa wealth and the fear of coastal raids. **Hinge Question:** Why did so many buried Roman silver hoards turn up in eastern Britain near the North Sea coast?
source_context.Source D: Built of neat limestone blocks and red tile bands around AD 306, York's Multangular Tower reminds us that Britain's cities, roads, alphabet, and calendar stand on Roman roots. **Hinge Question:** Which Roman legacy shapes your own life more every day: stone towers like Source D, or our ABC alphabet and calendar?

items.question: In what year did Emperor Claudius invade Britain to make it part of the Roman Empire?
items.explanation: Four Roman legions landed in AD 43, beginning nearly 370 years of Roman rule in Britain.

items.question: Which Iceni queen burned Colchester, London, and St Albans during her AD 60–61 rebellion?
items.explanation: Queen Boudicca led a fierce rebellion before her defeat at the Battle of Watling Street.

items.question: Why did Emperor Hadrian build a 73-mile wall across northern Britain in AD 122?
items.answer: To stop northern raids from Caledonia and collect taxes at guarded milecastle gates
items.explanation: Hadrian's Wall controlled the northern frontier from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway.

items.question: What famous piece of writing by Claudia Severa survived in wet mud at Vindolanda Fort?
items.answer: A wooden ink birthday party invitation — the oldest surviving Latin handwriting by a woman
items.explanation: Written around AD 100, Tablet 291 invited her friend Sulpicia Lepidina to her birthday celebration.

items.question: From which three continents did auxiliary soldiers come to guard Hadrian's Wall?
items.answer: Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa
items.explanation: Batavians, Syrian archers, and North African Aurelian Moors all served along the northern frontier.

items.question: What wooden sighting tool helped Roman surveyors build 10,000 miles of straight stone roads?
items.explanation: Surveyors used a wooden groma to lay straight, cambered stone roads with drainage ditches.

items.question: How did a Roman hypocaust heat bathhouses like Aquae Sulis and wealthy villas?
items.answer: Hot air from a furnace flowed beneath raised floors resting on stacks of brick tiles (pilae)
items.explanation: Hypocaust central heating warmed mosaic floors and steaming bath rooms.

items.question: While rich leaders built mosaic villas like Fishbourne Palace, how did almost nine in ten Britons live?
items.answer: Farming in the countryside inside thatched roundhouses while paying Roman taxes
items.explanation: Most ordinary families in rural Britain continued living in roundhouses throughout the Roman era.

current_items.question: In what year did Emperor Honorius tell British towns they must defend themselves?
current_items.answer: AD 410
current_items.explanation: In AD 410, with Italy itself under attack, Emperor Honorius wrote that Rome could send no more troops to Britain.

current_items.question: Which raiders crossed the North Sea to attack eastern Britain around AD 400?
current_items.answer: The Angles and Saxons
current_items.explanation: While Picts raided from Scotland and Scotti from Ireland, Angles and Saxons sailed across the North Sea.

current_items.question: Name two famous buried Roman silver treasures found centuries later in Suffolk.
current_items.answer: The Hoxne Hoard and the Mildenhall Treasure
current_items.explanation: Wealthy families buried chests of coins, spoons, and silver dishes underground for safekeeping and never returned.

current_items.question: What Latin word for a Roman fort gave towns like Manchester and Lancaster their names?
current_items.answer: Castra
current_items.explanation: British place-names ending in -chester, -caster, or -cester mark the site of a Roman castra (fort).

current_items.question: Which two calendar months are named after Julius Caesar and Rome's first emperor Augustus?
current_items.answer: July and August
current_items.explanation: Our 12-month Roman calendar still honours Julius Caesar (July) and Emperor Augustus (August).

vocab.definition: A secret collection of valuable coins, silver, or jewellery buried underground to keep it safe in dangerous times.

narrative_blocks.title: Raiders on Every Coast & Leaving in AD 410
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.1] Around **AD 400**, after nearly four hundred years in Britain, the **Roman Empire** faced fierce attacks everywhere. **Picts** from Scotland, **Scotti** from Ireland, and seafaring **Angles and Saxons** raided Britain's coasts. Meanwhile, **Visigoth** [VIZ-ih-goth] armies invaded **Italy** and threatened **Rome** itself.

[6.2] Roman legions sailed away across the Channel to defend Italy. When worried British towns begged for help in **AD 410**, **Emperor Honorius** [hoh-NOR-ee-us] replied that Rome had no spare soldiers left, so **British towns must defend themselves**.

narrative_blocks.title: Buried Silver Treasure & Crumbling Bathhouses
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.3] Once the Roman army left Britain, fresh **Roman coins** stopped arriving to pay soldiers' **wages**. Busy town markets shrank and pottery workshops closed their doors. Nobody fixed leaky stone **aqueducts**, **hypocausts**, or **bathhouses**, so grand buildings slowly **crumbled** into silent ruins.

[6.4] Fearing coastal raiders, rich families buried wooden chests of gold coins, spoons, and silver plates underground in a secret **hoard**. Many owners never came home! Centuries later, **Suffolk** farmers ploughed up the glittering **Hoxne Hoard** [HOKS-un] and **Mildenhall Treasure**.

narrative_blocks.title: Roman Footprints Still Shaping Britain Today
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.5] Even after the legions left, Rome left a lasting **legacy** all around us today. **Londinium** grew into **London**, and straight modern **A-roads** follow old Roman highways. Town names ending in **-chester** or **-caster**, like Manchester and Lancaster, mark Roman army forts (**castra** [KAS-truh]).

[6.6] Every day we write with the **Latin** **ABC alphabet** and read **Roman numerals** (**I, V, X**) on clocks. Our **12-month calendar** names **July** and **August** after Roman leaders, and Rome brought **Christianity**, **apples**, **cabbages**, **rabbits**, and **stinging nettles**!

tasks.title: 1. Primary Evidence Detective
tasks.question: Read Zosimus's words beside Emperor Honorius's gold coin in Source A. Why couldn't Honorius send legions to Britain in AD 410?
tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, Emperor Honorius could not send fresh soldiers to defend Britain in AD 410 because...
hints: Identify Emperor Honorius on the gold coin and Zosimus’s account of AD 410.
Explain what crisis was happening closer to Rome as enemy armies like the Visigoths attacked Italy.
State Honorius’s message telling Romano-British towns to look to their own defences.
tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, Emperor Honorius could not send fresh soldiers to defend Britain in AD 410 because enemy armies such as the Visigoths were attacking Italy and Rome itself. With zero spare legions left, Honorius wrote telling British cities they must guard themselves against Pictish, Irish, and Saxon raiders.

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Why did the Roman army leave Britain around AD 410, and what happened to Roman coins and stone bathhouses afterwards?
tasks.starter: The Roman army marched away from Britain around AD 410 because the Roman Empire...
hints: Name the enemies attacking Britain (Picts, Scotti, Angles, and Saxons) AND the Visigoths attacking Italy and Rome itself.
Explain Emperor Honorius's AD 410 reply telling British towns they must defend themselves.
Trace the knock-on effect of soldiers leaving: why did stopping army wages make town markets shrink and bathhouses crumble?
tasks.model_answer: The Roman army marched away from Britain around AD 410 because the Roman Empire was under attack everywhere at once. While Picts from Scotland, Scotti from Ireland, and Angles and Saxons across the North Sea raided Britain, Visigoth armies invaded Italy and threatened Rome itself. Legions were called back to save Italy, and in AD 410 Emperor Honorius told British towns they must defend themselves. Without soldiers' wages arriving, new Roman coins disappeared, town workshops shut down, and leaky aqueducts, hypocausts, and stone bathhouses slowly crumbled into ruins.

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: Why did the Roman army leave Britain around AD 410, and what did the Romans leave behind for us today?
tasks.starter: Even though the Roman legions marched away in AD 410, Rome changed Britain forever by leaving behind...
hints: Include towns and travel: Londinium becoming London, -chester/-caster fort towns (from castra), and modern A-roads along straight Roman routes.
Include reading, numbers, and time: the Latin ABC alphabet, Roman numerals (I, V, X), and the 12-month calendar (July and August).
Choose which single Roman legacy you think matters MOST to your daily life today (such as our ABC alphabet, cities, laws, Christianity, or foods like apples and cabbages) and explain why!
tasks.model_answer: Even though the Roman legions marched away in AD 410, Rome changed Britain forever by leaving behind a legacy we still use every single day. On our maps, Londinium grew into our capital city London, towns ending in -chester or -caster mark Roman forts (castra), and modern A-roads still follow straight Roman highways. Even more importantly, Rome gave us the Latin ABC alphabet we read and write with, Roman numerals (I, V, X) on clocks, the 12-month calendar including July and August, written laws, Christianity, and everyday foods and wildlife from apples and cabbages to rabbits and stinging nettles!

quiz.question: Which groups raided Roman Britain from Scotland, Ireland, and across the North Sea around AD 400?
quiz.q: Which groups raided Roman Britain from Scotland, Ireland, and across the North Sea around AD 400?
options: Picts, Scotti, and Angles and Saxons
quiz.answer: Picts, Scotti, and Angles and Saxons
quiz.a: Picts, Scotti, and Angles and Saxons
quiz.explanation: Around AD 400, Picts raided from Scotland, Scotti from Ireland, and Angles and Saxons sailed across the North Sea.

quiz.question: Why were Roman legions called away from Britain in the early fifth century?
quiz.q: Why were Roman legions called away from Britain in the early fifth century?
options: To sail across the Atlantic Ocean
Because British winters had turned tropical
To defend Italy and Rome itself against invading armies like the Visigoths
quiz.answer: To defend Italy and Rome itself against invading armies like the Visigoths
quiz.a: To defend Italy and Rome itself against invading armies like the Visigoths
quiz.explanation: Roman troops marched away from Britain to defend Italy and Rome itself as Visigoth armies attacked the heart of the Empire.

quiz.question: In what year did Emperor Honorius send his famous reply telling British towns to defend themselves?
quiz.q: In what year did Emperor Honorius send his famous reply telling British towns to defend themselves?
quiz.explanation: In AD 410, Emperor Honorius wrote to British cities warning that Rome could send no troops and they must guard themselves.

quiz.question: What message did Emperor Honorius send to the cities of Britain in AD 410?
quiz.q: What message did Emperor Honorius send to the cities of Britain in AD 410?
options: Ten new legions and war elephants were on their way
Everyone in Britain must move to Rome
Hadrian's Wall would be rebuilt in marble
quiz.explanation: Emperor Honorius warned British towns that they had to look to their own safety and defend themselves.

quiz.question: Where did the Picts and the Scotti sail and march from when raiding Roman Britain around AD 400?
quiz.q: Where did the Picts and the Scotti sail and march from when raiding Roman Britain around AD 400?
options: Picts from Italy and Scotti from Egypt
Picts from Scotland and Scotti from Ireland
Picts from Spain and Scotti from Greece
Picts from Syria and Scotti from Gaul
quiz.answer: Picts from Scotland and Scotti from Ireland
quiz.a: Picts from Scotland and Scotti from Ireland
quiz.explanation: Around AD 400, Picts raided south from Scotland, Scotti sailed across from Ireland, and Angles and Saxons crossed the North Sea.

quiz.question: Why did fresh shipments of new Roman coins stop arriving in Britain after the legions left?
quiz.q: Why did fresh shipments of new Roman coins stop arriving in Britain after the legions left?
options: There were no longer Roman soldiers in Britain receiving army wages
Gold mines on the Moon closed down
quiz.answer: There were no longer Roman soldiers in Britain receiving army wages
quiz.a: There were no longer Roman soldiers in Britain receiving army wages
quiz.explanation: Rome shipped new coins mainly to pay soldiers' wages; once the legions departed, fresh coinage stopped arriving.

quiz.question: What happened to many Roman stone bathhouses, aqueducts, and hypocausts after AD 410?
quiz.q: What happened to many Roman stone bathhouses, aqueducts, and hypocausts after AD 410?
options: They were turned into railway stations
They were covered in solid gold
They were shipped brick by brick back to Italy
Nobody repaired them, so they slowly crumbled into overgrown ruins
quiz.answer: Nobody repaired them, so they slowly crumbled into overgrown ruins
quiz.a: Nobody repaired them, so they slowly crumbled into overgrown ruins
quiz.explanation: Without town wealth and engineers to maintain them, leaky aqueducts, hypocausts, and bathhouses fell into ruin.

quiz.question: Why did anxious wealthy families bury chests of silver plates, spoons, and coins underground as a hoard?
quiz.q: Why did anxious wealthy families bury chests of silver plates, spoons, and coins underground as a hoard?
options: To grow silver trees in their orchards
To hide their valuables safely from raiders, hoping to dig them up when danger passed
To pay taxes to Queen Boudicca
quiz.answer: To hide their valuables safely from raiders, hoping to dig them up when danger passed
quiz.a: To hide their valuables safely from raiders, hoping to dig them up when danger passed
quiz.explanation: Fearing raiders and unrest, wealthy families buried precious silver hoards for safekeeping — though many never returned.

quiz.question: Name two famous buried Roman silver treasures discovered centuries later by farmers in Suffolk.
quiz.q: Name two famous buried Roman silver treasures discovered centuries later by farmers in Suffolk.
options: The Sutton Hoo Ship and the Rosetta Stone
The Battersea Shield and the Snettisham Torc
The Hoxne Hoard and the Mildenhall Treasure
quiz.answer: The Hoxne Hoard and the Mildenhall Treasure
quiz.a: The Hoxne Hoard and the Mildenhall Treasure
quiz.explanation: Suffolk farmers unearthed both the Mildenhall Treasure (including the Great Silver Dish) and the Hoxne Hoard (including the Empress Pepper Pot).

quiz.question: What happened to town markets and pottery workshops in Britain once Roman army wages stopped arriving?
quiz.q: What happened to town markets and pottery workshops in Britain once Roman army wages stopped arriving?
options: Every village opened ten new marble shopping forums
Markets shrank rapidly and potters' workshops closed their doors
Potters began exporting millions of plates to China
Emperor Honorius paid every potter in solid gold
quiz.answer: Markets shrank rapidly and potters' workshops closed their doors
quiz.a: Markets shrank rapidly and potters' workshops closed their doors
quiz.explanation: Without soldiers spending silver coins, busy Roman town markets shrank and mass-produced pottery workshops closed.

quiz.question: Which Roman port on the River Thames grew into Britain's modern capital city?
quiz.q: Which Roman port on the River Thames grew into Britain's modern capital city?
quiz.explanation: Roman Londinium on the River Thames grew into London, the capital city of the United Kingdom today.

quiz.question: What does a British town name ending in -chester or -caster (like Manchester or Lancaster) reveal?
quiz.q: What does a British town name ending in -chester or -caster (like Manchester or Lancaster) reveal?
options: It was an Iron Age roundhouse farm
It was founded by Julius Caesar's elephants
It grew on the site of a Roman fort (castra)
quiz.answer: It grew on the site of a Roman fort (castra)
quiz.a: It grew on the site of a Roman fort (castra)
quiz.explanation: Town names ending in -chester or -caster come from castra, the Latin word for a Roman camp or fort.

quiz.question: Which two months of our 12-month calendar are named after Julius Caesar and Emperor Augustus?
quiz.q: Which two months of our 12-month calendar are named after Julius Caesar and Emperor Augustus?
quiz.explanation: July honours Julius Caesar and August honours Rome's first emperor, Augustus, in our 12-month Roman calendar.

quiz.question: Along with the Latin ABC alphabet and Roman numerals (I, V, X), which foods and wildlife did the Romans introduce to Britain?
quiz.q: Along with the Latin ABC alphabet and Roman numerals (I, V, X), which foods and wildlife did the Romans introduce to Britain?
options: Apples, cabbages, rabbits, and stinging nettles
quiz.answer: Apples, cabbages, rabbits, and stinging nettles
quiz.a: Apples, cabbages, rabbits, and stinging nettles
quiz.explanation: The Romans introduced cultivated apples, cabbages, rabbits, and stinging nettles to Britain alongside Christianity and written laws.

quiz.question: What do modern British main roads ("A-roads") and clockface numbers like I, V, and X have in common?
quiz.q: What do modern British main roads ("A-roads") and clockface numbers like I, V, and X have in common?
options: Both were invented by Iron Age Druids before AD 43
Both are lasting Roman legacies still used across Britain every day
Both arrived from North America in the 1900s
Both were banned by Emperor Hadrian
quiz.answer: Both are lasting Roman legacies still used across Britain every day
quiz.a: Both are lasting Roman legacies still used across Britain every day
quiz.explanation: Many straight modern A-roads follow Roman highways, and clockfaces still display Roman numerals (I, V, X)!

cards.heading: Raiders Strike & AD 410 Reply
cards.stat: Emperor Honorius Tells Towns to Guard Themselves
cards.connective: Why did the Romans leave Britain, and what did they leave behind?
cards.html: Around AD 400, Picts, Scotti, and Saxons raided Britain while Visigoths threatened Italy itself. Legions sailed away, and in AD 410 Emperor Honorius told British towns to defend themselves.
cards.spoken: Why did the Romans leave Britain, and what did they leave behind? <short pause> Around AD 400, Picts, Scotti, and Saxons raided Britain while Visigoths threatened Italy itself. Legions sailed away, and in AD 410 Emperor Honorius told British towns to defend themselves.

cards.heading: Crumbling Baths & Silver Hoards
cards.stat: Hoxne & Mildenhall Silver Buried for Safety
cards.connective: Without Roman soldiers or fresh coins, town life quickly shrank.
cards.html: Unrepaired stone bathhouses and aqueducts slowly crumbled as town markets closed. Fearing coastal raiders, wealthy families buried silver chests like the Hoxne Hoard and Mildenhall Treasure underground.
cards.spoken: Without Roman soldiers or fresh coins, town life quickly shrank. <short pause> Unrepaired stone bathhouses and aqueducts slowly crumbled as town markets closed. Fearing coastal raiders, wealthy families buried silver chests like the Hoxne Hoard and Mildenhall Treasure underground.

cards.heading: Roman Clues All Around Today
cards.stat: London, Straight A-Roads, Latin ABC & Calendar
cards.connective: Even after the army left, Roman ideas stayed woven into Britain.
cards.html: Londinium became London, modern A-roads follow Roman highways, and -chester towns mark old forts. Rome also left our Latin ABC alphabet, Roman numerals, calendar months, apples, and rabbits!
cards.spoken: Even after the army left, Roman ideas stayed woven into Britain. <short pause> Londinium became London, modern A-roads follow Roman highways, and -chester towns mark old forts. Rome also left our Latin ABC alphabet , Roman numerals, calendar months, apples, and rabbits!

cards.heading: Four Centuries That Shaped Us
cards.stat: Roads, Cities, Language & Laws Still Used Today
cards.connective: Nearly four hundred years of Roman rule left deep footprints behind.
cards.html: Though legions departed in AD 410, Rome's legacy never disappeared from island Britain. Every straight highway, -chester city, and printed page still carries Roman history today.
